summary:
Recorded one finding. Review complete.

The PR adds `lib/multipart.js`, the multipart body builder that `request.js` already requires and calls. I read the whole file and traced its callers (`request.js:27,138,422,551,1142-1148`).

The added code reproduces CVE-2017-16026: `add(part.body)` at `lib/multipart.js:86` forwards a numeric body to `new Buffer(part)` at line 71, allocating N bytes rather than sending the number. On Node < 8 those bytes are uninitialized heap memory (I reproduced non-zero memory under Node 6.17.1), so a remote server receives client process memory. On Node ≥ 8 the buffer is zero-filled but the wrong N-byte body is still sent. The fix is the upstream coercion of numbers to strings.

I found no other issue worth reporting; the remaining quirks (error-then-continue in `isChunked`, unsanitized part header values) are upstream behavior with no trust-boundary crossing. I filed nothing for them.

findings.title: Numeric multipart body sends N bytes of process memory instead of the number
findings.body:
A multipart part whose `body` is a number is passed to the `Buffer` constructor as a size, so `request` sends that many bytes of process memory instead of the number. On Node.js versions where `new Buffer(size)` returns uninitialized memory (Node < 8), those bytes leak client memory to the remote server. This is CVE-2017-16026 / GHSA-7xfp-9c55-5vqj.

**Preconditions:** A multipart request where one part's `body` is a number (for example a value forwarded from untrusted JSON), running on Node.js < 8, which this package's `engines` field still permits (`node >=0.8.0`).

**Evidence:** `lib/multipart.js:86` calls `add(part.body)` for every part; `add` at `lib/multipart.js:70-72` forwards a non-chunked part to `new Buffer(part)`. `new Buffer(500)` allocates a 500-byte buffer rather than the string `"500"`. Running the same expression under Node 6.17.1 produced a buffer with 164 non-zero bytes out of 500. Upstream fixed exactly this by converting numbers to strings in `add` (request/request commit 29d81814, PR #2022); this added file matches the pre-fix version.

**Impact:** A remote server can receive arbitrary contents of the client process's heap (other requests' data, credentials, tokens) that it was never sent. Reach crosses a trust boundary because process memory is exposed to a remote party; the leak is permanent. Severity is medium after one discount: it requires a numeric multipart body rather than the ordinary string/buffer/stream body, and full disclosure requires a legacy Node.js runtime (on Node >= 8 the buffer is zero-filled, though the wrong N-byte body is still sent).

**Fix:** Coerce numeric bodies to their string form before buffering, e.g. in `add` add `if (typeof part === 'number') part = part.toString()`, and add a test that a numeric `body` sends its decimal text.

summary:
The change re-adds `lib/routes/statics.js`, the static-file route that maps each request path onto `process.cwd()` and streams the file. That path mapping is unchecked, so I reproduced unauthenticated directory traversal: with the route mounted as in `lib/cli.js:138`, a request for `/../secret.txt` returned content from outside the served directory (200, full body). I recorded that as one high finding with a containment fix.

The rest of the file's oddities — `Last-Modified` set to a future time, a 304 branch that sets fewer headers than the 200, a 500 instead of 404 for directory paths, a cacheable 404 leaking statics' headers — are cache-correctness nits a change like this should ideally clean up but that do not fail safely. The OPTIONS-after-headers crash I found in the same stack is pre-existing: it reproduces identically with `statics.js` absent, so it is out of scope here.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read files outside the served directory via ../ in the request path
findings.body:
The static file handler concatenates the request path onto the server's working
directory without normalising or containing it, so any HTTP client can read files
outside the directory being served.

**Evidence:** `lib/routes/statics.js:23-24` builds the path as
`process.cwd() + (resource.pathname || '/')`. `url.parse().pathname` returns the
request target unnormalised, so `..` segments survive:

    var resource = url.parse('/../secret.txt');
    resource.pathname; // '/../secret.txt'

Reproduced against the real route stack (`lib/server.js` + this handler) with
`/tmp/hroot` as cwd and `/tmp/secret.txt` outside it:

    Listening on 3999
    200 GET /../secret.txt 46ms
    STATUS 200
    BODY "SECRET-DATA\n"

`fs.stat` at line 27 and `fs.createReadStream` at line 52 both follow the same
unchecked path, so the escape works for every route through this handler with no
authentication and no special flags. `lib/cli.js:138-142` mounts it as the first
route on every request, and `lib/server.js:114` listens on all interfaces
(`listen(port)` with no host).

**Impact:** An unauthenticated network peer reads any file the server process can
read — SSH keys, `~/.npmrc`, `.env`, `/etc/passwd` — one directory level per `../`.
The README states the server hosts "only files in current directory structure", so
this crosses the documented trust boundary. Disclosure cannot be undone, which is
permanent; the actor is unprivileged and remote. Severity high.

**Fix:** Resolve the request path against the root and reject anything that lands
outside it before `fs.stat`:

    var path = require('path');
    var root = process.cwd();
    var filePath = path.resolve(root, '.' + resource.pathname);
    if (filePath !== root && filePath.indexOf(root + path.sep) !== 0) {
      return next();
    }

Keep the trailing-slash `index.html` append after the check. Decode
(`decodeURIComponent`) before resolving so `%2e%2e` is judged by the same rule, and
reject paths containing a null byte.

summary: The change restores `lib/stats.js`, the platform backends (`proc`, `ps`, `win`) that `index.js` already required, so it is entirely new code rather than a modification. Tests pass on Linux, and I reproduced the shell injection at `stats.ps` (unvalidated pid concatenated into `child_process.exec`), which is the published advisory for this package and affects the darwin/BSD/AIX path; I also confirmed an uncaught crash in the Windows parser when wmic yields no data row, and a weaker path-traversal side effect of the unvalidated pid on the Linux path. All three are recorded, with the injection graded `high` under this run's severity policy.

findings.title: Untrusted pid reaches child_process.exec in stats.ps, allowing shell command injection
findings.body:
`stats.ps` builds a shell string by concatenating `pid` onto `ps -o pcpu,rss -p ` and hands it to `child_process.exec`, so a pid containing shell metacharacters runs arbitrary commands as the process user. lib/stats.js:97-103.

**Preconditions:** the host runs on darwin, sunos, freebsd or aix, where index.js:20-24 maps the platform to `ps`. Linux (`proc`) and Windows (`win`) do not reach this code through `pidusage.stat`. A caller must pass a pid it does not fully control, e.g. an id taken from an HTTP request or a config file.

**Evidence:** on Linux, calling the method directly with a hostile pid:
```
$ cat /tmp/inj.js
var stats = require('.../lib/stats')
stats.ps("1; echo INJECTED-$((7*7)) > /tmp/pwned.txt; ps -o pcpu,rss -p 1", {}, function(err, st){ ... })
$ node /tmp/inj.js
err: null
stat: { cpu: 0.2, memory: 1388544 }
file: INJECTED-49
```
The trailing `ps` keeps the output well-formed, so the callback still reports a normal stat and the caller sees nothing. Nothing in lib/stats.js or index.js validates or coerces `pid`. This is the injection tracked as GHSA-h2p3-h48h-9jj7 / npm advisory 356, fixed upstream in 1.1.5 by `pid = parseInt(pid, 10)` before the command is built (pu1.1.5 lib/stats.js:101).

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution across a trust boundary with permanent effect: the attacker's commands run with the privileges of the monitoring process, so secrets on the host and the availability of the service are exposed. Severity is capped at high per this run's policy; the advisory calls it critical.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that only a numeric pid reaches the shell. Coerce once at the entry points (`pid = parseInt(pid, 10)`, reject non-positive values) or drop the shell entirely by using `execFile('ps', ['-o', 'pcpu,rss', '-p', String(pid)])`.

findings.title: Unvalidated pid lets the Linux path read a stat file outside /proc
findings.body:
On the Linux path the caller-supplied pid is joined into a filesystem path without validation, so a pid containing `..` makes pidusage read a file outside `/proc` and report it as a process stat. lib/stats.js:45.

**Evidence:**
```
$ mkdir -p /tmp/pz && printf '1 (evil) S 0 1 1 0 -1 4194560 0 0 0 0 111 0 0 0 20 0 1 0 500 1000 333 ...\n' > /tmp/pz/stat
$ node -e "require('.../lib/stats').proc('../../tmp/pz',{},function(e,r){console.log(e&&e.message,r)})"
null { cpu: 0.012676283131064775, memory: 1363968 }
```
`p.join('/proc', '../../tmp/pz', 'stat')` resolves to `/tmp/pz/stat`. Because `join` (not `resolve`) is used, an absolute pid such as `/etc/passwd` does not escape, and only files named `stat` can be reached; the contents are only reflected as derived cpu/memory numbers.

**Impact:** a caller-controlled pid reads files whose name is `stat` anywhere the process can read, and files the parsed record into `history` under that key. No file content is returned verbatim and the attacker must already be able to influence the pid, so the practical damage is negligible: info.

**Fix:** same invariant as the shell-injection finding: coerce pid to a positive integer at the entry points and reject anything else before it reaches `p.join` / `fs.readFile`.

findings.title: A pid wmic reports with no data row crashes the Windows path with an uncaught TypeError
findings.body:
`stats.win` parses wmic output inside its `close` handler without checking that a data row exists, so a pid wmic answers with a single line throws an uncaught `TypeError` out of the event emitter. The `done` callback is never called and the host process dies. lib/stats.js:160.

**Preconditions:** Windows host, and wmic exits with code 0 while printing only one line, e.g. the header-only output for a pid that no longer exists. `!stdout || code !== 0` (lib/stats.js:146) does not catch this, because stdout is non-empty and the exit code is 0.

**Evidence:** with a stub `wmic` on PATH that prints a header line and exits 0:
```
$ node -e "require('.../lib/stats').win(424242,{},function(e,r){console.log('cb',e&&e.message,r)})"
lib/stats.js:156
      stdout = stdout.split(os.EOL)[1].replace(/\s\s+/g, ' ').split(' ')
                                      ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')
    at ChildProcess.<anonymous> (lib/stats.js:156:39)
    at ChildProcess.emit (node:events:514:28)
exit code 1
```
The callback never fired. I could not exercise real wmic here, so the exact single-line reply of wmic for a missing pid is inferred, not reproduced.

**Impact:** a monitoring call for a pid that has just exited crashes the whole caller instead of returning an error, so every Windows user that polls pids from a request or a pid file can be killed by that input. Contained to one call and cleared by a restart, hence low.

**Fix:** parse defensively: split the output, drop the header, and if no data row remains call `done(new Error(...))` (or report NaN-free zeroes) rather than dereferencing `stdout[1]`.

summary:
**What the change does:** it adds `lib/multipart.js` (112 lines), the multipart body builder that `request.js:27` already requires. At baseline the module was absent, so `require('request')` failed outright; the file restores it and matches upstream request's fixed implementation (`v2.68.0`, blob `c128172`), including the `typeof part === 'number'` guard in `add()` (`lib/multipart.js:71-76`).

**Verification:** I installed dependencies and reproduced both sides of CVE-2017-16026 — with the guard removed, `multipart: [{body: 12345}]` sends 12 438 bytes of raw allocation; with the PR's guard, it sends the string `12345` (98 bytes) in both the buffered and chunked (`transfer-encoding: chunked`) paths. `eslint lib/ *.js`, `tests/test-multipart.js` (148), `tests/test-multipart-encoding.js` (70) and `tests/test-errors.js` (11) all pass, and the diff is confined to the one new file.

**Assessment:** the change closes the memory-exposure path cleanly for every call site of the only caller-fed `Buffer` allocation, with no other numeric-allocation route reachable from multipart parts, so I filed no findings. I also left the invalid-input path (`lib/multipart.js:19-36`, which emits `error` and then falls through to a `parts.forEach` `TypeError` when a callback is supplied) unreported: it is upstream behaviour pinned by `tests/test-errors.js:62-89` and only fires on malformed options from the library's own caller.

The change adds the whole `lib/routes/statics.js` static-file route (the file was stripped from the baseline), wiring in path filtering, ETag/`Cache-Control` handling, and streamed responses. The path filter it introduces is ineffective: it strips only one `"/.."` and one `"../"` per request, so `/../../../../etc/passwd` still resolves outside the served directory — I reproduced a 200 response containing `/etc/passwd` through the same module wiring `lib/cli.js` uses, and recorded that as a high-severity finding. The remaining handler logic (caching validators, directory requests, error paths) has real rough edges but nothing I could trace to a concrete, exploitable failure in normal use; several candidates turned out to be pre-existing defects in `lib/server.js` or operator-supplied CLI input.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read files outside the served directory via chained ../ in the URL
findings.body:
The path filter at `lib/routes/statics.js:27` removes at most one `"/.."` and one `"../"` per request, so request paths with two or more leading `../` segments survive it and are appended verbatim to `process.cwd()` at line 28. A remote client can therefore read any file the server process can read, outside the directory the operator chose to serve.

**Evidence:** request `/../../../../etc/passwd` against the route wired exactly as `lib/cli.js:96` wires it:

```js
process.chdir('/tmp/pub');
require('./lib/server')({port:31999})
  .use(require('./lib/routes/statics')())
  .use(require('./lib/routes/notfound')())
  .start();
```

`GET /../../../../etc/passwd` returns `200` with `root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash...`. Trace for that path: `/\/\.\./` strips the first `"/.."` → `/../../../etc/passwd`; `/\.\.\//` strips the next `"../"` → `/../../etc/passwd`; `filePath` becomes `/tmp/pub/../../etc/passwd`, i.e. `/etc/passwd`. Single-segment paths (`/../secret.txt`) are blocked, which is why the filter looks effective. On Windows the filter does nothing for backslash separators: `GET /..\..\boot.ini` contains neither `"/.."` nor `"../"` and is used as-is, so one traversal level is enough there.

**Impact:** unauthenticated arbitrary file read across a trust boundary, and permanent — disclosed bytes (private keys, `.env`, `/etc/shadow` where readable) cannot be recalled. `lib/server.js:114` calls `listen(port)` with no host, so the server binds every interface by default, and `lib/server.js:103` adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so any web page can read the responses through a victim's browser. The only bound is the OS permissions of the serving user. The filter is the whole defense for a route whose only job is serving one directory, so this is `high`.

**Fix:** stop trying to strip dangerous substrings; resolve the request path against a fixed root and verify containment, e.g. `var root = process.cwd(); var filePath = path.resolve(root, '.' + path.normalize(decodeURIComponent(resourcePathname)));` then reject with `next()` unless `filePath === root || filePath.indexOf(root + path.sep) === 0`. Normalizing before the check also covers chained `..`, repeated slashes, and Windows backslashes; `fs.realpath` on the resolved path additionally blocks escape through symlinks.

summary:
## Review summary

PR #1 restores `lib/stats.js`, the missing module `index.js` already required; the added file is byte-identical (md5 `3b8cf65…`) to upstream pidusage v1.1.5, the release that fixes CVE-2017-16034. The fix's core property holds: `pid` is coerced with `parseInt(pid, 10)` at all three command-construction points (`lib/stats.js:42`, `:100`, `:123`), so the `exec('ps … ' + pid)` and `spawn('wmic', args.split(' '))` calls cannot receive shell metacharacters — I drove the public `stat()` through the `darwin` (ps) path with `'1; touch /tmp/pwned_e2e ;'` and the injected command did not run. `npm test` passes (3/3), and the `/proc` and `ps` paths return sane values on Linux.

The remaining defects are all in the newly added code and concern reported metrics rather than security: the first Windows sample returns lifetime CPU time as a rate (recorded, low), and the undocumented `childrens` option re-adds cumulative child CPU on every call so the percentage grows without bound (recorded, low, reproduced against real `/proc`). A third, info-level finding records that unguarded `ps`/`wmic` output parsing throws inside an async callback and kills the host process; I could not reproduce a real trigger, so it rests on the demonstrated throw only. No blocking issue — the change is safe to merge.

findings.title: childrens option adds cumulative child CPU time on every sample, inflating cpu %
findings.body:
When a caller passes `{childrens: true}`, each `stat()` call adds the process's cumulative child CPU time (`cutime + cstime`) to the delta since the last call, so the reported cpu percentage grows with the process's age even while children are idle.

**Preconditions:** caller passes `options.childrens` (undocumented, not exercised by the test suite).

**Evidence:** `lib/stats.js:71` computes `childrens` from the raw cumulative counters parsed at `lib/stats.js:63-64`, while the self terms on `lib/stats.js:73` subtract history. `cutime`/`cstime` are stored in history at `lib/stats.js:82` but never read back. Reproduced against the real `/proc` with a spawned busy child: reported cpu tracked `(dSelf + cumulative_child)/dt` — 654.84, 312.35, 396, 443.59, 513.16 % while the true interval values were 6.65, 61.85, 59.64, 63.53, 60.38 %. A synthetic run with children idle but 360 CPU-seconds of child time in the past reports ≈36000 % on every call.

**Impact:** low. The option is off by default and affects only the caller's own metric, so reach is contained; the error does not clear while the process lives, but it is a wrong number rather than lost data.

**Fix:** treat the child counters like the self counters: `var childrens = options.childrens ? stat.cutime - (history.cutime || 0) + stat.cstime - (history.cstime || 0) : 0`.

findings.title: First Windows cpu sample reports lifetime CPU time as a one-second rate
findings.body:
On Windows, the first `stat()` call for a pid returns a cpu percentage equal to the process's entire lifetime CPU time (in CPU-seconds × 100) instead of a rate. A process that has burned 43,200 CPU-seconds reports `cpu = 4320000`.

**Preconditions:** platform is Windows, and the pid has no entry in `stats.history` — i.e. the first sample, or any sample after `unmonitor(pid)`.

**Evidence:** with an empty history, `lib/stats.js:170-171` makes the numerator the full cumulative `kernelmodetime + usermodetime` (`history.* || 0`), and `lib/stats.js:174-176` sets the denominator to 1 when there is no previous `uptime`. `lib/stats.js:181` then divides one by the other and multiplies by 100. Reproduced with a stubbed `wmic` emitting a realistic data row: first call `cpu = 12845.68` for a process with 128.46 s of CPU time; a 12 h-CPU process gives `cpu = 4320000`. The second call, once `os.uptime()` has advanced, matches the true interval (150 % and 25 % where expected). The `/proc` path avoids this by dividing the first sample by process age (`lib/stats.js:78`).

**Impact:** low. Every Windows caller of the library gets one impossible sample (far above the 100 % × core-count ceiling), which can trip single-shot monitoring or alerting on first poll; it corrects itself on the next call, and `unmonitor` re-triggers it. Metric-only, no data loss.

**Fix:** give the first sample the same baseline the `/proc` path uses — divide by process age derived from `os.uptime()` and the process start time — or return no cpu value until a second sample exists.

findings.title: Unguarded ps/wmic output parsing throws in an async callback, terminating the caller's process
findings.body:
`ps` and `wmic` output is indexed without checking its shape, so an unexpected-but-successful child run throws inside an async callback. Nothing catches it, so the caller's process exits instead of receiving an error through the callback.

**Preconditions:** the child command exits 0 while writing output without the expected second line. For `wmic`, `trim()` at `lib/stats.js:147` makes this any single non-empty line with code 0. For `ps`, it needs stdout with no newline at all (or empty stdout) and `err === null`.

**Evidence:** with `child_process` stubbed to succeed: `lib/stats.js:160` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')` for `stdout = "No Instance(s) Available."` and for a header-only line; `lib/stats.js:111` throws the same for a single line without a newline. With `index.js:36-38` forwarding the callback, the exception escapes the caller's `try/catch` and a child process running `pusage.stat(999999, cb)` dies with exit code 1 and no callback. I could not reproduce a real trigger: on Linux `ps -o pcpu,rss -p <gone-pid>` exits 1 (so `lib/stats.js:107` returns early), and the upstream convention on the other `ps` platforms is also exit 1 for an unmatched pid; the reported real-world wmic no-match case writes to stderr with empty stdout and is absorbed by the guard at `lib/stats.js:150`.

**Impact:** info. Worst case is termination of the monitoring host process (recoverable by restart), but the output shape needed was not observed on any real platform, so severity rests on the demonstrated throw, not a demonstrated trigger. Header-only `ps` output with a trailing newline does not throw — it silently returns `cpu: NaN, memory: NaN` (`lib/stats.js:114-115`).

**Fix:** validate before indexing — require at least two lines and the expected field count, and call `done(new Error(...))` when the layout is unexpected.

summary:
Reviewed the change: the PR adds `lib/hide-sensitive.js`, the module that builds a regex from sensitive environment variables and redacts their values in log output (used by `index.js:245`, `cli.js:59`, `lib/utils.js` and `lib/definitions/plugins.js`). The file matches the shape of the upstream 17.2.3 fix and differs from it only in formatting, so the new behaviour is concentrated in the pattern built at `lib/hide-sensitive.js:14-19`.

I reproduced two defects in that pattern with the repo's own module, both introduced by the added Web-encoded alternative:

- Any secret containing `(` or `)` makes `new RegExp` throw (`Unterminated group` / `Unmatched ')'`), which aborts every run before masking hooks exist and carries the escaped secret in the error message — recorded as low.
- The encoded alternative uses `encodeURI` and is escaped before encoding, so it never matches the credential form actually produced by `url.format` in `lib/get-git-auth-url.js` for values containing `@`, `+`, `=`, `[`, etc., leaving the token recoverable in git error output — recorded as medium.

The plain-value masking path itself is correct: escaping, `GOPRIVATE` exclusion, the `SECRET_MIN_SIZE` cutoff and the empty/no-match returns all behave as intended.

findings.title: Secrets containing parentheses throw at regex construction and abort every run
findings.body:
A secret whose value contains an unbalanced `(` or `)` makes `hideSensitive(env)` throw a `SyntaxError` while it builds the masking regex, so semantic-release never starts.

**Preconditions:** an environment variable whose name matches `/token|password|credential|secret|private/i` and whose trimmed value is at least `SECRET_MIN_SIZE` (5) characters and contains `(` or `)`. A password such as `Pass(word)1` is enough.

**Evidence:** `lib/hide-sensitive.js:16` appends `${encodeURI(escapeRegExp(env[envVar]))}` as a second alternative. `encodeURI` percent-encodes the backslash that `escapeRegExp` inserted, but leaves `(` and `)` alone, so the escaped group syntax survives into the pattern:

```
$ NODE_PATH=... node -e "require('./lib/hide-sensitive')({GH_TOKEN:'abc(def'})"
Invalid regular expression: /abc\(def|abc%5C(def/g: Unterminated group
```

`abc)def` fails the same way with `Unmatched ')'`. Before this change the pattern was only `escapeRegExp(value)`, which is always a valid regex, so no value could throw.

The throw happens at `index.js:245` (`hookStd(..., hideSensitive(env))`) and at every `hideSensitiveValues` call in `lib/utils.js:10`, i.e. before any masking hook exists. In the CLI path `cli.js:59` builds `hideSensitive(env)` again inside its own `catch`, which throws a second time, so `bin/semantic-release.js` swallows the rejection and the process exits `1` with no output at all. Programmatic callers see an error whose message contains the escaped secret (`abc\(def`), which decodes to the secret if they print it.

**Impact:** any user whose token or password contains a parenthesis cannot run semantic-release at all — it fails closed with no diagnostic — and the error object carries the secret pattern for anyone who logs it. Contained to that user's run and recoverable by changing the credential, so `low`.

**Fix:** escape the secret *after* URL-encoding it, i.e. `escapeRegExp(encodeURI(env[envVar]))` (or `encodeURIComponent`), so the second alternative is always a literal match for the encoded secret and never contains unescaped group syntax.

findings.title: URL-encoded secrets are still logged unmasked for characters the downstream encoding escapes
findings.body:
Percent-encoded forms of a secret are still printed unmasked whenever the secret contains a character that the URL encoding used downstream actually escapes, so the credential this change is meant to hide still reaches the logs.

**Preconditions:** a sensitive environment variable whose value is at least 5 characters and contains a character that `encodeURI` leaves alone but that percent-encoding of the git credential escapes — `@`, `+`, `=`, `&`, `,`, `;`, `$`, `(`, `)`, `*`, `!` — or any regex metacharacter.

**Evidence:** `lib/hide-sensitive.js:16` adds a second regex alternative built as `encodeURI(escapeRegExp(value))`. Two problems:

1. `encodeURI` is not the encoding applied downstream. `lib/get-git-auth-url.js:25-36` embeds the credential with Node's `url.format`, which uses `encodeURIComponent`: `https://x-access-token:ab@cd@github.com/o/r.git` becomes `https://x-access-token:ab%40cd@github.com/...`. `encodeURI('ab@cd')` is `ab@cd`, so the alternative never matches `ab%40cd`.
2. Escaping before encoding destroys the escaping. For `abc[def`, `escapeRegExp` yields `abc\[def`, `encodeURI` yields `abc%5C%5Bdef`, which does not match the encoded secret `abc%5Bdef`; for any value containing `.`, `*`, `$` etc. the alternative is a mangled literal.

Reproduced with the repo file:

```
hideSensitive({GH_TOKEN:'ab@cd'})('Command failed: git push https://x-access-token:ab%40cd@github.com/o/r.git HEAD:main')
  -> ... https://x-access-token:ab%40cd@github.com/o/r.git HEAD:main   // not masked
hideSensitive({GH_TOKEN:'abc[def'})(...) -> 'abc%5Bdef' left in place
hideSensitive({GH_TOKEN:'pass word'})(...) -> '[secure]'             // only plain-encoding-safe values are covered
```

`lib/git.js:205-212` runs `git push --dry-run --no-verify <authUrl> HEAD:<branch>`; a failing push produces an execa error whose message includes the full URL, and that error is written to stderr through `hideSensitive` in `cli.js:59` and through `hideSensitiveValues` for plugin failures (`lib/definitions/plugins.js:100,106`).

**Impact:** the token appears in CI logs in a form that decodes to the credential in one step, which is the disclosure this change aims to prevent. Reach crosses a trust boundary (anyone reading the log), storage of the log is permanent; discounted one tier because it needs a credential containing one of the characters above and an error path that echoes the URL, so `medium`.

**Fix:** percent-encode the value the same way the credential is encoded downstream (`encodeURIComponent`), and escape the *encoded* string before putting it in the regex — `escapeRegExp(encodeURIComponent(value))` alongside the plain-text alternative — so both forms match literally.

summary:
Both findings are recorded. Summary of the review:

**What the change does:** adds `src/browser.js`, the browser build of `safer-eval` — the file `package.json:19-21` already mapped to in place of the node `vm`-based `src/index.js`. It is byte-identical to upstream v1.3.4's `src/browser.js`, so this is a faithful port rather than a hand-written change; the code builds a `Function` body from the context keys and evaluates the caller's `code` in the page realm.

**Assessment:** the file is clean in the mechanical sense but its security premise is not sound. The two escapes the accompanying tests assert against are blocked, yet any value literal (`[].constructor.constructor(...)`) still reaches the real `Function` and the page's global object, so the browser build gives nothing close to isolation for untrusted code — I reproduced a full escape, and separately reproduced code execution from a crafted context key name. The rest of the file (options asymmetry with the node build, the unused `opts.freeze` doc) is harmless.

findings.title: Untrusted code escapes the new browser sandbox through any literal's constructor chain and gets the page globals
findings.body:
The new browser build evaluates untrusted `code` with a `Function` built in the page
realm, and its only guard against reaching the page globals is bypassable, so evaluated
code gets full `window` access.

`runInContext` assembles one source string (`src/browser.js:42-48`). Line 42 tries to cut
the escape path by reassigning `this.constructor.constructor`; lines 44-46 try to hide
globals by declaring a `var` for each context key (`window`, `document`, `fetch`, ... are
set to `undefined` by `createContext`, `src/common.js:20-33`). Neither prevents the code
from reaching the real `Function` constructor through any value literal, whose
`.constructor` chain is not shadowed:

```js
saferEval("[].constructor.constructor('return document.cookie')()")
```

**Evidence:** harness loading `src/common.js` + `src/browser.js` with `global.window = {}`
set before `require` (this makes `common.js` take its `hasWindow` branch, i.e. the browser
code path):

- `"[].constructor.constructor('return this')().process.version"` → `"v24.22.2"`
- `"''.constructor.constructor('return this')().process.version"` → `"v24.22.2"`
- `"(function(){}).constructor('return this')().process.version"` → `"v24.22.2"`
- `"RegExp.prototype.constructor.constructor('return this')().process.version"` → `"v24.22.2"`

The returned object is the host global, not the `__context` object; in a page the same
call returns `window`, so `document`, `localStorage`, cookies and `fetch` are all
reachable. Only the two paths that go through reassigned built-ins are blocked
(`this.constructor.constructor(...)`, `Object.constructor.constructor(...)` — the cases the
spec asserts in `test/saferEval.spec.js`).

**Impact:** `package.json:19-21` maps the browser build to this file, so every browser
consumer of `saferEval` gets a function that runs attacker-supplied code with page
privileges: it can read and exfiltrate session data, or drive the page's authenticated
requests. The code change introduces the exposure — before it, the mapped
`lib/browser.js` did not exist, so browser bundling failed instead of silently providing
pseudo-isolation. Severity is high rather than critical: reach crosses the trust boundary
and the theft is permanent, but `README.md:20-22` states upfront that the browser version
has no real sandboxing, which bounds what a reader was promised.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that evaluated code cannot reach the host realm's globals.
In-browser that needs a real realm boundary: evaluate inside a sandboxed iframe
(`<iframe sandbox>`, null origin) or a Web Worker and pass only the context in/out by
`postMessage`. Shadowing identifiers and reassigning `Function`-adjacent built-ins cannot
hold. If that is out of scope for this PR, remove the browser mapping and the
constructor-guard code, and state in the docs that the browser build provides no isolation
— rather than shipping a guard that a one-line payload defeats.

findings.title: Context key names are spliced into evaluated source, so a crafted key runs code
findings.body:
Context property names are concatenated into the generated function body without
escaping, so a context whose key names come from untrusted data executes statements in
the sandbox even when `code` is a harmless literal.

`src/browser.js:45` builds `src += 'var ' + key + ' = __context[\'' + key + '\'];\n'`. The
only filter is `isIdentifier` (`src/common.js:11-13`), which rejects keys starting with a
digit, containing `-`, or equal to a reserved word. It is a name check, not an escaping
check, so a key such as

```js
const key = 'x = console.log("INJECTEDFROMKEY") ; var y'
saferEval('2 + 2', { [key]: 1 })
```

passes the filter and yields the body
`var x = console.log("INJECTEDFROMKEY") ; var y = __context['x = console.log(...) ; var y'];`.

**Evidence:** the harness above prints `INJECTEDFROMKEY` and then returns `4`.
`isIdentifier(key)` returns `true`. The node build has no such sink: the same key becomes
an ordinary vm context property (`src/index.js:25-33`) and `saferEval('2+2', {[key]: 1})`
returns `4` without executing anything.

**Impact:** low. The host must pass attacker-controlled key names as `context` (for
example building the context object from user-supplied JSON keys), which `README.md:47-49`
already warns against, and an attacker who controls `code` instead has the broader escape
recorded separately. Still, this turns a data-only context into a code sink and is a new
failure mode created by this file.

**Fix:** never place an unvalidated key in source position. Keep keys strictly identifier-
safe before splicing — validate with `/^[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*$/` in
`runInContext` (or tighten `isIdentifier`) — and quote the property access with
`JSON.stringify(key)`.

summary:
Review complete. Findings are recorded.

**What the change does:** it adds `index.js`, the whole validator engine, as the upstream 2.0.x → 2.1.0 refactor (`fdab855`, the commit that fixes CVE-2019-19507): comparison logic moves into `compareCommon`/`iterate` with an `options` object, and the type check becomes constructor identity (`value.constructor === pattern.constructor`, index.js:119-121) instead of `constructor.name` string comparison.

**Assessment:** the CVE payload from issue #6 — `{should_be_arrary: {"a":1, constructor:{name:'Array'}}}` against `{should_be_arrary: []}` — is now rejected (`false`), and the documented README examples still validate correctly, so the security fix itself holds. The refactor did, however, drop the per-branch early returns the pre-patch code had, which makes one property's failure recoverable by a later success — the most serious issue I found, reproducible in both standard and strict mode. Two smaller defects (nested schema keys skipped when the input supplies an array; uncaught `TypeError` on input keys that shadow `hasOwnProperty`/`toString`) are recorded at low severity, the latter carried over from the pre-patch code rather than introduced here.

findings.title: A failing property is overwritten by a later passing property, so validate() accepts invalid JSON
findings.body:
`iterate()` stores every property's result in one shared `valid` flag and keeps
looping after a property fails, so a later property that passes sets `valid` back
to `true`. `validate()` then returns `true` for JSON that failed the pattern.

The pre-refactor code returned `false` immediately on the first failing branch;
this file (index.js:230 `valid = (() => {...})()`, loop at index.js:227, no
`if (!valid) return false;` after `pull` at index.js:272) only ever *assigns* the
result, so the last checked property wins.

**Preconditions:** a pattern with two or more keys, where the checked order puts a
failing key before a passing one. JSON key order is attacker-controlled.

**Evidence:** run against this checkout:

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({age:'notnum', name:'bob'}, {age:'(number)', name:'(string)'})   // true
jpv.validate({email:'nope', status:'OK'}, {email:'[email]', status:'OK'})     // true
jpv.validate({b:'OK'}, {a:1, b:'OK'})                                         // true (a is missing)
jpv.validate({b:'OK'}, {a:1, b:'OK'}, {mode:'strict'})                        // true
jpv.validate({x:{a:'NO', b:1}}, {x:{a:'OK', b:1}})                            // true
```

The pre-patch commit `e93d2f6` returns `false` for the first three calls: the same
regression also hides the missing-key check performed by `compareExistence`
(index.js:161-176).

**Impact:** the value returned by `validate()` is the gate callers put in front of
untrusted input. Ordering the failing fields first and one valid field last makes
the whole object pass, in both standard and strict mode. Reach is broad (every
caller with a multi-key pattern), and the bypass can be retried at will.

**Fix:** restore first-failure propagation: after `pull(options, level)`
(index.js:272) add `if (!valid) return false;`, as upstream 2.1.1 does, or check
`valid` before each per-property assignment.

findings.title: Nested schema keys are never validated when the input supplies an array
findings.body:
When a schema key expects a nested object and the input supplies an array there,
the schema object's keys are never validated. `validate()` returns `true` for a
payload whose nested object is entirely unchecked.

In `iterate()` the array branch (index.js:246-257) is chosen from the *pattern's*
property, but the existence pass calls `iterate(pattern, json, compareExistence)`,
so in that pass the "pattern" argument is the input JSON. The input array makes
`value[property].constructor !== Array` true (index.js:249) and hands the schema
object plus the array to `compareExistence`, which only checks that the value is
defined (index.js:168-179) and returns `true`. The schema's inner keys are never
visited by either pass.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({x:[1,2]}, {x:{b:'[url]'}})          // true, expected false
jpv.validate({x:[1,2]}, {x:{b:1, c:2}})           // true, expected false
const old = require('/tmp/vuln/index.js');          // pre-patch commit e93d2f6
old.validate({x:[1,2]}, {x:{b:'[url]'}})           // false
```

A related gap uses the same guard: `validate({a:{}}, {a:{b:1}})` also returns
`true`, because the recursion test at index.js:265-267 inspects the input object
(`Object.keys(value[property]).length !== 0`) — an empty input object skips
recursion there too. That one also fails on the pre-patch commit, so it is older
than this change.

**Impact:** a caller that requires `body.x.b` to be a URL gets no validation of
`x` at all when the client sends an array (or `{}`); downstream code reads fields
that were never checked.

**Fix:** decide recursion from the schema's shape, not the input's: recurse
whenever the schema value is a plain object with own keys, regardless of whether
the input value is an array or an empty object, and reject a non-object input
where a keyed object is required.

findings.title: validate() throws TypeError on input JSON containing a hasOwnProperty key
findings.body:
`validate()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` when the input JSON contains a key
named `hasOwnProperty`. Any caller validating a request body has to catch this or
the request fails harder than a validation error.

`iterate()` calls the method through the instance: `value.hasOwnProperty(property)`
(index.js:228). A JSON object with an own `hasOwnProperty` key shadows
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`, so the call is on a non-function. The same
class of bug exists for primitive coercion: `String(value)` (index.js:62, 76, 90,
101) throws `Cannot convert object to primitive value` for input such as
`{toString:'x'}` when the pattern is a regex or a `[...]` / `{...}` pattern.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({hasOwnProperty: 1}, {})                       // TypeError: value.hasOwnProperty is not a function
jpv.validate({a: {hasOwnProperty: 1}}, {a: {b: 1}})         // TypeError: pattern.hasOwnProperty is not a function
jpv.validate({a: {toString: 'x'}}, {a: /^[0-9]+$/})         // TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
```

Upstream fixed the first form in commit `e3eec12` by switching to
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, String(property))`.

**Impact:** contained and transient, but it is a request-triggered crash in a
library whose input is untrusted JSON: an HTTP handler returns 500 instead of a
validation result, and an unhandled rejection or uncaught throw outside a handler
terminates the Node process. The pre-patch commit throws the same way, so this is
not a regression, only a flaw carried into the file this change adds.

**Fix:** use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, property)` and wrap the
`String(value)` conversions so a hostile `toString`/`valueOf` cannot throw.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** re-adds `lib/hide-sensitive.js` (17 lines), the module that masks sensitive environment values in `stdout`/`stderr`, error output, and plugin results. Three call sites already `require` it (`index.js:9`, `cli.js:3`, `lib/definitions/plugins.js:5`, `lib/utils.js:3`), so the file's content is what determines whether secrets are masked.

**Assessment:** the content is byte-identical to upstream v17.2.2 (blob `60984962c9`) — the version affected by CVE-2020-26226 — not the fixed v17.2.3. It masks only the literal value, so a credential containing characters that `url.format` percent-encodes (e.g. `tok en#1` → `tok%20en%231`) is written to CI logs verbatim; I reproduced this against the real `formatAuthUrl` code path. All other upstream behavior in the file checks out (I ran every assertion from `test/hide-sensitive.test.js`), and the fix is the 7-line upstream patch `ca90b34c` plus its test. One high finding recorded; no other defects in the change's surface.

findings.title: Secrets containing URL-encoded characters are written to logs unmasked
findings.body:
`hideSensitive` only masks the literal environment value, so a secret that gets
percent-encoded when it is embedded in a git URL passes through unmasked. This is
CVE-2020-26226; the added file is the pre-fix version (blob `60984962c9`, identical
to upstream v17.2.2).

**Preconditions:** a token/password/credential/secret/private env var whose value
contains a character that `url.format` percent-encodes (space, `#`, `%`, `?`, `@`
inside the auth part) and is at least `SECRET_MIN_SIZE` (5) chars.

**Evidence:**
`lib/get-git-auth-url.js:25-33` builds the auth URL with `url.format({auth: gitCredentials})`,
which encodes the credentials; `lib/hide-sensitive.js:14` builds its regexp from the
raw `env[envVar]` only.

```
$ node -e "..."
auth URL : https://gitlab-ci-token:tok%20en%231@gitlab.com/o/r.git
masked   : https://gitlab-ci-token:tok%20en%231@gitlab.com/o/r.git   # secret disclosed
raw form : token=[secure]
```

The leak reaches users because every stdout/stderr write is run through this function
(`index.js:243-246`), and the console error path writes `util.inspect(error)`
(`cli.js:59`). Errors from `git` and `debug` output routinely contain the auth URL, so
the encoded secret is written verbatim to CI logs.

**Impact:** CI credentials that contain encoded characters are published in build logs
unmasked, where every other secret is replaced with `[secure]`. Anyone who can read the
logs gets the credential; logs persist. Upstream rates this high
(GHSA-r2j6-p67h-q639); the file re-introduces the vulnerable behavior.

**Fix:** also match the URI-encoded form of each value, as upstream did in
`ca90b34c`:

```js
const regexp = new RegExp(
  toReplace
    .map((envVar) => `${escapeRegExp(env[envVar])}|${encodeURI(escapeRegExp(env[envVar]))}`)
    .join('|'),
  'g'
);
```

and add the accompanying test (`hideSensitive({privateKey: 'secret '})(...)` masks
`https://host.com?token=secret%20`).

summary: The PR restores `lib/reduce_object.js`, the helper the object and function adapters require for merging own properties, adding a `__proto__` guard intended to close CVE-2019-10750. The guard depends on a `behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys` flag that `flags.js` does not define, so both sides of the comparison are `undefined` and the check is skipped — I reproduced `Object.prototype` pollution from a plain `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{...}}')` payload. The helper also reads `this` as its context while all three callers pass it as a bare function, so the documented opt-in cannot work and the safety decision comes from the global object. Both issues are recorded; the security one needs the missing flag entry in `flags.js` alongside the new file.

findings.title: Merging a `__proto__` key pollutes Object.prototype because the safety flag is never defined
findings.body:
Merging an object that carries a `__proto__` own key still writes into `Object.prototype`. The guard added in `lib/reduce_object.js:23` never runs under default flags.

**Preconditions:** none beyond normal use — the library merges untrusted JSON (form bodies, config payloads, API responses) with default flags.

**Evidence:** the guard's condition is
`context.allowDangerousObjectKeys !== behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys && isUnsafeKey(key)`
(`lib/reduce_object.js:23`). `flags.js:3-8` defines only `useCustomAdapters` and `useCustomTypeOf`, so `behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys` is `undefined`. Inside `reduceObject` `this` is the global object (see the paired finding), where the property is also `undefined`, so `undefined !== undefined` is `false` and the key is merged. Reproduced:

```
$ node -e "var d=require('./index.js');
  d({}, JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\":{\"polluted\":\"yes\"}}'));
  console.log(({}).polluted)"
yes
```

Nested payloads (`{"a":{"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}}}`) pollute as well. `merge` reads `acc['__proto__']` as `Object.prototype`, and `adapters/object.js:20` merges the attacker's keys straight into it.

**Impact:** an attacker who controls merge input can set arbitrary properties on `Object.prototype` for the whole process — the prototype-pollution issue this guard was written for (CVE-2019-10750). Every object then inherits the injected properties, which enables gadget-based denial of service and, in applications with suitable sinks, remote code execution. Reach crosses a trust boundary (data supplier gains process-wide capability) and the pollution is permanent for the process lifetime. Graded **high**.

**Fix:** restore the flag the guard compares against, so the default is fail-closed like the other flags in `flags.js`:

```js
allowDangerousObjectKeys: 'deeply:allowDangerousObjectKeys:' + Math.random(),
```

findings.title: Dangerous-key guard reads the global object instead of the merge context, so `allowDangerousObjectKeys` opt-in never works
findings.body:
The new guard in `lib/reduce_object.js:18,23` reads its setting from `this`, but every caller invokes `reduceObject` as a plain function, so `this` is the global object rather than the merge context. Two consequences: the `allowDangerousObjectKeys` opt-in described by the code cannot be used, and the safety decision is taken from process-global state.

**Evidence:** callers: `adapters/object.js:20`, `extra/functions_clone.js:27`, `extra/functions_extend.js:26` — all bare `reduceObject(to, from, merge)` calls, while `merge` binds the context and passes it down to adapters via `adapter.call(this, ...)` (`merge.js:37`). With the flag added to `flags.js` (see the paired finding) the guard blocks by default, but the opt-in silently fails:

```
$ node -e "var m=require('./index.js');
  m.mutable.call({allowDangerousObjectKeys: m.behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys},
                 {}, JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\":{\"p\":1}}'));
  console.log(({}).p)"        // undefined — expected 1
```

Conversely, setting the token on `global` instead of the context *does* disable the guard: `global.allowDangerousObjectKeys = m.behaviors.allowDangerousObjectKeys` re-enables pollution, which confirms `context` is the global object.

**Impact:** the documented escape hatch is dead code, and the dangerous-key check is governed by a variable on `globalThis` that no caller intends to set there. A contained correctness defect: it fails closed for security, so the severity is **low**.

**Fix:** forward the merge context to the helper — `reduceObject.call(this, to, from, merge)` in `adapters/object.js:20` and the two `extra/` adapters — so `this` inside `reduceObject` is the context that `merge` was called with.

summary:
Findings recorded.

**What the change does:** This PR adds `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts` — the row-dispatch layer that drives `Scanner`/`RowParser`, handles BOM stripping, comments, and empty-row filtering. It is the rewritten parser that also replaced the regex-based empty-row test with a `RowParser.isEmptyRow` helper.

**Assessment:** The parser logic itself matches the upstream design and its control flow looks sound, but the file was added without the `RowParser.isEmptyRow` static it calls. That is a hard type error (the package `compile` script is plain `tsc`, and Jest runs through ts-jest), and with types erased the same call throws `TypeError: RowParser.isEmptyRow is not a function` for every caller using `ignoreEmpty`. I verified both: a tsc run on the sources reports TS2339 at `Parser.ts:80`, and a bundled runtime reproduction with `ignoreEmpty: true` throws. One medium finding recorded; no other issues found in the changed surface or its callers.

findings.title: Parser calls RowParser.isEmptyRow, which does not exist, so the parse package does not build
findings.body:
The new `Parser.parseRow` calls `RowParser.isEmptyRow(row)`, but `RowParser` in this tree has no `isEmptyRow` static member, so the parse package does not type-check and throws at runtime when `ignoreEmpty` is enabled.

**Preconditions:** Compiling the package always hits this; the runtime `TypeError` needs `ignoreEmpty: true`.

**Evidence:**
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:80` — `if (this.parserOptions.ignoreEmpty && RowParser.isEmptyRow(row))`.
- `packages/parse/src/parser/RowParser.ts:7-26` defines only `parse`, `getStartToken`, and `shouldSkipColumnParse`. `grep -rn isEmptyRow packages/` matches only the call site; `git show f270d35:packages/parse/src/parser/RowParser.ts` confirms the baseline never had it.
- Type check on the sources with tsc 4.1: `src/parser/Parser.ts(80,57): error TS2339: Property 'isEmptyRow' does not exist on type 'typeof RowParser'`. `tsc` is the package `compile` script, so `npm run build` (and ts-jest, the Jest preset) fails.
- Runtime, with types erased: `new Parser(new ParserOptions({ ignoreEmpty: true })).parse('a,b\n,,\n', false)` throws `TypeError: RowParser.isEmptyRow is not a function`.
- The related `Parser.spec.ts` case "should ignore empty rows if ignoreEmpty is true" exercises exactly this path.

**Impact:** The parse package cannot be built as committed, and any caller that uses `ignoreEmpty` (a documented parse option) gets an uncaught `TypeError` thrown from the transform stream instead of parsed rows. Reach is every consumer of the package and the outcome is undone by adding the helper, so medium.

**Fix:** Add the missing helper the caller expects, matching the rest of the change: `static isEmptyRow(row: RowArray): boolean { return row.join('').replace(/\s+/g, '') === ''; }` in `RowParser`, or inline that check in `Parser.parseRow` so the file has no dependency on an absent member.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded: 5 (1 medium, 3 low, 1 info).

**Summary:** PR #2 adds `index.js`, the complete Json Pattern Validator (`jpv` 2.0.1) implementation: `validate()` walks the untrusted JSON against a pattern object, dispatching to regex, native-type, functional, and constructor-based comparisons with standard/strict modes. The implementation is vulnerable in the way CVE-2019-19507 / GHSA-rh46-3fgc-mvrf describes — `compareCommon` reads `value.constructor.name` from the attacker's own object, so a crafted `constructor` field defeats the library's only type guard — and I reproduced that bypass plus three further validation/crash defects in the same code (prototype-named keys throwing, primitives satisfying object schemas, strict-mode presence checks skipping array elements), all documented with runnable reproductions. The change is not safe to merge as-is: the core type check and the untrusted-key handling need reworking before this validator can be used on untrusted input.

findings.title: Attacker-supplied constructor field makes a JSON value pass any array or object schema
findings.body:
`compareCommon` decides an object pattern's type by reading `value.constructor.name`,
which is a plain data property of the attacker's own JSON object. Any payload that
sends `"constructor": {"name": "Array"}` is treated as an Array, so it passes every
pattern whose meaning is "this value must be an array" — including array-of-schema
patterns whose per-element checks are then skipped entirely.

**Preconditions:** the caller validates untrusted JSON with a pattern that describes an
object, an empty-object, or an array (`README.md:207-264` documents these as the way to
enforce Array/object types). No other precondition.

**Evidence:** (`index.js:117-125`, the comparison is line 122)

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
// documented "value must be an array" pattern
jpv.validate({tags: {length: 0, constructor: {name: 'Array'}}}, {tags: ['[email]']});
// -> true   (control {"tags":["a@b.com"]} -> true, {"tags":["not-an-email"]} -> false)
jpv.validate({should_be_arrary: {a: 1, constructor: {name: 'Array'}}}, {should_be_arrary: []});
// -> true   (an object satisfies the "must be an Array" schema)
```

The same line also throws on `{"key": {"constructor": null}}` (`TypeError: Cannot read
properties of null (reading 'name')`) instead of returning false.

**Impact:** an attacker who supplies the JSON being validated can make a value look like
an Array and so skip element-level validation or type enforcement. The validator's only
strong type guard reads attacker-controlled data, which defeats the library's purpose.
Severity is medium: the bypass crosses the validation trust boundary, but the damage that
follows depends on how the calling application uses the value, and it lasts only for the
request that carries the payload (this is CVE-2019-19507 / GHSA-rh46-3fgc-mvrf).

**Fix:** stop reading `constructor` from the value. Compare `Object.getPrototypeOf` on a
known prototype, e.g. `pattern.constructor === value.constructor` is still spoofable, so
use `Array.isArray(value)` for arrays and compare an explicit tag/native check for other
object types; at minimum reject values whose own `constructor` property exists.

findings.title: A JSON key named toString or hasOwnProperty makes validate() throw instead of returning a boolean
findings.body:
`iterate` looks up pattern values with `obj2[property]`, so a JSON key that names an
`Object.prototype` member resolves to the inherited function instead of `undefined`.
Validation then falls through to `compareCommon`, which throws (line 127). Keys named
`hasOwnProperty` crash earlier still, at line 208, because the untrusted object's own
property shadows the method the code calls.

`validate()` is documented to return a boolean (`README.md:47`); the file has no
`try/catch`, so every one of these payloads raises an exception out of `validate()`.

**Preconditions:** the payload must be an object (any object pattern, including `{}`,
triggers it).

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"toString":5,"a":1}'), {a: '(number)'});
// throws a *string*: "error: don`t use function as a pattern value, insted of it use string format"
jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"valueOf":5}'), {});            // same throw
jpv.validate(JSON.parse('{"hasOwnProperty":1,"a":2}'), {a: 2});
// TypeError: obj1.hasOwnProperty is not a function
```

Top-level and nested objects both hit this (`index.js:232`, `index.js:224` recursion);
no pattern key needs to mention the offending name.

**Impact:** any untrusted client can make validation throw by including a key named
`toString`, `valueOf`, `constructor`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, or
`hasOwnProperty`. In a request handler this is a 500 per request at best, and an
uncaught-exception/process exit in callers that do not wrap `validate`. Low severity: a
single request is affected and nothing persists; the damage is bounded by the caller's
error handling.

**Fix:** never read pattern members through the prototype chain — test with
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj2, property)` before using `obj2[property]`,
and call `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj1, property)` at line 208.

findings.title: Primitive JSON values and primitive array elements satisfy object schemas
findings.body:
When the JSON side is a primitive, `iterate` iterates its properties (`for (var property
in obj1)` over a number/boolean/null yields none), returns `true`, and the mirror pass
`iterate(pattern, json, compareExistence)` sees only "value is defined" (`index.js:166-181`).
The schema's keys are never compared, so a primitive passes any object or array schema —
at the top level and as an element of an array.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
const S = {a: '(number)', b: '(string)'};
jpv.validate(null,  S, {mode: 'strict'}); // -> true
jpv.validate(5,     S, {mode: 'strict'}); // -> true
jpv.validate(true,  S, {mode: 'strict'}); // -> true
jpv.validate(7, [4]);                     // -> true  ("must be an array")
jpv.validate({}, S, {mode: 'strict'});    // -> false (correct, for comparison)
jpv.validate({users: [7]}, {users: [{id: '(number)', name: '(string)'}]}, {mode: 'strict'});
// -> true (the element schema is never applied)
```

Relevant code: `index.js:200-202` (primitive-pattern shortcut and the property loop),
`index.js:224` (array elements are recursed into the same `iterate`), `index.js:254`/`263`
(the two passes).

**Impact:** a caller doing `jpv.validate(JSON.parse(body), schema)` accepts a body of
`null`, `5`, or `true` as a valid document, and accepts numbers as valid array elements
inside an otherwise enforced list. Severity is low: the validation gate is defeated for
these payloads, but a non-object body usually fails on the caller's next property access,
so the concrete damage depends on the application.

**Fix:** in `iterate`, before the property loop, return `false` when the pattern is a
non-null object and the value is not an object (`typeof value !== 'object' || value ===
null`); that one guard covers both the top-level and array-element cases.

findings.title: Strict mode does not check for missing keys in array elements after the first
findings.body:
Strict mode is documented to require the same key hierarchy in the JSON and the pattern,
but the presence pass only reaches the first element of an array. A required key may be
absent from every element after the first and validation still returns `true`.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
const P = {users: [{id: '(number)', name: '(string)'}]};
jpv.validate({users: [{id: 1, name: 'a'}, {id: 2}]}, P, {mode: 'strict'});
// -> true   (element 2 has no "name")
jpv.validate({users: [{id: 1}]}, P, {mode: 'strict'});   // -> false (element 1 is checked)
```

The presence pass (`index.js:263`, standard mode `index.js:254`) walks the pattern, and
for an array property it loops `i < obj1[property].length` where `obj1` is the *pattern*
(`index.js:223-227`), so it visits only as many elements as the pattern declares. The
value-side pass only compares keys the element actually has, so the missing key is never
reported.

**Impact:** strict mode silently accepts documents that violate the declared schema, so a
required field can be dropped from any element after the first. Type checks inside those
elements still run, which makes the hole easy to miss. Low severity: only the presence
check is skipped and the absent field reads as `undefined` downstream.

**Fix:** drive the array iteration from the value array in both passes (or, in the
presence pass, recurse with `iterate(obj2[property][i], obj1[property][i], ...)`) so every
element of the validated array is checked against the element pattern.

findings.title: Debug logging enabled by one call stays on for every later validate() call
findings.body:
`debug` is module-level state (`index.js:17`) assigned from the per-call option at
`index.js:281`. Nothing ever sets it back to `false`, so one call that passes
`{debug: true}` turns on logging for every later call in the process, including calls
made for other users.

**Evidence:**

```
const jpv = require('./index.js');
jpv.validate({a: 1}, {a: '(number)'}, {debug: true});
jpv.validate({password: 'hunter2'}, {password: '(number)'});
// stdout: The value of ["hunter2"] does not match with ["(number)"]
```

`log` (`index.js:22-26`) prints the failing value verbatim.

**Impact:** in a server, a single debug-enabled code path makes the library write other
requests' values to stdout for the life of the process, which can put secrets or personal
data into logs. Info severity: it needs a non-default setting (`debug: true`) and the
exposed values are ones that already failed validation.

**Fix:** pass a per-call options object carrying `debug` through `compareStandard`,
`compareStrict` and `compareExistence` instead of mutating a module-level flag.

summary:
## Summary

The PR adds `src/browser.js`, the browser counterpart of safer-eval's `vm`-based node build, which `package.json`'s `browser` field swaps in for bundlers (the file is byte-identical to what upstream published in 1.3.2–1.3.4; I checked by unpacking both from npm). The implementation is sound for evaluating permitted expressions, but it is not a sandbox: the code string is compiled by the page's own `Function` constructor in non-strict mode, so `this` is `window`, `(function(){}).constructor` is the real `Function`, and the single constructor guard only blocks its literal test-suite form. A second, smaller defect is that the guard is implemented by assigning through `this`, so every call permanently rewrites the host page's `Window.constructor` (plus `Function.constructor` via `common.js:56`). Both findings are recorded; the escape is the blocking issue, and no local patch fixes it without a separate realm.

findings.title: Browser build evaluates untrusted code in the page realm, so page globals and credentials are reachable
findings.body:
`src/browser.js` is the browser build; `package.json` maps `./lib/index.js` to
`./lib/browser.js`, so bundlers swap the vm-sandboxed node build for this file.
`SaferEval#runInContext` (src/browser.js:36-50) pastes the caller's code into a non-strict
function body compiled by the host realm's `Function` constructor and invokes it with
`.call(null, __context)`. In a browser that makes `this` the page's `window`, and every
function literal in the evaluated code is a page-realm function whose `.constructor` is the
real `Function`. The allow-list only shadows identifiers (src/browser.js:44-46), and the
single guard (src/browser.js:42) blocks only the literal form `this.constructor.constructor(...)`.

**Preconditions:** the `code` string is untrusted (the module's documented use), and the
bundle resolves the browser build, which webpack/browserify do automatically through the
`browser` field in package.json:19-21.

**Evidence:** run node with `global.window = global` set before requiring src/browser.js
(this models the browser, where the global object is `window`), set
`window.sessionToken = 'SECRET-TOKEN'`, then call `saferEval`:

| snippet | result |
|---|---|
| `this.sessionToken` | `"SECRET-TOKEN"` |
| `this.eval('sessionToken')` | `"SECRET-TOKEN"` |
| `(function(){}).constructor('return sessionToken')()` | `"SECRET-TOKEN"` |
| `arguments.callee.constructor('return sessionToken')()` | `"SECRET-TOKEN"` |
| `this.constructor.constructor.constructor('return sessionToken')()` | `"SECRET-TOKEN"` |
| `this.constructor.constructor('return sessionToken')()` (the guarded form) | throws `TypeError` |

Only the exact form exercised by the test suite (test/saferEval.spec.js:290-308) is
blocked. The node build has the same shape of guard but runs the body in a strict-mode
wrapper inside `vm` (src/index.js:43-50), so `this` is `undefined` there.

**Impact:** untrusted code evaluated in a browser bundle gets full page-realm execution:
`this.document.cookie`, `this.localStorage`, any page global can be read and overwritten,
and `this.eval` / `(function(){}).constructor` return the real page `Function`. Reach crosses
a trust boundary (untrusted input gains the page's credentials and capabilities) and the
effect is permanent (exfiltrated tokens do not come back), so high. The file and README do
warn that there is "no real sandboxing" in the browser, which limits what the module
promises, but the allow-list and the guard are presented as the mitigation and the tests
assert the constructor walk is closed, so a caller who follows the README advice of passing
only selected context props still hands over the whole page.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — evaluated code must not be able to name the host realm's
`Function` or global object. No local patch achieves this: a strict-mode wrapper removes
`this`, but `(function(){}).constructor` still yields the page's `Function`. Either evaluate
in a separate realm (Worker or sandboxed iframe), or stop shipping the browser build and
remove the ineffective guard and the tests that claim it works.

findings.title: Browser build permanently rewrites the page's Window.constructor and Function.constructor
findings.body:
`src/browser.js:42` writes through `this`, which in a browser is the page's global object:
`this.constructor.constructor = function () {}` sets the `constructor` property of the
`Window` function (`window.constructor`), replacing `Function`. It runs on every
`runInContext` call and nothing restores the old value. A second write happens at
`src/common.js:56` (`context.Object.constructor.constructor = 'function () {}'`), reached
from the `SaferEval` constructor (src/browser.js:25-27) whenever `window` exists: it sets the
page's `Function.constructor` to the string `'function () {}'`.

**Evidence:** node, with `global.window = global` before requiring src/browser.js:

```
before ctor : Function.constructor is function, Object.constructor === Function
after  ctor : Function.constructor is string "function () {}",   // common.js:56
after  call : Object.constructor !== Function,                   // browser.js:42
              window.constructor.constructor !== Function
```

**Impact:** merely calling `saferEval` — even on trusted code — leaves the page realm
permanently changed: `window.constructor !== Window` and `Function.constructor` is no longer
callable, so any host code that inspects or calls those properties gets wrong results. The
damage is real but small, since these properties are rarely read, so low.

**Fix:** do not write through the host global. Evaluate the body in strict mode so `this` is
`undefined`, shadow any guard value with a local variable, and drop the host-state write at
src/common.js:56.

summary: **Summary:** PR #2 re-adds `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts` (88 lines), the row/comment orchestration layer for `@fast-csv/parse`, including the `ignoreEmpty` emptiness check. That check (`Parser.ts:7`, `Parser.ts:82`) runs a backtracking regex over `row.join('')`; I reproduced a stall of ~60 s from a single 32 KB cell, and the same predicate silently drops non-empty rows such as `",","` because the delimiters are stripped by `join('')`. The rest of the file (comment handling, row loops, BOM stripping) reads correctly and terminates on all paths I traced through `Scanner`/`RowParser`. One finding recorded: the ReDoS/data-loss issue in the `ignoreEmpty` check, whose smallest fix is a per-column emptiness test that also removes the regex.

findings.title: Crafted CSV cell with a long whitespace run stalls the parser for minutes via EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP
findings.body:
A parsed row's emptiness check runs a backtracking regular expression over the whole row, so one
crafted CSV cell blocks the Node event loop for minutes. Any service that parses untrusted CSV
with `ignoreEmpty: true` stops serving all other requests while that row is tested.

**Preconditions:** `ignoreEmpty: true` (the default is `false`); attacker-controlled CSV content;
no limit on line or cell length. No other option matters.

**Evidence:**
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:7` — `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP = /^\s*(?:''|"")?\s*(?:,\s*(?:''|"")?\s*)*$/`.
  Each iteration of the outer group wraps an optional token between two greedy `\s*` runs, and the
  whole expression is anchored with `$`, so a long whitespace run that is followed by one
  non-matching character forces the engine to retry every way of splitting that run.
- `packages/parse/src/parser/Parser.ts:82` — `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP.test(row.join(''))` applies it to
  every parsed row whenever `ignoreEmpty` is set.
- Reproduction with the package compiled as-is (`ParserOptions({ignoreEmpty: true})`, one line, one
  cell, no other data; timings on this machine):

  | cell content | time in `parse` |
  |---|---|
  | `" " x 8000 + "x"` | 0.5 s |
  | `" " x 16000 + "x"` | 2.9 s |
  | `" " x 32000 + "x"` | 59.9 s |

  Growth outruns the input: a 32 KB cell is enough to stall the process for a minute, and a 1 MB
  cell for hours. `" " x 32000 + "x"` in an unquoted cell (kept when `trim` is off) takes 0.5 s, so
  even modest lines from a real file are enough.

**Impact:** A crafted row makes the whole parsing process unresponsive — every concurrent request
or job sharing that process waits for the regular expression to finish. DoS affects all users of
the process (broad reach) and is re-triggerable at will, but leaves no persistent damage
(recoverable). The non-default `ignoreEmpty` option keeps it below `high`; per the policy in
"Reviewing a change" (broad/recoverable = medium) it is filed as `medium`.

**Fix:** Restore per-column emptiness and delete `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP`, e.g.
`if (this.parserOptions.ignoreEmpty && row.every(col => col === '')) return true;`.
Testing the joined values is also wrong in the other direction: `row.join('')` drops the delimiters,
so a non-empty two-cell row `",","` joins to `,,` and matches the regex (same for a single cell
`''`), and is silently discarded. Upstream fixed this in 4.3.6 by replacing the regex with a
per-row emptiness helper in `RowParser`.
