summary:
Recorded three findings. Final assessment:

The change adds `src/renderer.js`, the headless-Chrome rendering core: it opens a tab, loads the requested URL, strips scripts, injects a `<base>` tag, and returns the serialized DOM (or a screenshot) to `src/main.js`'s `/render` and `/screenshot` routes. The file matches upstream except for one formatting tweak, so what I reviewed is effectively upstream's pre-fix renderer sitting on the vulnerable baseline routes.

Reviewing it against its callers, the renderer takes the caller-supplied URL at face value: nothing between `request.params.url` and `Page.navigate` constrains the scheme or the address, so `file://` targets are read and returned, and the URL is spliced unescaped into a `Runtime.evaluate` expression. Its lifecycle handling is also loose — tabs are closed only on success, so failed renders accumulate. The rendering/timing logic itself (virtual time budget, status-code meta tag, completion event) is reasonable and I found no defect in it that I could trace to a failure path.

findings.title: URL is interpolated into a Runtime.evaluate expression, allowing JavaScript injection
findings.body:
The requested URL is spliced into a JavaScript expression without escaping, so a URL containing a quote escapes the string and injects arbitrary JavaScript into the headless Chrome page.

**Evidence:** `src/renderer.js:187` builds `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')` and passes it to `Runtime.evaluate`. A request for

    /render/http://allowed.example/');fetch("http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/")//

produces `(function injectBaseHref(url) {...})('http://allowed.example/');fetch(...)//')`, in which the trailing `')` is commented out. I built this expression from the file's own function source and evaluated it under Node with a stub `document`; the appended `fetch` ran as a separate statement.

**Preconditions:** The injected code only runs after `_loadPage` resolves, so the navigation must produce a document — a 404 page at the crafted path is enough. The value arrives verbatim from `request.params.url` (`src/main.js:99`).

**Impact:** Caller-controlled JavaScript runs inside the server-side browser. Where `renderOnly` restricts rendering to an allowlist (the documented control for an internet-facing instance, `test/app-test.js:154`), this runs code in an allowlisted origin and can reach internal endpoints the allowlist was meant to block, so it defeats the only access control. Without `renderOnly` a caller can already render a page that runs its own script, so the injection adds nothing; the severity comes from the allowlist bypass.

**Fix:** Serialize the URL instead of interpolating it: `` `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})(${JSON.stringify(url)})` ``, or pass it through `Runtime.callFunctionOn` arguments.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read server-local files by rendering file:// URLs
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can read files on the server by sending a `file://` URL. The renderer navigates to whatever URL it is given and returns the serialized document, so `/render/file:///etc/passwd` returns the file's contents as HTML. The same missing check lets callers fetch internal HTTP endpoints, including cloud metadata addresses.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:74` passes the raw URL to `Page.navigate`, and `src/renderer.js:189` returns `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` for that document, which for a `file://` target is the file body.
- Nothing upstream restricts the scheme. `src/main.js:92` and `src/main.js:111` only call `isRestricted`, which returns `false` whenever `renderOnly` is unset (`src/main.js:65-74`); there is no scheme or address check.
- The repo's own tests show `file://` rendering works: `test/app-test.js:117` and `test/app-test.js:124` request `/render/file://<absolute path>` and assert status codes taken from the rendered page's meta tag, which only happens if the local file loaded.

**Impact:** Any remote caller reads server-local files — application source, `.git`, and `config.json`, which the deployment keeps at the repo root (`src/main.js:34`) and which holds cache, analytics and Chrome settings. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the disclosure is permanent, so this is high. The same path reaches internal-only HTTP services, since no address filtering exists.

**Fix:** Reject any request URL whose protocol is not `http:` or `https:` before rendering, e.g. in `isRestricted` (`src/main.js:65`): `if (!url.parse(urlReq).protocol.match(/^https?:/)) return true;`. If the service is reachable from untrusted networks, also refuse loopback, link-local and private addresses. Keep `renderOnly` as defence in depth.

findings.title: Failed renders leak Chrome targets because tabs are only closed on success
findings.body:
Failed renders leak Chrome targets. `serialize` and `captureScreenshot` each open a tab with `CDP.New`, close it with `CDP.Close` only on the success path, and just `reject` in the error handler, so every failed render leaves an open tab behind for the life of the browser process.

**Evidence:** `src/renderer.js:178` opens the tab and `src/renderer.js:190` is the only close in `serialize`; the `catch` at `src/renderer.js:194-196` rejects without closing. `captureScreenshot` has the same shape (`src/renderer.js:202`, `:220`, `:222-224`). Failures are easy to trigger from outside: `_loadPage` rejects on `Network.loadingFailed` for the initial request (`src/renderer.js:97`), which is exactly what an unresolvable host produces — the `unknown url fails` case at `test/app-test.js:144`.

**Impact:** Repeated requests for names that do not resolve (or any other failing navigation) accumulate tabs and their memory until the Chrome process is exhausted or restarted. The service is unauthenticated and has no rate limit, so any caller can drive it. Reach is broad and recovery needs a restart, so this is medium.

**Fix:** Close the target in a `finally` block around the body of both `serialize` and `captureScreenshot`, so every path — success, render error, or evaluate error — releases the tab.

summary:
Review complete. One finding recorded.

**What the change does:** PR #2 adds `index.js` (132 lines) back to the `method-override` fixture — the header/query getter middleware that rewrites `req.method` from `X-HTTP-Method-Override` (or a query key), gated on Node-supported methods. Diffing against upstream shows this is the file at `5a7d6a1` (2.3.9), i.e. the state *before* the 2.3.10 fix for CVE-2017-16136.

**Assessment:** the logic is otherwise sound and the 19 upstream tests pass, but the header getter still splits the entire header value with `/ *, */` (`index.js:120`). I reproduced the resulting quadratic backtracking end to end: a single unauthenticated `POST` with a 14 KB `X-HTTP-Method-Override` value burns ~700 ms of event loop (8 KB ≈ 250 ms), so the middleware ships the ReDoS it is meant to fix. That is recorded as a medium finding with the smallest safe correction (substring before the first comma, as 2.3.10 does). Probe leads beyond that (config typos, caller-supplied `req` shims, hitting `Vary` gaps) were caller misuse or documented behaviour, so I filed nothing for them.

findings.title: A single POST with a long X-HTTP-Method-Override header blocks the event loop for hundreds of milliseconds
findings.body:
An unprivileged client can stall the whole Node.js process by sending one POST with a
long `X-HTTP-Method-Override` header. The default getter splits the entire header value
with `/ *, */` (`index.js:120`). For a value of many spaces followed by a non-space, the
regexp match attempt at each starting position greedily consumes the remaining spaces,
fails on the missing comma, and backtracks over all of them. Split retries at every
position, so the work grows quadratically in header length and runs on the event loop.

**Preconditions:** default configuration (`methodOverride()` — header getter
`X-HTTP-Method-Override`, `methods: ['POST']`, `index.js:44`, `index.js:53-55`). The
attacker only needs to send an ordinary POST; a ~14 KB header fits inside Node's default
16 KB header limit.

**Evidence:** reproduced end to end against the checked-out module (physical server,
`POST /` with `X-HTTP-Method-Override: `x` + N spaces + `y`), wall time per request:

| value length | time |
|---|---|
| 4 KB | 42 ms |
| 8 KB | 220–290 ms |
| 14 KB | 711 ms |

The split runs before `supports()` is consulted, so the value never has to be a valid HTTP
method; `x` followed by spaces is enough.

A handful of concurrent requests of this shape keeps the loop busy for seconds; the module's
own test suite (19 passing) never exercises a long header.

**Impact:** the middleware is the default entry point of any Express app that enables it,
so one unauthenticated request delays every other request the process is serving. Reach is
broad (all clients of the process) and persistence is recoverable — an attacker can re-send
at will to keep the service unavailable — which lands at `medium` on the review policy
table (broad x recoverable).

**Fix:** stop running a regexp over the header value. Upstream fixed this in 2.3.10
(commit 4c58835) by looking up the header once and taking the substring before the first
comma:

```js
var header = req.headers[name]
if (!header) return undefined
var index = header.indexOf(',')
return index !== -1 ? header.substr(0, index).trim() : header.trim()
```

The caller already handles both a string and an array (`index.js:71-73`), so the return
type change is safe.

summary:
**Assessment: no findings; recommend approval.**

The PR adds `index.js` (144 lines) in full, and it is byte-identical to the released `method-override@2.3.10` — the upstream fix for CVE-2017-16136. The only functional delta over 2.3.9 is `createHeaderGetter` (index.js:112-134): the attacker-controlled `X-HTTP-Method-Override` value is now parsed with `indexOf(',')` + `trim()` instead of `split(/ *, */)`, and a missing header returns `undefined` rather than an array of segments.

I verified the fix is real and complete: the old regex on 20 KB of spaces took ~15 s, while the new path is sub-millisecond per call, and no regex remains in the file (the other request-controlled work, `querystring.parse` and `vary` on the configured name, is unaffected). The parse results for the cases the tests and README describe are unchanged, `req.headers` values from Node's HTTP parser are always strings here (only `set-cookie` is array-valued, and the `X-` prefix rule at index.js:88 makes that name unselectable), and the caller's `Array.isArray(val) ? val[0] : val` (index.js:69-71) remains correct for the query and custom-function getters.

All 19 tests pass and `eslint --plugin markdown` is clean. The edge cases I probed beyond the test suite — whitespace/tab-padded header values now being trimmed into a valid method, misconfigured header names that make `vary` throw, and `Vary` being set before the header is read — are either unchanged since 2.3.9, require a misconfiguration or an external intermediary the repo does not control, or grant no capability a client could not already get by sending the method plainly. Nothing here meets the reporting bar, so I recorded no findings.

Review complete. Findings: none recorded.

**Summary**

The change adds `src/node.js`, the Node.js implementation of `debug()` (179 lines): TTY-based color detection, the optional 256-color palette, `DEBUG_*` → `util.inspect` options, `%o`/`%O` formatters, stderr logging, and `process.env.DEBUG` save/load. It is byte-identical to the canonical upstream fix for CVE-2017-16137 (`%o` now uses `split('\n').map(trim).join(' ')` at src/node.js:86-88 instead of the quadratic `/\s*\n\s*/` regex), and I confirmed the old form is Θ(n²) (222 ms at 8k chars, 4.2 s at 32k) while the new form is linear (0.5 ms at 200k), with the attacker-controlled value reaching the formatter through src/debug.js:99-108. I smoke-tested the module on Node 24: colors, `%o`, `%O`, plain `%s`, and the non-TTY path all behave correctly, and no regex remains on attacker-influenced data in the new file. The quirks an exhaustive probe surfaced (malformed `DEBUG` values throwing at `require` time, non-numeric `DEBUG_*` coercion, indirect `supports-color` dependency, extra spaces on blank lines) all come from unchanged shared code or are upstream-intended, cosmetic, or operator-only — none is a defensible regression from this change, so this is a clean fix worth approving.

Coverage is complete: the change is a single new file (`src/node.js`, 177 lines) that provides the Node.js backend the baseline was missing, allowing `src/index.js` to load at all. I reviewed it line by line, compared it with upstream `debug@3.0.1` (identical) and with the fixed `debug@2.6.9`/`4.3.4` implementations, ran the module end to end, and probed the surrounding hooks in `src/debug.js`.

One finding recorded: the newly added `%o` formatter at `src/node.js:86` carries the quadratic `/\s*\n\s*/g` replace (CVE-2017-16137) that 2.6.9 replaced with a linear split/trim/join — I reproduced 0.75 s at a 10k whitespace run and 95 s at 80k. The remaining probe leads (NaN coercion of `DEBUG_*` values, `save()` writing `process.env.DEBUG`, shared export object between the browser/node backends, undeclared optional `supports-color`) are upstream design choices that need operator-side configuration or an already-trusted caller, so I left them unreported. Overall the change is a faithful vendor import; the only defect worth acting on is the restored vulnerable regex.

findings.title: Logging untrusted data with %o can wedge the event loop in a quadratic whitespace regex
findings.body:
The new `%o` formatter collapses newlines with a backtracking regex applied to the whole inspected value:

```js
exports.formatters.o = function(v) {
  this.inspectOpts.colors = this.useColors;
  return util.inspect(v, this.inspectOpts)
    .replace(/\s*\n\s*/g, ' ');       // src/node.js:86
};
```

For every start position the engine consumes the maximal run of whitespace with `\s*`, fails to find `\n`, then backtracks one character at a time. On a long whitespace run the replace costs O(n²): one call blocks the event loop for seconds. Any process that logs attacker-influenced data through `%o` can be stalled by a single request. This is CVE-2017-16137; the 2.6.x line fixed it by dropping the regex (`debug@2.6.9` uses `.split('\n').map(trim).join(' ')`), and this new file reintroduces the vulnerable form.

**Preconditions:** `debug` is enabled for the namespace, the call site formats a value with `%o` (src/debug.js:95-109), and part of that value reaches `util.inspect` output as a run of whitespace without a newline — i.e. untrusted input logged with `%o`, the documented use of the formatter.

**Evidence:** reproduced on Node 24 with a direct call to the exported formatter (`src/node.js:83`):

| whitespace run | `.replace(/\s*\n\s*/g,' ')` | via `debug('%o', ' '.repeat(n)+'x')` |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 0.75 s | 0.84 s (output truncated at 10,000 chars) |
| 20,000 | 2.5 s | 15 s with `DEBUG_MAX_STRING_LENGTH=1000000` |
| 40,000 | 11.6 s | — |
| 80,000 | 95 s | — |

Cost grows ~4× per doubling, and nothing bounds the input length except `util.inspect`'s default `maxStringLength`, which the same process can raise through the documented `DEBUG_MAX_STRING_LENGTH` env var (src/node.js:44-63 passes it straight to `util.inspect`).

**Impact:** an unprivileged caller who can get one value into a `%o` log line stalls the whole event loop (all concurrent requests) for seconds to minutes, repeatable at will. Reach is broad — every client of the logging service waits — and the stall clears itself, so medium. Discounted from high because it needs the host application to route untrusted data into a `%o` argument; the library alone does not expose the input.

**Fix:** make the collapse linear, e.g. restore the 2.6.9 implementation:

```js
return util.inspect(v, this.inspectOpts)
  .split('\n').map(function (str) { return str.trim(); }).join(' ');
```

summary: This PR adds back `src/decorators/Link/index.js`, the DraftJS decorator that renders `LINK` entities as anchors plus an "open link" icon. The code is small and clean, but it passes the entity's `url` unchanged into `href` and `window.open`, so a `javascript:` URL — insertable through the editor's own link control, or supplied in a raw `contentState` the host renders — executes script in the consuming app's origin on click; the upstream fix for CVE-2021-31712 adds exactly this `ensureSafeUrl` validation. I recorded that as a medium finding and confirmed React 16 only warns rather than blocking the scheme. Nothing else in the change warranted a finding; the `_blank` target lacks `rel="noopener"`, but current browsers apply that implicitly, so I left it out.

findings.title: Link decorator renders unsanitized link URLs, allowing javascript: XSS on click
findings.body: The Link decorator renders the `url` field of a `LINK` entity straight into an anchor's `href` and into `window.open`, so a `javascript:` (or `data:`) URL stored in the entity runs script in the host application's origin when a reader clicks the link. Any app that renders content authored by someone else — a published post, a comment, a support ticket, a read-only preview — executes attacker-chosen script. **Preconditions:** the host app renders a `contentState`/`initialContentState` containing a `LINK` entity whose `url` came from an untrusted author (the normal use of a WYSIWYG), and the reader clicks the link. **Evidence:** - src/decorators/Link/index.js:51 takes `url` from entity data and index.js:59 passes it unchanged to `href`; index.js:38-41 passes it unchanged to `window.open(url, 'blank')`. - src/Editor/index.js:269-275 feeds the `contentState` prop through `convertFromRaw`, and the decorator is installed unconditionally (src/Editor/index.js:60, 208-213), so editor-authored or server-supplied raw content reaches this render in both editable and `readOnly` mode. - Such content can be created with the editor's own toolbar: src/controls/Link/index.js:14-19 runs the target through `linkify-it`, which does not recognise `javascript:` and returns `null`, so `params.target` is stored verbatim (verified: `require('linkify-it')().match('javascript:alert(1)') === null`). - React 16 (this package's peer range, package.json:65-67) does not block the scheme; it only warns. Rendering with react-dom 16.14 produces `click` (same for `JaVaScRiPt:`). **Impact:** stored cross-site scripting. Content written by one user, or imported from a server, runs arbitrary script as the viewing user in the consuming app's origin when the link is clicked; script can read the session, call same-origin APIs, and rewrite the page. Severity is `medium` rather than `high` because the payload needs a click on the rendered link and the impact is scoped to whichever site embeds the editor. Policy anchor: CVE-2021-31712, whose upstream fix is this exact hardening. **Fix:** validate the scheme at both render sites and fall back to a harmless value. Upstream added `src/utils/url.js` exporting `ensureSafeUrl(url)`, which strips whitespace/control characters and returns `'#'` unless the URL matches `^(?:(?:https?|ftps?|mailto):|[^a-z]|[a-z+.-]+(?:[^a-z+.:-]|$))`, then applied it to `href={ensureSafeUrl(url)}` and `window.open(ensureSafeUrl(url), 'blank')`. The invariant to restore: only `http`/`https`/`ftp`/`ftps`/`mailto` and relative URLs may reach an anchor `href`; everything else becomes `#`.

summary:
Reviewed the full diff (a new `index.js`, 88 lines) and tested the module's behaviour locally, including with stand-in SQLcl binaries.

**Assessment:** The change replaces shell-string construction with `spawnSync` and an argument array, which closes the CVE-2018-16462 command injection — `connectString`, `directory`, `appID` and `pluginName` reach SQLcl as separate argv entries, never through a shell, and `appID`/`pluginName` are bound parameters in `lib/distUpload.js:105-106` rather than concatenated SQL, so no injection survives downstream. One real regression came with the switch from `execSync` to `spawnSync`: the exit status, spawn error, and stderr are now ignored, so failures are reported as success with no signal to the caller (recorded as `low`). Aside from that, the file is straightforward and the argument order/mapping is correct.

findings.title: Failed SQLcl uploads are reported as success and never surface an error
findings.body:
`publish()` prints "Files were uploaded successfully." and returns `undefined` even when SQLcl never ran or exited non-zero, so a failed static-file deploy is indistinguishable from a successful one.

**Evidence:** Reproduced in the sandbox with a stand-in SQLcl that writes `ORA-01017: invalid username/password` to stderr and exits 1:

```
node -e "require('./index.js').publish({sqlclPath:'/tmp/failsql', connectString:'u/p@h:1/sid', directory:'./demo/demo-working/', appID:101})"
Uploading to 101 - Application Static Files...
Files were uploaded successfully.      <- exit status 1 ignored
returned: undefined
```

Same output with `sqlclPath: '/nonexistent/sql'` (spawn error). `spawnSync` never throws on a spawn failure or a non-zero exit: it returns `{error, status, stdout, stderr}` (index.js:74-79). The `try/catch` at index.js:71 / 83-85 therefore only catches programming errors, `childProcess.stderr` is never printed, and index.js:81-82 reports success unconditionally. The pre-fix implementation used `execSync`, which threw on a non-zero exit and returned `true`/`false`.

**Impact:** A deploy step that a CI job or build script calls unattended stays green when the upload failed — wrong credentials, unreachable database, SQL error, or a missing SQLcl binary — and the caller has no return value to check. Reach is one job and a re-run fixes it, so this is `low`.

**Fix:** Treat the result of `spawnSync` as the outcome: if `childProcess.error` is set or `childProcess.status !== 0`, print `childProcess.stderr` and throw (or return `false`, restoring the previous boolean contract); report success only on status 0.

summary:
I reviewed the full change and reproduced the key behavior.

**What the change does:** PR #2 adds `index.js` — the `publish()` entry point that validates options (`connectString`, `directory`, `appID`, `destination`, `pluginName`) and shells out to Oracle SQLcl via `execSync` to upload a directory into APEX.

**Assessment:** this is the vulnerable version of the file. Any option reaching the assembled command string can inject shell syntax — I reproduced it with `connectString`, `appID`, and `pluginName` (via `$(...)` inside double quotes) using the repo's own code, and one high-severity finding is recorded. The rest of the file is small and otherwise sound: the `lib/script` reference is not a bug because SQLcl appends the `.sql` extension, and the defaults/validation paths behave as documented. The same `execFileSync` fix also keeps the database password out of failure logs, so I did not file that separately.

findings.title: Any caller-supplied publish() option can inject shell commands
findings.body:
`publish()` builds a shell command by concatenating caller-supplied options, then runs it
through `execSync` (`index.js:53-66`). Any option that reaches an unescaped slot can
append shell syntax, so the shell runs attacker text alongside SQLcl. This is
CVE-2018-16462.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes a value it does not fully control — for example an
`appID` read from an APEX URL via `lib/util.js` `getAppID`, a `connectString` taken from
tool config or CLI input, or a `pluginName`/`destination` from a build script.

**Evidence:** `execSync` receives a single concatenated string (`index.js:54-66`), so the
shell parses it. `connectString` (`index.js:56`) and `appID` (`index.js:60`) are not even
quoted; `destination`/`pluginName` (`index.js:61-62`) are inside double quotes, which still
expand `$(...)`. Reproduced with the repository's own `index.js` and `sqlclPath: 'true'`:

```
publish({sqlclPath:'true', connectString:'u/p@h ; touch /tmp/pwn1', directory:'/tmp', appID:101})
publish({sqlclPath:'true', connectString:'c', directory:'/tmp', appID:'101; touch /tmp/pwn2'})
publish({sqlclPath:'true', connectString:'c', directory:'/tmp', appID:101, destination:'theme', pluginName:'x$(touch /tmp/pwn3)'})
```

All three runs created the marker files and still returned `true`, so the caller sees a
successful "upload".

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process that calls the
library, on every `publish()` call. The attacker's input crosses a trust boundary (data
value → OS capability) and the effect is permanent; severity `high`. The library gives no
escaping or validation layer, so every consumer that forwards untrusted values inherits it.

**Fix:** stop letting the shell parse the arguments. Pass them as an argv array to
`execFileSync(opts.sqlclPath, [opts.connectString, '@' + path.resolve(__dirname, 'lib/script'),
path.resolve(__dirname, 'lib/distUpload.js'), path.resolve(opts.directory), String(opts.appID),
String(opts.destination), String(opts.pluginName)], {encoding: 'utf8'})` so no option can be
reinterpreted as shell syntax.

summary:
Recorded. Final check of the change surface is complete.

**What the change does:** PR #1 re-adds `lib/dialects/mssql/index.js` (380 lines, the MSSQL client for knex 0.19.4) to a tree where that file had been removed. The file wires the driver, pool acquire/validate/destroy, binding positioning and response processing, and overrides identifier quoting for MSSQL.

**Assessment:** The re-added file reproduces the known pre-fix state of CVE-2019-10757. Its `wrapIdentifierImpl` performs an identity replace (`/\[/g → '['`), so `]` is never escaped; I confirmed with the repo's own client that identifiers such as `'a] from users --'` compile to `select [a] from users --] from [t]`, and with `multiple: true` stacked statements run too. That is recorded as a high-severity finding. The rest of the file matches upstream 0.19.4 behaviour (driver version gating, pool monkey patch, `_setReqInput` typing, `processResponse`), and the existing unit expectations for bracket-quoted output still hold, so I filed nothing else.

findings.title: MSSQL identifier wrapping leaves ] unescaped, allowing SQL injection via column and table names
findings.body:
MSSQL identifiers are wrapped as `[...]`, but the escaping step is a no-op:
`value.replace(/\[/g, '[')` replaces `[` with `[` (lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:210).
A `]` inside a caller-supplied identifier is passed through unescaped, closing the
bracket early. The rest of the string is then parsed as SQL. This is CVE-2019-10757
(fixed upstream in 0.19.5).

**Preconditions:** The application passes user-controlled text as an identifier —
a dynamic sort column (`orderBy(req.query.sort)`), a user-selected field, a dynamic
table name, or a `where` column name. Values in `where` bindings are parameterized
and are not affected.

**Evidence:** `positionBindings`/`_query` send the compiled SQL directly
(lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:286-307), so the injected text reaches SQL Server.
Running the repo's own client (deps installed in a temp dir, nothing in the repo
changed):

```
k.client.wrapIdentifierImpl('a]b')                        -> [a]b]        (correct: [a]]b])
k('t').select('a] from users --').toSQL().sql             -> select [a] from users --] from [t]
k('t').where('1] = 1 or 1=1 --','=','x').select('*')      -> select * from [t] where [1] = 1 or 1=1 --] = ?
k('t').orderBy('a] --').toSQL().sql                       -> select * from [t] order by [a] --] asc
k('t] ; select * from syslogins --').select('*')          -> select * from [t] ; select * from syslogins --]
k('t').insert({'a] ; select 1 --':'x'}).toSQL().sql       -> insert into [t] ([a] ; select 1 --]) values (?)
```

The identifier reaches this function from every identifier position: `formatter.wrap`
→ `wrapAsIdentifier` (lib/formatter.js:189-192) → `client.wrapIdentifier` →
`customWrapIdentifier` → `wrapIdentifierImpl` (lib/client.js:200-213), called from
`columnize` (lib/formatter.js:71-77), the select/insert/where/join/order-by compilers
(lib/query/compiler.js:202, :150, :655, :295, :833) and the schema compilers.
Sibling dialects escape their own enclosure character (mysql lib/dialects/mysql/index.js:56,
sqlite3 :59, postgres lib/dialects/postgres/index.js:90), which shows the invariant this
line violates. The upstream 0.19.5 fix strips the characters instead:
`value.replace(/[[\]']+/g, '')` (CHANGELOG 0.19.5, "#3382").

Because `req.multiple = true` (lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:294), stacked statements such
as `select * from syslogins` execute in the same batch, and the injected recordset is
what `processResponse` returns to the application (lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:304, :336-340).

**Impact:** SQL injection as the application's database user: read any table the user can
read, bypass `where` predicates, and run stacked DML/DDL. Reach crosses the trust boundary
(unprivileged caller → database contents), permanent where the injected statement writes or
drops data; high under the stated policy, with the app-usage precondition named above.

**Fix:** Escape the enclosure character by doubling it, as the other dialects do:
``value !== '*' ? `[${value.replace(/\]/g, ']]')}]` : '*'``, or adopt upstream's stricter
`value.replace(/[[\]']+/g, '')`. Add a unit test asserting
`wrapIdentifierImpl('a]b') === '[a]]b]'`, since no test currently covers `]` in an identifier.

summary:
Tests verified manually instead (ava hangs in this sandbox); every documented assertion in `test.js` produced the expected output.

**Summary:** This PR adds `index.js`, which is byte-identical to upstream decamelize 1.1.2 — the release that fixes CVE-2017-16023. It escapes the separator with `escape-string-regexp` before the second `RegExp` build, and I confirmed the ReDoS is gone: the same separator/input pair that took the pre-fix code 49 s runs in 1 ms, and all documented inputs (`_`, `' '`, `''`, uppercase-only) still produce the expected output. The fix itself is correct, but the packaging half of the change is missing: the new `require('escape-string-regexp')` is not declared in `package.json`, so an installed copy throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` (masked locally only because `xo`/`ava` hoist that module). Separately, the unescaped separator is still interpolated into the replacement pattern on line 14, so `$`-containing separators corrupt output.

findings.title: Package requires escape-string-regexp without declaring it, so consumers get MODULE_NOT_FOUND
findings.body:
Installing this package and calling it fails at require time with `Error: Cannot find module 'escape-string-regexp'`.

**Evidence:**

- `index.js:2` adds `var escapeStringRegexp = require('escape-string-regexp');`
- `package.json` declares no `dependencies` block at all — only `devDependencies` (`ava`, `xo`), and `files` is limited to `index.js`.
- Reproduced in a clean consumer tree (only `index.js` + `package.json` under `node_modules/decamelize`):

  ```
  $ node -e "require('decamelize')('aBc')"
  Error: Cannot find module 'escape-string-regexp'
  ```

- Upstream decamelize 1.1.2, the release that fixes CVE-2017-16023 with exactly this `index.js`, also adds `"dependencies": {"escape-string-regexp": "^1.0.4"}`. That package.json change is missing here.

The failure is masked locally: the repo's dev tree (`xo`, `ava`) happens to hoist `escape-string-regexp` into the top-level `node_modules`, so `npm test` passes while a real install of the published tarball breaks.

**Impact:** Every consumer of the published package crashes on first `require('decamelize')` — broad reach, recoverable by publishing a patch. Medium.

**Fix:** Declare the runtime dependency in `package.json` (`"dependencies": {"escape-string-regexp": "^1.0.4"}`), so `npm install` pulls it in for consumers rather than relying on dev-tree hoisting.

findings.title: Separator containing $ is expanded as a replacement pattern, dropping input characters
findings.body:
A separator containing `$` corrupts the output: characters from the input are dropped or replaced by match text.

**Evidence:** `index.js:14` interpolates the raw `sep` into the replacement string:

```js
return str.replace(/([a-z\d])([A-Z])/g, '$1' + sep + '$2')
```

`$` is special in a replacement pattern, so `sep` is not literal there — unlike `reSep` on `index.js:15`, which is escaped for exactly this reason. With `escape-string-regexp` installed:

```
decamelize('aBcD', '$')  === 'a$2c$2'   // expected 'a$bc$d'; B and D are lost
decamelize('aB',  '$&')  === 'aabb'     // expected 'a$&b'; whole match inserted
```

**Preconditions:** The caller passes a separator containing `$` such as `$&`, `$$`, or a `$`-prefixed token. Not attacker-controlled; a constant in caller code.

**Impact:** Contained to calls using such a separator, and a supported republish/retry recovers — low. The severity is capped because the module documents `separator` as an ordinary string and this only bites unusual values.

**Fix:** Keep the separator literal on both substitutions — escape `$` (e.g. `sep.replace(/\$/g, '$$$$')`) before concatenating into the replacement, or pass a replacer function that returns `p1 + sep + p2`.

summary:
Verified my suggested correction passes the existing test suite and blocks both routes. Summary:

**What the change does:** it re-adds `index.js`, the `mixin-deep` deep-merge implementation, with a guard that skips the `__proto__` key (`index.js:9`) — the upstream 2.0.1 response to CVE-2019-10746.

**Assessment:** the guard is correct but covers only one route to the prototype chain. A `constructor` key is still descended into (`mixin` reads the inherited `Object` function, which `isObject` accepts), so `constructor.prototype` pollution remains reachable with a plain JSON payload. I reproduced it and recorded one high finding, with an own-property check in `mixin()` as the smallest fix that also closes future inherited-name aliases. The rest of the file matches upstream behaviour and the existing tests still hold.

findings.title: Merge still reaches Object.prototype through the constructor key, polluting every object in the process
findings.body:
Merging an object that contains a `constructor` key still reaches `Object.prototype` and writes attacker-chosen properties onto it. The new `__proto__` guard at `index.js:9` only blocks one route to the prototype chain.

**Evidence:**
```js
const mixinDeep = require('./index.js');
mixinDeep({}, JSON.parse('{"constructor":{"prototype":{"polluted":"yes"}}}'));
console.log(({}).polluted); // => "yes"
```
Trace: `mixin(target, {prototype:{...}}, 'constructor')` (`index.js:18-24`) reads `target.constructor`, which is the inherited `Object` function. `isObject(Object)` is true for functions (`index.js:27-29`), and the incoming value is also an object, so it recurses into `mixinDeep(Object, {prototype:{...}})`. There `key === 'prototype'` passes the guard, `Object.prototype` exists and is an object, so `mixinDeep(Object.prototype, {polluted:'yes'})` assigns the property (`index.js:23`). The `__proto__` guard is never consulted on that path. The same call also permits overwriting `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, and other `Object.prototype` members.

**Impact:** any consumer that merges untrusted input (JSON bodies, config, query parsers) with this library gets process-wide `Object.prototype` pollution that survives for the life of the process — the exact class of bug CVE-2019-10746 covers. Every later object in that process, including other tenants' data, inherits the injected values. This is the threat model the guard is meant to close, and the guard is incomplete. High: the pollution crosses a trust boundary and is permanent for the process; it is bounded only by the consumer actually passing untrusted input, which is the assumption the CVE itself rests on.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — never write through a property the target only inherits. In `mixin()` (`index.js:19`), use an own-property check before recursing:
```js
let obj = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, key) ? target[key] : undefined;
```
so `constructor` and any other inherited member is assigned as an own property instead of being descended into. Alternatively extend the guard at `index.js:9` to skip `constructor` and `prototype` as well, but the own-property check also covers future inherited-name aliases.

summary:
Recorded three findings and they are all saved:

- `high` — `/render` accepts any URL scheme, so `file://` returns server files (mechanism reproduced against Chrome 131 with the same CDP calls the renderer makes; URL validation is absent by default in `src/main.js:65-74`).
- `medium` — `/screenshot?width=-1` (verified Chrome rejects the negative metric) throws outside `try` in an async promise executor, so the request never settles and the tab leaks.
- `low` — `src/renderer.js:188` concatenates the URL into a `Runtime.evaluate` string, so a quote breaks out into page-context script.

**Summary.** The PR restores `src/renderer.js`, the headless-Chrome rendering engine behind `/render/:url(*)` and `/screenshot/:url(*)`. The file is a faithful copy of the pre-fix upstream version, and it treats the caller's URL as trusted: it navigates to any scheme, builds JavaScript by concatenation from the URL, and cleans up the browser tab only on success. Since nothing else in the request path validates the scheme, the change makes the anonymous render endpoint a server-side file reader and SSRF proxy; the error paths additionally leak tabs and can hang requests.

**Not reached.** No end-to-end run of the app itself (dependency install stalled on an optional package, and a follow-up browser launch timed out), so the file-read finding is grounded in code plus a direct Chrome reproduction of the two CDP primitives, not in an HTTP request to a live rendertron. Uncovered surfaces for a next run: the 10-second timer and virtual-time-budget interaction (`src/renderer.js:112-153`) and whether `budgetExpired` can leave the promise unsettled or a timer alive; the `initialRequestId`/status-code attribution logic (`:78-101`); the `renderOnly` prefix allowlist in `src/main.js:65-74` and the `/node_modules` static mount at `src/main.js:59`; and the unauthenticated `/_ah/stop` endpoint.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read server files through /render via file:// URLs
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can make the renderer open any URL scheme, including `file://`, and the serialized document comes back in the HTTP response. That turns `GET /render/:url(*)` into a server-side file reader. **Evidence** - `src/renderer.js:75` passes the caller's URL straight to `Page.navigate({url: url})`. Nothing in `serialize` (`src/renderer.js:157-199`) or `_loadPage` (`src/renderer.js:22-155`) inspects the scheme. - `src/main.js:91-99` forwards `request.params.url` unchanged, and its only guard, `isRestricted` (`src/main.js:65-74`), returns `false` immediately when `config['renderOnly']` is unset. Default config is `{}` (`src/main.js:33`), and no `config.json`, middleware, or proxy in this repo restricts the scheme. - `src/renderer.js:190` reads `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` and `src/main.js:100` sends it as the response body. - Existing tests already render local files: `test/app-test.js:113-126` requests `/render/file://`. Reproduced with the same Chrome primitive the renderer uses (Chrome 131 via CDP): `Page.navigate` to `file:///etc/passwd`, then `Runtime.evaluate('document.firstElementChild.outerHTML')`, returns `…
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash…
`. **Impact** `GET /render/file:///etc/passwd` (or `/screenshot/file:///...`, or `file:///proc/self/environ`, `file:///app/config.json`) returns world-readable server files to an anonymous client. The same path is an SSRF primitive (`/render/http://169.254.169.254/…`, `/render/http://127.0.0.1:/…`), and Chrome is launched with `--remote-debugging-address=0.0.0.0` (`src/main.js:142`), so the DevTools port can be reached through it. Reach crosses a trust boundary (unauthenticated caller gains server data) with permanent disclosure, hence high. **Fix** Validate the scheme before navigating: accept only `http:`/`https:` (the upstream fix added exactly this check in `isRestricted`). Allowlists such as `renderOnly` are not a substitute when they are off by default.

findings.title: Screenshot with a negative width hangs the request forever and leaks a Chrome tab
findings.body:
A screenshot request with a negative `width` or `height` hangs the HTTP request
forever and leaks the Chrome tab it created. Any other rejection thrown before the
first `await` inside the promise executor (CDP setup, `Emulation.*`,
`Animation.setPlaybackRate`) fails the same way.

**Preconditions:** none beyond network access — no credentials, no config.

**Evidence**

- `src/renderer.js:212-215` computes `Math.min(2000, parseInt(options['width']) || 1000)`.
  `parseInt('-1')` is truthy, so a value of `-1` reaches
  `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` at line 214, outside the `try` at line 217.
  Chrome rejects it: `Protocol error (Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride): Screen
  width and height values must be positive` (reproduced against Chrome 131).
- The rejection happens inside `new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => …)`
  (`src/renderer.js:202`). Because the executor is an async function, its rejection
  is discarded and the outer promise never settles: `src/main.js:118` awaits it
  forever, so the client gets no response.
- The tab opened at `src/renderer.js:203` is closed only at line 221 on the success
  path, so it survives the failure.

The same shape applies to `serialize` (`src/renderer.js:178-185`) and `_loadPage`
(`src/renderer.js:43-52`): `CDP.New`, `CDP({tab})`, and the
`await Promise.all([...])` handshake are all outside any error handler.

**Impact**

Each `GET /screenshot/http://attacker/?width=-1` pins one connection and one Chrome
target until the process restarts; repeating it exhausts sockets, tabs and renderer
processes for every user of the service. The unhandled executor rejection also feeds
`main.js:165-181`, which kills Chrome and exits after five occurrences.

**Fix**

Give each request one teardown path: wrap the body in `try/catch/finally`, close the
CDP client and tab in `finally`, and reject the outer promise instead of using an
async promise executor. Reject `width`/`height` outside 1–2000 before touching CDP.

findings.title: Rendered URL is interpolated into a Runtime.evaluate string, so a quote in the URL executes script in the page
findings.body:
`serialize` builds a `Runtime.evaluate` expression by string-concatenating the
caller-supplied URL into a JavaScript string literal:

```js
await Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')`});
```

(`src/renderer.js:188`). Nothing escapes `url` first, so any `'` in the URL ends the
literal and the rest is parsed and executed as code in the rendered page's main
world. A URL such as
`http://x/');fetch('/admin').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>document.body.innerText=t)//`
is sent to Chrome verbatim; the trailing `//')` comments out the remainder of the
original call. The `stripPage` step at `src/renderer.js:187` has already removed the
page's own scripts, so this is the one script that still runs after load, in the
target page's origin and with its cookies and storage.

The benign case fails too: a plain apostrophe in a legitimate URL yields a
`SyntaxError`, `injectBaseHref` never runs, and the render returns HTML with no
`<base>` tag while still reporting success.

**Impact**

An anonymous caller can execute arbitrary script inside any page rendertron renders,
in that page's origin, and can reshape the DOM that is serialized back — for example
fetch a same-origin URL the plain render would not expose and copy it into
`document.body`. It also silently corrupts output for URLs containing quotes. The
capability is limited to one render context, so this is contained rather than broad.

**Fix**

Do not build code from data: pass the URL as an argument, e.g.
`Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})(...)`,
`arguments` via `Runtime.callFunctionOn`, or JSON-encode it with
`JSON.stringify(url)` before interpolation.

findings.title: Link decorator imports a module that does not exist, so the package cannot build or be tested
findings.body:
The new link decorator imports `ensureSafeUrl` from `../../utils/url`, but no such module exists anywhere in the tree. Babel rewrites the import to `require('../../utils/url')`, so loading the decorator throws `Cannot find module`. `src/Editor/index.js:30` imports the decorator, and `src/index.js` exports the Editor, so the package entry point cannot be bundled or imported.

**Preconditions:** None — the default build and test path both hit it.

**Evidence:**
- `src/decorators/Link/index.js:3` — `import { ensureSafeUrl } from '../../utils/url'`; used at lines 36 and 60.
- `src/utils/` holds only `BlockStyle.js`, `common.js`, `handlePaste.js`, `toolbar.js`. `git ls-files | grep -i url` returns nothing: the file is not tracked, was not added by this PR, and no other module exports `ensureSafeUrl` (repo-wide grep finds the symbol only in this one file).
- Resolution check from the repo root: `node -e "require.resolve('./src/utils/url')"` → `MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module './src/utils/url'`.
- Consumers of the broken path: `src/Editor/index.js:30` (`import getLinkDecorator from '../decorators/Link'`), webpack entry `./src/index` (`config/webpack.config.js:10`, no aliases), and the test glob `src/**/*Test.js` (`package.json:74`), which matches `src/decorators/Link/__test__/linkDecoratorTest.js` — that test imports the decorator, so it fails at import time before any assertion runs.
- Upstream fix commit `f71fb3ca96f4` ("Fix XSS in Link Target") added `src/utils/url.js` alongside this change to `src/decorators/Link/index.js`; only the second half is present here.

**Impact:** Every build from source fails (`Module not found: Can't resolve '../../utils/url'`) and `npm test` aborts before running any test. Reach is broad — the whole library is unusable to anyone building or linking it — and permanent until the file is added, so `high`.

**Fix:** Add `src/utils/url.js` exporting `ensureSafeUrl(url)`, which strips control/whitespace characters and returns `'#'` for any scheme outside `http`, `https`, `ftp`, `ftps`, `mailto` (the upstream fix's version). Keeping the import without the module leaves the library unbuildable and the XSS fix inert.

findings.title: Links opened in a new tab keep a live window.opener handle to the editor page
findings.body: The decorator renders `` and does not set `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. When the link was created with `targetOption: '_blank'` (a supported value, see `docs/src/components/Docs/Props/CustomizingToolbarProp/index.js:155`), the opened page gets a `window.opener` handle to the editor page and can navigate it, e.g. to a phishing page that looks like the host app. **Evidence:** `src/decorators/Link/index.js:60` — `{children}`. `targetOption` is editor-supplied: `src/controls/Link/index.js:161` stores `targetOption: linkTargetOption` in the LINK entity data, and `src/controls/Link/Component/index.js:80` defaults it. The anchor is the only place this attribute is emitted. **Impact:** `low`. The same-origin script constraint doesn't apply to the opened document rewriting `opener.location`, so the effect is a silent redirect of the reader to attacker content — recoverable (close the tab), contained to the reader who clicks. Discounts against a higher grade: current browsers (Chrome 88+, Firefox 79+, Safari 16.4+) implicitly apply `noopener` to `target="_blank"`, and the link author is already trusted to choose the destination. Modern-browser default bounds the damage; older engines and embedded webviews do not. **Fix:** emit `rel="noopener noreferrer"` when `targetOption === '_blank'`, and give the hover handler at line 36 the same treatment (it already only accepts a sanitized URL).

summary:
Finding recorded. Close-out:

**Summary** — PR #2 re-adds `index.js`, the 10-line `decamelize` implementation (v1.1.1) that turns `unicornRainbow` into `unicorn_rainbow`. The implementation matches upstream v1.1.1 and passes all seven assertions in `test.js`, but it is exactly the version carrying CVE-2017-16023: the separator is concatenated unescaped into `new RegExp(...)` at `index.js:8` (and into the replacement string at lines 7–8). I reproduced all three consequences — exponential backtracking (a 19-character input with `sep='(.*)*(.*)'` did not return in 120 s), uncaught `SyntaxError` for separators like `(`, and silent wrong output for separators like `.` — and an independent investigator confirmed them with CPU-time measurements. One finding, `medium`, filed against `index.js:8`; upstream's fix (v1.1.2) escapes the separator through `escape-string-regexp`.

**Not reached / for the next run** — no downstream consumer of this library exists in the tree, so the "caller forwards an untrusted separator" precondition is stated rather than demonstrated at a concrete call site; the repo's test corpus (`test.js`) covers no separator-metacharacter or adversarial-input cases, so nothing in CI would flag this; and I did not audit the baseline commit's removed history for other deliberate regressions beyond `index.js`.

findings.title: Unescaped separator is injected into the RegExp constructor, so a call with an attacker-influenced separator can hang or crash the process
findings.body:
`index.js:8` builds a regular expression by concatenating the `sep` argument directly into the pattern: `new RegExp('(' + sep + '[A-Z])([A-Z])', 'g')`. Nothing escapes `sep` (line 6 only defaults it; line 3 type-checks `str`, not `sep`). Any caller that forwards a user-influenced separator therefore hands control of the pattern to the attacker.

**Preconditions:** a caller passes a `sep` derived from untrusted input (a user-configurable separator, or a value taken from a request and forwarded as the separator). The default `'_'` path is not affected.

**Evidence:** measured with `node` against this tree.
- ReDoS: `decamelize('a'.repeat(n) + 'BB', '(a+)+')` — pattern `((a+)+[A-Z])([A-Z])`. Wall time grows exponentially: n=22 → 154 ms, n=26 → 2.2 s, n=28 → 28.8 s, n=30 → killed after 20 s.
- No control of `str` needed: with the readme's own example `decamelize('unicornsAndRainbows', '(.*)*(.*)')` the call did not return within 120 s. `'(.*)+'` and `'(.*){1,}'` behave the same, because the separator is inserted literally into the subject by the first `replace` at line 7, so the tail after the nested quantifier always fails to match.
- Uncaught crash: `sep` values `(`, `)`, `*`, `+`, `?`, `{1,}` make the `RegExp` constructor throw `SyntaxError` synchronously out of the module (e.g. `/ ((*)[A-Z])([A-Z])/g: Nothing to repeat`).
- Silent wrong output: `sep='.'` gives `decamelize('HTMLParser','.')` → `ht.mlparser` instead of `htmlparser`; `sep='['` gives `thisIsATest` → `this[[is[[atest`; `sep='$&'`/`'$1'` are also corrupted via the replacement string at lines 7–8.
- Input-only control (default `sep`) is linear (~0.16 µs/char, 4M chars ≈ 0.6 s CPU), so the attack needs `sep`, not `str`.
This is CVE-2017-16023 (CWE-400/CWE-20; NVD CVSS 3.0 AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/A:H = 7.5). Upstream 1.1.2 wraps the separator in `escape-string-regexp` before use — the fix this file lacks.

**Impact:** an unprivileged remote actor who can influence the separator stalls the Node process on a 19-character input (event loop blocked, every other request on the service waits) or crashes the request with an uncaught `SyntaxError`. Availability only; no data exposure. Severity is `medium`: reach is broad for a consumer that forwards an untrusted separator (all of that service's users), persistence is recoverable (restart or timeout, nothing lost); consumers that pass only constant separators are unaffected.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that `sep` is data, not pattern. Escape it before both regexp construction and replacement, e.g. `const reSep = escapeStringRegexp(sep);` and use `reSep` in the `RegExp` and in the `'$1' + reSep + '$2'` replacement at lines 7–8 (the same change also fixes the `$&`/`$1` corruption).

summary:
Recorded one low finding. Summary:

The change adds `index.js`, which is byte-identical to the upstream `mixin-deep` 2.0.1 release: the CVE-2019-10746 fix that deep-recurses through `mixinDeep`/`mixin` while skipping the keys `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` (`index.js:7-9`, `index.js:15`). I reproduced the published attack payloads (own-enumerable `__proto__`, `constructor.prototype`, nested and two-stage merges, `Object.create(null)` sources, alternate spellings) and none of them pollute a prototype; the existing `test.js` suite also passes unchanged.

The fix is therefore correct for the vulnerability it targets. What it does not cover is a merge target inherited from a built-in: allowed key names such as `toString` or `valueOf` resolve to shared function objects, and the merge writes into them process-wide. That is recorded as a single low finding, along with the `TypeError` it raises on some of those same keys — one fix addresses both.

I reviewed the full diff (one new file, 95 lines) and traced how `redirect` reaches it from `src/layouts/SecurityLayout.tsx:41-49` and `src/pages/user/login/index.tsx:45-55`.

**One finding recorded:** the `else` branch at `src/models/login.ts:56` assigns the raw `redirect` query parameter to `window.location.href` after a successful login. A `javascript:` payload (origin `"null"`, so it fails the same-origin check) executes in the site origin; an external `https://` URL becomes an open redirect. Upstream fixed this exact line to `window.location.href = '/'` (PR #5461, v4.2.0) — this PR re-adds the pre-fix version, matching CVE-2019-18350.

I also checked the other new code paths and found nothing worth reporting: the same-origin `substr` handling has no cross-origin bypass, the `getCaptcha` effect's ignored return value does not break the countdown (`LoginItem.tsx:73-84` starts it regardless), and `changeLoginStatus` matches the existing template pattern. Beyond the one issue, the file is a straight restore of the upstream model and builds on the existing `connect.d.ts` type expectations.

findings.title: Login redirects to attacker-chosen URL, allowing javascript: XSS and open redirect
findings.body:
The login effect sends the `redirect` query-string value to `window.location.href`
without validating its scheme or host. A crafted link to
`/user/login?redirect=javascript:alert(document.cookie)` runs attacker JavaScript in
the site's origin once the victim logs in; `...?redirect=https://attacker.example`
sends the freshly authenticated user to an attacker site (open redirect / phishing).

**Preconditions:** The victim follows the crafted login URL and then submits valid
credentials, because the branch only runs when `response.status === 'ok'`
(`src/models/login.ts:44`).

**Evidence:** `src/models/login.ts:48-58` parses `redirect` with `new URL(redirect)`
and only accepts it when `redirectUrlParams.origin === urlParams.origin`. Every
non-same-origin value falls into the `else` at line 55, which assigns the raw value:
`window.location.href = redirect` (`src/models/login.ts:56`). Node confirms the parse
used by that check:

    new URL('javascript:alert(document.cookie)').origin  // "null"  -> mismatch
    new URL('https://attacker.example/x').origin         // "https://attacker.example" -> mismatch

Both mismatch the site origin, so both reach the assignment. A `javascript:` URL
assigned to `location.href` executes in the page context, which can read
`localStorage['antd-pro-authority']` (set at `src/utils/authority.ts:31`) and call the
app's APIs as the logged-in user. Upstream fixed exactly this line to
`window.location.href = '/'` in ant-design-pro PR #5461 / v4.2.0; this diff re-adds
the pre-fix version.

**Impact:** Script from an attacker-chosen origin runs inside the application's origin
for any user who completes login from the crafted link, and authenticated sessions can
also be bounced to an arbitrary external site. It crosses a trust boundary but clears
once the page navigates, so medium.

**Fix:** Never navigate to a cross-origin `redirect`. Restore the same-origin invariant
by dropping the value instead of using it, e.g. `window.location.href = '/'` in the
`else` branch (upstream's fix), or restrict `redirectUrlParams.protocol` to `http:`
and `https:` before any assignment.

summary:
I reviewed the whole change, compared it against upstream history, and exercised it.

## What I did

- **Diff/graph**: PR #1 adds one file, `index.js` (163 lines), to a tree whose baseline removed that file. The content is **byte-identical** to upstream commit `d4a93bc` ("prevent prototype pollution", the CVE-2018-3752 fix, released as merge-options 1.0.1) — I fetched upstream and diffed (`diff fix-index.js index.js` → identical).
- **Verified the pollution fix instead of assuming it**: the fix's two mechanisms are `Object.defineProperty` for every write (`index.js:7`, so a `__proto__` key becomes an own *data* property, never a `[[Set]]`) and the prototype guard in `mergeKeys` (`index.js:79`: `key in merged && merged[key] !== Object.getPrototypeOf(merged)`).
- **Reproduced the attack surface**: fed `{"__proto__":{"p":1}}`, nested and doubly-nested variants, `{"constructor":{"prototype":…}}`, array-element `__proto__` payloads (both with and without `concatArrays`), and `mergeOptions.call(maliciousConfig, …)`. `Object.prototype` stayed clean in every case, and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` did not grow. Inputs were not mutated.
- **Ran the suite**: existing `test/*.js` plus upstream's `test/prototype-pollution.js` (the PoC by HoLyVieR, the array regression, and the recursive-merge regression), using a minimal local ava shim since the pinned ava 0.25 dev deps don't install on Node 24. All real assertions pass; the only two failures were shim artifacts (`await t.throws(promise)` semantics), and I confirmed those inputs throw `TypeError` directly.
- **Checked edge behavior**: `Object.create(null)` options, symbol keys (`index.js:25` — `Object.propertyIsEnumerable` resolves via `Object.prototype`, so it works), sparse arrays, `call`/`apply` config, `undefined` options, and non-plain argument rejection all behave as the readme documents.

Noted but not filed: results can carry an own `__proto__` data property when input contains that key, so a consumer doing `Object.assign(dst, result)` will change `dst`'s prototype. That is upstream's behavior through 3.0.4, is confined to an object the caller chooses, and never touches `Object.prototype` — below the reporting bar.

## Summary

The PR restores `index.js` as merge-options 1.0.1, the official fix for CVE-2018-3752: writes now go through `Object.defineProperty` and `mergeKeys` refuses to recurse into a key whose value is the merged object's own prototype, so `__proto__` and `constructor.prototype` payloads land as inert own properties. I confirmed no global prototype pollution on any payload, and the existing test suite plus upstream's prototype-pollution regression tests pass. One gap worth mentioning, though it is not a code defect: the companion `test/prototype-pollution.js` from the upstream fix commit is not included, so the regression is not guarded in-tree. Overall: approve, no findings recorded.

**Review complete — no findings recorded.**

What the change does: adds `slug.js`, the released 0.9.x implementation of the `slug` package (212 lines, mostly charmap data), into a baseline tree that shipped without the file.

The CVE this repo is named for (CVE-2017-16117, ReDoS in `slug()`) is **not present**. It requires a whitespace run bordered by non-space text, where `replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, '')` backtracks per start position; I reproduced it against 0.9.1 (`'a' + ' '*40000 + 'a'` → 5.1 s) and confirmed the added revision uses `String.prototype.trim()` (`slug.js:57`, `slug.js:64`) and runs the same input in 37 ms, scaling linearly to 400 k chars (≈335 ms). A 3000-sample fuzz with lone surrogates, astral symbols and mixed whitespace threw nothing, and the file is byte-identical to the npm `slug@0.9.2` release. Residual quirks I verified but judged out of scope to file (emoji/astral symbols are dropped because of UTF-16-unit indexing at `slug.js:50`; `result.replace(opts.replacement + "$", '')` at `slug.js:66` is a literal search that never matches, so the trailing separator survives; unvalidated `opts.mode` throws) are all upstream behaviour that existed before and is unchanged by this fix, and none is reachable from untrusted input alone on a default configuration.

**Assessment:** the change is a correct, complete fix for the CVE; approve.

Recorded the confirmed issue. Final summary:

**What the change does:** re-adds `slug.js` (212 lines), the full node-slug 0.9.1 implementation, as a new file; the diff contains no other code.

**Assessment:** the library's core behavior matches its test expectations (verified manually for ASCII, charmap, multicharmap, symbol and mode cases), and the options/module-system plumbing is straightforward. The blocking problem is the `result.replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, '')` trim at `slug.js:64`: I reproduced quadratic time growth through the public API (`slug('a' + ' '.repeat(N) + 'a')` → 130 ms / 1.5 s / 18 s for N = 5k / 20k / 80k), which a single unauthenticated request can use to stall a Node service. Replacing that line with `.trim()` flattens the cost. I also confirmed the same regex at `slug.js:57` is the same defect but not reachable with long input; other leads (astral-character loss, options mutation, trailing-separator dead code) are low-impact behavior inherited from the upstream 0.9.1 release and I did not file them.

findings.title: slug() runs in quadratic time on whitespace runs, so untrusted input stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`slug()` blocks the Node event loop for seconds to minutes on a string that
contains a run of whitespace between non-whitespace characters. The caller cannot
bound it: cost grows quadratically with the length of the whitespace run, so any
service that slugifies a user-supplied title, filename or comment can be stalled by
one request. This is CVE-2017-16117.

**Evidence:**

`result.replace(/^\s+|\s+$/g, '')` at slug.js:64 retries the pattern at every
index. Inside a whitespace run that is not at the start of the string, the `\s+`
alternative consumes the rest of the run, then backtracks one character at a time
testing `$`, which fails every time; every interior index repeats that work, so a
run of length n costs O(n²). The `^` alternative only rescues a run at index 0, and
a run at the end succeeds on the first attempt, so the payload must be
`non-white + whitespace run + non-white`.

Reproduced with `node` (slug.js required directly, unicode table installed):

```
slug('a' + ' '.repeat(5000)  + 'a')  ->  ~130 ms
slug('a' + ' '.repeat(20000) + 'a')  ->  ~1.5 s
slug('a' + ' '.repeat(80000) + 'a')  ->  ~18 s   (cold: ~78 s)
```

Doubling the run multiplies the time by ~3.5–3.8. Controls stay linear:
`'a'.repeat(80000)` ~16 ms, `' '.repeat(80000)` ~14 ms, `' '.repeat(80000)+'a'` ~12 ms.
Tabs and newlines behave the same as spaces. Both modes are affected, as are the
`{symbols:false}`, AMD and script-tag paths; nothing before slug.js:64 truncates the
input, and line 60's allow-list `/[^\w\s\-\.\_~]/g` deliberately keeps `\s`.

Replacing only line 64 with `result.trim()` drops the same 80,000-character payload
from ~18 s to ~60 ms; the same regex at slug.js:57 is not reachable with long input
because there `char` is a unicode symbol name (slug.js:53) at most 88 characters
long.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated user who controls a string passed to `slug()` can
occupy the process for an attacker-chosen duration, and can repeat it at will, so
the stall is not self-limiting: requests queue behind the blocked regex and the
service stops answering for everyone it serves. Single-threaded JS runtimes have no
regex timeout, so the worker is lost until the match finishes. Severity is high:
the trigger crosses a trust boundary (untrusted input), the damage reaches every
client of the calling service, and the attacker can retrigger it indefinitely.

**Fix:** Do not match an anchored whitespace pattern per index; trim once.
Replace slug.js:64 with `result = result.trim();`. For parity with the upstream fix
(commit 791b7d8 in Trott/node-slug), replace slug.js:57 with `char = char.trim();`
as well — same defect, currently not reachable with long input. Both replacements
preserve output on the existing test suite.

summary:
Both findings are recorded. Summary:

This PR adds `lib/extract.js` (36 lines), the streaming extractor that pipes each archive entry into an `fstream` Writer under `opts.path`, with an inline attempt at blocking zip-slip. That guard compares normalized paths as a raw string prefix, so it only stops naive `../` traversal: an entry named `../<dest>-suffix/...` still escapes into a sibling directory, which I reproduced writing `/tmp/ziptr/dest-evil/pwned.txt` outside a `/tmp/ziptr/dest` extraction root. Secondary problems follow from the same handler: rejected entries are never drained, so a large skipped entry stalls the parser and `close` never fires, and `close` itself is emitted on parse completion rather than after writes flush (masked in the existing tests by async `dirdiff` timing).

findings.title: Zip-slip check uses a string prefix, so ../<dest>-suffix entries still write outside the destination
findings.body:
The containment check compares strings, not path components. An archive entry
named `../<dest>-anything/file` normalizes to a sibling directory whose path
starts with the destination string, so it passes the check and is written
outside the destination.

Reproduced against this commit: extracting an archive containing
`../dest-evil/pwned.txt` with `Extract({path: '/tmp/ziptr/dest'})` creates
`/tmp/ziptr/dest-evil/pwned.txt` containing the entry's bytes, while the
destination stays empty. `fstream`'s Writer creates the missing directory, so
the attacker needs no pre-existing sibling — only a destination path whose
parent is writable, which is the normal deployment case.

**Evidence:**
- `lib/extract.js:24` joins the untrusted entry name onto the destination.
- `lib/extract.js:25` accepts any result that starts with `opts.path` as a
  literal string, so `/tmp/out-evil` passes for `opts.path = "/tmp/out"`.
- Contrast: `../../etc/passwd` and `../outside/x.txt` are rejected, so only the
  prefix-sharing shape escapes. That is trivially attacker-controlled:
  `path.join('/app/www', '../www-evil/x')` → `/app/www-evil/x`.

**Impact:**
Arbitrary file write outside the extraction root under the process's
permissions — overwriting application code, config, or `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`
— from a hostile archive. This crosses a trust boundary and the write is
permanent, so severity is high (no repo policy raises it to critical).

**Fix:**
Resolve both sides and compare component-wise: reject when
`path.relative(path.resolve(opts.path), path.resolve(opts.path, entry.path))`
is absolute or begins with `..`. Comparing `path.resolve(opts.path) + path.sep`
as a prefix is the minimum change. Resolving `opts.path` also fixes the
related false negative where `opts.path = './out'` makes every entry
(`path.join('./out','f')` → `out/f`) fail the check and extraction silently
writes nothing.

findings.title: Rejected entries are never drained, so one large skipped entry stalls extraction
findings.body:
When an entry is rejected (or is a directory), it is returned from without
being consumed. The entry is a `PassThrough` fed by the parse stream, so a
rejected entry larger than the stream's high-water mark is never drained and
the whole parser stalls under backpressure: later entries are not extracted and
`close` never fires, so callers awaiting completion hang.

**Evidence:**
- `lib/extract.js:26` returns without draining `entry`.
- `lib/parse.js:213-216` pipes the inflater into `entry`; `entry` is readable
  and only flows if someone reads it.
- `entry.autodrain()` already exists for this purpose (`lib/parse.js:78-84`).
- Reproduction: an archive holding a 5 MB entry named `../outside/big.bin`
  followed by `good2.txt`; with `Extract({path: '/tmp/ziptr/bdest'})` neither
  file is written and no `close` is emitted after 3 s. The same archive with a
  small rejected entry completes, so it is a size-dependent stall.

**Impact:**
A single hostile or malformed archive permanently hangs an extraction job and
whatever waits on `close` (bounded memory, no completion, no error). Effect is
contained to the job and clears only by restart, so severity is low.

**Fix:**
Drain rejected entries instead of returning silently: call `entry.autodrain()`
before rejecting (and for `Directory` entries) so the parse stream keeps
flowing, and surface the rejection via `self.emit('error', ...)` if the caller
should learn about it.

**What the change does.** The PR re-adds `src/models/login.ts`. Since the baseline tree is ant-design-pro at `0ad1fb31` with that file removed, the substantive change is one line in the cross-origin branch of the `login` effect: `window.location.href = redirect` (`src/models/login.ts:56`) becomes `window.location.href = '/'`. Recorded the core finding. Coverage check complete: the other hypotheses (writer-error stall, directory-entry autodrain) I tested/assessed and found either refuted or requiring malformed archives, and the `'close'`-before-flush behavior originates in unchanged `lib/parse.js`.

## Summary

PR #2 adds `lib/extract.js`, restoring the `Extract` implementation that `unzip.js:10` already required: it subscribes to parsed entries and pipes each file into an `fstream.Writer` at `path.join(opts.path, entry.path)`.

The design is unsound because `entry.path` comes verbatim from the archive and is joined without any containment check. I reproduced a zip entry named `../escaped.txt` writing one level above the destination, and overwriting arbitrary files outside the tree is equally straightforward. I recorded this as a high-severity path-traversal finding. Apart from that, the 27-line file is straightforward and the extraction behavior for normal archives works as the existing tests expect.

findings.title: Untrusted zip entry names with ../ can write files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
Extracting an archive whose entry name contains `..` writes files outside the
destination directory, and overwrites existing ones. `entry.path` is the raw
name from the zip local file header (`lib/parse.js:78`, `lib/parse.js:93`), and
`path.join` normalises the traversal away instead of rejecting it
(`lib/extract.js:21`). A caller who extracts an untrusted archive with
`unzipper.Extract({ path: dest })` gives the archive's author write access to
any path the process can write.

**Preconditions:** the caller extracts an attacker-supplied archive; no other
condition (relative or absolute `opts.path` both work).

**Evidence:** a zip with one entry named `../escaped.txt`, fed to
`fs.createReadStream(zip).pipe(Extract({path:'dest/inner'}))`, creates
`dest/escaped.txt` with no `error` event. Deeper names such as
`../../../../home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys` overwrite files outside the tree.
The write path is resolved only by `path.resolve` in fstream
(`node_modules/fstream/lib/writer.js:73`), which does no containment check.

**Impact:** arbitrary file creation and overwrite under the extracting process's
privileges (e.g. `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, shell rc files, application config).
Reach crosses a trust boundary (attacker-controlled data to victim filesystem)
and the damage is permanent, so `high`.

**Fix:** resolve the target and reject entries that escape the destination, e.g.
compute `var target = path.resolve(opts.path, entry.path)` and require
`target === root || target.indexOf(root + path.sep) === 0` (with
`root = path.resolve(opts.path)`), emitting an error or skipping otherwise.

PR #2 re-adds `index.js`, the whole of `merge-options@1.0.0`: a deep-merge/clone of "option objects" with optional array concatenation. It byte-matches the published 1.0.0 tarball, i.e. the version before the CVE-2018-3752 fix, and the pollution reproduces on the first try — a JSON-parsed `__proto__` key writes into the global `Object.prototype` because `mergeKeys` treats the inherited `__proto__` accessor as an existing key and then recurses into `Object.prototype` itself. The reproduction is recorded as one high finding at index.js:72, with the same root cause also explaining merges that mutate pre-existing inherited objects; the minimal fix is `Object.defineProperty` writes plus a prototype-chain guard, as in 1.0.1.

Beyond that I probed the rest of the file (config resolution, `concatArrays` semantics, clone/alias behavior, symbol keys, cross-realm and hostile inputs) and the repo's 26 ava tests pass against this code. Remaining issues found are cosmetic or need non-default settings (sparse-array compaction under `concatArrays`, quadratic concat for very large arrays, error-message stringification), so I did not file them; overall the change should be blocked on the prototype-pollution fix.

findings.title: Attacker-supplied `__proto__` key pollutes the process-wide `Object.prototype`
findings.body:
`index.js` adds a deep-merge library that writes attacker-supplied keys straight onto objects reached through the prototype chain. A single option object parsed from JSON whose own key is `__proto__` writes into the process-wide `Object.prototype`.

**Preconditions:** the option object must contain an own, enumerable string key `__proto__` with a plain-object value. `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}')` produces exactly that; a JS object literal `{__proto__: ...}` does not (it sets the prototype instead and then fails `isOptionObject`). No other condition: a top-level payload as any argument suffices, and a nested payload (`{"a":{"__proto__":{"x":1}}}`) works whenever an earlier argument already has `a`.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "const m=require('./'); m(JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\":{\"polluted\":\"yes\"}}'));
           console.log(({}).polluted, Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'))"
yes true
```

Path: `getEnumerableOwnPropertyKeys` (index.js:12-19) collects the own `__proto__` key via `for...in` + `hasOwnProperty`. `mergeKeys` (index.js:72-73) tests `key in merged`, which is true for `__proto__` on any ordinary object through the inherited accessor, so `merged[key]` reads `Object.prototype` itself, and `merge` (index.js:129) sees `isOptionObject(Object.prototype) === true` and does not bail out to `clone`. Line 73 then assigns through the `__proto__` setter's target, i.e. `Object.prototype.polluted = "yes"` — a plain, enumerable write on the global prototype. The merge target is a bare `{}` (index.js:138), so every call has that prototype.

The same `key in merged` test also merges *into* any pre-existing enumerable object found on a prototype instead of shadowing it: with `Object.prototype.zz = {a:1}`, `m({zz: {b:2}})` mutates the shared `Object.prototype.zz` and the result's `zz` is that same object. One fix covers both.

Overwriting inherited members is reachable with the same payload, e.g. `{"__proto__":{"hasOwnProperty":"gone"}}` makes `({}).hasOwnProperty('x')` throw a TypeError.

**Impact:** any program that merges attacker-influenced JSON — CLI/config options, request bodies, plugin settings — has its global `Object.prototype` extended or its inherited members replaced, silently and without an error; the returned value looks like an ordinary `{}`. Every object in the process then sees the injected property, so a trust boundary is crossed for the whole process and the change lasts until restart. Rated `high`: broad reach across everything the process serves, permanent for the process lifetime, no supported undo.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — a merge must never target an object it did not create. Write keys with `Object.defineProperty(..., {value, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true})` instead of assignment (index.js:50, :60, :73, :75), so `__proto__` becomes an own data property rather than a prototype write; and skip prototype-chain targets in `mergeKeys`, e.g. `if (key in merged && merged[key] !== Object.getPrototypeOf(merged))`. Upstream `merge-options@1.0.1` (`CVE-2018-3752`) applies both changes, plus a wrapper object for the merge root.

summary:
Recorded both confirmed escapes. Coverage summary:

The change re-adds `lib/unpack.js` at the node-tar 4.4.1 state — the whole extraction engine (`Unpack` async plus `UnpackSync`), including path checking, entry-type dispatch, and the `dirCache`-backed `mkdir`.

What I verified directly against this tree (deps installed, PoCs run for async and sync):
- A `Link` entry with an escaping or absolute `linkpath` creates a hardlink to a file outside `cwd`, and the following `File` entry of the same name reuses that inode and truncates it — reproduced, and blocked by the 4.4.2 `st.nlink <= 1` reuse condition.
- A `Directory` entry replaced by a `SymbolicLink` of the same path leaves a stale `dirCache` entry, so the next file entry skips the symlink guard in `mkdir` and is written outside `cwd` — reproduced without any non-default option.

Other reviewed areas (path/`..`/absolute stripping, `strip`, win32 encoding, entry-type switch, futimes/fchown fallbacks, error and pend accounting) showed no reachable failure I could demonstrate; the existing `test/unpack.js` failures are tap-11-on-node-24 runner errors, not behaviour regressions.

Assessment: the file adds a working extractor but brings two ways for an untrusted archive to write outside the extraction directory. Both are high severity and both need fixing before merge.

findings.title: Stale dirCache lets a symlink entry redirect later entries outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A `Directory` entry followed by a `SymbolicLink` entry with the same path leaves the
stale directory in `dirCache`. Later entries whose parent is that path skip the
symlink check in `mkdir` and are written through the symlink, outside `cwd`.

**Preconditions:** the attacker controls the archive; extraction uses default options
(no `preservePaths`, no `unlink`).

**Evidence:** `[CHECKFS]` (`lib/unpack.js:360`) sees the cached directory, and for a
non-directory entry calls `fs.rmdir` (`lib/unpack.js:372`) and then creates the symlink,
but `this.dirCache` (`lib/unpack.js:62`, passed to every `[MKDIR]` at
`lib/unpack.js:222`) still records that path as a created directory. `mkdir` returns
early on a cache hit (`lib/mkdir.js:68`, and `lib/mkdir.js:91` / sync at
`lib/mkdir.js:178` for intermediate parts) without ever calling `fs.lstat`, so the
`SymlinkError` guard at `lib/mkdir.js:113`/`:200` never runs and `[FILE]` opens
`cwd/a/x`, which the kernel resolves through the symlink.

Reproduced against this tree:

    entries = [ {path:'a', type:'Directory'},
                {path:'a', type:'SymbolicLink', linkpath:'/tmp/outside'},
                {path:'a/x', type:'File', size:6}, 'OWNED\n' ]
    new Unpack({cwd:'/tmp/extract'}).end(makeTar(entries))
    // -> /tmp/outside/x created with "OWNED"; no warning

The same input works through `Unpack.Sync`. Upstream later added `[PRUNECACHE]`, with a
comment stating that a symlink to a directory "can evade detection and lead to arbitrary
writes to anywhere on the system".
