**Impact:** An archive writes new files anywhere the extracting user can write, with
attacker-chosen contents. Attacker input crosses a trust boundary and the write is
permanent, so this is `high`.

**Fix:** Never trust `dirCache` for a path whose type changed during extraction. When an
entry replaces a cached directory (in particular any `SymbolicLink`), drop that path and
its descendants from `dirCache`, or drop the whole cache on a symlink entry, so the next
`mkdir` re-validates the real filesystem. Apply to both `Unpack` and `UnpackSync`.

findings.title: Hardlink entries can target files outside the extraction directory and overwrite them
findings.body:
Extracting an archive can overwrite any file the extracting user can write, outside the
extraction directory. A `Link` (hardlink) entry whose `linkpath` points outside `cwd` is
created without any check, and a following `File` entry with the same path then reuses
that inode and truncates it.

**Preconditions:** none beyond extracting an attacker-supplied archive with default
options (`unlink` false, `preservePaths` false).

**Evidence:** `lib/unpack.js:337` resolves the link target as
`path.resolve(this.cwd, entry.linkpath)` and never checks that the result stays inside
`cwd` — unlike `entry.path`, which is validated in `[CHECKPATH]` (`lib/unpack.js:143`).
`[CHECKFS]` (`lib/unpack.js:363`) then treats any existing regular file as reusable
(`entry.type === 'File' && !this.unlink && st.isFile()`), ignoring `st.nlink`, so
`[FILE]` opens the hardlinked inode with `'w'` (`lib/unpack.js:250`, sync path
`lib/unpack.js:459`) and writes through it.

Reproduced against this tree with `test/make-tar.js`:

    // /tmp/victim/v.txt contains "SECRET"
    entries = [ {path:'pwn', type:'Link', linkpath:'../victim/v.txt'},
                {path:'pwn', type:'File', size:6}, 'OWNED\n' ]
    new Unpack({cwd: '/tmp/extract'}).end(makeTar(entries))
    // -> /tmp/victim/v.txt now contains "OWNED"

The same happens with an absolute `linkpath` and in `Unpack.Sync`. No warning is
emitted. Replacing the `unpack.js` in `lib/` with the 4.4.2 file (which only adds the
`st.nlink <= 1` reuse condition) keeps the victim file intact, confirming the reuse is
what turns the escaping hardlink into an overwrite.

**Impact:** A malicious archive overwrites arbitrary files writable by the extracting
process, with contents the attacker chose. The attacker crosses a trust boundary (the
archive is untrusted input, the target file is outside the extraction directory) and the
damage is permanent, so this is `high`.

**Fix:** Restore one invariant — an extraction never writes outside `cwd`. Reject a
`Link` entry whose resolved `linkpath` is not inside `cwd` (same `..`/absolute check
used for `entry.path`, and apply it to `entry.linkpath`), and in `[ISREUSABLE]` only
reuse an existing file when `st.nlink <= 1`, so an inode reachable by another name is
unlinked and recreated instead of written through. Apply both to `Unpack` and
`UnpackSync`.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded:

- **high** — `index.js:26` command injection: `pdfFilePath`, derived output paths, and `convertOptions` go into `child_process.exec` strings unescaped (reproduced with `$(...)`, embedded `"` break-out, and option injection).
- **low** — `index.js:133` `convertFile` never settles when `pdfinfo` fails or when `combineImages` rejects (reproduced: promise still pending after 4s).
- **low** — `index.js:140` lexicographic `imagePaths.sort()` misorders pages from page 10 onward (reproduced: `p-0, p-1, p-10, p-2, …`).

I also cleaned up the temporary `node_modules`/`package.json` edit used for the reproduction; the checkout is back to its original state.

The PR re-adds `index.js`, the single-file library `pdf-image`, and this content is the **pre-fix** revision of CVE-2018-3757 — upstream's fix (commit `54679496`) replaces `exec` with `spawn` plus an argv array. The core injection is real, trivially reachable from the documented Express usage in the README, and should block the change; the two low-severity promise/ordering bugs are worth fixing in the same pass since they live in the same file.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled PDF path and convert options reach the shell, giving arbitrary command execution
findings.body:
`PDFImage` builds every external command as a string and runs it through
`child_process.exec`, which means `/bin/sh -c` (index.js:8, 44, 116, 170). The values
substituted into those strings are never escaped or validated, so any caller that
passes an untrusted PDF path — the usage shown in README.md:63-74 reads it straight
from a URL — gets arbitrary command execution as the Node process user.

Injection sinks:

- `constructGetInfoCommand`: `pdfinfo "%s"` with `this.pdfFilePath` (index.js:26-29).
- `constructConvertCommandForPage`: `"%s[%d]"` with `this.pdfFilePath` (index.js:88-93).
- `constructConvertOptions`: `optionName + " " + value`, joined raw and unquoted
  (index.js:103-110, used at index.js:91).
- `constructCombineCommandForFile`: `imagePaths.join(' ')`, unquoted (index.js:95-101).
- `combineImages` cleanup: `exec("rm " + imagePaths.join(' '))` (index.js:125).

Double quotes are not protection: the shell still performs `$(...)` and backtick
substitution inside them, and an embedded `"` closes the quote entirely. The output
paths are equally reachable because `pdfFileBaseName` defaults to
`path.basename(pdfFilePath, ".pdf")` (index.js:79) and `outputDirectory` is taken
verbatim from options (index.js:21).

**Evidence:** with `tests/test.pdf` copied to `/tmp/injtest/my.pdf`:

```
var p = new PDFImage("/tmp/injtest/my$(touch /tmp/injtest/PWNED).pdf");
p.convertPage(0);
// command: convert "/tmp/injtest/my$(touch /tmp/injtest/PWNED).pdf[0]" ...
// -> /tmp/injtest/PWNED created

new PDFImage('/tmp/injtest/q" ; touch /tmp/injtest/quotePWNED ; "z.pdf').getInfo();
// command: pdfinfo "/tmp/injtest/q" ; touch /tmp/injtest/quotePWNED ; "z.pdf"
// -> /tmp/injtest/quotePWNED created

new PDFImage("/tmp/injtest/my.pdf",
  {convertOptions: {"-density": "300; touch /tmp/injtest/optPWNED"}}).convertPage(0);
// command: convert -density 300; touch /tmp/injtest/optPWNED "/tmp/injtest/my.pdf[0]" ...
// -> /tmp/injtest/optPWNED created
```

All three markers appeared even though `pdfinfo` is not installed in the test
container and the `convert` call itself failed: the shell expansion happens before
the command runs.

**Impact:** an actor who controls the PDF path, file name, or convert options — a
remote HTTP client in the documented Express usage — runs arbitrary shell commands
with the service's privileges. That crosses a trust boundary and is permanent
(files, credentials and network access are exposed; nothing in the library undoes
it), so high.

**Fix:** stop passing command lines to a shell. Build `{cmd, args}` pairs and call
`child_process.execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array (what upstream's 2.0.0 fix
does): `["pdfinfo", this.pdfFilePath]`, `["convert", ...options, pdfFilePath + "[" + pageNumber + "]", outputImagePath]`,
`["convert", "-append", ...imagePaths, outputImagePath]`, and `["rm", "--", ...imagePaths]`.
That single change closes every sink above; `convertOptions` keys/values must then be
validated as plain option tokens so they cannot masquerade as extra paths.

findings.title: Page images are sorted as strings, scrambling output for PDFs with 11 or more pages
findings.body:
`convertFile` collects page image paths as conversions finish and then re-sorts them
with `imagePaths.sort()` (index.js:140). The default sort is lexicographic on the
file name, which is only correct while page numbers are single-digit. From page 10
on, `-10` sorts between `-1` and `-2`.

**Evidence:** for an 11-page PDF the array handed to `combineImages`, captured by
stubbing `convertPage`, is:

```
p-0.png p-1.png p-10.png p-2.png p-3.png ... p-9.png
```

so `convert -append` stacks page 10 between pages 1 and 2 (index.js:96-101). With
`combinedImage: false` the same misordered array is resolved to the caller, contrary
to the documented `[slide-0, slide-1, ...]` order in README.md:38-40.

**Impact:** any PDF with 11 or more pages produces a scrambled combined image or a
mis-ordered result array; exactly 10 pages — the test fixture — hides it. Contained
to that conversion and fixable by re-running on a corrected version, so low.

**Fix:** sort numerically on the page index, e.g. sort the paths by the integer
between the last `-` and `.`, or simply resolve pages in index order by storing
results in a pre-sized array (`results[pageNumber] = imagePath`).

findings.title: convertFile never settles when pdfinfo fails or image combination fails
findings.body:
`convertFile` can return a promise that never settles, so the caller waits forever
with no error and no timeout.

Two independent paths:

1. **`numberOfPages()` rejection is dropped.** index.js:132-161 wraps the work in a
   `new Promise` but attaches only `.then` to `pdfImage.numberOfPages()` (index.js:133).
   There is no `.catch`, and the executor's `reject` is only reachable from inner
   callbacks, so a rejection from `getInfo` (index.js:46: `pdfinfo` missing, PDF
   unreadable or nonexistent, stat failure) leaves the outer promise pending.
2. **`combineImages()` rejection is dropped.** index.js:151 calls
   `pdfImage.combineImages(imagePaths).then(...)` and discards the returned promise.
   The `.catch` at index.js:157 is attached to the chain started at index.js:149,
   whose callback returns `undefined`, so it never sees the combine failure. A failed
   `convert -append` (disk full, unreadable page image, `EMFILE` from the unbounded
   parallel converts at index.js:136-146) leaves `convertFile` pending and, on Node
   15+, also raises an unhandled rejection, which terminates the process by default.

**Evidence:** with `pdfinfo` absent and a nonexistent PDF path (the default in a
container without poppler-utils):

```
var p = new PDFImage("/tmp/injtest/nonexistent.pdf");
var settled = false;
p.convertFile().then(() => settled = "resolved", () => settled = "rejected");
setTimeout(() => console.log(settled), 4000);   // logs: false
```

Path 2 reproduces the same way when `combineImages` is made to reject: the internal
`convertPromise` resolves, but `convertFile` never settles and an
`unhandledRejection` fires.

**Impact:** a library user gets a hang instead of an error for ordinary failures
(missing `pdfinfo`, bad path) and for any post-conversion failure. For an HTTP
handler using the documented usage this holds the request open until the client or
server times out, and the `combinedImage` path can crash the process. Contained to
the call that triggers it and cleared by a retry or restart, so low.

**Fix:** return the `numberOfPages()` chain and chain the combine step, e.g.
`return this.numberOfPages().then(...)` with `return pdfImage.combineImages(...)`
inside the callback, so both rejections propagate to the caller.

summary:
Findings recorded. Summary:

The PR adds `index.js`, a rewrite of `pdf-image`'s process handling that replaces `child_process.exec` with string-built shell commands by `spawn(cmd, args)` from `child-process-promise` — the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3757's command injection (`exec("rm " + imagePaths.join(" "))`, `exec(convertCommand)`). The injection itself is genuinely closed: every external program is now invoked with an argument array and no shell.

The port is incomplete and introduces regressions. `package.json` still lacks the new `child-process-promise` dependency, so the module does not load after a clean install; the cache-hit branch of `convertPage` lost its final `resolve`, so re-converting an already-rendered page hangs forever (and takes `convertFile` with it); the `graphicsMagick` option now spawns the literal program name `"gm convert"` and always fails with ENOENT. The existing `tests/test-main.js` also still asserts the old string-returning API and fails, which the upstream commit updated alongside the code.

findings.title: Module fails to load: child-process-promise is required but not declared in package.json
findings.body:
Loading the module throws on a clean install. `index.js:7` requires `child-process-promise`,
but `package.json` (unchanged by this PR) declares only `es6-promise` as a dependency, so
`npm install` never fetches it and every `require("pdf-image")` fails.

**Evidence:** in this checkout, `npm install` then `node -e "require('./')"` gives
`Error: Cannot find module 'child-process-promise'` from `index.js`. The upstream commit this
file is taken from also added `"child-process-promise": "^2.2.1"` to `dependencies`; that
`package.json` edit is missing here.

**Impact:** the published package is unusable for all consumers until they manually add a
transitive dependency that the package never declares. Reach is broad (every install),
persistence recoverable (installing the missing module fixes it); policy: no repo policy
override, so `medium`.

**Fix:** declare the new dependency in `package.json` (and its lockfile), matching the
`require` in `index.js`.

findings.title: convertPage never settles when the cached image is newer than the PDF
findings.body:
`convertPage` never settles when the page image already exists and is newer than the PDF —
the documented cache-hit path (`index.js:192-218`). The `if (imageFileStat.mtime < pdfFileStat.mtime)`
branch resolves after re-converting, but there is no `else`: when the image is up to date,
neither `resolve` nor `reject` is called and the returned promise stays pending forever.

**Evidence:** create `/tmp/test.pdf`, create `/tmp/test-3.png` with a newer mtime, then call
`new PDFImage("/tmp/test.pdf").convertPage(3)` — the promise has not settled 3 s later.
The removed upstream line was `return resolve(outputImagePath);` after the timestamp check.
`convertFile` (`index.js:131-144`) inherits this: it waits for every page's promise, so one
cached page means `convertFile` never resolves either.

**Impact:** re-converting a PDF that was already rendered hangs the caller instead of
returning the existing image path. In the documented Express usage every request for an
already-converted page leaks a never-settled promise, so trivial repetition is a DoS on the
hosting process. Reach broad, persistence recoverable (delete the image / restart);
policy: no repo override, so `medium`.

**Fix:** settle the promise in the cache-hit case too — `resolve(outputImagePath)` when
`imageFileStat.mtime >= pdfFileStat.mtime`.

findings.title: graphicsMagick option spawns "gm convert" as a program name and always fails
findings.body:
The `graphicsMagick: true` option is broken: `constructConvertCommandForPage` and
`constructCombineCommandForFile` set `cmd: "gm convert"` (`index.js:85`, `index.js:94`), and
`spawn` receives that whole string as the program name. `child_process.spawn` does not split
on spaces, so the executable is looked up literally as `gm convert` and fails.

**Evidence:** `new PDFImage("/tmp/gm.pdf", {graphicsMagick: true}).convertPage(0)` rejects with
`{"message":"Failed to convert page to image","error":"spawn gm convert ENOENT"}`.
It worked before the change because the command was passed to a shell through `exec`.

**Impact:** every user of the documented GraphicsMagick switch gets a rejection on every
conversion. Reach broad for that option, persistence recoverable (ImageMagick works);
only non-default setting affected, so `low`.

**Fix:** pass the program name and subcommand separately — `cmd: "gm"` with `"convert"`
prepended to `args`.

summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/unpack.js` (extraction was entirely absent in the baseline tree) at exactly npm `tar@4.4.2`'s version, i.e. upstream commit b0c58433 "only reuse file fs entries if nlink = 1" — the fix for CVE-2018-20834, on an otherwise 4.4.1 tree. I confirmed the fix by PoC: a hardlink entry pointing at a file outside `cwd` followed by a `File` entry at the same path leaves the victim untouched (`st.nlink > 1` forces the unlink at `lib/unpack.js:385-386`), and that holds for `OldFile`/`ContiguousFile` and multiple-hardlink variants too. The fix itself is correct and I found no regression from it on POSIX; the two recorded findings are separate from the CVE — a reproducible escape that still writes outside `cwd` via a cached-directory/symlink swap, and the Windows unlink-before-write data-loss side effect upstream patched in 4.4.3.

Note: `package-lock.json` shows as modified because I ran `npm install` to build PoCs; no source files were touched.

findings.title: Crafted archive can write outside the extraction cwd by replacing a cached directory with a symlink
findings.body:
A tarball can make `tar.x` write a file outside the extraction `cwd`. The archive
creates a real directory, replaces it with a symlink to any target, then ships a file
entry under that path. The file is written through the symlink. Default options, no
warning or error, async and sync.

**Preconditions:** extraction of an archive the caller does not fully trust, with default
options (`preservePaths:false` still allows this — `linkpath` is never checked).

**Evidence:** entry sequence, reproduced against this tree:

```
Directory  'link'
SymbolicLink 'link' -> /tmp/poc/outside
File       'link/victim.txt'  ("PWNED BY TARBALL")
```

`new Unpack({cwd})` (also `new Unpack({cwd, sync:true})`) turns
`/tmp/poc/outside/victim.txt` from `ORIGINAL` into `PWNED BY TARBALL`; `cwd` only ever
contains the symlink `link`. 10/10 runs in each mode.

Causal chain:
- the `Directory` entry mkdirs `cwd/link` and memoises it: `lib/mkdir.js:58`
  (`cache.set(dir, true)`).
- the `SymbolicLink` entry rmdirs it and creates the symlink, but the cache entry is
  left behind: `lib/unpack.js:377-384` (async), `lib/unpack.js:441-446` (sync). No
  `dirCache` invalidation anywhere in the file.
- the `File` entry calls `[MKDIR]` on `cwd/link`, which returns success straight from
  the cache without touching the filesystem or noticing the symlink:
  `lib/mkdir.js:68-69` (async), `lib/mkdir.js:150-151` (sync).
- the write opens the unresolved path: `lib/unpack.js:251-254` (`fsm.WriteStream`) and
  `lib/unpack.js:471` (`fs.openSync`).

The direct form (symlink entry with no preceding directory at the same path) is caught
by `lib/mkdir.js:113-114` (`Cannot extract through symbolic link`); only the cached
directory path escapes.

**Impact:** whoever controls the archive chooses the destination path and overwrites or
creates it with the extracting process's privileges — arbitrary file write outside the
sandbox, permanent, and silent. Not introduced or fixed by the `nlink` change this PR
carries; it is reachable in the extraction code this PR adds.

**Fix:** when an entry removes a directory or replaces a path with a link, drop that
path (and anything under it) from `dirCache` before continuing — in `[CHECKFS]` at
`lib/unpack.js:377-386` and `:439-448`, in both classes. Upstream later did exactly this
with a `[PRUNECACHE]` helper. Verifying the parent's realpath against `cwd` before the
open is the belt-and-braces alternative.

findings.title: Overwrites on Windows now unlink first, so a pending delete can remove the newly written file
findings.body:
On Windows, this change makes every overwrite of an existing regular file unlink it
first. Windows unlinks are not atomic, so the pending delete can land after the
replacement file is written and remove it. Upstream shipped a rename-then-delete
workaround one release later for this exact reason.

**Preconditions:** Windows extraction that writes over an existing path (re-extraction,
or an archive containing the same path twice). Linux/macOS are unaffected.

**Evidence:** `[ISREUSABLE]` returns false on win32 by design (`lib/unpack.js:363`), so
`[CHECKFS]` now always falls through to `fs.unlink` / `fs.unlinkSync` before creating the
new file (`lib/unpack.js:385-386`, `:447-448`). Before this change the inline condition
`entry.type === 'File' && !this.unlink && st.isFile()` reused the existing inode on
Windows too, so no unlink happened. npm `tar@4.4.3` replaced both unlink calls with
`unlinkFile`/`unlinkFileSync`, which rename then delete, with this comment:

> Unlinks on Windows are not atomic. This means that if you have a file entry, followed
> by another file entry with an identical name, and you cannot re-use the file [...]
> the unlink will be committed to the disk AFTER the new file has been written over the
> old one, deleting the new file. See: https://github.com/npm/node-tar/issues/183

**Impact:** on Windows the extracted file can end up missing after an overwrite — the
extraction reports success while the output is gone. Recoverable by extracting again
(`medium`→`low` discount: I have no Windows host and did not reproduce it; the evidence
is the upstream follow-up fix). The security fix itself is still correct on Windows; this
is the data-loss side effect of routing every overwrite through unlink.

**Fix:** on win32, rename the existing path to a temporary name and unlink that, instead
of unlinking the target path directly — the `unlinkFile`/`unlinkFileSync` helpers from
`tar@4.4.3`.

summary:
The PR adds `lib/contextify.js` to a checkout whose other files already match vm2 3.6.11, but the added file is the 3.6.10 version with only the EvalError/URIError branches backported — the 3.6.11 security hunk (`patriksimek/vm2@4b22d70`) that moves the `Decontextified.has` / `Contextify.proxies.has` lookups inside the surrounding `try` is missing.

I reproduced the resulting CVE-2019-10761 escape on this checkout (`new VM().run(...)` returns `uid=0(root)`), and bisected it: restoring only the `Contextify.value` hunk blocks the escape, restoring only the `Decontextify.value` hunk does not. Recorded as a high finding on lib/contextify.js:624.

No other defect was found in the 699 added lines; aside from that hunk the file is identical to the 3.6.11 release, and the surrounding `main.js`/`sandbox.js` wire its exports correctly. My assessment: the change must not merge in this form — it ships a known sandbox escape.

findings.title: Sandboxed code can escape vm2 with a raw host RangeError and run host code

summary:
I finished the review. One finding recorded.

**Summary:** PR #1 adds the 934-line generated grammar parser (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js`) that `src/parser.js:3` imports, replacing the vulnerable array-literal `eval` with a `trimEdges(...).split(',')` action — i.e. it is the generated half of the fix for CVE-2020-6836. The file is byte-identical to upstream's fixed artifact and the whole test suite passes with it (only 4 pre-existing floating-point financial assertions fail). The gap is that the fix exists only in the generated output: the `.jison` grammar it comes from still contains the `eval`, so the repository's own `npm run generate-parser` step silently rewrites the vulnerability back in; that is the recorded finding. The committed `dist/` bundles also still contain the `eval`, but CONTRIBUTING.md tells contributors not to edit `dist/` (maintainers rebuild it), so I did not file that.

findings.title: Regenerating the parser from its jison source restores the eval-based code execution
findings.body:
The PR removes the `eval` from the ARRAY action only in the generated file
(`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:225`, now `yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',')`),
but the grammar it is generated from still evaluates the array token:
`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison:191` reads
`var arr = eval("[" + yytext + "]");`. Running the repository's own parser build
step, `npm run generate-parser` (`package.json:20`, jison), overwrites the fixed
file with one that calls `eval` on the raw formula text again, so the
CVE-2020-6836 fix is reverted by a routine build and the next release ships the
arbitrary-code-execution path.

**Preconditions:** someone runs `npm run generate-parser` (or otherwise
regenerates the parser from the `.jison` source) before building or publishing.

**Evidence:** with the repository's installed jison 0.4.18, copy
`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison` to a scratch directory and run
`jison grammar-parser.jison`; the output contains
`var arr = eval("[" + yytext + "]");` (line 226 of the generated file) where the
committed file has the `split` action. The two artifacts disagree today, so the
source of truth is still the vulnerable one.

**Impact:** formula input reaches `eval` again, so an application that passes
user-controlled text to `Parser#parse` runs attacker-chosen JavaScript in its own
process. Reach is broad (every consumer of the rebuilt package) and the effect is
permanent (code execution), discounted one tier because the vulnerable artifact is
only produced by a maintainer build action; the code committed in this PR is
itself safe. Policy: the table in the review contract, no repository-specific
severity rules.

**Fix:** make the same change in `grammar-parser.jison` (replace the `eval` block
with `$$ = yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',');`) and regenerate
`grammar-parser.js` from it, so the checked-in parser and its source agree.

summary:
Recorded one finding; covering the rest of the file.

**Summary:** The PR adds `lib/validation.js`, restoring the schema validation module that the baseline tree had removed; the file is byte-identical to upstream fastify 2.15.0 and its exports (`build`, `validate`, `serialize`, `isValidLogger`, `buildSchemaCompiler`, symbols) match every call site in `lib/route.js`, `lib/handleRequest.js`, `lib/reply.js` and `lib/logger.js`, so the module integrates correctly. The one real defect is the restored default `allErrors: true` in the shared Ajv instance (`lib/validation.js:174`), the exact line upstream changed in 2.15.2 because a single failing request can make Ajv collect ~1M errors, block the event loop for up to a second, and emit a ~50 MB 400 response — reproducible with a 1 MB body, so I filed it as medium (CVE-2020-8192). I checked but did not file the other edge cases the review surfaced (header-schema lowercasing gaps, `useDefaults`/`removeAdditional` mutating `request.headers`, `querystring` vs `query` in `validationContext`, `ret.value` falsy handling): they are upstream 2.15.0 behavior on non-default schema shapes, not regressions this change introduces.

findings.title: Default Ajv allErrors lets one request build a 50 MB error message and exhaust memory
findings.body:
`buildSchemaCompiler` creates the shared Ajv instance with `allErrors: true`
(`lib/validation.js:174`), so every route that declares a `body`, `querystring`,
`params` or `headers` schema collects *all* validation errors for each discarded
request and turns them into one huge error message. A remote client can send a
single ~1 MB body that fails validation and make the server build a 50 MB response
after blocking the event loop for ~0.5-1 s and retaining ~400 MB of heap. A few
concurrent requests exhaust memory; repeating them keeps the service unavailable.

**Preconditions:** a route with any of those schemas (normal use). The default
`bodyLimit` of 1048576 (`lib/configValidator.js:15`) caps the request, not the
amplification.

**Evidence:** reproduced with ajv@6.12.0 and the options from
`lib/validation.js:170-176`, run through a copy of `validate`/`schemaErrorsText`:
a 1,020,009 B body against `{type:'object', properties:{arr:{type:'array',
items:{type:'object', required:['a','b','c']}}}}` yields 1,020,000 errors,
451-977 ms of `validate`, +385 MB heap, and a 50.3 MB 400 response body; the same
input with `allErrors: false` yields 1 error and <=1 ms. Nested arrays/`anyOf`
scale worse (117 KB -> 240,000 errors). Compilation happens once per route, so the
cost is per request: `lib/route.js:269` -> `lib/validation.js:59-61`, then
`lib/handleRequest.js:83` -> `lib/validation.js:101`, with the uncapped
stringification at `lib/validation.js:157-165` and the whole message serialized at
`lib/reply.js:493-501` (`error.validation` also keeps every error object alive
until the reply is sent). Upstream fixed this by setting `allErrors: false`
(fastify 2.15.2, with the comment "When set to `true`, a DoS attack is possible");
NVD CVE-2020-8192 describes it as resource exhaustion via the allErrors option.

**Impact:** unauthenticated availability loss for every service on a schema-validating
route. Reach is broad (all users of the service), persistence is recoverable (the
process recovers when the traffic stops, but the attacker can retrigger at will),
so medium.

**Fix:** set `allErrors: false` in the default Ajv options and update the
documented default in `docs/Server.md:389` / `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md`;
callers that want all errors can still pass `customOptions: { allErrors: true }`.

summary:
Reviewed the change and finished coverage. Summary:

The PR adds one file, `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js`, a jison-generated parser that `src/parser.js` imports; the rest of the repo is unchanged. Byte-for-byte it is the pre-fix upstream revision (94413609), so the review reduces to whether that generated code is safe to ship — and it is not: its `expseq : ARRAY` action passes attacker-controlled formula text to `eval` (grammar-parser.js:226), which I reproduced as code execution through the public `Parser.parse()` API. I recorded that as one high-severity finding; no other deviations from the fixed upstream file exist, so there is nothing else to report.

The full test suite runs (505 passing) with four financial-formula numeric mismatches (`CUMPRINC`, `FV`, `IPMT`, `IRR`) that come from the `@handsontable/formulajs` dependency and are unrelated to this change.

findings.title: Formula array literals are eval'd, allowing arbitrary code execution
findings.body:
Formula text passed to the array-literal rule is executed with `eval`, so a formula string can run arbitrary
JavaScript in the parser's host process. The ARRAY token matches the whole bracket group with the greedy
lexer rule `^(?:\[(.*)?\])` (src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:925), and the `expseq : ARRAY` action then
evaluates that raw input as code: `eval("[" + yytext + "]")` (src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:226).
Anything a caller can write inside a `[...]` argument of a function call is executed.

**Preconditions:** the application parses a formula string it does not fully trust (a spreadsheet cell, an
uploaded workbook, or an API value). This is the library's normal input.

**Evidence:** through the public API, with dependencies installed (`BABEL_ENV=commonjs node -r babel-register`):

```js
const {Parser} = require('./src/index.js');
const p = new Parser();
p.parse('SUM([require("fs").writeFileSync("/tmp/pwned_by_formula","owned")])');
// => {error: null, result: 0}
```

The file `/tmp/pwned_by_formula` is created, and `parse()` reports no error. `SUM([process.pid])` likewise
returns the process id, proving arbitrary expression evaluation rather than data parsing. The exception
thrown by a failing payload is swallowed by `Parser.parse`'s catch (src/parser.js:52-60), so failures are
silent.

**Impact:** an attacker who controls a formula string gets code execution in the process that parses it —
typically the server or the browser tab of another user in a spreadsheet application. That crosses a trust
boundary and is permanent (secrets and files reachable by the process). This is CVE-2020-6836; the added
file is byte-identical to the vulnerable pre-patch revision (94413609) instead of the fixed one (396b089).

**Fix:** parse the array literal without evaluating it — upstream replaced the action with
`this.$ = yy.trimEdges(yytext).split(',');` (commit 396b089, which also shifted the surrounding `case`
numbers). Apply the same change to `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison` (its `expseq : ARRAY` action
still contains the `eval`), otherwise `npm run generate-parser` regenerates the vulnerable code.

summary:
Working tree is clean and both findings are recorded.

**Summary**

PR #1 adds `lib/validation.js`, the request-validation and response-serialization module that `lib/route.js:11-12` and `lib/reply.js:22-23` already require, and it is byte-identical to upstream fastify v2.15.2's file — the fix for CVE-2020-8192, which sets the private Ajv instance's `allErrors` to `false`. I confirmed the mitigation works here: a 400-property required schema answered with `{}` returns a 39-byte error message instead of a 17 KB one, and the option cannot be re-enabled by a request, only by the operator via `ajv.customOptions`. The two issues I recorded are second-order: the repository's docs and tests still encode the old `allErrors: true` contract (five tests in `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` fail, which CONTRIBUTING's green-CI rule blocks), and a latent truthiness check in `build()` skips a request part declared with the boolean `false` schema. Overall the fix itself is correct and faithful; the remaining work is aligning docs and tests, plus the one-line boolean-schema presence check.

findings.title: Disabling allErrors by default leaves docs and tests advertising the vulnerable Ajv setting
findings.body:
The default Ajv options in this new module disable `allErrors` (lib/validation.js:174-176), which is the fix for CVE-2020-8192, but nothing else in the tree was updated to match. Two things still describe the old behaviour:

- `docs/Server.md:384-391` lists `allErrors: true` inside the documented `ajv.customOptions` default block, and `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:336-343` lists it in the "baseline ajv configuration", with the same value again in the "create your own instance" recipe at `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:352-360`. A user who follows either recipe explicitly re-enables the setting the CVE is about. `docs/Validation-and-Serialization.md:669` and `:718` repeat it in the `customOptions` examples.
- `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` still asserts the multi-error contract: `:63`, `:219-232`, `:258`, `:288` and `:381` expect two errors (`"... required property 'name', ... required property 'work'"` and a two-element `error.validation` array).

**Evidence:** with the PR applied,
`npx tap --no-esm -J test/validation-error-handling.test.js test/output-validation.test.js` fails tests 2, 6, 7, 8 and 11 of `validation-error-handling.test.js` (found `body should have required property 'name'` vs wanted the two-error message at :60). With `allErrors: true` restored, those five pass; tests 9 and 10 and the `output-validation.test.js` shorthand cases fail in both runs, so they are unrelated/environmental. CONTRIBUTING.md requires "All integrated CI services must be green before a pull-request can be merged", so the change cannot land as-is.

**Impact:** the code change itself is correct and the mitigation works — a route schema with 400 required properties answered with `{}` produces a 39-byte error message here versus a 17,088-byte one with `allErrors: true`. The defect is the surrounding contract: the documented defaults still advertise the vulnerable setting, and the repo's own tests encode the old single-pass behaviour. No trust boundary is crossed, and an application can restore the old behaviour with `ajv.customOptions.allErrors: true`, so severity is low.

**Fix:** update the two default blocks and the two `customOptions` examples to `allErrors: false` (with the DoS note), and change the five expectations in `test/validation-error-handling.test.js` to the single-error contract, as upstream did in the same security release.

findings.title: Boolean false request-part schema is skipped, so any request reaches the handler unvalidated
findings.body:
A route that declares a boolean `false` schema for a request part gets no validation at all, so any request reaches the handler with that part unchecked. JSON Schema uses `false` to mean "nothing is valid"; for `body` that also means "this route accepts no body".

**Evidence:** every request-part check in `build()` is a truthiness test — `lib/validation.js:59` (`body`), `:63` (`querystring`), `:67` (`params`) — and `:33`-`:53` for `headers`. When the schema is `false` the branch is skipped, no symbol is set on the context, and `validate()` at `lib/validation.js:97` sees an `undefined` validator and passes.

Reproduced against this checkout:

```js
const app = Fastify()
app.post('/', { schema: { body: false } }, (req) => { console.log('handler ran, body =', JSON.stringify(req.body)); return 'ok' })
// POST / with {"a":1} and content-type: application/json
// -> ready err: undefined / handler ran, body = {"a":1}   (no 400)
```

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller sends a body to a route whose schema forbids one (or bypasses any request part declared `false`), and the precondition the handler was written against is gone. It needs the route to use a boolean `false` schema, which is valid JSON Schema but uncommon, and the fix is local, so the severity is low.

**Fix:** test for presence instead of truthiness, e.g. `if (context.schema.body !== undefined)` (and likewise for `querystring`, `params`, `headers`), letting the compiler produce the always-failing validator.

summary:
**Verification performed**

- Diff vs. upstream: the added `lib/contextify.js` is byte-identical to `patriksimek/vm2` commit `4b22d70` ("Fixes sandbox escape #197", released as v3.6.11), the fix for CVE-2019-10761; the baseline file was the pre-fix version.
- Mechanism: the pre-fix `Contextify.value` / `Decontextify.value` made their first host-realm call (`Contextified.has` / `Decontextified.has`) before the `try` block, so a stack-exhausted (`RangeError`) host exception escaped to the sandbox at `lib/contextify.js:331` and `:625`; moving those lookups inside `try` turns it into a `null` return.
- Reproduced on Node 11.8.0: the issue #197 PoC (`Buffer.prototype.write` + deep recursion) returns `RESULT: root` against the pre-fix file and never escapes against the fixed file.
- Test suite (mocha, Node 11.8.0): 61 passing, 2 pending, 1 failing — the failing `VM timeout` test asserts a `"Script execution timed out."` message and fails identically before and after the change (Node version artifact), so it is not a regression.
- Checked for regressions from the new `null`-on-exception path: `WeakMap.has/get` do not throw for ordinary values, so normal contextification is unchanged; the extra swallowing only affects the overflow case.

**Summary**

The change adds `lib/contextify.js`, the contextification layer that `lib/main.js:11,145` loads into the sandbox; relative to upstream it is exactly the CVE-2019-10761 fix, which moves the proxy WeakMap lookups inside the surrounding `try` so a host-realm stack-overflow `RangeError` can no longer reach sandbox code. I reproduced the reported escape against the pre-fix file and confirmed it no longer works against the fixed file, and the existing test suite behaves the same before and after (the single failure is a Node-version message-mismatch present on both). I found no defect introduced by the change and recorded no findings.

Note on limit: I could not get a runtime for the "ideal" reproduction matrix beyond Node 11.8.0 (modern Node lacks `process.binding('natives')` and `Reflect.enumerate`), and I could not confirm any further stack-exhaustion route (e.g. the unguarded `host.Array.isArray(args)` at `lib/contextify.js:390`) by reproduction, so I did not file it.

Recorded one finding. The probe surfaced several upstream API quirks (`setMaxSockets(0)`, in-place `reverse()`, `buffer` state handling), but those are pre-existing 0.6.3 behaviour and misuse/edge cases rather than defects this PR introduces, so I did not file them.

Summary: the PR restores `lib/node-http-proxy.js`, the package entry point, at the pre-0.7.0 state of node-http-proxy 0.6.3. The added `stack()` middleware composer throws on `next(err)`; I reproduced a real HTTP server process exit when a middleware reports an asynchronous error, which is CVE-2017-16014. The rest of the file matches upstream and the newly reachable submodules look consistent with that release. Overall the change should not merge as-is; the error path in `stack()` needs the 0.7.0 fix.

findings.title: Middleware errors in httpProxy.stack() throw and crash the proxy process
findings.body:
A middleware that reports an error through `next(err)` in `httpProxy.stack()` throws from the request handler instead of ending the response. Because middleware normally calls `next` asynchronously, the throw escapes the HTTP server's call stack and becomes an uncaught exception, which terminates the Node.js process. Every client served by that proxy loses the service, and a remote client that can make the failing middleware run can repeat the crash at will.

**Evidence:** `lib/node-http-proxy.js:223-231` — the error branch is `throw err;` with a TODO noting that no error response is implemented. Reproduction with a middleware that defers `next(new Error(...))` by 10ms:

```
$ NODE_PATH=/tmp/nm node repro.js
listening
.../lib/node-http-proxy.js:225
          throw err;
          ^
Error: downstream lookup failed
    at Timeout._onTimeout (repro.js:5:35)
```

The process exits with status 1 while serving the request. This is CVE-2017-16014 / GHSA-9xw9-pvgv-6p76, fixed upstream in 0.7.0 by writing a 500 response (or destroying the response if headers were already sent) instead of throwing.

**Impact:** The proxy process crashes for all users. Reach is broad (one failing request takes the whole server down) and persistence is recoverable (restart restores service, but the trigger can be repeated). That gives medium under the review severity policy, not `high`, because the failure depends on a consumer using the `stack` middleware API and on a middleware that propagates an error.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that a middleware error is contained in the response: in the `if (err)` branch, log the error, then send `500 Internal Server Error` with `res.end()`, or destroy the response if its headers are already sent, and return without calling `child`.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** commit b985b8c restores `index.js` (238 lines) as the upstream `serialize-javascript@3.1.0` implementation — 3.0.0 plus the CVE-2020-7660 fix: a 128-bit crypto-random placeholder `UID` (`index.js:37-44`) instead of `Math.random`, and a backslash-aware placeholder regexp with a guard (`index.js:14`, `index.js:202-208`).

**Assessment:** the security logic holds up. A delegated investigation tried ~10k attacker-reachable payloads (quotes/backslashes before placeholder text, placeholder lookalikes in keys, values, Map/Set entries, regexp sources, all option combinations) and could not produce a substitution or an unescaped HTML char without knowing the UID, and no channel leaks the UID. Escaping of strings and regexp sources is correct, and the 66 unit tests pass. The change does break the package: `index.js:9` requires `randombytes`, but `package.json`/`package-lock.json` were not updated, so a fresh install cannot load the module and `npm test` fails — recorded as one medium finding. Other defects I checked (function bodies spliced in after the escape pass, `flags`/`toISOString` interpolation, `ignoreFunction` mutating caller objects, class serialization) are unchanged upstream behaviour from 3.0.0 and not made reachable by this commit, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: Package declares no randombytes dependency, so requiring the module throws MODULE_NOT_FOUND
findings.body:
`index.js:9` now requires `randombytes`, but `package.json` still declares no runtime `dependencies` and `package-lock.json` has no `randombytes` entry. Installing the package installs nothing, and `require('serialize-javascript')` throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before any code runs.

**Evidence:**
- `git diff 599f858...b985b8c` touches only `index.js`; `package.json:3` still says `"version": "3.0.0"` and has no `dependencies` key; `grep -c randombytes package-lock.json` → `0`.
- Fresh clone at b985b8c: `npm ci && npm test` fails with `Error: Cannot find module 'randombytes'`; `node -e "require('./index.js')"` fails at `index.js:9`. The 66 unit tests only pass after `npm i randombytes` by hand.
- Upstream `serialize-javascript@3.1.0` ships the same `index.js` plus `"dependencies": {"randombytes": "^2.1.0"}` in `package.json`; the two index files are byte-identical, so only the manifest change is missing.

**Impact:** Every consumer of the published package fails at import time unless `randombytes` happens to be hoisted from an unrelated dependency; the repo's own test command fails too. The security fix this change is meant to deliver never takes effect. Library-wide reach, recoverable by installing the missing module — medium.

**Fix:** Add `randombytes` (`^2.1.0`) to `dependencies` in `package.json` and regenerate `package-lock.json`; bump `version` to `3.1.0` in the same edit so the release carrying the CVE-2020-7660 fix is published under a new version.

summary:
I reviewed the full 43-line addition (the only changed file) and reproduced the file-serving handler's behaviour in isolation.

**Summary:** PR #2 re-adds `server.js`, the package's `main` entry point: a demo static-file server on port 8080 plus a `ws` echo/broadcast server on `localhost:8090`. The static handler joins `__dirname` with the raw request URL (`server.js:9`), which is a path traversal; I reproduced it locally and recorded it as a high-severity finding. The remaining code (echo, stdin broadcast, uncaught-exception handler, `clients` bookkeeping) has no reachable path to data crossing a trust boundary beyond what the demo already exposes on loopback, so I filed nothing else.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read any file on the host via .. in the static server URL
findings.body:
`server.js:7-19` builds a static file path by concatenating `__dirname` with the raw
request URL, so `..` segments in the URL escape the package directory. Any file the
node process can read is returned to the caller.

**Preconditions:** the HTTP listener is reachable. `hserver.listen(8080)` at
`server.js:38` passes no host, so it binds all interfaces, not just loopback. Because
`package.json:10` sets `"main": "./server.js"`, any consumer that does
`require('pooledwebsocket')` also starts this listener as a side effect.

**Evidence:** reproduced with the same code shape (a `createReadStream(__dirname + req.url)`
handler, `--path-as-is` to stop the client from normalising the URL):

```
$ curl -s --path-as-is 'http://127.0.0.1:8099/../tsecret.txt'
secret
```

The server logged `url: "/../tsecret.txt"` — Node's HTTP parser does not normalise
`req.url`, so the `..` reaches `fs` intact. The same handler's error path at
`server.js:16-18` confirms the traversal in its message:
`Error: ENOENT: ... open '/tmp/tdir/../../tsecret.txt'`.

**Impact:** unauthenticated remote read of arbitrary files readable by the node user —
application config, `~/.ssh` keys, `/etc/passwd` — with no write or execution needed,
and nothing to undo afterwards. Reach crosses a trust boundary (a network actor gains
data its role denies) and persistence is permanent, so `high`: this is CVE-2017-16107,
a path traversal in the `pooledwebsocket` package.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the resolved path must stay inside the intended
document root. Resolve the joined path and reject anything outside it, e.g.
`var root = __dirname, p = path.resolve(root, '.' + req.url);
if (p.indexOf(root + path.sep) !== 0) { res.statusCode = 403; return res.end(); }`
then stream `p`. Skip the traversal entirely for package consumers: the demo server
should not be `main`.

summary:
Verified the change and its downstream effects. No findings to record.

**What the change does:** PR #1 adds `library.js` back to the plugin at the snapshot from upstream commit `cf43beed` ("fix: CSRF issues", tagged 0.7.0) — the commit NVD lists as the fix for CVE-2020-15156 (CWE-352). Compared with the plugin's 0.6.3 code, the only semantic delta is `middleware.applyCSRF` on the two state-changing routes (`library.js:251-252`).

**Assessment — the fix holds:** `middleware.applyCSRF` is csurf with default settings (`/tmp/nbb/src/middleware/index.js:34`), so any POST without a session-bound `_csrf` fails closed before `replyToComment`/`publishArticle` run; the plugin's routes are registered after body parsing and session middleware (`/tmp/nbb/src/webserver.js:166-185`, `src/routes/index.js:113,144`), and both client forms already submit a `_csrf` field populated from the `token` field in the JSON response (`public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:15,29,64,89`, `library.js:105`), so the fix is functionally complete and not a regression. The CORS response that exposes that token is gated by an exact-match allowlist against the configured blog URLs (`library.js:62-74`), so an unlisted origin cannot read it. These routes are the only state-changing endpoints the plugin registers.

Remaining defects I considered and did not file: the unescaped `url` sink in `addLinkbackToArticle` (`library.js:219`) is unreachable on NodeBB 1.12 because the `filter:posts.custom_profile_info` payload no longer carries the post and no template renders it (`/tmp/nbb/src/posts/user.js:98,111`); the unvalidated `res.redirect` targets (`library.js:131,134,193`), unguarded `JSON.parse` (`library.js:145,182`) and `meta.config['blog-comments:cid'].toString()` (`library.js:162`) are all pre-existing in 0.6.3 and untouched by this fix, and their worst outcomes (open redirect to a self-chosen URL, 500s) are not reachable by an attacker without the victim's token. The change is a correct, minimal security fix and can be approved.

**Summary**

The change re-adds `lib/node-http-proxy.js`, the package entry point, and its one behavioural difference from the version the rest of the tree was built against is inside `exports.stack()` (`lib/node-http-proxy.js:222-243`): a middleware error passed to `next(err)` now answers `500` (or destroys the response when headers are already out) instead of re-throwing. That is exactly upstream commit `0e36912` — the fix for CVE-2017-16014 (file blob `ea05ab1` matches both) — applied over the tree's own parent commit `0c71119e`; everything else in the file is byte-identical, and no other file differs from upstream. I reproduced the new branch with a stubbed response (500 before headers, `destroy()` after headers, error logged and no re-throw) and checked that `res._headerSent` and `OutgoingMessage.prototype.destroy` are real properties on the declared Node `0.4.x || 0.5.x` runtimes, so the guard is sound where the package claims support. Residual crash paths I found (a synchronous throw from a middleware layer, and `_headerSent` being a private API that later Node versions dropped, which would make the guard dead and `setHeader` throw) are either unchanged upstream design or outside the declared engine range, so I filed nothing. The change is clean and I recommend approval.

The pull request adds `index.js` — the full implementation of `serialize-javascript` v3.0.0 (byte-identical to upstream tag `v3.0.0`), which serializes RegExp, Date, Map, Set, function, `undefined` and `Infinity` values by substituting placeholders into JSON text after the HTML-unsafe-character escaping pass.

That ordering is the root of the most serious problems: placeholder matches are resolved inside the finished string, so attacker-supplied strings that look like placeholders get replaced (the bug upstream fixed in 3.1.0 as CVE-2020-7660), and function bodies bypass escaping entirely. I reproduced the code-injection sink in the `RegExp.flags` / `Date.toISOString` concatenation, the destructive `ignoreFunction` mutation of caller objects, and two stateful/unanchored-regex defects that silently emit unparseable output.

I did not fully reproduce code execution from string-only attacker input against the placeholder grammar (the inserted regexp source is escaped, and the surrounding tail blocks a clean breakout), so that finding is graded medium rather than high despite the CVE label. Overall the code is a faithful copy of a version that upstream later patched six ways; I would not merge it without the placeholder, flags/date and function-body fixes.

findings.title: Attacker strings that match the placeholder grammar are replaced with code from other fields
findings.body:
A string value can be re-interpreted as a generated placeholder and replaced with code from
another field, so attacker-supplied text is silently turned into a live object, into output
that is not valid JavaScript, or into a thrown exception.

`index.js:10-11` builds the placeholder grammar and a 40-bit UID with
`Math.floor(Math.random() * 0x10000000000).toString(16)`. `index.js:180` escapes unsafe
characters in the JSON text, then `index.js:190-218` runs a global placeholder replacement
over that text. The replacement text is inserted after escaping, so it is never escaped
itself. The regexp matches anywhere in the JSON text, including inside a string literal
where the opening quote is escaped.

**Preconditions:** The attacker can place strings into an object that is serialized together
with at least one RegExp, Date, Map, Set, function or `Infinity` (so the replacement step
runs), and the UID for the process is known. The UID is a single per-process constant of 40
bits derived from `Math.random()`, and serialized output acts as an oracle: a request whose
output changes shows the guess was right. One guess per string value is possible, so a
single object can carry thousands of candidates.

**Evidence:** With `Math.random` pinned to `0.5` so the UID (`8000000000`) is known:

    S({a: '@__R-8000000000-0__@', r: /safe/})
    -> {"a":new RegExp("safe", ""),"r":new RegExp("safe", "")}

    S({foo: /1" + console.log(1)/i, bar: '"@__R-8000000000-0__@'})
    -> {"foo":new RegExp("1\" + console.log(1)", "i"),"bar":"\new RegExp("1\" + console.log(1)", "i")}
    eval('(' + out + ')')  // SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token

The second case is the one upstream fixed in v3.1.0 (commit f21a6fb, CVE-2020-7660) by
capturing the preceding backslash, `new RegExp('(\\\\)?"@__(F|R|D|M|S|U|I)-' + UID + ...)`,
and rejecting matches that follow one. Keys are affected too: `{'@__U-8000000000-0__@': 1}`
serializes the key as `undefined`. An out-of-range index throws out of `serialize()`:
`{a: '@__S-8000000000-99__@', s: new Set([1])}` -> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading 'values')`.

**Impact:** Attacker-controlled strings are replaced with values taken from other fields of
the same object (a string becomes a RegExp, Date, Map, Set, function, `undefined` or a
number), and a value whose opening quote is escaped turns the rest of the object into code
position, producing output that does not parse. I reproduced corruption and a thrown
`TypeError`, not execution of attacker-chosen code: the inserted regexp source is itself
serialized and escaped, and the fixed tail `, "<flags>")` blocks a clean breakout in the
roughly 240k payload permutations I tested. So the demonstrated impact is data corruption,
unparseable output for consumers that `eval` it, and a request-level `TypeError`, not the
XSS/code execution the CVE label implies. The UID precondition also discounts this. I stop
at medium; the placeholder grammar must not match data.

**Fix:** Make the placeholder unforgeable and never rewrite text that came from data. Both
were done upstream in v3.1.0: generate the UID with `crypto.randomBytes` (16 bytes) and
require the placeholder not be preceded by a backslash
(`if (backSlash) return match;`). Also validate `valueIndex` against the collected array
before indexing it.

findings.title: Unvalidated RegExp.flags and Date.toISOString values are concatenated into generated code
findings.body:
`RegExp#flags` and `Date#toISOString()` results are concatenated into generated JavaScript
without validation, so an attacker-supplied object can inject arbitrary code into the
serialized output.

`index.js:192` emits `new Date("` + `dates[i].toISOString()` + `")` and `index.js:196` emits
`new RegExp(" + serialize(source) + ', "' + regexps[i].flags + '")`. The regexp source is
escaped through a nested `serialize()` call; the flags string and the date text are not
checked for quotes or code characters at all.

**Preconditions:** The serialized graph contains a `RegExp` or `Date` whose `flags` or
`toISOString` is not the built-in implementation — an object created with
`Object.create(RegExp.prototype)` plus own `source`/`flags` properties, a `defineProperty`
override, or a patched `RegExp.prototype.flags` / `Date.prototype.toISOString`. Plain
`JSON.parse` data cannot produce this; an in-process actor or a prototype-patching
dependency is required.

**Evidence:**

    var re = /abc/g;
    Object.defineProperty(re, 'flags', {value: 'g"),x:console.log("PWNED-flags"),y:("'});
    serialize({re: re})
    -> {"re":new RegExp("abc", "g"),x:console.log("PWNED-flags"),y:("")}
    eval('(' + out + ')')   // prints PWNED-flags

    var d = new Date(0);
    Object.defineProperty(d, 'toISOString', {value: function () { return '"),x:console.log("PWNED-date"),y:("'; }});
    serialize({d: d})       // eval prints PWNED-date
    -> {"d":new Date(""),x:console.log("PWNED-date"),y:("")}

**Impact:** Code chosen by whoever controls the `flags`/`toISOString` value runs in every
consumer that evaluates the output, and the injected text is not escaped even with the
default options. Upstream fixed this in commit 2e609d0 ("fix(CVE-2020-7660): fix for
RegExp.flags and Date.prototype.toISOString"), which serializes `flags` as a JSON string
and validates the date text. Severity is limited because the attacker must already be able
to hand `serialize()` a spoofed RegExp/Date, which implies code in the producing process.

**Fix:** Treat both values as data: emit `", " + serialize(String(flags)) + ")"` and
`new Date(" + serialize(isoString) + ")`, and reject a non-string or malformed result
instead of concatenating it.

findings.title: Stateful /g native-code guard lets every second native function through as invalid output
Function bodies bypass unsafe-character escaping, so </script> reaches HTML-inlined output raw
findings.body:
Function bodies are spliced into the serialized output after the escaping pass, so `<`, `>`,
`/`, U+2028 and U+2029 inside a function value reach the output raw even with the default
(safe) options.

`index.js:179-181` escapes the JSON text and its own comment at `index.js:176-178` notes the
ordering; `index.js:215-217` then inserts `serializeFunc(fn)` — the result of
`fn.toString()` (`index.js:114`) — with no escaping. Any consumer that embeds the output in
an HTML script element, which is the documented use of this library in `README.md`, gets a
truncated script element.

**Preconditions:** The attacker can influence a function value in the serialized graph (for
example a plugin handler, a callback taken from configuration, or code built with
`new Function`). Ordinary values and function bodies written by the developer are not
affected.

**Evidence:**

    serialize({f: function () { return '</script>'; }, s: '</script>'})
    -> {"f":function () { return '</script>'; },"s":"\u003C\u002Fscript\u003E"}

The sibling string is escaped; the identical text inside the function body is not.
`serialize({f: new Function('return "A\u2028B"')})` also returns a raw U+2028, which is a
line terminator for older engines. `{unsafe: true}` does not help — the default already
emits raw characters.

**Impact:** Cross-site scripting in any page that inlines the serialized output, with no way
to opt into escaping. Upstream treated this as a security fix later (commit 738a8e9
"security: sanitize function bodies", refined in 2864b3c and ffda9f1). Severity is low
because the attacker must control a function *value*, not just data.

**Fix:** Run the same `UNSAFE_CHARS_REGEXP` escaping over the text returned by
`serializeFunc` before inserting it.

findings.title: Unanchored function-detection regexes emit methods with nested arrows or functions as invalid JS
findings.body:
`IS_PURE_FUNCTION` and `IS_ARROW_FUNCTION` test the whole function source instead of its
head, so a concise method whose body merely contains `function(` or `=>` is emitted unchanged
as a method and the serialized output does not parse.

`index.js:14-15` define unanchored `/function.*?\(/` and `/.*?=>.*?/`, tested at
`index.js:120` and `index.js:125`. When either matches, `serializeFunc` returns
`fn.toString()` as-is, skipping the rewrite at `index.js:140-143` that turns a method into a
function expression.

**Evidence:**

    serialize({m(){ return [1].map(x => x); }})        -> {"m":m(){ return [1].map(x => x); }}
    serialize({m(){ return function inner(){}; }})     -> {"m":m(){ return function inner(){}; }}
    serialize({m(){ /* => */ return 1; }})             -> {"m":m(){ /* => */ return 1; }}

All three outputs are `SyntaxError` when evaluated, although each input is an ordinary
object with a method. A comment containing `=>` is enough to trigger it.

**Impact:** Round-tripping silently produces unusable output for common method bodies, with
no error at serialization time. Upstream anchored both patterns and added an `IS_CLASS`
check in commit fdb853d ("Fix methods containing nested functions and arrows"). Impact is
contained to code shape, so this is low.

**Fix:** Anchor the detection to the start of the source, e.g. `^(?:async\s+)?function\b`
and `^(?:async\s+)?(?:\([^)]*\)|[^\s()]+)\s*=>`, so only a leading function or arrow is
treated as already-serialized code.

findings.title: ignoreFunction deletes properties from the caller's objects instead of skipping them
findings.body:
`serialize(obj, {ignoreFunction: true})` deletes function-valued properties from the caller's
object graph instead of skipping them, so serializing an object can permanently destroy
state that the process still uses.

`index.js:67-69` calls `deleteFunctions(value)` from the replacer, and `index.js:34-44` walks
`for...in` and runs `delete obj[key]` on the real object. Objects reached through arrays,
Maps and Sets are mutated the same way, because those containers are serialized with the
same options at `index.js:200` and `index.js:204`.

**Preconditions:** The caller passes `ignoreFunction`, which is not the default.

**Evidence:**

    var victim = {a: 1, f: function () {}};
    serialize(victim, {ignoreFunction: true});
    Object.keys(victim)   // ['a'] — `f` is gone from the caller's object

    serialize(require('fs'), {ignoreFunction: true});   // leaves fs with 4 of its 104 keys
    serialize(Object.freeze({a: 1, f: function () {}}), {ignoreFunction: true});
    // TypeError: Cannot delete property 'f' of #<Object>

Because the module is `'use strict'` (`index.js:7`), deleting a non-configurable property
throws, so a frozen or sealed input aborts serialization after part of the object has
already been modified.

**Impact:** The caller's data — including shared module singletons and freeze-protected
objects — is silently mutated or the call throws mid-way. Upstream fixed this in commit
45e5397 ("fix: ignore functions without mutating input objects"). Reach is contained (the
caller's own objects) and it needs a non-default option, so it is low.

**Fix:** Do not mutate the input. Walk a copy (or build the output from a filtered clone) so
functions are omitted without deleting them from the source object.

summary:
PR #1 adds `server.js`, a small demo server: a `ws` WebSocket server on `localhost:8090`, an `http` static-file server on port 8080 that streams `__dirname + normalized(req.url)`, and a stdin broadcast loop. The static handler has no document root and listens on all interfaces, and failures are returned as `200` with the raw error string.

My main suspicion — the CVE-2017-16107 `../` traversal — did not reproduce on POSIX: `req.url` always starts with `/`, so `path.normalize` clamps at `/`, and llhttp rejects relative request targets. An independent investigator reproduced the same result, and confirmed the real exposure instead: any readable file in the package (including `.git/config`) is served to unauthenticated network clients. On Windows the guard does leak, but only as a bounded `..` hop above the package directory; that is folded into the medium finding's evidence rather than filed separately.

The change is a demo/dev server, so the two zero-severity-consequence items are `info`; nothing here justifies blocking the merge on its own once the handler gets a document root and an explicit bind address. Three findings recorded (one medium, two info), and the working tree is unchanged.

findings.title: Unauthenticated clients can read any file in the package directory
findings.body:
The HTTP handler on port 8080 serves any readable file under `__dirname` to anyone who
can reach the port, with no document root and no authentication.

`server.js:10` builds the path as `__dirname + path.normalize(req.url).replace(...)` and
passes it straight to `fs.createReadStream`. Nothing checks that the resolved path stays
inside a directory meant to be served, and every name under the package root is therefore
reachable. `hserver.listen(8080)` (`server.js:34`) has no host argument, so it binds all
interfaces — the WebSocket server by contrast passes `host: 'localhost'`
(`server.js:4-7`).

**Preconditions:** the demo server is running (it is the package `main` and the
`npm start` target, `package.json:7,26`), and a client can reach port 8080.

**Evidence:** reproduced with a byte-identical copy of `server.js` plus a stub `ws`
module:

- `GET /package.json` → 200 + full `package.json`
- `GET /.git/config` → 200 + git config; `.git/FETCH_HEAD` and `.git/logs/HEAD` are
  equally readable, and a configured remote URL normally carries credentials
- `GET /server.js`, `GET /node_modules/ws/index.js` → 200
- reachable over a non-loopback address (`http://172.17.0.2:18081/.git/config` → 200);
  `/proc/net/tcp6` shows the listener on `::`

The regex guard does not make this containment. `'../'` payloads do not escape on POSIX:
`req.url` always starts with `/`, so `path.posix.normalize` clamps at `/`, and llhttp
answers 400 for relative request targets. On Windows the guard leaks: every URL starting
with `//` survives as a UNC-shaped path, e.g. `//../../x` → `\\..\..\x`, and
`'C:\\app' + '\\\\..\\..\\x'` is dot-trimmed by Win32 to `C:\x`, above `__dirname`.

**Impact:** a developer running the demo on a shared network exposes the whole checkout —
sources, `package.json`, and `.git` metadata that often holds remote credentials. Reach is
unauthenticated and remote; damage is bounded to files readable under the package
directory on POSIX, which is why this is medium rather than high.

**Fix:** restore one invariant — the resolved path must stay inside a fixed document
root. Serve from `const root = path.join(__dirname, 'public')`, resolve
`path.resolve(root, '.' + req.url)`, answer 403 when the result is neither `root` nor
prefixed by `root + path.sep`, and give `listen()` an explicit host.

findings.title: Failed requests return 200 with the server's absolute path in the body
findings.body:
Every response, including failures, is sent as HTTP 200 with the raw error string as the
body, so the server's absolute filesystem paths are disclosed to clients.

`server.js:17-19` calls `res.end(e + '')` and never sets `res.statusCode` or a status
line, so a missing file yields `200 OK` with a body like
`Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/srv/app/etc/passwd'`. A request for `/`
returns `200` with `Error: EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, read`.

**Evidence:** `curl -s --path-as-is -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8080/../t/secret.txt`
→ `200` with the message `open '/tmp/t/app2/t/secret.txt'`, i.e. the install path; same for
`/` and `/%00`.

**Impact:** discloses the server's absolute install path and lets a client probe for file
existence. Clients also treat the error text as a successful resource. The worst outcome
is genuine but negligible, hence info.

**Fix:** set `res.statusCode` (404 for `ENOENT`, 403 for `EACCES`, 500 otherwise) and send
a short generic body instead of the error object's `toString()`.

findings.title: Web pages can attach to the demo WebSocket and read the console broadcast
findings.body:
Any web page loaded in a browser on the host can open a socket to the demo WebSocket
server and receives everything the server's operator types on its console.

The WebSocket server (`server.js:23-33`) has no `verifyClient` or `Origin` check, so a
cross-origin page may connect to `ws://localhost:8090`. `process.stdin.on('data')`
(`server.js:35-39`) then sends every chunk read from stdin to all sockets in `clients`,
including the page's socket.

**Preconditions:** the demo server is running and the operator visits a hostile page;
the operator must type something of interest into the server's console.

**Evidence:** `server.js:35-39` iterates `clients` and calls `ws.send(data)` with no
authentication; the constructor at `server.js:4-7` sets only `host` and `port`, so `ws`
accepts any handshake regardless of `Origin`.

**Impact:** the browser-side attacker reads console input echoed by the demo server while
the page is open. Value is limited to what the operator types into a demo console, so
info.

**Fix:** require authenticated clients (a token compared in `verifyClient`) or at least
check `Origin` against an expected value before adding a socket to `clients`.

summary:
Review complete.

The change adds `library.js`, the 0.6.3-era version of the Blog Comments plugin: it exposes a public JSON feed of a forum topic plus two POST handlers that reply to and publish topics on behalf of the caller. The dominant issue is the one upstream fixed in 0.7.0 — both POST routes are registered without `middleware.applyCSRF` (unlike the GET beside them), and NodeBB 1.12 applies CSRF only per route and sets no `SameSite` on its session cookie, so a hostile page can post replies, and publish topics and rewrite the article-id mapping, under a logged-in user's identity (CVE-2020-15156).

I also confirmed the unescaped `url`-into-HTML linkback at `library.js:219` is dead code on supported NodeBB versions (the `filter:posts.custom_profile_info` payload has no `pid` since 0.5.6), so I did not report it. Two smaller issues are recorded: an open redirect through the reply handler's body-supplied `url`, and a missing readability check on the comments feed. Separately, `ozone knowledge save` accepts writes but never persists them; I filed an environment report for that.

findings.title: Cross-site POSTs can post replies and articles as a logged-in user because the plugin's POST routes skip CSRF verification
findings.body:
The plugin registers its two state-changing routes without CSRF verification, so any page a logged-in user visits can make the forum post as them.

**Preconditions:** The victim is logged in to NodeBB and visits an attacker-controlled page. For `/comments/publish` the victim must be an administrator or a member of the `publishers` group; for `/comments/reply` any logged-in user is enough.

**Evidence:**
- `library.js:250` puts `middleware.applyCSRF` on the GET, but `library.js:251-252` register `POST /comments/reply` and `POST /comments/publish` with no middleware at all. The plugin's own forms already submit `_csrf` (`public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:15,64,89`), so the token is collected and never checked.
- NodeBB 1.12 does not apply CSRF globally. `src/middleware/index.js:34` only aliases `csrf()` into `middleware.applyCSRF`; every one of the 12 call sites is per-route (`src/routes/index.js:37,102`, `src/routes/api.js:13,40`, `src/routes/authentication.js:67,114-118`, `src/routes/admin.js:12`, `src/middleware/header.js:32`), and `src/webserver.js:133-209` installs no CSRF middleware. Plugin routes are mounted on the same router (`src/routes/index.js:94,113,144`), so a tokenless cross-site POST reaches the handlers.
- NodeBB 1.12 also sets no `SameSite` on the session cookie (`src/webserver.js:219-240`, `setupCookie()` sets only `maxAge`/`domain`/`secure`/`path`), so a browser that honours the attribute only when present attaches the session cookie to the forged POST.
- An attacker-chosen form body then flows straight into core: `library.js:124` calls `topics.reply({tid, uid, content})` with the victim's `uid` and attacker-chosen `tid`/`content`, and `library.js:178-192` calls `topics.post(...)` plus `posts.setPostField(pid, 'blog-comments:url', url)` and `db.setObjectField('blog-comments', commentID, tid)` with attacker-chosen `title`, `markdown`, `url`, `cid`, `tags` and `id`. `topics.reply`/`topics.post` do check category privileges for the *victim's* uid (`src/topics/create.js:113-136,207-283`), but nothing binds the request to the victim.
- This is exactly what upstream 0.7.0 fixed: commit `cf43beedb05131937ef46f365ab0a0c6fa6ac618` ("fix: CSRF issues") only adds `middleware.applyCSRF` to these two lines (CVE-2020-15156, GHSA-43m5-c88r-cjvv).

**Impact:** A third party can post replies and, when the victim is an admin or publisher, publish topics and overwrite the `blog-comments` article-id mapping — all attributed to the victim. That crosses a trust boundary (an outsider acts through another user's account) and is recoverable (a moderator can delete the posts), so high. Two limits, named: a browser that defaults cookies to `SameSite=Lax` blocks the cookie on a cross-site top-level POST, so this lands on browsers/configurations that do not; and the victim must take the bait.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that every state-changing route verifies a token issued to the same session: add `middleware.applyCSRF` to both POST registrations, as upstream did.

findings.title: Reply handler redirects to an arbitrary URL supplied in the request body
findings.body:
Both POST handlers send the browser to a URL taken verbatim from the request body, so a link hosted anywhere can bounce visitors to an attacker's site under a legitimate-looking forum interaction.

**Evidence:** `library.js:121` reads `url = req.body.url`, then `library.js:131` and `library.js:134` do `res.redirect(url + '?error=' + ...)` / `res.redirect(url + '#nodebb-comments')`. Nothing compares `url` with `blog-comments:url` (the host allowlist used at `library.js:62-74,148-160`) or validates the scheme. A page at `evil.example` posting `<form action="https://forum.example/comments/reply" method="post"><input name="url" value="https://evil.example/phish">…</form>` gets a `302 Location: https://evil.example/phish#nodebb-comments`. The error branch fires even without a session, because `topics.reply` rejects `uid = 0` and the handler still redirects.

**Impact:** Phishing pivot: the victim leaves a forum-originated form submit on an attacker-chosen page. No data or capability crosses the trust boundary, and the redirect is a one-shot action, so low.

**Fix:** Redirect only to a URL whose origin is in the configured `blog-comments:url` list, or derive the target from the post's stored `blog-comments:url` field and fall back to `/` when the request value does not match.

findings.title: Comments endpoint returns posts and category data for topics the caller cannot read
findings.body:
The public comments endpoint serves a topic's posts, its category and its main post to any caller, including guests, without checking that the caller may read that topic or its category.

**Evidence:** `library.js:36-60` calls `topics.getTopicPosts(tid, ..., uid, true, next)`, `topics.getTopicField(tid, 'postcount', next)`, `topics.getCategoryData(tid, next)` and `topics.getMainPost(tid, uid, next)` directly with `uid = req.user ? req.user.uid : 0` (`library.js:30`), and returns the results as JSON at `library.js:100-113`. None of these are authorization layers: `Topics.getTopicPosts` (`src/topics/posts.js:27-44`), `Topics.getMainPosts` (`src/topics/index.js:305-316`) and `Topics.getCategoryData` (`src/topics/data.js:61-70`) read storage and filter only on `deleted`. NodeBB's own topic page checks first — `topicsController.get` calls `privileges.topics.get(tid, req.uid, …)` and refuses when `readable` is false (`src/controllers/topics.js:34-50`) — and the plugin has no equivalent. The only gate on the route is CSRF middleware for token minting (`library.js:250`).

**Preconditions:** The comment/topic id must be present in the `blog-comments` hash, and the topic must sit in a category the caller cannot read (a restricted or staff-only category, or a category whose privileges changed after the comments were created). Ids are small integers, so they are enumerable.

**Impact:** A guest can read posts, author data, category metadata and the article body of a topic the category privileges deny them. The disclosure is limited to content that already lives in the forum and needs a non-public category, so low.

**Fix:** Before returning data, check readability for the caller (`privileges.topics.get(tid, uid)` or `topics.isReadable`) and answer with an error when it fails, the same way core's topic controller does.

findings.title: Credential handlers and requestOptions.headers still send Authorization to a different hostname on redirect
findings.body:
The new redirect guard deletes `authorization` only from the `headers` argument, but the
redirected request is built by `_prepareRequest`, which re-merges
`requestOptions.headers` and re-runs every `IRequestHandler.prepareRequest` on the new
header set. Credentials injected that way are sent to the different hostname anyway, so
the leak this PR is meant to close stays open in the library's primary auth paths.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:389-397` strips from `headers`; `index.ts:400` then calls
`_prepareRequest`, which does `info.options.headers = this._mergeHeaders(headers)`
(`index.ts:553`, re-adding `requestOptions.headers` at `index.ts:574-579`) and then
`handler.prepareRequest(info.options)` (`index.ts:562-563`, which assigns `Authorization`
at `auth.ts:13`, `auth.ts:42`, `auth.ts:70`).

Reproduced against two local servers, origin `http://127.0.0.1:P1` returning
`302 Location: http://localhost:P2/x`, capturing the request headers at `P2`:

| client configured with | header seen at the redirect target |
|---|---|
| `get(url, {authorization: 'SECRET'})` | none (fixed) |
| `new BearerCredentialHandler('SECRET')` | `Bearer SECRET` |
| `new PersonalAccessTokenCredentialHandler('SECRET')` | `Basic UEFUOlNFQ1JFVA==…` |
| `new BasicCredentialHandler('user','SECRET')` | `Basic dXNlcjpTRUNSRVQ=…` |
| `{headers: {authorization: 'SECRET'}}` in requestOptions | `SECRET` |

**Impact:** An origin (or anyone who can make the origin answer with a cross-host
redirect) still receives the action's Basic/Bearer/PAT credential, which is exactly the
token exposure CVE-2020-11021 describes. Reach crosses a trust boundary — the receiving
host is a third party the caller never addressed — and a disclosed secret cannot be
un-disclosed, so `high` under the standard reach×persistence table. The documented
handler path (README: "Basic, Bearer and PAT Support out of the box") is affected for
every hop to a different hostname.

**Fix:** Strip after every header source is applied. Simplest: in `request`, remember the
original hostname and, when the redirect target differs, call `_prepareRequest` and then
delete any `authorization` key from `info.options.headers` (case-insensitively) before
`requestRaw`; alternatively stop applying `handlers`/`requestOptions.headers` for a
cross-host redirect hop.

findings.title: Cross-host redirect deletes Authorization from the caller's headers object, so later requests lose auth
findings.body:
The redirect guard calls `delete headers[header]` on the object the caller passed in, not
