on a copy. After one cross-host redirect the caller's reusable header map has lost its
authorization entry, so later requests made with the same object silently go
unauthenticated; a frozen or sealed header object makes the request throw instead.

**Evidence:** `index.ts:390-397` mutates the caller's `headers` (the same object
`get`/`post` receive, `index.ts:164-207`). Reproduction:

```
const headers = {authorization: 'Bearer TOKEN'}
await client.get('http://127.0.0.1:A/a', headers)   // A answers 302 to http://localhost:B/
await client.get('http://127.0.0.1:A/b', headers)   // same trusted origin
// server A receives: [null]
```

`await client.get(url, Object.freeze({authorization: 'Bearer T2'}))` through the same
redirect throws `TypeError: Cannot delete property 'authorization' of #<Object>` after
the redirect response body was already consumed, so the request fails with an error
unrelated to the HTTP exchange.

**Impact:** Contained to the calling process and recoverable (the caller can rebuild the
header map), but it silently downgrades authenticated requests to anonymous ones, which
surfaces as 401/404 from the API rather than a clear error. `low`.

**Fix:** Copy before stripping, e.g. `headers = {...headers}`, or delete from
`info.options.headers` after `_prepareRequest` instead of from the caller's object.

summary:
I reviewed the full 182-line addition (the `attach-hhvm` deep-link handler in `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js`) and delegated independent verification of the hostname-to-notification path plus a broad probe for other failure modes in the file.

The change adds a deep-link handler that connects to a remote host, opens a file, optionally sets a breakpoint, and attaches the HHVM debugger. The main problem is that the hostname parsed from the link is used unvalidated in HTML-rendered notifications, so a crafted `atom://` link gives script execution in the editor renderer — this matches the upstream CVE fix (host character validation), which this version lacks. I also confirmed a second, functional defect: the breakpoint request calls a method the vended debugger service does not have, so that flow silently fails.

findings.title: Attacker-supplied hostname in attach-hhvm deep link is rendered as HTML in an Atom notification
findings.body: The `attach-hhvm` deep-link handler takes the hostname from the URL, checks only that it looks like a remote Nuclide URI, and interpolates it raw into `atom.notifications.addInfo(...)`. Atom notifications render their message as HTML, so a hostname containing markup executes script inside the editor renderer, which has Node integration — an `atom://` link becomes code execution. The same unescaped value is used in the error notification at `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:136` and as `displayTitle` at line 131. **Preconditions:** The victim opens a crafted `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm?...` link (e.g. from a web page; the browser asks to hand it to Atom). No remote project, SSH host, or successful connection is needed: the notification is created at line 117, before `createRemoteConnection` is awaited at line 127. **Evidence:** Params reach the handler unvalidated from Atom's URI handler (`lib/main.js` `handleURI` → `sendDeepLink`, delivered through `DeepLinkService.subscribeToPath`, `pkg/nuclide-deep-link/lib/DeepLinkService.js:107`). The guard at `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:84-87` only requires `nuclideUri.isRemote(nuclidePath)` (a `startsWith('nuclide://')` test, `modules/nuclide-commons/nuclideUri.js:55-57`); the value is then `decodeURIComponent`-ed (line 92) and split at the first `/` by `getHostname`/`parse` (`nuclideUri.js:126-147,157-184`), which accepts any characters, including `<`, `>`, `"`, `=` and spaces. The decoded host is then put into the notification message at line 117-121. Input `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm?nuclidePath=nuclide://%3Cimg%20src=x%20onerror=alert(document.domain)%3E/tmp/hack/x.php&hackRoot=/tmp/hack` yields `host = ` and the message `Connecting to and attaching debugger...`. That notification messages are HTML is stated in this repo (`pkg/nuclide-atom-notifications/lib/main.js:65`: "Markdown and HTML can be used with Atom notifications") and relied on by other call sites, e.g. `pkg/nuclide-remote-projects/lib/notification.js:22` wraps values in ``. **Impact:** An unauthenticated remote party who gets the link followed gains script execution in the Atom renderer, i.e. arbitrary command execution with the developer's privileges on their machine and on any host their SSH agent reaches — code execution, permanent, across a trust boundary. The one discount applied: the victim must follow the link and approve the protocol handoff. **Fix:** Reject hostnames that are not valid per RFC 952 before using them, e.g. `if (host.match(/[^A-Za-z0-9\-._]+/) != null) { atom.notifications.addError('The specified host name contained invalid characters.'); return; }` after line 115 (this is the upstream fix), or HTML-escape the host wherever it is placed in a notification message.

findings.title: attach-hhvm deep link with addBreakpoint=true throws on a missing service method and never starts the debugger
findings.body:
When an `attach-hhvm` deep link asks for a breakpoint
(`addBreakpoint=true` plus a line number), the handler calls
`debuggerService.addBreakpoint(navUri, lineNumber - 1)` at
`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:170`. The object returned by
`consumeFirstProvider('nuclide-debugger.remote')` has no `addBreakpoint`
method, so the call throws a `TypeError`. Because the throw happens before
`startDebugging` (line 173), the debugger never attaches, and because the
deep-link subscriber at lines 65-67 neither awaits nor catches the promise,
the rejection is lost and the "Connecting to ..." notification created at
line 117 is never dismissed.

**Evidence:** Both providers of `nuclide-debugger.remote` vend the
`RemoteControlService` class: `pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/main.js:973-975` and
`pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/main.js:886-888`. Its public methods are
`startDebugging`, `getCurrentDebuggerName`,
`canLaunchDebugTargetInTerminal`, `launchDebugTargetInTerminal`
(`pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/RemoteControlService.js:39,47,68,73`, and the same
set in `pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/RemoteControlService.js`). Breakpoints
are set through other objects: `DebuggerActions.addBreakpoint`
(`pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/DebuggerActions.js:448`) and
`DebugService.addBreakpoints`
(`pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/vsp/DebugService.js:988`). Upstream later
replaced this line with
`atom.commands.dispatch(atom.views.getView(atom.workspace), 'debugger:add-breakpoint')`.

**Impact:** The documented breakpoint-on-attach flow fails silently: no
debugger session starts and the user sees a stuck dismissable notification
instead of an error. Contained to the one deep link and cleared by dropping
the flag, hence low.

**Fix:** Set the breakpoint through a supported path — dispatch
`debugger:add-breakpoint` after opening the file, as the later upstream
version does — instead of calling a method that the vended service does not
have.

summary:
Review complete. Six findings recorded, each reproduced against a build of the tree.

**What the change is:** a single new file, `index.ts` (760 lines) — the whole `@actions/http-client` entry point, including its redirect handling, credential handlers wiring, proxy/agent selection, retries and JSON helpers. The baseline had no `index.ts` at all, so every behaviour in it is new surface.

**Assessment:** the redirect code that tries to keep credentials on the origin host is the highest-risk part, and it does not hold: it strips only per-call headers while handlers and client-level headers re-inject `Authorization` on every hop, which I reproduced end to end with `Bearer`, PAT and Basic credentials arriving at a second host. The rest are confirmed but narrower: a body-read that never settles on a broken connection, an `ignoreSslError` client mutating the process-wide global agent, relative `Location` targets losing their host, keep-alive agent reuse across protocols, and 303 redirects replaying the verb and body. Correctness elsewhere (retry/backoff, proxy tunnel setup, header merging, response parsing) read as intended given its upstream design.

findings.title: Redirect to another hostname re-sends handler and client-level Authorization headers
findings.body:
Following a redirect to a different hostname re-sends a credential that came from a
credential handler or from the client-level `requestOptions.headers`. Only an
`authorization` header passed per call is stripped.

The strip block at index.ts:389-397 deletes `authorization` from the caller's
per-request `headers` object. That object is not what gets sent: `_prepareRequest`
builds `info.options.headers` as a fresh object via `_mergeHeaders`
(index.ts:553, 570-583), then re-runs every `IRequestHandler.prepareRequest`
(index.ts:561-565), which writes `Authorization` unconditionally (auth.ts:13,
auth.ts:42, auth.ts:70). Each redirect hop calls `_prepareRequest` again
(index.ts:400), so the header is re-injected regardless of what the strip removed.

**Preconditions:** the client carries a credential handler (the documented auth
path, and what `@actions/*` callers use) or `requestOptions.headers.Authorization`;
a followed redirect targets a different hostname. Both are defaults.

**Evidence:** built the tree (`npm install && npx tsc`) and ran two local servers —
A on `127.0.0.1` answers `302 Location: http://localhost:<port>/final`, B records
received headers:

- `new HttpClient('ua', [new BearerCredentialHandler('SECRET')])` → B saw
  `authorization: Bearer SECRET`
- `new HttpClient('ua', [], {headers: {authorization: 'Bearer SECRET2'}})` → B saw
  `Bearer SECRET2`
- `PersonalAccessTokenCredentialHandler('PATSECRET')` → B saw
  `Basic UEFUOlBBVFNFQ1JFVA==` (`PAT:PATSECRET`)
- control `get(url, {authorization: 'Bearer X'})` → stripped, which is the only
  case the new tests cover (__tests__/basics.test.ts:182, :205)

**Impact:** a redirect to any other host (compromised or attacker-influenced
endpoint, an open redirect on a trusted host, or a legitimate CDN hop) receives the
Bearer token, PAT, or Basic password. The secret crosses a trust boundary and the
exposure is permanent, so this is `high` under the standard reach/persistence
table; no discount applies because redirects and credential handlers are both
default paths.

**Fix:** enforce the invariant after the headers are assembled, not on the caller's
object: when the redirect hostname differs from the original hostname, delete
`authorization` from `info.options.headers` between index.ts:400 and index.ts:401
(and skip re-adding it in later hops). Leave the caller's `headers` untouched.

findings.title: ignoreSslError disables TLS verification for unrelated https requests in the process
findings.body:
One client built with `ignoreSslError: true` turns off TLS certificate
verification for every other https request in the process that uses the global
agent.

`_getAgent` falls back to `https.globalAgent` when there is no tunnel or keep-alive
agent (index.ts:660-662) and then assigns `rejectUnauthorized: false` onto that
shared object's `options` (index.ts:664-670). The comment above it says the point
is to avoid a process-wide effect; mutating `https.globalAgent` is exactly that
effect.

**Preconditions:** one caller passes `ignoreSslError: true` (non-default); other
https requests in the same process then use the global agent.

**Evidence:** with the built tree, `new HttpClient('ua', [], {ignoreSslError:
true}).getAgent('https://example.com')` leaves
`require('https').globalAgent.options.rejectUnauthorized === false`, and
`new HttpClient('ua2').getAgent('https://example.org') === https.globalAgent` —
the unrelated client gets the same unverified agent.

**Impact:** any subsequent https request in the process silently accepts invalid
certificates, so a network attacker can intercept it and its credentials. Reach is
broad but the setting is non-default, which discounts the severity to `low`.

**Fix:** never mutate `https.globalAgent.options`; create a dedicated
`https.Agent({rejectUnauthorized: false})` for the requesting client and keep it in
`this._agent`, or set `rejectUnauthorized` on the per-request options.

findings.title: Relative redirect Location is never resolved, so the follow-up request has no host
findings.body:
A redirect whose `Location` is relative (`/next`) is parsed without a base URL, so
the follow-up request has no host. Over http it is sent to `127.0.0.1:80`; over
https it throws a misleading "Redirect from HTTPS to HTTP protocol" error and the
request fails.

`url.parse(redirectUrl)` at index.ts:374 yields `hostname: null` and
`protocol: null` for a relative target. `_prepareRequest` then sets
`info.options.host = null` (index.ts:546), and Node dials `localhost`. For an
https origin, the downgrade guard at index.ts:375-383 compares `'https:'` against
`null` and throws.

**Preconditions:** a server returns a relative `Location` and redirects are
enabled (default). Relative `Location` headers are common.

**Evidence:** local http server answering `302 Location: /final`, client
`get('http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start')` → `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:80`.
Same server over https → `Redirect from HTTPS to HTTP protocol. This downgrade is
not allowed for security reasons.`

**Impact:** redirects to relative targets, a documented feature, break: over https
the call fails with an error that misdirects the user into enabling
`allowRedirectDowngrade`, and over http the request (with any credential headers)
is sent to a local service instead of the origin. Contained to the affected call
and it fails loudly, so `low`.

**Fix:** resolve the target against the current URL, e.g.
`url.resolve(requestUrl, redirectUrl)` (or `new URL(redirectUrl, current).href`),
before comparing protocols and preparing the next request.

findings.title: readBody never settles when the connection breaks mid-body, hanging the caller
findings.body:
`readBody()` never settles if the connection breaks after the response headers
arrive, so `get()`/`post()` and every `<verb>Json` helper hang forever instead of
failing.

`HttpClientResponse.readBody` (index.ts:79-91) listens only for `'data'` and
`'end'`. A destroyed or reset socket after headers emits `'aborted'`/`'error'`, not
`'end'`, so both branches are skipped and the promise stays pending. The request
timeout at index.ts:495-500 only ends the socket; it does not settle the body
promise. The same hang blocks the redirect path, which awaits
`response.readBody()` before following (index.ts:387).

**Preconditions:** the server or an intermediate proxy closes the connection
mid-body — a truncated download or a proxy reset is enough.

**Evidence:** local server sends `Content-Length: 100`, writes `partial`, then
destroys the socket. `await res.readBody()` still had not settled 3 seconds later;
`_processResponse` awaits the same promise (index.ts:716), so an entire action step
hangs with no error.

**Impact:** reach is contained to the affected call, but nothing recovers the
pending promise except process exit, so a CI step stalls indefinitely where the
documented behaviour is to return or throw. That fits `medium` on the
reach/persistence table.

**Fix:** reject on `'error'` and `'aborted'` in `readBody` (and call `reject` in
the existing executor), so a broken connection surfaces as an error.

findings.title: keepAlive client reuses one cached agent across http and https, failing every other protocol
findings.body:
A client created with `keepAlive: true` cannot reach both http and https targets:
the first agent it creates is cached in `_agent`/`_proxyAgent` and reused for every
later host and protocol.

`_getAgent` assigns `this._agent` (or `this._proxyAgent`) on first use
(index.ts:648-657) and returns the cached agent before looking at the target's
protocol or proxy (index.ts:605-616). The cache key is the client, not the
destination.

**Preconditions:** `keepAlive: true` and a client whose requests mix protocols
(or two different proxies).

**Evidence:** with the built tree, `get('https://127.0.0.1:<port>/')` succeeded,
then `get('http://127.0.0.1:<port>/')` on the same client threw
`Protocol "http:" not supported. Expected "https:"`. `getAgent('https://…') ===
getAgent('http://…')` is true.

**Impact:** the second request fails outright for any client that reuses one
`HttpClient` across http and https endpoints, which is common in Actions code that
targets both `http://` and `https://` API hosts. Contained to that client and
fails loudly, so `low`.

**Fix:** key the cached agents by protocol (and by proxy URL), e.g. keep
`_agent`/`_proxyAgent` in a map keyed by `${protocol}|${proxyUrl}`.

findings.title: 303 See Other redirect replays the original verb and body
findings.body:
A 303 (See Other) redirect is followed with the original verb and body, so a POST
is re-sent to the redirect target and can repeat the write it just performed.

`HttpCodes.SeeOther` is listed in `HttpRedirectCodes` (index.ts:57-63), but the
redirect loop reuses `verb` and `data` unchanged when preparing the next request
(index.ts:400). RFC 7231 requires a 303 to be followed with GET and no body.

**Preconditions:** the server answers a non-GET request with 303; redirects are on
by default.

**Evidence:** local server answers `POST /start` with `303 Location: <abs>/final`
and records requests: it received `POST /start` with body `PAYLOAD`, then
`POST /final` with body `PAYLOAD`.

**Impact:** a server that uses 303 to redirect after a create gets the create
request applied again at the new location (duplicate issue, duplicate upload,
double charge for non-idempotent endpoints). Contained to the caller's request and
depends on the server's choice of 303, so `low`.

**Fix:** when the status code is 303, follow with `GET` and no body; for 307/308
keep the verb and body.

summary:
The change adds `lib/index.ts`, the whole `fs-git` API surface (`open`, `fileList`, `file`, `exists`, `readFile`, `showRef`, `revParse`) built on `git` subprocesses. It is a faithful copy of upstream fs-git before the 1.0.2 fix, so the security-relevant construction (`_buildCommand` plus `child_process.exec`) and the untyped `exec` output both ship as-is; comparing against current upstream shows the later fix replaced the shell string with `execFile` argument arrays and requested `encoding: "buffer"`.

I read all 143 lines, reproduced the shell injection end to end against the bundled bare fixture (through both the ref and the file-path arguments), and reproduced the binary read corrupting bytes and the stdout leak on a repository path containing a space. Three findings are recorded; the high one is the shell injection, which is the defect the upstream fix addresses. Beyond those, the code is a small, straightforward wrapper with no other failure paths I could reach — overall the change needs the injection fix before merge.

findings.title: User-supplied ref, git path, or file path executes as shell commands
findings.body:
`_buildCommand()` joins `this.path`, the ref, and the file path into one string that `child_process.exec()` hands to `/bin/sh`. Any shell metacharacter in those values runs as a separate command under the caller's OS privileges. The values are `open(path, ref)`, `revParse(ref)`, `file(path)`, `exists(path)`, and `readFile(path)` arguments — the ref and file path normally come straight from an application's user input.

**Evidence:** `_buildCommand` at lib/index.ts:125-127, used at lib/index.ts:36, 62, 83, 100. Reproduced against `test/fixture/bare.git` with a faithful port of the class: `open(repo, "master; touch /tmp/pwned_ref #").fileList()` and `readFile("subdir/test.txt; touch /tmp/pwned_path")` both resolved successfully and created their `/tmp/pwned_*` files. The commands executed were `git --git-dir=./test/fixture/bare.git rev-parse master; touch /tmp/pwned_ref #` and `git --git-dir=./test/fixture/bare.git show master:subdir/test.txt; touch /tmp/pwned_path`.

**Impact:** A consumer that passes a ref or path taken from a request (a common use for a "fs-like API for git repositories") lets an unprivileged user run arbitrary commands as the service. This crosses a trust boundary and the result is permanent (data exfiltration or writes), so `high`. The same missing quoting also breaks benign values: any git directory or file name containing a space splits into extra arguments and the call fails.

**Fix:** Never build a shell string. Pass the arguments as an array to `child_process.execFile` (`git`, `["--git-dir=" + this.path, "rev-parse", ref]`) or `spawn`, so no shell parses them. Do not try to escape values by hand.

findings.title: readFile returns a UTF-8-decoded string instead of the declared Buffer, corrupting binary files
findings.body:
`readFile(path)` is declared to return `Promise<Buffer>` (lib/index.ts:57) but resolves with whatever `exec()` yields. `child_process.exec` defaults to UTF-8 decoding, so callers get a string, and binary blobs are mangled by replacement characters before they reach the caller.

**Evidence:** reproduced against a repo containing a committed PNG. `readFile("img.png")` returned `typeof === "string"`, `Buffer.isBuffer === false`; the original `89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 ff fe` came back as `ef bf bd 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a 00 00 ef bf bd ef bf bd`. The resolve site is lib/index.ts:71; the `exec` call at lib/index.ts:64 sets no `encoding`.

**Impact:** Any consumer using the documented no-options overload to read an image, archive, or other non-UTF-8 blob silently receives corrupted data, and TypeScript gives it no warning because the declared type is `Buffer`. The read itself changes nothing, so the damage is limited to the wrong result — `low`.

**Fix:** Read the blob as bytes: use `execFile("git", [...], { encoding: "buffer" })` (or `spawn`) and resolve the raw `Buffer` when no `opts.encoding` is given. Keep the declared overloads as they are.

findings.title: rev-parse failures print the git command to stdout
findings.body:
`revParse()` logs the assembled git command to stdout whenever the command fails. A library has no business writing to its consumer's stdout, and the line contains the repository path and the caller-supplied ref.

**Evidence:** lib/index.ts:88. Opening a repository at `/tmp/my repo/.git` printed `git --git-dir=/tmp/my repo/.git rev-parse master` before the promise rejected.

**Impact:** Consumers that use stdout for their own output (CLI tools, JSON pipelines) get a stray line, and repository paths — potentially sensitive filesystem layout — end up in shared logs. Nothing persists and no capability is granted, so `info`.

**Fix:** Delete the `console.log(command)` line; the rejection already carries the failing command in `error.cmd`.

summary:
PR #1 adds `index.js` (201 lines) to a tree where the package's entry file was missing. The added blob is byte-identical to the post-fix sibling of upstream commit `b1338128` (PR #35), i.e. the release that fixed CVE-2017-18077: line 109 uses `m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0` instead of the exponential `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/`.

I confirmed the CVE path is gone rather than simply absent from the diff: against upstream 1.1.6 the hostile body `'a,'*n + '\n'` (the newline defeats `.`, forcing full backtracking) takes 1.8 s at n=22 and doubles per comma, while this file stays flat at ~2 ms; the other regexes in the file are linear. The `indexOf` replacement is semantically equal to the old regex on every line-terminator-free body and strictly more permissive when a body contains `\n`, which is the bug being fixed, and the full test suite passes (172/172). One real availability defect remains in the imported code — a zero step (`{1..3..0}`) makes the sequence loop spin to heap OOM — which I recorded as `low`; note also that `package.json` still declares version `1.1.6` while the source is the fixed one, so advisory tooling will still flag the package.

findings.title: Step of zero in a brace sequence loops until the process runs out of memory
findings.body:
A brace sequence with an explicit step of zero never terminates: `expand('{1..3..0}')` spins in the
sequence loop, pushing one entry per iteration, until V8 runs out of heap and aborts. The same
happens for alpha sequences (`{a..c..0}`) and reverse ranges (`{5..1..0}`).

`incr` is `Math.abs(numeric(n[2]))` (index.js:153-155), which is `0` when the step is `0`; the loop
at index.js:166 then runs `test(i, y)` with an unchanging `i` (`i += 0`), so the condition is true
forever while `N.push(c)` grows. Bash treats a zero step as 1 (`echo {1..3..0}` prints `1 2 3`).

**Preconditions:** none beyond a pattern reaching the module. `expandTop` (index.js:65) hands any
string containing `{x..y..0}` straight to `expand`; there is no length, depth or count guard.

**Evidence:** from the repo root (dependencies installed):

```
$ timeout 3 node -e "require('./index.js')('{1..3..0}')"; echo $?
124                                  # still running after 3s
$ timeout 60 node --max-old-space-size=64 -e "require('./index.js')('{1..3..0}')"
# ... FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

`{1..3}`, `{a..c}` and `{5..1}` return normally, so the trigger is the zero step alone.

**Impact:** an 11-byte pattern handed to the library blocks the calling process's event loop —
every concurrent request in a Node service — and then crashes it with a heap OOM. Upstream releases
carry the same loop, so this is not a regression of the ReDoS fix this file brings; adding `index.js`
is what makes the path reachable in this repository. Reach is broad (all callers of the process),
recovery is a restart, and the defect predates the change, so severity stays low. Later upstream
releases bound the loop with a maximum expansion count instead.

**Fix:** treat a zero step as one, so the loop always advances, e.g. right after the reverse
handling at index.js:158-160:

```js
if (incr === 0) incr = 1;
```

summary:
The PR adds `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js`: the `attach-hhvm` deep-link handler that validates the hostname against an RFC 952 character allowlist (the CVE-2018-6333 mitigation, blocking HTML injection through the notification message), then opens an SSH remote project and optionally attaches the HHVM debugger. I confirmed the allowlist sits before every message that interpolates `host` (`main.js:119-135`, `147`), so the CSP/CWE-79 sink the CVE describes is closed here.

Two defects remain in the new file: the `addBreakpoint=true` branch calls a method the `nuclide-debugger.remote` service does not implement (both providers verified), so that link variant always rejects before `startDebugging` and leaves its notification behind; and the handler decodes already-decoded query params, so any legit remote path containing `%` throws `URIError`. Neither reaches across a trust boundary; the security fix itself looks correct and complete for this file.

findings.title: Deeplink with addBreakpoint=true throws TypeError and the HHVM debugger never attaches
findings.body:
Opening the HHVM attach deeplink with `addBreakpoint=true` throws before the debugger starts, so the debug session never begins and the "Connecting to …" notification stays on screen.

**Preconditions:** the link is followed with a numeric `line` and `addBreakpoint=true`, e.g. `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm?nuclidePath=nuclide://host/a.php&hackRoot=/a&line=10&addBreakpoint=true`.

**Evidence:** `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:181` calls `debuggerService.addBreakpoint(navUri, lineNumber - 1)`. `debuggerService` comes from `consumeFirstProvider('nuclide-debugger.remote')` (`main.js:174`), which returns the provider object verbatim (`pkg/commons-atom/consumeFirstProvider.js:22-31`). There are exactly two providers of that service — `pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/main.js:973` and `pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/main.js:886` — and neither `pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/RemoteControlService.js:39-108` nor `pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/RemoteControlService.js:34-120` defines `addBreakpoint`; the service surface is `startDebugging`, `getCurrentDebuggerName`, `canLaunchDebugTargetInTerminal`, `launchDebugTargetInTerminal`. Breakpoints are only on `DebuggerActions.addBreakpoint` (`pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/DebuggerActions.js:448`) and `IDebugService.addBreakpoints` (`pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/types.js:353`). The call therefore throws `TypeError: debuggerService.addBreakpoint is not a function` and `startDebugging` at `main.js:184` is never reached. The subscriber at `main.js:66` drops the returned promise, so the failure is an unhandled rejection with no error notification, and `notification.dismiss()` (`main.js:189`) is skipped, leaving the dismissable "Connecting to …" info notification behind.

**Impact:** contained and recoverable — one user action, that link only, nothing persisted — so `low`. The `addBreakpoint` option of this deep link is always broken and its failure is silent.

**Fix:** insert the breakpoint through a supported API and keep it inside a `try`/`catch` that dismisses the notification: open the location first, then `atom.commands.dispatch(atom.views.getView(atom.workspace), 'debugger:add-breakpoint')`, or await `getDebuggerService()` and call `addBreakpoints(uri, [{line: lineNumber - 1}])` on the debug service rather than the remote-control service.

findings.title: Deep links whose remote path contains % abort with URIError and no feedback
findings.body:
An `attach-hhvm` link whose remote path contains a literal `%` aborts with `URIError: URI malformed` before any parameter check, so the link silently does nothing.

**Evidence:** Atom hands packages the already-decoded query object: `package.json:26-29` registers `handleURI`, Atom's `URIHandlerRegistry.handleURI` parses with `url.parse(uri, true)` (query values percent-decoded) and calls it. Nuclide forwards that object unchanged (`lib/main.js:356-365`, `_handleURI({pathname, query})` → `sendDeepLink(..., query)`). The handler then decodes a second time: `pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:92-93` `decodeURIComponent(String(nuclidePath))` / `decodeURIComponent(String(hackRoot))`. A path containing `%` — sent as `%25`, e.g. `hackRoot=/home/u/100%_done` — arrives as `%` and `decodeURIComponent('%')` throws. The throw happens before the argument check at `main.js:83` and before the notification at `main.js:128`, and the subscriber at `main.js:66` drops the returned promise, so the user sees no error at all.

**Impact:** `info` — contained and transient; only the followed link fails and nothing is persisted. The practical effect is that deep links for legitimate paths containing `%` never work and give no feedback.

**Fix:** remove the redundant `decodeURIComponent` (the params are already decoded), or wrap both decodes in `try`/`catch` and report a bad-argument notification.

summary:
I've completed the review. Verification steps I ran:

- Read the full diff; the added `lib/index.ts` is byte-identical to upstream vvakame/fs-git commit `eb5f70e` ("fix(fs-git): fix command injection"), the published fix for CVE-2017-16087.
- Confirmed all four git invocations in `lib/index.ts:32,58,80,96` go through `child_process.execFile(base, args, …)` with an argv array and no `shell` option; the `--git-dir=<path>` prefix is a single argv element (`lib/index.ts:119-124`), so the old shell-string injection is gone. Empirically, `--git-dir=/tmp/x; touch /tmp/marker` reaches git literally and creates no file.
- Compiled the file with the pinned TypeScript 1.7.5 and exercised the built module against `test/fixture/bare.git`: `showRef`, `fileList`, `file`, `exists`, `readFile` (both Buffer and `{encoding}` overloads), plus branch and tag refs all behave as the specs expect.
- Checked the Node 4.3 target named in `circle.yml`/`appveyor.yml`: `execFile`'s `encoding: "buffer"` is supported there (node v4.3.0 `lib/child_process.js:162`), so the `readFile(): Promise<Buffer>` overload is not regressed on the supported runtime.

The change replaces shell command construction with argv-based `execFile` across every git call site and adds no new dependencies or public API change. It is a complete, minimal fix; the residual weaknesses in the file (regex parsing of `ls-tree` output, lack of `--` argument separators before caller-supplied `ref`/`path`) predate this change and need an application that forwards untrusted refs to reach, so I found nothing worth filing.

The change re-adds `index.js` from brace-expansion 1.1.6, the bash-style brace-expansion library. The code is functional and its 172 tests pass, but the added `expand()` has two denial-of-service paths reachable from an untrusted pattern: the comma/newline regex backtracking fixed upstream in 1.1.7 (CVE-2017-18077), and a zero-increment sequence loop that allocates until the heap is exhausted. Both were reproduced against the checked-out code and recorded as findings.

findings.title: expand() hangs exponentially on comma-heavy brace patterns containing a newline
findings.body:
`expand()` hangs when a brace body contains many commas followed by a character that `.` does not match (for example a newline). The `isOptions` check at `index.js:109` uses `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/`, which backtracks over every way of partitioning the comma runs once the trailing newline makes the match fail. Each extra comma roughly doubles the work, so a ~30-byte pattern blocks the caller indefinitely.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes an untrusted string to `expand()` (directly, or through a consumer such as `minimatch`/`glob` matching a user-supplied pattern). No other setting is needed.

**Evidence:** measured with the checked-out code (`node -e`, timing `require('./index.js')('{' + 'a,'.repeat(n) + 'a\n}')`):

- n=18: 195 ms
- n=20: 637 ms
- n=22: 3021 ms
- n=24: 9164 ms
- `'{' + ','.repeat(25) + '\n}'` did not finish within 15 s (30 commas exceeded a 120 s timeout).

A plain body without a newline (`{,}`, `{a,a,a}`) matches immediately, because `.` consumes everything up to `$`; the newline (or `\r`, `\u2028`, `\u2029`) is what forces the failing backtrack.

**Impact:** availability-only denial of service. In a Node server, one small unauthenticated input pins the single event loop where `expand()` runs, so every request served by that process stops responding. The runaway call does not terminate on its own; the process has to be restarted, and an attacker can repeat the input at will. Reproduced above, so the severity is set from demonstrated impact rather than the CVE rating alone.

**Fix:** replace `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/.test(m.body)` with a linear check for the presence of a comma, `m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0`. That preserves the "is a comma set" meaning (the regex has no other constraint) and removes the backtracking, which is the upstream fix in brace-expansion 1.1.7.

findings.title: Zero-increment sequences loop forever and exhaust memory
findings.body:
A numeric or alphabetic sequence whose increment is `0` never advances the loop at `index.js:166`. `incr = Math.abs(numeric(n[2]))` (`index.js:153-155`) yields `0`, the `for (var i = x; test(i, y); i += incr)` condition stays true, and every iteration pushes another string into `N`. The call allocates until the heap is exhausted.

**Evidence:** `expand('{1..5..0}')` aborted with `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory` after ~5 s under `node --max-old-space-size=256`. `expand('{a..z..0}')` takes the same path. Bash treats a zero increment as 1 (`printf '%s\n' {1..5..0}` prints 1..5), so this is also incorrect expansion, not just resource use.

**Impact:** availability-only denial of service from a 9-byte unauthenticated input; the process must be restarted. Every caller that expands an untrusted pattern can be taken down. The bug is present in upstream brace-expansion through 2.0.2, but the whole of `index.js` is added by this change, so it is new code in this branch.

**Fix:** reject or default a zero increment before the loop, e.g. `var incr = n.length === 3 ? Math.abs(numeric(n[2])) : 1; if (!incr) incr = 1;`, matching Bash's behaviour.

summary: The change re-adds `lib/extend.js` (the only file in the diff), a port of jQuery.extend, with `index.js` as the entry point. I reproduced prototype pollution against this tree: `extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"polluted": "yes"}}'))` makes `({}).polluted === "yes"`, via `src = target[name]` resolving to `Object.prototype` and the deep branch recursing into it (lib/extend.js:43-61). The `constructor.prototype` variant does not pollute, so it was refuted; the existing suite passes 83/83 because it has no `__proto__` case. One high finding recorded; the fix is an own-property guard or defineProperty-based access as in upstream 2.0.1.

findings.title: Deep extend on untrusted input pollutes Object.prototype
findings.body:
Deep merges let an attacker write to `Object.prototype`, so every object created
afterwards in the same process carries the attacker's properties. Trigger: any
caller that deep-extends untrusted data, e.g. JSON from a request body or config
file.

**Preconditions:** the consumer calls `extend(true, target, source)` where
`source` contains an own `__proto__` key — the normal shape of attacker-supplied
JSON (JSON.parse creates `__proto__` as an own, enumerable property).

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:43-44` reads the source key with plain bracket
access, so for `name === '__proto__'` `src` resolves to `Object.prototype`
through the prototype chain instead of the caller's own data. `is.hash(src)` is
true, so line 57 picks `clone = src` — the real `Object.prototype` — and line 61
recurses with it as the target, writing the attacker's keys onto it.

Reproduced against this tree:

```js
var extend = require('./index');
extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"polluted": "yes"}}'));
({}).polluted; // "yes" — inherited by every object in the process
```

The nested form `{"a": {"__proto__": {...}}}` pollutes the same way. The
regression suite (`test/index.js`) has no `__proto__` case, so it passes (83/83)
despite the bug.

**Impact:** Untrusted input gains write access to the shared `Object.prototype`
of the host process — a capability no caller grants it. Anything that relies on
object shape afterwards (auth checks like `user.isAdmin`, template rendering,
cache lookups, `for...in` loops, option defaults) can be steered by the
attacker. Reach is broad (every consumer of the library) and crosses a trust
boundary, so **high** under the review policy; persistence is recoverable — the
pollution is re-triggerable at will and cleared only by a process restart.

**Fix:** never let a merge read or write `__proto__` through the prototype
chain. Smallest change: add a guard at the top of the loop
(`if (name === '__proto__') { continue; }`), or follow node.extend 2.0.1, which
reads keys via an own-property-aware `getProperty` and writes them with
`Object.defineProperty` in `setProperty`. Add a test asserting `({}).polluted`
is still undefined after `extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"polluted": 1}}'))`.

summary:
The PR adds `lib/print.js`, the console/debug helper module (`print`, `log`, `err`, `print_options`, `plugin_options`, `print_tree`) that `seneca.js` and the other internal modules require. The file itself is sound structurally, declares only existing dependencies, and loads cleanly; I also ran the fatal-error path end to end to check the one security-relevant behavior in it.

One issue recorded: the crash-report sink `Print.err` (`lib/print.js:138`) writes a report that embeds the full `process.env` (`lib/common.js:345`) in cleartext whenever `debug.print.fatal` is `'full'` and test mode is on — reproduced locally, and confirmed suppressed by the upstream `debug.print.env: false` gate. Severity `low` because it needs two non-default debug settings and only reaches the process's own stderr.

findings.title: Fatal error report sends the full process environment to stderr in cleartext
findings.body:
A fatal error makes Seneca write the whole process environment to stderr in cleartext.
`Print.err` (`lib/print.js:138`) is the sink for the crash report built in
`exports.makedie`, whose `PROCESS :::` line appends
`', env=' + Util.inspect(process.env)` (`lib/common.js:345`) whenever
`debug.print.fatal` is `'full'`. Callers that emit it: `lib/common.js:416` and
`lib/common.js:437`. Every variable in the host environment — database passwords,
API keys, cloud credentials — reaches the process log through a helper whose only
job is to write to the console.

**Preconditions:** options `debug.print.fatal: 'full'` (default is `'summary'`,
`seneca.js:81`) and test mode (`so.test`, i.e. `Seneca({test: true})` or the
`SENECA_TEST` environment variable, `lib/optioner.js:91-92`); then any unhandled
fatal error, e.g. a plugin init failure.

**Evidence:** setting `SECRET_TOKEN=super-secret-value-123` in the environment and
running

```js
Seneca({ test: true, debug: { print: { fatal: 'full' } } }).die(new Error('boom'))
```

prints `env={  HOSTNAME: ..., SECRET_TOKEN: 'super-secret-value-123', ... }` to
stderr, twice (close path and death-delay path). Gating the segment on a
`debug.print.env` flag suppresses it (tested: zero occurrences).

**Impact:** anyone who reads the service's logs — a log aggregator, a hosted log
vendor, a support engineer — receives the full environment of the process, which is
permanently retained in the log store. The leak needs two non-default debug
settings and only reaches the process's own stderr, which keeps it below high.

**Fix:** make environment printing opt-in: gate `lib/common.js:345` on a new
`debug.print.env` option defaulting to `false` (upstream fixed it this way in
`b0565ba`). The same module also dumps entire option objects
(`lib/print.js:51`, `lib/print.js:149`), but those paths are separate, explicitly
requested features, not part of this leak.

summary:
Recorded two findings. Summary of the review:

The PR re-adds `lib/extend.js` (106 lines), restoring node.extend's implementation — byte-identical to the released node.extend@2.0.1, including the `__proto__` guards (`setProperty` writes `__proto__` via `Object.defineProperty`, `getProperty` returns `undefined` unless `__proto__` is an own property). I probed the prototype-pollution surface empirically: 5,440 key-path/target-shape combinations plus inherited-key, accessor, array, `constructor.prototype`, null-prototype and `is.hash`-spoofing vectors all leave `Object.prototype` clean, and the unpatched 2.0.0 file served as a positive control. The CVE-2018-16491 path is closed.

The file was added without the rest of its upstream commit, which breaks the package and the build: the new `require('has')` has no matching `dependencies` entry (production installs throw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at require time, masked in this repo because devDependencies pull `has` in transitively), and the new 3-parameter helper trips the repo's `max-params` eslint rule so `npm test` exits 1. Merge behavior changes I saw (caller-object aliasing, frozen-target `TypeError`, cycle stack overflow) match the pre-existing 2.0.0 semantics and are not introduced here.

findings.title: Production install fails at require: the file needs the undeclared 'has' dependency
findings.body:
`lib/extend.js` requires the module `has`, but `package.json` declares only `is` under
`dependencies`. A production install of the package (`npm install --omit=dev`, which is what
every consumer gets) installs `is` alone, so `require('node.extend')` throws
`Error: Cannot find module 'has'` before any code runs. The library is unusable for every
consumer.

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:13` (`var has = require('has');`) versus `package.json:14-16`
(`"dependencies": { "is": "^3.2.1" }`). Reproduced in a scratch copy:

```
cp -r <repo> /tmp/t2 && cd /tmp/t2 && npm install --omit=dev
node -e "require('./index.js')"
> Error: Cannot find module 'has'
> Require stack: /tmp/t2/lib/extend.js -> /tmp/t2/index.js
npm ls has   # node.extend@2.0.0 -- (empty)
```

The failure is masked in this repo's own CI: `tape`/`covert` pull `has` in transitively, so
with devDependencies installed `has` happens to be present and `node test` passes 83/83.

**Impact:** Every production consumer of the published package gets a hard module-load
failure — the package's whole surface is dead, on all platforms, deterministically. Reach is
broad (all consumers) and persistence permanent (nothing in the package undoes it; a new
release is required), so this is `high`. The mitigation is that it fails loudly at require
time rather than silently misbehaving.

**Fix:** Declare the dependency the code already uses: add `"has": "^1.0.3"` to
`dependencies` in `package.json` (and ship a release whose dependencies match
`lib/extend.js`).

findings.title: Added file trips the repo's max-params lint rule, so npm test exits 1
findings.body:
The added file triggers a lint error under the repository's own config, so the project's
test script fails: `npm test` runs `pretest` -> `npm run lint` -> `npm run jscs && npm run
eslint .` and `eslint` exits 1.

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:19` defines `setProperty = function setP(target, name, value)`
— three parameters. `.eslintrc` extends `@ljharb`, whose `max-params` rule is
`[2, 2]` (`node_modules/@ljharb/eslint-config/.eslintrc:168`, in the oldest version the
range allows: 13.0.0). Reproduced after a dev install:

```
npm test
/tmp/t1/lib/extend.js
  19:19  error  Function 'setP' has too many parameters (3). Maximum allowed is 2  max-params
EXIT=1
```

`jscs` passes; only `eslint` fails. The upstream tree this file came from carries
`"max-params": [2, 3]` in `.eslintrc`; this repo's `.eslintrc` does not, and the PR adds only
`lib/extend.js`.

**Impact:** `npm test` (and therefore CI) is red for the repository after this change, and
the failure is attributed to the newly added file, blocking merging and any automated
verification of the rest of the suite. Damage is limited to tooling and is trivially
reversible, hence `low`.

**Fix:** Restore the matching config alongside the file — add `"max-params": [2, 3]` to the
`rules` block of `.eslintrc` — or add an inline `// eslint-disable-next-line max-params`.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded: five, one high.

**What the change does:** it adds `src/main.js`, the Express front end for Rendertron (routes `/`, `/render/:url(*)`, `/screenshot/:url(*)`, `/node_modules/*`, `/_ah/health`, `/_ah/stop`; config loading; one shared Chrome launched at startup; process-level crash handling). It is byte-identical to upstream at `16ade320`, i.e. the state immediately before the commit that fixed CVE-2017-18353.

**Assessment:** the file is the vulnerable side of that CVE. `/_ah/stop` (`src/main.js:136`) is an unauthenticated instance-control route that kills the only Chrome process and never relaunches it, and follow-on render requests then hang and drive `process.exit(1)` after six unhandled rejections while `/_ah/health` keeps reporting OK. Two further issues matter: the render handlers accept `file://` URLs (local file read, no scheme check) and reflect the requested URL unescaped into a `text/html` 400 body, which reaches the same-origin `/_ah/stop`. The remaining two are low-severity hygiene: the entire `node_modules` tree is served statically, and the analytics call has no error listener. All four areas match the hardening the upstream follow-up commit shipped, which raises my confidence in the findings.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GET /_ah/stop kills the shared Chrome instance and disables all rendering
findings.body:
Anyone who can reach the service can shut down its rendering capability with a single unauthenticated `GET /_ah/stop`. The route kills the one Chrome process that every `/render` and `/screenshot` request depends on, and nothing relaunches it.

**Evidence:**
- `src/main.js:136-139` registers the route unconditionally on the same public listener that serves `/render` (`src/main.js:152`). Nothing in the repo authenticates it: `compression()` is the only global middleware, `renderOnly` is checked only inside the render handlers (`src/main.js:92`, `111`), and the outbound proxy in `middleware/` never sits in front of the listener. `app.yaml` has no path filtering, and `Dockerfile:40` starts `node src/main.js` directly.
- Chrome is launched once at module load (`src/main.js:141-147`) and `config.chrome` / `config.port` are assigned once. `app.setConfig` deliberately preserves them (`src/main.js:50-55`), and `chromeLauncher.launch` is never called again, so there is no recovery path inside the process.
- After the kill, `config.port` is a dead DevTools port. `renderer.serialize` and `renderer.captureScreenshot` both do `await CDP.New({port: config.port})` *outside* their `try` blocks, inside an `async` promise executor (`src/renderer.js:179-184` and `203-217`). The rejection is therefore an unhandled rejection, not a rejected promise: the HTTP request hangs and never reaches the 400 path.
- Each of those unhandled rejections increments `exceptionCount` in `logUncaughtError` (`src/main.js:164-176`), which calls `process.exit(1)` once the count exceeds 5. Six render requests after the kill take the whole Node process down.
- `/_ah/health` (`src/main.js:134`) returns a hard-coded `OK` and never probes Chrome, so load balancers and GAE health checks keep sending traffic to the dead instance.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated actor gains an instance-control capability reserved for the operator (crossing a trust boundary) and destroys the service's only function for the process lifetime. A restart undoes it, but nothing in the system triggers one: Docker (README:150) has no restart policy, and GAE flex only recycles the instance if the process exits. Reach is broad — every client of the deployment.

**Fix:** keep the shutdown action internal. Remove the `/_ah/stop` route and expose `app.stop()` for the process's own shutdown path (as the upstream fix does); if a remote stop is required, put it behind an authenticated, orchestrator-only channel.

findings.title: Render handlers accept file:// URLs and return local file contents
findings.body:
Both render handlers hand the caller's URL straight to Chrome without a scheme check, so `GET /render/file:///...` returns the contents of a local file. `isRestricted` (`src/main.js:65-74`) only runs when the non-default `renderOnly` config is set, and even then it does a plain prefix match with no protocol validation.

**Evidence:**
- `src/main.js:92-99` and `111-118` pass `request.params.url` to `renderer.serialize` / `renderer.captureScreenshot`, which call `Page.navigate({url: url})` (`src/renderer.js:75`) and then return `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` (`src/renderer.js:189`). Chrome renders `file://` on navigation, and the resulting text file body is serialized back to the caller.
- Rendering `file://` is a working, tested path in this exact tree: `test/app-test.js:117` and `:124` request `/render/file://<repo>/test/resources/...` and expect rendered output. So the scheme is not blocked anywhere.
- With `renderOnly` configured, the check is `url.startsWith(config['renderOnly'][i])` (`src/main.js:69`) — still no scheme restriction, so `file://` URLs simply fail the prefix match and return 403 only when the operator opted in.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller can read files the Chrome process can read. In the Docker layout (`COPY . /app/`) that includes `config.json` (`analyticsTrackingId`, `renderOnly`) and the app sources, plus anything mounted into the container and `/proc/self/environ`. Reach crosses a trust boundary; disclosure is permanent. I graded it medium rather than high because I could not run Chrome in this sandbox to reproduce, and the leak is limited to files Chrome can display as text (binary content serializes uselessly) — but the capability itself needs no configuration. The upstream fix closes it by rejecting any URL whose protocol is not `http`/`https`.

**Fix:** make the scheme check unconditional in `isRestricted`: parse the URL and return restricted unless the protocol is `http:` or `https:`, before the `renderOnly` prefix loop.

findings.title: Render error responses reflect the requested URL into a text/html body
findings.body:
The 400 responses from both render handlers echo the requested URL, unescaped, into a `text/html` body. A crafted link executes script on the rendertron origin.

**Evidence:**
- `src/main.js:103-106` builds `Cannot render ${request.params.url}` and passes the string to `response.send`. Express 4.15.3 (`yarn.lock`) sets `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` for a string body when no type is set, and sets no `X-Content-Type-Options`, so the browser parses it as HTML.
- Route params are URI-decoded by express (`decodeURIComponent` in `router/layer.js`), so `GET /render/%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E` arrives as `<script>alert(1)</script>`. `:url(*)` captures slashes and colons, so the whole payload stays in the path.
- The catch block is reached on ordinary bad input: `test/app-test.js:136-140` asserts `/render/abc` returns 400, which means `renderer.serialize` rejects and the message is built. The same applies to a page whose load fails (`src/renderer.js:96-101`), and to the screenshot handler, where the swallowed rejection at `src/main.js:118` makes `new Buffer(undefined)` throw into the identical catch at `src/main.js:126-131`.
- No CSP, `nosniff`, or escaping exists anywhere in `src/` (grep for `content-security`, `x-content-type`, `escape`, `helmet` finds nothing).

**Impact:** the attacker's script runs same-origin with the service, so it can call `/_ah/stop` (`src/main.js:136`), read arbitrary `/render/file://` output, and drive renders from the victim's browser — a link is enough to trigger the outage reported separately. Graded medium, not high: the rendertron origin holds no cookies, session, or credentials, so this is defacement and a delivery vector rather than a session compromise.

**Fix:** stop reflecting input. Send a constant message and log the error server-side: `console.error(err); response.status(400).send('Cannot render requested URL');`.

findings.title: Whole node_modules tree is served over static /node_modules
findings.body:
`src/main.js:59` mounts the whole installed dependency tree at `/node_modules`, so any client can download `node_modules/<pkg>/package.json`, sources, and source maps for every server dependency.

**Evidence:** `app.use('/node_modules', express.static(path.resolve(__dirname, '../node_modules')))` is registered before the routes and serves every file under the directory, with directory indexes and `.map` files included. `src/index.html` only needs `progress-bar-element`, so the mount is far wider than the one asset the page uses.

**Impact:** unauthenticated disclosure of the exact dependency versions and library source, which maps directly to known CVEs for this pinned tree (`package.json` pins old express, chrome-remote-interface, chrome-launcher). The content is third-party code that is public on npm, so I graded it low rather than higher — treat it as fingerprinting aid, not a secret leak. The upstream fix narrows the mount to the single file the page loads.

**Fix:** mount only the asset the page needs (`app.use('/progress-bar.html', express.static(...))`) instead of the directory.

findings.title: Analytics request without an error listener can crash the process
findings.body:
`track()` issues an `https.request` with no `'error'` listener, so a DNS or socket failure on the Google Analytics call raises an uncaught exception on a normal render.

**Evidence:** `src/main.js:78-88` creates the request, writes the payload and calls `post.end()`. No `post.on('error', ...)` and no response handler are attached, and the response is never consumed. Node emits `'error'` on a `ClientRequest` with no listener as an `uncaughtException`, which reaches `logUncaughtError` (`src/main.js:164-176`); after six such errors the handler calls `process.exit(1)`. Requests are awaited nowhere, so this is per render, not per instance.

**Impact:** with `analyticsTrackingId` configured (a documented option, `README.md` Config section) and Google Analytics unreachable — blocked egress, DNS failure, or a reset connection — six renders bring the process down. Precondition is a non-default setting plus a network fault, so I graded it low; reach would be broad once those hold.

**Fix:** attach an error listener (and a timeout) to the request, or fire the analytics call with a catch-all: `post.on('error', () => {})` / wrap `track` in try/catch, so a failed analytics ping can never escalate to a process exit.

summary:
The PR re-adds `index.js` — a 123-line implementation of `get`/`set`/`delete`/`has` for dot paths — identical to sindresorhus/dot-prop 5.1.0. I reviewed it against the readme and test contract and reproduced the behaviour under Node with `is-obj@2`.

Assessment: the traversal and path-parsing code is otherwise faithful to the documented API, but `set` and `delete` descend with plain property reads, so a path containing `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype` reaches `Object.prototype`. I reproduced the write, the nested write, and the `delete`-based removal of `Object.prototype.toString`, and recorded it as a high-severity finding (CVE-2020-8116). `get` is not affected because it gates on `propertyIsEnumerable`. The remaining oddities I probed — `has` using `in`, `set` clobbering non-object intermediates, backslash-escape asymmetry, and throws on frozen targets — are upstream design choices in unchanged code and are not separable defects in this change.

findings.title: Prototype pollution: set() and delete() write through __proto__ paths into Object.prototype
findings.body:
`set()` and `delete()` walk the path segments with plain property reads, so a path
containing `__proto__` (or `constructor.prototype`) reaches `Object.prototype` and
writes or deletes there. Any object created afterwards in the same Node process
inherits the change. This is CVE-2020-8116.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes an attacker-influenced string as `path`. The
`object` argument and `value` may be fully attacker-controlled; the library is
commonly fed user input (query-string keys, config keys, JSON field paths).

**Evidence:** `set` at index.js:62-74 reads `object[p]` without an own-property
check and drills into whatever it finds. `isObj(Object.prototype)` is `true`
(is-obj returns true for any non-array object), so index.js:65 does not replace
`__proto__` with `{}`; index.js:73 then rebinds `object` to `Object.prototype`,
and the next iteration writes the value there via index.js:70. `delete` has the
same traversal at index.js:86-99 and removes the property at index.js:90.

Reproduced against the file at this commit (is-obj@2):

```js
const dotProp = require('./index.js');
dotProp.set({}, '__proto__.polluted', 'yes');
({}).polluted;                                  // => 'yes'
dotProp.set({}, 'constructor.prototype.injected', 'bad');
({}).injected;                                  // => 'bad'
dotProp.set({}, 'a.__proto__.deep', 1);         // nesting also works
({}).deep;                                      // => 1
dotProp.delete({}, '__proto__.toString');
typeof ({}).toString;                           // => 'undefined'
```

`get` is not a read vector: index.js:31 gates on `propertyIsEnumerable`, so
`get({}, '__proto__.polluted')` returns `undefined`. `has` uses `in` (index.js:111)
and will report `true` for polluted names, but it does not itself mutate.

**Impact:** a hostile path permanently pollutes `Object.prototype` for the whole
process. Every later `{}` in the application, its dependencies, and the framework
carries the injected keys, which is the classic route to authentication bypass,
privilege escalation, or gadget-chain RCE in the host service. The write escapes
the boundary between the caller's object and the shared global prototype, and no
supported API undoes it. Reach crosses a trust boundary; persistence is permanent
for the process lifetime, so this is `high`. The fix that restores the invariant —
`set`/`delete` must only ever mutate own properties of the objects they were given
— is the same change that closes the `delete` variant.

**Fix:** reject the three prototype-traversing names before writing. In
`getPathSegments` or at the top of each loop, skip segments equal to `__proto__`,
`prototype`, or `constructor` (the upstream fix for this CVE adds that guard in
`get`, `set`, `has` and `delete`). Alternatively, test
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(object, p)` before descending in `set` and
`delete`, which keeps traversal inside the caller's own object graph.

summary:
Verified independently before finishing: the added module is byte-identical to upstream `senecajs/seneca` v3.8.4 `lib/print.js`, and the baseline tree is upstream `f505dc6` with only that file missing.

**Review summary**

The change restores `lib/print.js` (151 lines, identical to upstream v3.8.4): command-line handling for `--seneca.print.tree` / `--seneca.print.options`, the `archy` action-tree printer, and the `print` / `log` / `err` / `plugin_options` helpers that `seneca.js`, `lib/common.js`, `lib/logging.js` and `lib/plugins.js` already require — without the file the package fails to load at `seneca.js:30`. I ran the shipped `test/print.test.js` (3/3 pass on Node 12; the non-zero lab exit is the repo-wide `globalThis` leak check, which also fails on untouched test files) and exercised every export, including boolean/numeric `print.tree` forms, `log:'print'` logging, and full boot.

The module itself behaves as documented and I found no defect in the new lines: the `--seneca.print.options` flag does reach the "before plugins" dump (my own check refuted the plausible ordering suspicion), and `print_tree` filtering, delay handling and recursion are sound. Two non-blocking observations I did not file: `lib/print.js:14` parses argv with minimist 1.2.0, a second prototype-pollution sink that already exists unchanged at `lib/optioner.js:55`, and `print_options` prints options unredacted by design.

One real issue is recorded: the crash-report path that this change puts back in working order interpolates the entire `process.env` at `lib/common.js:345` when `debug.print.fatal: 'full'` and test mode are both on (CVE-2019-5483), which I reproduced with a fake secret appearing on stderr. Overall the change is a faithful, low-risk restore; the remaining risk is the unguarded environment dump in the fatal handler, not the added file.

findings.title: Fatal-error report dumps the whole process environment, leaking secrets to stderr
findings.body:
A fatal error can write every environment variable of the process to stderr,
including credentials. `exports.makedie` builds the process description as

```js
(!full ? '' : ', env=' + Util.inspect(process.env).replace(/\n/g, ''))
```

at `lib/common.js:345`, where `full` is `'full' === so.debug.print.fatal`
(`lib/common.js:295-296`). The assembled report is then written with
`Print.err(stderrmsg)` (`lib/common.js:411-421`, `436-443`), i.e. via
`console.error`. Any secret held in the environment (cloud keys, DB passwords,
tokens) lands in the crash output, which commonly ends up in log aggregation,
CI logs, or a support ticket. Defaults are safe: `debug.print.fatal` defaults to
`'summary'` (`seneca.js:78-82`) and the report is only printed when the instance
runs in test mode.

**Preconditions:** `debug: { print: { fatal: 'full' } }` **and** test mode on —
`test: true`, `seneca.test()`, `SENECA_TEST`, or `--seneca.test`
(`lib/optioner.js:91-93`, `seneca.js:58-59`). `fatal: 'full'` alone prints
nothing, because the report emission is gated on `so.test`
(`lib/common.js:411`, `lib/common.js:436`). A fatal trigger is also needed: a
plugin whose definition or init throws (`lib/api.js:252-255`,
`lib/plugins.js:166-170`), `emit('error')` (`seneca.js:500`), a transport
listen/client failure (`lib/api.js:453`, `540-547`), or a direct `die()`
(`seneca.js:481`).

**Evidence:** with Node 12,

```js
process.env.LEAKY_KEY = 'SECRET-XYZ'
var seneca = Seneca({ debug: { print: { fatal: 'full' } }, test: true })
seneca.use(function bad() { throw new Error('boom') })
```

exits 1 and stderr contains `PROCESS ::: pid=… env={ … LEAKY_KEY: 'SECRET-XYZ' }`;
stdout is clean. Replacing the options with the defaults produces zero bytes on
stderr. The reviewed change restores `lib/print.js`, which `seneca.js:30` and
`lib/common.js:12` require — without that file `require('seneca')` throws, so
this failure path cannot run at all; the change makes the crash-report path
live again without a guard on the environment dump.

**Impact:** Secrets readable by anyone with access to the process's stderr or
log pipeline: broad reach, permanent once written, but it needs two non-default
settings and a crash, so `low`. Upstream rated the same issue LOW
(CVE-2019-5483 / GHSA-2xwv-3cc9-fp7c).

**Fix:** gate the environment on its own opt-in flag that defaults to false —
`debug.print.env` — and only interpolate `process.env` when it is set (this is
the upstream 3.9.0 change, senecajs/seneca commit `b0565ba`). `full` should
control stack/detail verbosity only, not secret disclosure.

summary:
Reviewed and reproduced the change end to end.

**Summary:** The commit adds `lib/processNested.js`, the implementation behind the documented `parseNested` option that folds flat multipart field names (`hobbies[0]`) into nested objects for `req.body`/`req.files`. Its prototype-pollution guard only blocks the literal `__proto__` segment while the traversal still follows inherited properties, so a request field named `constructor[prototype][x]` writes onto `Object.prototype` — I confirmed this through a real multipart POST against the middleware (that finding is recorded). Apart from that, the parsing logic is sound and the existing `processNested`/multipart tests pass; the one failing test in `test/fileFactory.spec.js` concerns `file.mv()` error propagation in untouched code and appears to be environment-related, not caused by this change.

findings.title: Multipart field name constructor[prototype][x] pollutes Object.prototype when parseNested is enabled
findings.body:
A multipart field name containing `constructor[prototype][x]` makes the server
write `x` onto `Object.prototype` (CVE-2020-7699). The filter at
`lib/processNested.js:22` blocks only the literal segment `__proto__`, but the
walk at `lib/processNested.js:29-30` follows any existing truthy property, so
`constructor` resolves to the global `Object` and `prototype` to its prototype
object. The final assignment at `lib/processNested.js:27` then lands on
`Object.prototype`.

**Preconditions:** `parseNested: true` (`lib/index.js:19` defaults it to
`false`; README.md:114 documents it). No authentication is required — any
multipart field reaches `processNested` via `lib/processMultipart.js:132`.

**Evidence:** with `express-fileupload({ parseNested: true })` mounted, a POST
to an upload route with one field `constructor[prototype][polluted]=yes`
returns 200 and afterwards `({}).polluted === 'yes'` in the server process.
Reproduced with `request().post('/upload').field('constructor[prototype][polluted]','yes')`.
The same holds for nested prefixes such as `a[constructor][prototype][polluted]`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated upload can modify `Object.prototype` for the
whole Node process, so every subsequent request, middleware and dependency sees
the injected properties; gadget chains in template engines, serializers or
`child_process` options can turn this into code execution. The write survives
until restart and is repeatable at will. Severity is `medium`: the effect is
process-wide and cross-boundary, but the non-default `parseNested` option is
required and a restart clears it (policy: severity table, discounted for a
non-default setting).

**Fix:** restore one invariant — a key segment may only be followed when it is
an own, non-builtin property of the object being extended. Reject
`__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` at every segment (not just the
first), and build containers with `Object.create(null)` or guard reads with
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, k)` so inherited properties are
never traversed.

summary:
Recorded one finding. Summary:

The PR re-adds `lib/processNested.js`, the helper that unflattens `field[sub]=value` multipart names when the middleware runs with `parseNested: true` (`lib/processMultipart.js:131`). Nothing else changes; the existing `test/processNested.spec.js` now passes.

The implementation descends attacker-supplied path segments on plain objects without guarding `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype`, so a single upload field pollutes `Object.prototype` process-wide — I reproduced this end-to-end through the middleware and recorded it as medium (broad and permanent, discounted for the non-default option). Benign input handling looked correct; I found no other issue in the changed lines.

findings.title: Multipart field names like __proto__[x] pollute Object.prototype for the whole process
findings.body:
`processNested` (`lib/processNested.js:1`) builds nested objects by walking
attacker-controlled multipart field names. It looks up each path segment on a plain
object without checking for `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`, so an upload
field named `__proto__[isAdmin]=true` assigns onto `Object.prototype`. Every object
created later in the process then inherits `isAdmin: 'true'`.

**Preconditions:** the middleware is mounted with `parseNested: true`
(`lib/index.js:19` sets the default to `false`), and the caller can send a
multipart/form-data POST to a route using it. No authentication is needed.

**Evidence:** end-to-end run against the middleware:

```js
app.use(fileUpload({ parseNested: true }));
app.post('/upload', (req, res) => res.json({ polluted: ({}).isAdmin }));
request(app).post('/upload').field('__proto__[isAdmin]', 'true')...
// -> {"polluted":"true"}   Object.prototype.isAdmin === true
```

Direct check of the module: `processNested({'constructor[prototype][x]':'y'})` also
sets `({}).x === 'y'`. Tests in `test/processNested.spec.js` cover only benign keys.

**Impact:** the pollution lasts for the process lifetime and is not undoable without
a restart, so every request served afterwards sees the injected property. Downstream
code that reads `obj.someFlag` inherits the attacker's value — the classic outcomes
are authorization checks passing (`if (user.isAdmin)`), required-field validation
being satisfied by an empty object, and object merges in templating or ORM layers
turning into RCE. Reach is broad (all users of the process) and persistence permanent,
which grades high; it is discounted one tier to **medium** because the feature is
off unless `parseNested: true` is set.

**Fix:** reject path segments equal to `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`
before descending, and only create containers with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`
checks (or `Object.create(null)`) instead of `if (!current[k])`.

summary:
Recorded. Final assessment:

**What the change does:** PR #2 re-adds `lib/index.js` (283 lines) — the full `mpath` 0.4.1 implementation, identical to the published 0.4.1 release apart from a `Map` shim — under a baseline that had the file removed.

**Assessment:** the library is correct for normal paths (the whole shipped suite exercises it), but it ships without the prototype-pollution guard. I reproduced writes onto `Object`, `String`, `Number` and constructor prototypes from `set()`, and deletion of inherited built-ins from `unset()`; upstream 0.5.1 fixed exactly these two functions with an `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` blocklist. That is the one blocking issue. The other oddities a scan turned up (lookup-adapter semantics, `has`/`unset` not supporting arrays or `Map` keys, `set` no-op on falsy intermediates, sparse-array handling) are long-standing upstream design behaviour present in every release, not regressions from this change, and I left them unreported.

findings.title: mpath.set and mpath.unset follow __proto__ and constructor.prototype paths into built-in prototypes
findings.body:
`mpath.set()` follows path segments into built-in prototypes and writes there, so a path containing `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype` pollutes `Object.prototype` (or `String`/`Number`/`Object` prototypes) for the whole process. `mpath.unset()` has the same gap and can delete inherited built-ins.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes a path derived from untrusted input. This is the normal use in the library's main consumer: Mongoose passes update/query paths through `mpath.set`, so a request body can reach it.

**Evidence:** reproduced against `require('./lib')`:

```js
mpath.set('__proto__.isAdmin', true, {});
({}).isAdmin                                  // true — inherited by every object
mpath.set('constructor.prototype.x', 1, {});   // ({}).x === 1
mpath.set(['__proto__', 'x2'], 1, {});         // ({}).x2 === 1
mpath.set('a.__proto__.x3', 1, {a: {}});       // ({}).x3 === 1
mpath.set('arr.__proto__.x4', 1, {arr: [{}]}); // ({}).x4 === 1
mpath.unset('__proto__.toString', {});         // true; typeof ({}).toString === 'undefined'
```

The traversal loop at `lib/index.js:191-228` resolves each segment with plain property access (`lib/index.js:221-224`), so `part === '__proto__'` returns `Object.prototype`; the final write at `lib/index.js:272` then lands on it. `unset` at `lib/index.js:122-145` checks only `parts[i] in cur` (`lib/index.js:134`) and deletes at `lib/index.js:138`, so `__proto__` traversal reaches the built-in and `delete` succeeds. Only two or more path parts are needed; a missing or falsy intermediate stops the walk at `lib/index.js:227`.

The upstream fix (mpath 0.5.1, the release that closes CVE-2018-16490) adds a blocklist and guards these two functions:

```js
var ignoreProperties = ['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype'];
// set(): pre-scan all parts, return early
// unset(): per-part check, return false
```

This tree has neither guard; `lib/index.js` is identical to 0.4.1 apart from the `Map` shim at `lib/index.js:1-2`.

**Impact:** a single `set()` call permanently makes an attacker-chosen property visible on every object in the process (authorization flags, option lookups, deserialisation behaviour), and `unset()` can remove built-ins such as `toString` globally. Nothing supported undoes it short of restarting the process, so the effect is broad and permanent. Severity is `high` per this review's impact model: untrusted path input crosses into shared server state and outlives the request.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that no path segment may name a prototype-related property. Add the `ignoreProperties` blocklist and reject any path containing a listed segment in `set` (return before the copy/traversal logic) and in `unset` (return `false`). That matches upstream 0.5.1 and leaves normal paths unaffected.

summary:
This PR re-adds `lib/index.js` at upstream commit `7e2977f`, the fix for CVE-2018-16490: it blocks `__proto__` segments in `set` (lib/index.js:186-192) and `unset` (lib/index.js:137-140). I verified the file is byte-identical to that upstream commit, so the guards are the only substantive delta from the pre-patch release.

The mitigation is incomplete: it matches only the literal string `__proto__`, so `set('constructor.prototype.x', …)` still walks to `Object.prototype` and writes there, and the same comparison is bypassed by non-string segments that coerce to `__proto__`. Upstream fixed exactly this in the next commit (`fe732eb`) by blocking `constructor` and `prototype` as well — I reproduced both bypasses on this checkout and recorded one medium finding. The rest of the file is unchanged upstream logic whose quirks (falsey intermediates, empty paths, Map/non-Map asymmetry in `has`) predate this change and are not regressions.

findings.title: set still pollutes Object.prototype through a constructor.prototype path
findings.body:
`set` still writes to `Object.prototype` through a `constructor.prototype` path. The
guard added in this change only rejects path segments that are the literal string
`__proto__`, so any other route to a prototype still lands the assignment on a
shared prototype object. An application that passes untrusted data as the path —
exactly the case the guard's comment at lib/index.js:187 names — remains polluted.

**Preconditions:** a consumer calls `mpath.set()` with a path derived from
untrusted input (form field names, query/body keys, mapping configs). Mongoose-style
`update`/`$set` handling is the realistic case.

**Evidence:** the guard loop at lib/index.js:186-192 compares each segment with
`'__proto__'`. Path `constructor.prototype.x` passes it and the walk then proceeds
normally: lib/index.js:236 resolves `o.constructor` → `Object`, then
`Object.prototype`, and lib/index.js:284 assigns `obj[part] = map(val)` there.
Reproduced with the checked-out tree:

    $ node -e "var m=require('./'); var o={}; m.set('constructor.prototype.p', 'yes', o); console.log(({}).p)"
    yes

It also works on a nested target and via a non-string segment, since the guard
compares raw segments with `===` before property-key coercion happens at
lib/index.js:236:

    $ node -e "var m=require('./'); var o={a:{}}; m.set('a.constructor.prototype.p', 1, o); console.log(({}).p)"
    1
    $ node -e "var m=require('./'); m.set([{toString:function(){return '__proto__'}}, 'q'], 1, {}); console.log(({}).q)"
    1

Upstream reached the same conclusion: the commit right after this one
(`fe732eb`, "prevent writing to constructor and prototype as well") replaces both
string comparisons with an `ignoreProperties = ['__proto__', 'constructor',
'prototype']` list and adds a `constructor.prototype.x` regression test.

**Impact:** `Object.prototype` gains an attacker-chosen key for the life of the
process. Every object in every request then sees that key, which enables
property-injection / authentication-bypass style attacks in the consuming service
and is not undone by any supported action. The fix here closes only one of the two
spellings of the same escalation. Severity is medium rather than high because the
pollution needs a downstream caller to feed an untrusted path into `set` — the
library alone is not reachable by an attacker.

**Fix:** make the guard semantic rather than a single literal — reject any segment
in `['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype']` (in both `set` at lib/index.js:189
and `unset` at lib/index.js:138), and coerce segments to strings (or reject
non-string segments) before the comparison so the check cannot be sidestepped by an
object with a coercing `toString`. One invariant to restore: `set`/`unset` never
write or delete on a prototype object.

summary:
The change re-adds `src/main.js` with the CVE-2017-18353 fix: the unauthenticated `/_ah/stop` route is gone, so no HTTP request can kill the shared Chrome instance; render errors are no longer echoed back to callers; and a protocol gate now rejects `file://` and other non-http(s) URLs, which closes local file reads like `/render/file:///etc/passwd`. The fix itself is sound and complete — `app.stop` is reachable only from the internal error counter (`src/main.js:176`), and no other file references `_ah/stop`.

Carrying over only `main.js` from the upstream fix commit leaves two collateral regressions, both recorded as low: the removed `/node_modules` mount breaks the homepage's progress-bar import (`src/index.html:209`, now 404), and the new 403 response code breaks three assertions in `test/app-test.js` that expect 400/401.
