Remaining weaknesses in `isRestricted`, such as the `startsWith` allow-list bypass (`http://allowed.example.com@evil.com`) and the fact that only the initial URL is checked, predate this diff and are documented in the README, so I did not file them.

findings.title: Homepage progress bar import 404s after the /node_modules static route is removed
findings.body:
The demo page at `/` no longer loads its `<progress-bar>` element: the app stopped
serving `/node_modules` and now serves only `/progress-bar.html`, but
`src/index.html:209` still imports
`node_modules/progress-bar-element/progress-bar.html`. That request now returns 404,
so the custom element never upgrades.

**Evidence:** `src/main.js:63` replaces the old
`app.use('/node_modules', express.static(<repo>/node_modules))` with
`app.use('/progress-bar.html', express.static(PROGRESS_BAR_PATH))`. Nothing in the
tree requests `/progress-bar.html`; the only consumer, `src/index.html:209`, still
uses the old path. Verified against the running app with `chrome-launcher` and
`renderer` stubbed: `GET /` → 200, `GET /node_modules/progress-bar-element/progress-bar.html`
→ 404, `GET /progress-bar.html` → 200. The old pre-change code served the same
request with 200.

**Impact:** Low. Reach is contained to the demo homepage, the failure is permanent
until fixed, and the visible effect is cosmetic — the progress indicator stays
absent while a render runs (`src/index.html:195,204` toggles `hidden` on an
undefined element without error). It does not affect `/render` or `/screenshot`.

**Fix:** Update the import in `src/index.html:209` to `progress-bar.html` so it
matches the route this change introduces.

findings.title: Non-http render requests now return 403, breaking three existing tests
findings.body:
Any render request that is not http(s) — including the bare `/render/abc` used by the
tests — now returns 403 instead of 400/401, so three assertions in `test/app-test.js`
fail.

**Evidence:** `src/main.js:69-72` adds a protocol gate that returns "restricted" when
`url.parse(urlReq).protocol` does not match `/^https?/`; `/render/:url(*)` at
`src/main.js:100-103` answers 403 for restricted URLs. Confirmed against the running
app with `renderer` stubbed:

- `/render/abc` → 403; `test/app-test.js:139` asserts 400.
- `/render/file://<path>?wc-inject-shadydom=true` → 403; `test/app-test.js:118`
  asserts 400 and `test/app-test.js:125` asserts 401.

The two `file://` fixtures exist to exercise the `render:status_code` meta-tag
feature (`src/renderer.js:27-32`), which now has no HTTP-reachable test path.

**Impact:** Low. The 403 is the intended hardening — it closes local file reads such
as `/render/file:///etc/passwd` — but the change ships without the matching test
updates, so `yarn test` fails on three tests and CI goes red.

**Fix:** Update the three assertions to 403 where a rejected URL is expected, and
serve `http-meta-status-code*.html` from the tests' local http server
(`test/app-test.js:25`) instead of `file://` so the meta-tag status-code path stays
covered.

summary:
Done. Coverage summary:

**What the change does:** PR #1 re-adds `index.js`, the dot-prop implementation with the CVE-2020-8116 prototype-pollution guard (`disallowedKeys` for `__proto__`/`prototype`/`constructor`, path validation inside `getPathSegments`, and early returns in `get`/`has`). I compared it byte-for-byte with published `dot-prop@5.1.1` — it is identical to the upstream fix, and the CVE-2020-8116 exploit is blocked (verified by hand-picked paths plus a 300k-case fuzz: `({}).someKey` stayed undefined, `Object.prototype` unchanged), and the existing ava suite passes.

**Assessment:** This is the correct fix for the CVE and I would approve it. Measured against the CVE's threat model it closes the hole; the one recorded finding covers a narrower gap the three-name guard does not address — `set()` follows inherited builtin method functions, so a path like `hasOwnProperty.call` still writes onto a realm-shared object (reproducible `TypeError` in `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`). That behavior also exists in released upstream versions, so it is a limit of the fix, not a regression; I filed it `low`. One cosmetic inconsistency I did not file: `get()` returns bare `undefined` instead of the caller's default for guarded paths (index.js:41-43), unlike every other miss path.

findings.title: set() follows inherited builtin methods, so paths like 'hasOwnProperty.call' write onto shared functions
findings.body:
`set()` descends through inherited values. When a path's leading segment names a
method that lives on `Object.prototype` or `Array.prototype`, `isObj(object[p])`
is true (is-obj counts functions as objects), so index.js:80 leaves it in place and
index.js:88 makes that shared builtin function the next write target. The caller's
value is then assigned as an own property of the builtin (index.js:85), for the
whole process.

**Preconditions:** the application passes an attacker-influenced path string to
`dotProp.set`, and its leading segment is a builtin method name (`hasOwnProperty`,
`toString`, `valueOf`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `toLocaleString`,
`push`, ...). This is the same trust assumption as the prototype-pollution bug the
change fixes.

**Evidence:**

```
const dp = require('./index.js');
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call({a: 1}, 'a');   // true
dp.set({}, 'hasOwnProperty.call', 'oops');
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call({a: 1}, 'a');   // TypeError: ... is not a function
```

Also `dp.set({}, 'toString.call', 'nope')` breaks `Object.prototype.toString.call`
and `dp.set({}, 'toString.x', v)` makes `({}).toString.x` readable from any other
call site. `dp.delete({}, 'hasOwnProperty.call')` restores the builtin.

**Impact:** A path string alone can shadow `call`/`apply`/`bind` on shared builtins,
which breaks the common `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key)` and
`Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` patterns process-wide, and can plant a value
readable by other requests in the same process. The three-name guard
(index.js:4-10) does not cover this because none of these segments is
`__proto__`/`prototype`/`constructor`. Severity is low: reach is broad but the
effect is recoverable (a restart or `delete()` undoes it) and it is not
`Object.prototype` pollution itself. The behaviour also exists in released upstream
dot-prop (checked 5.1.1, 6.0.1, 7.2.0), so this is a limit of the fix rather than a
regression introduced on top of it; it is reported because the whole file is new
here and the guard is meant to stop attacker-controlled paths from writing to
shared objects.

**Fix:** never use an inherited value as a write target. Test ownership, not
object-ness, when deciding whether to descend at index.js:80 — e.g.
`if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(object, p) || !isObj(object[p]))`. The
same own-property test should be applied in `delete` (index.js:105-109) so inherited
members are not deleted through.

Verified: with that condition at index.js:80 the existing suite still passes
(`npx ava`: 4 tests) and `set({}, 'hasOwnProperty.call', 'x')` no longer touches
the builtin.

summary: Reviewed the added `utils/find-opencv.js`, which re-adds the script that `binding.gyp` calls at build time and removes attacker-controlled `process.argv` from the `exec` call. That security goal is met, but the patch over-corrects: it pins `flag` to `--exists`, so the `--libs`/`--cflags` queries from `binding.gyp` are ignored and source builds lose their OpenCV link/include flags (and the Windows fallback always throws). One medium finding recorded.

findings.title: Hardcoded --exists flag breaks the --libs/--cflags contract used by binding.gyp
findings.body:
This patch hardcodes `flag` to `--exists`, so the script ignores the `--libs`
and `--cflags` arguments that `binding.gyp` passes it. `pkg-config` therefore
only performs an existence check and prints nothing useful. The native addon
gets no link libraries and, on Windows, the fallback throws.

**Preconditions:** Building the addon (`node-gyp rebuild` / `npm install`), which is every normal install of this package.

**Evidence:** `utils/find-opencv.js:5` sets `var flag = "--exists";` and never
reads `process.argv`. `binding.gyp:29` and `binding.gyp:109` invoke
`node utils/find-opencv.js --libs`; `binding.gyp:34`, `:114`, `:44`, `:69`,
`:125`, `:150` invoke it with `--cflags`. With a stub `pkg-config` that logs
its arguments:

```
$ PATH=/tmp/stub:$PATH node utils/find-opencv.js --libs
...
$ cat /tmp/stub/log
ARGS:opencv >= 2.3.1 --exists
ARGS:opencv >= 2.3.1 --exists
```

Both invocations receive `--exists`, not the requested flag. On Windows,
`printPaths` therefore reaches its final `else` and throws
`Error: unknown argument '--exists'` (`utils/find-opencv.js:70`), so the
fallback path can never succeed.

**Impact:** On Linux/macOS the `--libs` query returns no `-lopencv_*` flags, so
linking `opencv.node` fails with undefined OpenCV symbols; on Windows the build
aborts outright. The package can no longer be built from source on any platform,
which affects every consumer of the package. Reach is broad and the damage is
recoverable by correcting the script, so `medium`.

**Fix:** Restore argument forwarding while keeping untrusted input out of the
shell: map the accepted arguments to a fixed whitelist, e.g.
`var flag = ({'--cflags':'--cflags','--libs':'--libs'})[process.argv[2]] || '--exists';`
and keep interpolating only that validated value (and the fixed `opencv`
selection) into the `exec` call.

summary:
Recorded one finding.

The change re-adds `utils/find-opencv.js`, an 81-line build helper that `binding.gyp` runs during `node-gyp`/`npm install` to locate OpenCV via `pkg-config`, with a Windows fallback based on `%OPENCV_DIR%`. The file is the pre-fix revision of CVE-2019-10061: it interpolates `process.argv[2]` straight into a `child_process.exec` command string (`utils/find-opencv.js:19`), which I reproduced executing an injected shell command. Upstream's later version fixes this by whitelisting the flag through a lookup table; that one caveat — in-repo call sites pass literal flags — is why I graded it medium rather than high. The rest of the file is straightforward build plumbing with no further material risk.

findings.title: Command injection: find-opencv.js passes process.argv[2] into child_process.exec
findings.body:
`utils/find-opencv.js:19` builds a shell command by string concatenation and passes it to
`child_process.exec`. The second argument of the script, `process.argv[2]` (stored in `flag`
at line 5), is inserted unquoted, so any caller that forwards a non-constant flag value
executes arbitrary shell commands at build/install time.

**Evidence:** reproduced in this checkout:

```
$ node utils/find-opencv.js '--exists; touch /tmp/PWNED'
$ ls -l /tmp/PWNED
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 ... /tmp/PWNED
```

The command line becomes `pkg-config "opencv >= 2.3.1" --exists; touch /tmp/PWNED` and the
shell runs the trailing command. Even without a metacharacter, an empty or junk argument
reaches the shell verbatim. `binding.gyp:29,34,44,69,109,114,125,150` invokes the script
during `node-gyp`/`npm install`, so the injection happens in the build phase.

**Preconditions:** a caller passes an argument that is not a fixed literal — e.g. a wrapper
script, CI variable, or any code that re-uses this helper with forwarded input. The call
sites in this repository itself pass literals (`--libs`, `--cflags`), so the bug is reachable
through the script's public CLI contract but not through the packaged build.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution with the privileges of whoever runs the build. The
value crosses a trust boundary (data becomes shell syntax) but requires a caller that
forwards it, and the in-repo callers do not, so severity is medium rather than high.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that the flag can only be one of the supported pkg-config
options — map it through a whitelist before use, and keep the constant literals:

```js
var flags = { "--cflags": "--cflags", "--libs": "--libs" };
var flag = flags[process.argv[2]] || "--exists";
```

Then `exec("pkg-config " + opencv + " " + flag, ...)` can only ever run a known option.
Upstream's later revision does exactly this.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded:

- **high** — `util/utils.js:109`: extraction of a crafted archive writes files outside the target directory (Zip Slip / CVE-2018-1002204). Reproduced on Linux; the added file is what makes the library loadable, and the write sinks have no containment check.
- **low** — `util/utils.js:16`: `makeDir` repeats the first path segment for relative paths, so `writeZip("build/out.zip")` throws `ENOENT: mkdir 'build/build'`.
- **low** — `util/utils.js:146`: `writeFileToAsync` ignores the second `open` error and calls `fs.write(undefined)`, crashing the process with the callback never fired.

The PR re-adds `util/utils.js` verbatim from upstream `cthackers/adm-zip` at `e116bc18` (the CVE-2018-1002204 pre-patch commit) — I verified the blob hash matches upstream at both recorded commits. The baseline tree cannot even be required (`util/index.js:1` → `Cannot find module './utils'`), so the change restores a working library together with the unpatched extraction path: the real fix lives in `adm-zip.js` (`extractAllTo`/`extractAllToAsync`/`extractEntryTo` pass `pth.resolve(targetPath, entryName)` unchecked; the only sanitizer, `escapeFileName`, is Windows-only). Beyond that, the file is upstream code as-is, and the two low findings are genuine defects in the new code with reproductions.

findings.title: Extracting a crafted zip writes files outside the target directory
findings.body:
Extracting an archive whose entry names contain `../` or an absolute path writes
files outside the requested target directory, anywhere the process can write.
The new `util/utils.js` holds the write sink and is what makes the library
loadable at all, so the change puts this path back in service.

**Evidence:** `util/utils.js:92` (`writeFileTo`) and `:122` (`writeFileToAsync`)
open whatever path they get; no caller compares the destination with
`targetPath`. The paths come straight from the archive: `zipFile.js:38` copies
the central-directory name bytes into `entry.entryName`, and `adm-zip.js:430/444`
(`extractAllTo`), `:356/385` and `:374` (`extractEntryTo`), `:468/488`
(`extractAllToAsync`) pass `pth.resolve(targetPath, entryName)` to those sinks.
The only sanitizer, `escapeFileName` (`adm-zip.js:30`), is gated on
`isWin` (`adm-zip.js:10`), so it never runs on Linux.

Reproduced on Linux with an archive built by `python3 zipfile` (adm-zip's own
`writeZip` is broken on current Node, see `headers/entryHeader.js:216`):

    entry "../pwned.txt"   -> /tmp/zs/pwned.txt created outside /tmp/zs/target
    entry "/tmp/abs.txt"   -> created outside
    entry "../../d/" + "../../d/x.txt" -> directory and file created outside

Each escaped file lands with mode 0666 because `attr` is never passed
(`util/utils.js:118`). Baseline check: at `5f28835` `require("./adm-zip")`
throws `Cannot find module './utils'` from `util/index.js:1`, so before this PR
no extraction code could run.

**Impact:** an attacker who supplies the zip decides which file the victim
overwrites, with attacker-controlled contents and 0666 permissions (for example
a shell rc file or a cron entry). That crosses a trust boundary and leaves
persistent changes, so high.

**Fix:** restore the containment invariant before the write: after
`pth.resolve(targetPath, entryName)`, reject names whose resolved path is not
`targetPath` or under it, in `extractAllTo`, `extractAllToAsync` and
`extractEntryTo` (`adm-zip.js:444`, `:488`, `:385`, `:374`). Upstream fixed
CVE-2018-1002204 this way in commit 6f4dfeb. Do not rely on `escapeFileName`,
which only replaces characters and is Windows-only.

findings.title: Relative paths fail to create: makeDir repeats the first path segment
findings.body:
`Utils.makeDir` and `writeFileTo` create the first path component twice, so any
relative path with a missing parent fails with `ENOENT` instead of creating the
directory. `writeZip("./build/out.zip")` therefore throws whenever the folder
does not already exist.

**Evidence:** `util/utils.js:16` seeds `resolvedPath` with the first path
segment, then the loop at `:17-19` appends that same segment again:
`resolvedPath = path.split(PATH_SEPARATOR)[0]` followed by
`resolvedPath += PATH_SEPARATOR + name` for every segment including the first.
`makeDir("x/y/z")` runs `fs.mkdirSync("x/x")`
(`util/utils.js:23`) and throws `ENOENT: mkdir 'x/x'`. Reproduced in a fresh
directory:

    Utils.makeDir("x/y/z")                    -> ENOENT: mkdir 'x/x'
    Utils.writeFileTo("rel/out.txt", buf, 1)  -> ENOENT: mkdir 'rel/rel'
    new AdmZip().addFile(...); zip.writeZip("build/out.zip")
                                              -> ENOENT: mkdir 'build/build'

Absolute paths escape the bug only because `"/a/b".split("/")[0]` is `""`; the
extraction call sites resolve first (`adm-zip.js:437`, `:475`, `:103`), so they
are unaffected. The public `writeZip("build/out.zip")` path is affected
(`adm-zip.js:526` -> `util/utils.js:103`).

**Impact:** writing an archive, or writing a file, to a not-yet-existing
relative directory throws. The caller can work around it by passing an absolute
path, and no data is lost, so low.

**Fix:** build the prefix from the whole path instead of the first segment:
start `resolvedPath` empty (or at the root/drive) and let the loop append every
segment once, e.g. iterate over `path.split(PATH_SEPARATOR)` and use
`pth.dirname` on the absolute form.

findings.title: Failed async open writes with an undefined fd and crashes the process
findings.body:
When the extracting process cannot open the destination, `writeFileToAsync`
ignores the second `open` error and calls `fs.write` with an undefined `fd`,
which throws inside an fs callback. The exception is uncaught, so the process
exits instead of the error reaching the caller's callback.

**Evidence:** `util/utils.js:141-146` opens the file, and in `err` goes
straight to `fs.chmod` and a second `fs.open` whose `err`/`fd` are never
checked, then `fs.write(fd, ...)` at `:146`. Reproduced end to end: an archive
whose entry name is 300 characters (longer than one path component allows) and
`extractAllToAsync(target, true, cb)`:

    TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "fd" argument must be of type number.
    Received undefined
        at /workspace/repos/.../util/utils.js:146:44
        at FSReqCallback.oncomplete (node:fs:187:23)

The process exits 1 and `cb` is never invoked; the same happens for any reason
`open` fails twice (EACCES, EISDIR, ENAMETOOLONG). Triggering it directly:
`Utils.writeFileToAsync("/tmp/" + "x".repeat(300), buf, true, cb)`.

**Impact:** an attacker-supplied archive with one over-long entry name turns a
failed extraction into a process crash and a callback that never fires, so a
service that unzips uploads can be knocked over and callers that wait for the
callback hang. Restart recovers it, so low.

**Fix:** in both branches check the error from `fs.open`, and on failure call
`callback(false)` (or `callback(new Error(...))`) instead of writing with an
undefined descriptor. Keep `finally`-style cleanup so `fd` is closed exactly
once.

summary:
Review complete. Findings recorded: one high (path traversal), two low (uncaught throw crash, listing XSS).

**Summary:** This PR re-adds `crud-file-server.js`, the single-module HTTP file server behind CVE-2018-3726. The traversal guard `cleanUrl` is broken by a typo — `url.indexOf('..').length > 0` is always false because a number has no `length` — so the `while` loop never strips anything and the decoded request path reaches `fs` calls unchanged. I reproduced unauthenticated reads, PUT writes, and DELETE removals outside the served root against an unmodified copy, so the traversal is confirmed rather than argued; the rest of the file (query parsing, HEAD, JSON listing, error paths) behaves as intended apart from a crash-on-throw when `-v` is configured and unescaped file names in the HTML listing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read, write and delete files outside the served directory
findings.body:
`cleanUrl` never removes `..`, so any unauthenticated HTTP client can read, write,
rename, or delete files anywhere the server process can reach — not just inside the
exposed directory.

The loop condition is `url.indexOf('..').length > 0`. `indexOf` returns a number,
and a number has no `length`, so the condition is always `undefined > 0` — false. The
`while` body never runs; `cleanUrl` only calls `decodeURIComponent` and returns the
path unchanged. `relativePath` is then built by plain string concatenation
(`crud-file-server.js:53-55`), so `..` segments resolve at the filesystem call.

**Preconditions:** none. Reachable on the default configuration (`readOnly` false).
The same defect applies to `?rename=`, which also passes through `cleanUrl`.

**Evidence:** with the file served from `/tmp/repro/served`, all three requests
succeeded against an unmodified copy of this file:

    curl --path-as-is 'http://127.0.0.1:8098/../secret.txt'          -> "SECRET"
    curl --path-as-is 'http://127.0.0.1:8098/%2e%2e/secret.txt'      -> "SECRET"   (encoded form, decoded by cleanUrl)
    curl --path-as-is -X PUT --data-binary PWNED 'http://127.0.0.1:8098/../written.txt' -> 200, file created outside root
    curl --path-as-is -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8098/../secret.txt' -> 200, file removed

The server log shows the resolved path: `reading file /tmp/repro/served/../secret.txt`.

**Impact:** High. An unauthenticated caller crosses the trust boundary between
"visitor of the exposed directory" and the host filesystem: disclosure of any readable
file (`/etc/passwd`, private keys, other tenants' data), plus permanent damage via PUT
and DELETE over the whole filesystem the process can write. No discount applies — it
is the default configuration, no interleaving, no privileged action needed.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant "the request path must resolve inside the served root"
by comparing canonical paths instead of editing the string. Resolve the decoded path
with `path.resolve(root, relative)` and reject when the result does not start with
`root + path.sep`; apply the same check to the `?rename=` target. As a stopgap,
`while (url.indexOf('..') >= 0)` fixes the typo but remains a weak filter — deleting
`..` substrings does not stop all traversal forms.

findings.title: Request outside the virtual path throws uncaught, crashing the server
findings.body:
When the server is started with a virtual path (`-v`), a single request for any URL
that does not begin with that vpath kills the process.

`crud-file-server.js:47` runs `throw 'url [...] does not begin with vpath [...]'`
before the `try` block that starts at line 58. The exception escapes
`handleRequest`, propagates out of the `http.createServer` request listener in
`bin/crud-file-server:35-37`, and Node terminates the process. A request for `/`
(empty cleaned url) always fails the check, so the first client that opens the bare
host name takes the server down.

**Preconditions:** started with `-v` / `vpath` set (the form used in the README
example); `-v` is not the default.

**Evidence:** served with `vpath = 'filez'`:

    GET /x   -> connection closed, process exits:
    /tmp/repro/crud-file-server.js:47
            throw 'url [' + url + '] does not begin with vpath [' + vpath + ']';
    url [x] does not begin with vpath [filez]
    GET /filez afterwards -> connection refused

The same request wrapped in a try/catch returns normally, which confirms the throw —
not a crash inside `fs` — is the cause.

**Impact:** Low under the review policy: reach is broad (every client of that
deployment) and persistence recoverable (a restart restores service), giving medium,
discounted one tier because it requires the non-default `-v` option. On a deployment
that does use `-v`, the effect is a full, remotely triggerable outage from one
unauthenticated request.

**Fix:** Do not throw across the request-handler boundary. Respond with a 404/403 via
`writeError(..., 404)` and return.

findings.title: Unescaped file names in the HTML directory listing allow script injection
findings.body:
Directory listings render file names into HTML without escaping, so a file whose name contains markup executes script in the browser of anyone who lists that directory. `crud-file-server.js:143` writes the raw name into both the `href` and the link text: res.write('\r\n

' + name + '

'); `name` comes straight from `fs.readdir` (`:106`). A name containing `<`, `>` or a quote breaks out of the anchor. **Preconditions:** a file or directory with HTML in its name exists under the served root — either pre-existing, or placed by an unauthenticated `PUT` (allowed whenever `-r` is not set). **Evidence:** created `served/.txt`, then `GET /filez` returned: .txt **Impact:** Low. Script runs in the origin of the file server, which has no sessions, cookies, or authentication state, so there is no credential to steal and the attacker can already issue the same HTTP requests directly — the injected script adds little beyond nuisance and drive-by redirects against the person browsing the listing. **Fix:** HTML-escape `name` (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"`) before writing it, and URL-encode the path component used in `href`.

summary:
**Summary.** The PR adds one file, `util/utils.js`: the CRC32, directory-creation and file-writing primitives that every other module in the tree requires, so without it `require("./adm-zip")` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Restoring it makes the library functional again, and with it the unguarded extraction paths in the unchanged `adm-zip.js`, which pass attacker-controlled entry names through `pth.resolve` to these primitives — I reproduced CVE-2018-1002204 on this tree (an entry named `../../../../../../tmp/slip/pwned2.txt` wrote outside the target with no error), which is the blocking finding.

The restored code is byte-identical to upstream adm-zip's `util/utils.js` at both the pre- and post-fix commits, so nothing here is the CVE fix; that guard belongs in `adm-zip.js` and is absent. Beyond the traversal, three defects in the added file reproduced on modern Node: an unsigned CRC32 written with `writeInt32LE` breaks zip writing for about half of all contents, `mkdirSync` duplicates the first path segment so `writeZip("build/out.zip")` fails, and a failed `fs.open` in `writeFileToAsync` throws an uncaught `TypeError` that kills the process. Overall the change should not merge until the extraction containment guard is restored.

findings.title: Zip entries containing .. write files outside the extraction target
findings.body:
Extracting an archive whose entry names contain `..` writes files outside `targetPath`, anywhere the process can write.

`util/utils.js` is the only module that creates directories and writes files (`makeDir`/`mkdirSync` at util/utils.js:15-29, `writeFileTo` at util/utils.js:92-120). Both act on whatever absolute path they receive. Every extraction call site resolves the entry name against the target and passes the result straight through without a containment check: adm-zip.js:437 and adm-zip.js:444 (`extractAllTo`), adm-zip.js:374 and adm-zip.js:385 (`extractEntryTo`), adm-zip.js:475 and adm-zip.js:488 (`extractAllToAsync`). `pth.resolve` collapses `..`, so an entry named `../../../../../../tmp/slip/pwned2.txt` resolves outside the target and is written.

Note the change makes this reachable: before it, `require("./util")` (util/index.js:1) failed with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` because `util/utils.js` was missing, so no extraction path could run at all.

**Evidence:** reproduced on this tree with a zip built by the library itself:

```js
var AdmZip = require("./adm-zip");
var zip = new AdmZip();                                   // attacker side
zip.addFile("../../../../../../tmp/slip/pwned2.txt", new Buffer("owned by zip entry\n"));
zip.writeZip("/tmp/slip/evil2.zip");

var payload = new AdmZip("/tmp/slip/evil2.zip");          // victim side
payload.extractAllTo("/tmp/slip/out/a/b", true);          // no error thrown
```

`extractAllTo` returned normally, nothing was written under `/tmp/slip/out/a/b`, and `/tmp/slip/pwned2.txt` contained `owned by zip entry`. The same reachability applies through `extractEntryTo` and `extractAllToAsync`.

**Impact:** The documented use of this library is extracting archives from untrusted sources (plugins, uploads, build artifacts). Anyone who can supply an archive can create or overwrite any file the extracting process can write — `~/.bashrc`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, a reverse shell in a cron directory, another tenant's files — with attacker-chosen content that survives restart. This is CVE-2018-1002204. A trust boundary is crossed and the write is permanent, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Restore containment at each extraction call site: resolve the destination and reject it unless it lies inside the resolved `targetPath` (upstream fixed this in adm-zip.js with `if (!pth.resolve(targetPath, entryName).startsWith(pth.resolve(targetPath))) throw Utils.Errors.INVALID_FILENAME` before both `makeDir` and `writeFileTo`). Do not copy that check verbatim: string `startsWith` also accepts sibling directories such as `/tmp/out-evil` for target `/tmp/out`, so compare against `pth.resolve(targetPath) + pth.sep` or use `pth.relative(targetPath, target)` and reject results starting with `..`.

findings.title: Relative multi-segment paths are created one directory too deep, so writeZip fails
findings.body:
`writeZip` fails for any relative target name with more than one path segment. `mkdirSync` seeds `resolvedPath` with `path.split(PATH_SEPARATOR)[0]` (util/utils.js:16) and then re-appends that same first segment in its `forEach` loop (util/utils.js:17-19), so a relative path gains a duplicated leading directory: `build/out.zip` becomes `build/build/out.zip`, and a single-segment relative path becomes `name/name`. Absolute paths escape the bug only because their first split element is the empty string.

**Evidence:** `writeZip` passes the caller's file name un-resolved to `writeFileTo` (adm-zip.js:526), so the documented `zip.writeZip("build/out.zip")` reaches it directly:

```js
var z = new AdmZip(); z.addFile("a.txt", new Buffer("file2"));
z.writeZip("build/out.zip");   // ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir 'build/build'
```

`Utils.makeDir("a/b")` fails the same way (`mkdir 'a/a'`). Extraction is unaffected because those call sites pass `pth.resolve`d paths, which are absolute.

**Impact:** Creating a zip at a nested relative path — the common `writeZip("dist/out.zip")` pattern — throws instead of writing. Contained to the calling code and nothing is lost, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Do not re-add the first segment: start the loop at the segment after the root (`pth.parse(path).root`, or `path.slice(root.length).split(PATH_SEPARATOR)`), then append each remaining segment to the accumulated absolute prefix.

findings.title: CRC32 is returned unsigned but written with writeInt32LE, so writing zips throws RangeError
findings.body:
Writing a zip throws `RangeError` whenever an entry's CRC32 is 2^31 or larger — roughly half of all possible contents. `crc32` normalizes its result through a buffer into an unsigned 32-bit value (util/utils.js:76-77, returning e.g. `3633523372` for `"hi"`), `ZipEntry.setData` stores it verbatim (zipEntry.js:234), and `entryHeaderToBinary` writes it with `data.writeInt32LE(_crc, ...)` (headers/entryHeader.js:216). Modern Node range-checks the argument of `writeInt32LE`, so the write throws. The LOC header uses `writeUInt32LE` (headers/entryHeader.js:188) and is fine, which is why only the CEN-header path fails.

**Evidence:**

```js
var z = new AdmZip(); z.addFile("x.txt", new Buffer("hi"));   // crc32 = 3633523372
z.toBuffer();    // RangeError: ... must be >= -2147483648 and <= 2147483647. Received 3633523372
z.writeZip("/tmp/out.zip");  // same
```

Re-saving an archive that already contains such an entry fails the same way (`new AdmZip(file).writeZip(other)` → RangeError while `readAsText` still works), so loaded archives can be read but not rewritten or updated.

**Impact:** `addFile`/`writeZip`/`toBuffer`/`updateFile` fail for about half of real file contents, deterministically for a given content. Nothing is lost and the caller sees an exception, so this is a functional break rather than a data-integrity bug: broad reach over the write API, recoverable, severity medium.

**Fix:** Use one sign convention. Either write the CEN field with `writeUInt32LE` (matching the LOC header and the `readUInt32LE` already used at headers/entryHeader.js:153), or keep `crc32`'s result signed by returning `crc | 0`. Writing unsigned is preferable because the value is a checksum, not a number.

findings.title: Failed open in writeFileToAsync throws uncaught TypeError and kills the process

summary:
The change adds `crud-file-server.js`, a directory-exposing HTTP server with GET/HEAD/PUT/POST/DELETE, restored on top of a baseline that had the file removed. The whole file is new, so the review covered all of it, and I reproduced each failure against a running instance.

The core problem is that the traversal guard never runs — `url.indexOf('..').length` is always `undefined`, so unauthenticated clients can read, write, delete and rename files anywhere the process can reach. Two independent uncaught-exception paths (malformed percent-encoding, and a `"` in a listed file name) let any client kill the process, plus a third that a configured `-v` vpath trips on every `GET /`. The remaining note is a wrong status code for unsupported methods.

findings.title: Unauthenticated ../ traversal reads, writes, deletes and renames files outside the served directory
findings.body:
Any HTTP client can read, write, delete, and rename files outside the directory the server was told to serve. The traversal guard is inert: `cleanUrl` never removes `..`.

**Evidence:** `crud-file-server.js:6` — `while(url.indexOf('..').length > 0)`. `indexOf` returns a number, whose `.length` is `undefined`, so `undefined > 0` is false and the loop body never executes. `cleanUrl` therefore only percent-decodes the path. The decoded url is concatenated onto the root at `crud-file-server.js:55` and handed unchecked to `fs.stat`, `fs.readFile`, `fs.createWriteStream`, `fs.unlink`/`fs.rmdir`, and `fs.rename` (`:96`, `:172`, `:187`, `:214`, `:240`, `:248`). The rename destination (`path + query.rename`, `:214`) gets the same broken `cleanUrl` treatment at `:204`.

Reproduced against this checkout with the server serving `/tmp/cfs/root`:

```
GET  /../secret.txt                             -> 200 "SECRET-OUTSIDE"
GET  /..%2fsecret.txt                           -> 200 same (decode happens first, :5)
GET  /../../../../etc/passwd                    -> 200 /etc/passwd
PUT  /../written-outside.txt                    -> 200 file created beside the root
DELETE /../written-outside.txt                  -> 200 file removed
POST /served/moveme.txt?rename=../moved.txt     -> 200 file moved outside the root
```

**Impact:** The served directory is the only boundary this package claims (README: "exposes a directory and its children"). An unauthenticated network client gets read, write, delete and rename over every file the server process can reach — reading `/etc/shadow` or SSH keys, writing `authorized_keys` or a crontab. Crosses the trust boundary and the effects are permanent, hence high.

**Fix:** Restore one invariant: every path handed to `fs` must resolve inside the root. Resolve the root once and, per request, compute `var target = require('path').resolve(base, '.' + url)`; reject with 403 unless `target === base || target.startsWith(base + require('path').sep)`. Apply the same resolution to the `query.rename` destination. Stripping `..` substrings is not sound on its own — an encoded or nested form (`....//`, `..%5c`) can slip through — so the containment check must be the enforcement point.

findings.title: Malformed percent-encoding in a request URL crashes the server process
findings.body:
A single request with a malformed percent-escape terminates the server process. `decodeURIComponent` throws and nothing catches it.

**Evidence:** `crud-file-server.js:5` calls `decodeURIComponent(url)`; it runs from `crud-file-server.js:38`, which is above the `try` that only opens at `crud-file-server.js:57`. `decodeURIComponent('%')` throws `URIError: URI malformed`, which propagates out of the `http.createServer` request listener; `bin/crud-file-server` installs no `uncaughtException` handler, so Node exits.

Reproduced: `curl --path-as-is 'http://127.0.0.1:18081/%'` returned no response, and every following request was refused while stderr showed `Node.js v24.22.2` and a stack trace. The same path is reachable through `query.rename` at `:204` for POST.

**Impact:** Any unauthenticated client can stop the server at will, for any HTTP method; recovery needs a restart. Broad reach, recoverable (a restart is a supported action), so medium.

**Fix:** Put the preamble (decode, url normalisation, vpath check) inside the `try` at `:57` so `writeError` handles it, and have `cleanUrl` treat a decode failure as a 400 rather than propagating a `URIError`.

findings.title: File name containing a double quote crashes the server while rendering a directory listing
findings.body:
A file whose name contains a double quote makes every directory listing of that directory crash the server. The guard throws from inside an asynchronous callback, where no handler can see it.

**Evidence:** `crud-file-server.js:143` — `if(normalized.indexOf('"') >= 0) throw new Error('unsupported file name')`. It executes inside the `fs.readdir` callback (`:107`) that feeds the listing renderer, i.e. on a later tick, after the synchronous `try` at `:57` has already returned.

Reproduced: `PUT /served/a%22b` (200, file created — the server's own unauthenticated PUT is enough), then `GET /served/` kills the process; the socket is reset and the `<html><body>` already written at `:138` is left unterminated. The name is also attacker-influenced without PUT, since any user who can drop a file into the served tree can trigger it.

**Impact:** Unauthenticated denial of service of the whole server, re-triggerable, recovered only by restarting. Broad reach, recoverable persistence, so medium.

**Fix:** Do not throw on awkward names. Percent-encode the name for the `href` (`encodeURIComponent(name)`) and HTML-escape it for the label (including `"`), which removes the reason for the check.

findings.title: Request for / crashes the server when a virtual path is configured
findings.body:
With a virtual path configured (`-v`), a request for `/` — or the browser's automatic `/favicon.ico` — crashes the server.

**Evidence:** `crud-file-server.js:45-48` throws before the `try` that opens at `:57`. With vpath `filez`, `/` normalises to the empty string (`:41`, `:42`), so `''.indexOf('filez') != 0` is true and the throw escapes the request listener uncaught. `:41` partly causes this: `url.slice(0, url.length)` is a no-op, so a trailing slash is never actually stripped.

Reproduced with `-v filez`: `GET /` produced no response and the process exited; `GET /filez/served/inside.txt` afterwards was refused.

**Impact:** The documented `-v` deployment dies on the first browser visit. Broad reach and recoverable, discounted one tier because it needs the non-default vpath option, so low.

**Fix:** Report a bad virtual path through `writeError` (403/404) instead of throwing, move the preamble inside the `try`, fix `:41` to `url.slice(0, url.length - 1)`, and match the vpath on a `/` boundary (`url === vpath || url.indexOf(vpath + '/') === 0`) so `filez-private` is not mistaken for `filez`.

findings.title: Unsupported HTTP methods return 500 and leak an internal error instead of 405
findings.body:
Requests using an unsupported HTTP method get a 500 with an internal error string instead of the intended 405, because the message interpolates an undeclared variable.

**Evidence:** `crud-file-server.js:260` — `writeError('Method ' + method + ' not allowed', 405)`. There is no `method` binding; the request method is `req.method`. The resulting `ReferenceError` is thrown inside the `try` at `:57`, swallowed by the `catch` at `:264`, and re-sent as `writeError('unhandled error: ' + err)` with the default status 500.

Reproduced: `PATCH /served/inside.txt` returned `500` with body `"unhandled error: ReferenceError: method is not defined"`.

**Impact:** info — clients receive the wrong status code and a leaked internal error / stack-derived message for `PATCH`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, and lowercase method names.

**Fix:** Use `req.method` in the message and pass the 405 code through unchanged.

summary:
## Review summary

The change adds `src/ajax.js` (844 lines) to a tree where that file was removed. Its content corresponds to upstream jquery `a938d7b1` ("compress ajax", the post-fix commit for CVE-2020-7656), not to the pre-fix file that the surrounding tree (`c27dc018`) shipped.

The security-relevant difference is in `jQuery.fn.load` at `src/ajax.js:177`: the selector branch now inserts `jQuery.parseHTML( responseText )` instead of `responseText.replace( rscript, "" )`. I built the tree plus the added file (concatenated per `grunt.js`, Sizzle at the recorded submodule commit) and ran it under jsdom with a stubbed XHR: `<script>`, `</script >`, `</script\n>`, typed scripts and `onerror` payloads in a `load(url + " selector")` response neither execute nor survive in the DOM, while the same payloads do execute with the pre-fix file. The non-selector branch still evaluates scripts, which the repository's own tests require (`test/unit/ajax.js:1304`, `:1322`), and the file also loads and issues XHR/script/JSONP requests correctly against the older sibling modules (`src/ajax/script.js`, `jsonp.js`, `xhr.js`) left unchanged in the tree.

I found no defect to report: the added code removes the scripting vector rather than introducing one, and the remaining sharp edges in the file (`split( core_rspace )` on `dataType`, script evaluation in the non-selector branch) behave identically to the pre-existing version, so they are not regressions from this change. No findings were recorded.

Recorded one finding. Summary:

The PR adds the whole ajax module, `src/ajax.js` (872 lines), to a jQuery 1.9.0pre tree that previously had none; the file is byte-identical to upstream jquery/jquery at the baseline commit, and it wires in cleanly with the rest of the tree (`core_rspace`, `jQuery.now`, `parseJSON`, `parseXML`, `globalEval` all exist; build order in `grunt.js:65-68` is consistent).

The one real problem is in `jQuery.fn.load`: it strips `<script>` from fetched HTML with a regex that only recognizes the literal `</script>` end tag, so `<script>…</script >` survives, is inserted into the live document by `self.html()`, and is evaluated — cross-site scripting for any page that uses the selector form of `.load` on attacker-influenced HTML. I reproduced it end to end against a build of this tree in jsdom (attacker script ran; the `</script>` control did not).

Everything else in the file (URL/cross-domain parsing, anti-cache rewriting, prefilters/transports, `done`/`ajaxConvert`) matches upstream and I found no additional evidence-backed defect worth filing; the probe's other leads were upstream quirks or non-security behaviour.

findings.title: jQuery.fn.load runs attacker scripts when a closing tag is written `</script >`
findings.body:
`jQuery.fn.load( url, params, callback )` removes ``. Any script closed with whitespace — ``, which is valid HTML — or not closed at all survives the filter, is inserted into the page by `self.html()`, and is then executed by jQuery's own script evaluation. Fetched HTML that an attacker can influence therefore runs JavaScript in the victim page's origin. **Preconditions:** the calling page uses `$( el ).load( url + " #selector" )` (or a params argument) on a response whose body an attacker controls or influences. **Evidence:** `rscript` at `src/ajax.js:15` and its single use at `src/ajax.js:190`: ``` "" -> "" (stripped) "" -> "" (kept) ``` The kept script rides along inside the matched container: `jQuery("
").append( responseText.replace( rscript, "" ) ).find( selector )` (`src/ajax.js:186-193`) parses into a detached div, where `domManip` does not evaluate it because `jQuery.contains( doc, node )` is false (`src/manipulation.js:361`). `self.html( nodes )` (`src/ajax.js:183`) then appends that jQuery object into a live element, so the same `hasScripts` branch (`src/manipulation.js:351-377`) now passes the contains check and calls `jQuery.globalEval` at `src/manipulation.js:374`. Reproduced end to end against a build of this tree in jsdom, loading `/ws.html #c` where the response body is `
`: the target's HTML after load is `
` and `window.__ws === 1`. The same test with `` leaves `window.__ws` undefined and an empty container. **Impact:** attacker-supplied markup obtains script execution in the origin of the page that called `.load`, i.e. cross-site scripting against that page's users and any credentials or session the page holds. Reach crosses a trust boundary (untrusted response content reaches the page's script context); it is discounted once because the calling page must both use the selector form of `.load` and load attacker-influenced HTML, and the resulting script run is a single execution rather than stored state. This matches the CVE-2020-7656 report against jQuery's `load` method. **Fix:** stop hand-parsing the response. Keep the invariant "only markup chosen by the selector reaches `html()`", and let the library's inert parser do the stripping, e.g. `jQuery("
").append( jQuery.parseHTML( responseText ) ).find( selector )` (or pass the parsed nodes through `jQuery.buildFragment` with a detached context), so script nodes are dropped by construction rather than by a regex that enumerates end-tag spellings.

summary:
Reviewed the change: it adds `index.js` with the RNG switched from `Math.random()` to `math-random` (`index.js:83`) and exposes `module.exports.isCrypto` (`index.js:21`), i.e. the intended fix for insecure randomness. In Node the module behaves correctly once `math-random` resolves (`isCrypto === true`, output from `crypto.randomBytes`), and the rest of the file matches upstream byte-for-byte, so the argument-parsing, mask-building and `while (length--)` quirks are pre-existing upstream behaviour rather than regressions here.

One defect is attributable to the change: `index.js:12` requires `math-random`, which is declared in neither `package.json` nor `bower.json`, so a clean consumer install throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at load; the repo's own `npm test` hides this because `math-random` arrives transitively through dev dependencies. It is recorded as a medium finding with the reproduction.

findings.title: Package requires 'math-random' but never declares it, so consumers crash on require
findings.body:
`index.js` now requires `math-random` (`index.js:12`, used at `index.js:21` and `index.js:83`), but neither `package.json:31-34` nor `bower.json:13-16` declares it. Any consumer that installs this package declares only `is-number` and `kind-of`, so `require('randomatic')` throws before the library can be used.

**Evidence:** Reproduction with only the declared dependencies:

```
$ mkdir consumer && cd consumer && npm i is-number@4 kind-of@6 && cp <repo>/index.js .
$ node -e "require('./index.js')"
Error: Cannot find module 'math-random'
    at Module._resolveFilename (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1564:12)
    1 at Module._load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1218:12)
```

The failure is a load-time crash, not a degraded result: every call path through the module is unreachable. With `math-random` present the module works as intended (`isCrypto === true`, crypto-source output), so the only defect is the missing declaration.

The repo's own `npm test` does not catch it: `math-random` is only present transitively through dev dependencies (`benchmarked@1.1.1 -> micromatch@2.3.11 -> braces@1.8.5 -> expand-range@1.8.2 -> fill-range@2.2.4 -> randomatic@3.1.1 -> math-random@1.0.4`), so CI is green while the published package is broken.

**Impact:** Every install of the published package fails at `require` with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Reach is broad (all consumers) and the effect is undone by declaring the dependency and republishing, so medium.

**Fix:** Declare the dependency the new code already relies on — add `"math-random": "^1.0.1"` to `dependencies` in `package.json` (and `bower.json`), keeping `package-lock.json`/CI installs deterministic.

summary:
Findings recorded. Summary of the review:

The PR adds `lib/deep-extend.js`, the deep-extend implementation, to a baseline that was missing it, and it includes the `safeGetProperty` guard that blocks `__proto__` reads — the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3750. I verified empirically that the classic payloads (`__proto__` plain/nested, `constructor.prototype`, payloads inside arrays, 3000 randomized shapes) leave `Object.prototype` and `Array.prototype` untouched, while the pre-fix 0.5.0 code pollutes on the first payload; the 15 upstream tests also pass. So the security intent of the change holds; the two issues I recorded are a null-target crash (`deepExtend(null, x)` throws instead of returning `false`) and the merge writing into an object inherited from the target's prototype, which shares one caller's values with every instance of that prototype.

findings.title: deepExtend with a null first argument throws instead of returning false
findings.body:
`deepExtend(null, defaults)` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` instead of
returning `false` as the function's own contract states. A caller that passes a possibly
null first argument (for example `deepExtend(options.section, defaults)` where the section
is omitted) crashes the whole call.

**Evidence:** `lib/deep-extend.js:83` accepts `null`, because `typeof null === 'object'`, so
the guard does not return `false`; the doc comment at `lib/deep-extend.js:76` promises
`false` for "no target object". The null target then reaches `safeGetProperty(target, key)`
at `lib/deep-extend.js:105`, which evaluates `null[key]`:

```js
const d = require('./index.js');
d(null, { a: 1 });   // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'a')
d(5, { a: 1 });      // false  (non-object types are handled)
```

The upstream test suite only covers a null *second* argument (`test/index.spec.js:16`), so
the path is untested.

**Impact:** a contained, transient crash on invalid input; the merge never partially applies,
and the documented `false` return path is simply bypassed for `null`. Severity is below
`low` because it requires the caller to pass `null` where the docs already discourage it.

**Fix:** add `arguments[0] === null` to the guard at `lib/deep-extend.js:83` so a null
target returns `false` like any other non-object target.

findings.title: Merge mutates an object inherited from the target's prototype, leaking one caller's values to all instances
findings.body:
When the merged key exists as an object on the target's prototype chain, the merge writes
into that borrowed object instead of assigning a fresh one. Every other object sharing the
prototype sees the merged (attacker-supplied) values.

**Preconditions:** the target inherits an object-valued property, e.g. an instance created
from a constructor whose prototype holds a config/defaults object, and the value being
merged is supplied by someone other than the owner of that shared object.

**Evidence:** `lib/deep-extend.js:105` reads `src = safeGetProperty(target, key)`, which
walks the prototype chain, and `lib/deep-extend.js:137` then calls `deepExtend(src, val)`,
which mutates `src` in place:

```js
const deepExtend = require('./index.js');
function RequestState() {}
RequestState.prototype.config = { theme: 'light' };   // shared by all instances

const a = new RequestState();
deepExtend(a, JSON.parse('{"config": {"theme": "pwned"}}'));
a.config;                              // { theme: 'pwned' }  (own property)
new RequestState().config;             // { theme: 'pwned' }  (contaminated)
```

The library's own "doesn't change sources" test (`test/index.spec.js`) only covers the
arguments, not objects reached through the target's prototype, so nothing catches this.

**Impact:** in a long-lived server process, a value merged from one caller's input becomes
visible to every object sharing that prototype. Reach is contained to that prototype's
instances and the change is recoverable by overwriting the value, so this is `low`; the
default pattern (`deepExtend({}, input)`) is unaffected because a fresh object has no
inherited object properties.

**Fix:** only reuse `src` when it is an own property of the target — e.g. replace the read at
`lib/deep-extend.js:105` with an own-property check (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, key) ? target[key] : undefined`)
so an inherited object falls into the existing `target[key] = deepExtend({}, val)` branch.

summary:
Recorded three findings:

- **high** — unauthenticated LFI: `/render/file:///etc/passwd` returns local file contents (the CVE-2017-18354 defect; no scheme validation in `main.js:65` before `Page.navigate` at `renderer.js:75`).
- **medium** — failed renders leak a Chrome tab/CDP session because `CDP.Close` is only on the success path.
- **medium** — a negative `width`/`height` on `/screenshot` makes a pre-`try` CDP call reject inside an `async` Promise executor, hanging the request and feeding the 5-strike `process.exit` handler.

This PR adds `src/renderer.js`, the headless-Chrome render/screenshot driver, restoring Rendertron's rendering pipeline. The file is largely a faithful upstream copy, but it ships the pre-fix URL handling, so the rendering path it enables exposes the local filesystem to any caller; the resource-cleanup and screenshot-validation defects are real but less severe. I also reviewed the injected-URL `Runtime.evaluate` interpolation and the virtual-time/status-code logic and judged them non-reportable (no capability beyond what the rendered page already has, or bounded by the 10-second hard limit).

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can read arbitrary local files via file:// renders
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can read any file the renderer process can read. `/render/<url>`
(and `/screenshot/<url>`) pass the decoded path segment straight to Chrome's
`Page.navigate` with no scheme check, so a `file://` URL is rendered and its contents are
returned in the response body.

**Preconditions:** default configuration — no `config.json`, so `renderOnly` is unset.

**Evidence:**
- `src/main.js:65-74` — `isRestricted()` returns `false` when `config.renderOnly` is unset,
  and even when set it only does a prefix match on the URL string; it never inspects the
  scheme.
- `src/main.js:99` passes `request.params.url` to `renderer.serialize`, which reaches
  `Page.navigate({url: url})` at `src/renderer.js:75`.
- The serialized result is `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` (`src/renderer.js:190`).
  For `file:///etc/passwd` Chrome renders the file as a `<pre>`, so the returned HTML
  contains the file text. `stripPage()` (`src/renderer.js:162-165`) only removes scripts.
- Reproduction confirmed against headless Chrome with the unmodified renderer:
  `serialize('file:///etc/passwd')` returned `<html>...<pre>root:x:0:0:...`.
  `curl 'http://host:3000/render/file:///etc/passwd'` returns that body with status 200
  (`file://` produces no `Network.responseReceived`, so `statusCode` stays 200).
- The repo's own tests already render `file://` URLs (`test/app-test.js:117,124`), which
  confirms the scheme is not blocked.

**Impact:** crosses a trust boundary: a remote caller obtains local files such as
`config.json`, service-account keys, `/proc/self/environ`, or any file readable by the
Chrome user. Disclosure is permanent. This matches the published CVE-2017-18354 LFI.

**Fix:** reject any request URL whose parsed protocol is not `http:` or `https:` before
navigation, e.g. in `isRestricted()` (`src/main.js:65`) or at the top of `serialize` /
`captureScreenshot`, and return 403. A `renderOnly` prefix allowlist is not a substitute,
since it is off by default.

findings.title: Failed renders leak Chrome tabs and CDP sessions
findings.body:
Every failed render leaks the Chrome tab and CDP connection it created. `CDP.Close` is only
called on the success path, so a request that fails to load leaves a tab, a websocket and
Network/Console listeners alive on the shared Chrome instance until the process restarts.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:179` / `src/renderer.js:203` create a new target per request with
  `CDP.New`.
- `src/renderer.js:96-101` rejects `_loadPage` when the initial request fails
  (`Network.loadingFailed`, e.g. DNS failure or connection refused).
- The `catch` blocks in `serialize` (`src/renderer.js:194-197`) and `captureScreenshot`
  (`src/renderer.js:222-225`) only call `reject(error)`; neither calls `CDP.Close`
  (lines 191/221) nor closes the client.
- Reproduction: repeat `GET /render/http://127.0.0.1:1/`. Each request returns 400 from
  `src/main.js:102-107` and leaves one more open tab/session. Upstream later fixed exactly
  this by adding `closeConnection` to both catch blocks (commit ccb520c, PR #144).

**Impact:** broad and recoverable: an unauthenticated caller can leak tabs and file
descriptors without limit, eventually exhausting memory on the one Chrome instance that
serves every user, so all render requests fail until the service is restarted.

**Fix:** close the target in a `finally` block in both methods, awaiting the close and
swallowing close errors, instead of only on success.

findings.title: Screenshot with negative width hangs the request and can shut the service down
findings.body:
A screenshot request with a negative width or height makes the handler hang forever and
counts toward the process-exit counter. `captureScreenshot` runs its CDP setup calls before
its `try` block inside an `async` Promise executor. When one of those calls rejects, the
executor's promise rejects unseen and the outer Promise's `resolve`/`reject` are never
called, so no response is ever sent.

**Evidence:**
- `src/renderer.js:211-215`: `width`/`height` are `Math.min(2000, parseInt(value) || 1000)`,
  which keeps negative values, and are passed to `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` /
  `setVisibleSize` at lines 214-215, before the `try` at line 217.
- Verified against headless Chrome: `setDeviceMetricsOverride` with `width: -1` rejects with
  `Protocol error ... Width and height values must be positive`.
  `GET /screenshot/http://x?width=-1` reaches this call.
- The rejection of the async executor promise is unobserved; the outer promise never
  settles, so `src/main.js:110-125` waits forever and never writes a response.
- `process.on('unhandledRejection', logUncaughtError)` (`src/main.js:180`) counts each one;
  after more than 5, `src/main.js:170-175` kills Chrome and calls `process.exit(1)`.

**Impact:** broad and recoverable: an unauthenticated caller can hold request handlers open
and, with ~6 requests, shut the whole rendering service down.

**Fix:** reject early when `width`/`height` is not a positive integer, move the CDP calls
inside the `try`, and avoid an `async` function as a Promise executor — route every thrown
error to `reject`.

summary:
This PR re-adds `index.js`, the full `randomatic` generator (pattern → mask → string) at version 2.0.0, as a fixture for CVE-2017-16028. It is a single-file library addition whose behaviour the test suite (34 passing) does not question.

The main problem is the generator itself: every character is `Math.random()`-derived and the output is a pure function of that stream, so the library cannot produce unpredictable secrets despite being marketed for passwords and tokens. Two smaller defects come with the same file: unvalidated length values that can hang a caller's process, and a mask that silently picks up the string `"undefined"` when `?` is used without `chars`.

findings.title: Generated tokens are predictable: every character comes from Math.random
findings.body:
`randomatic` builds strings that are only as unpredictable as `Math.random()`. Every
character comes from one `Math.random()` draw:

```js
while (length--) {
  res += mask.charAt(parseInt(Math.random() * mask.length, 10));   // index.js:81
}
```

This library advertises itself as a password/token generator ("The original
generate-password", `password`/`generate-password` keywords in package.json:9-52),
so callers use its output as secrets: reset tokens, API keys, temporary passwords.

**Evidence:**

- The output is a pure function of the `Math.random()` stream. Stubbing
  `Math.random` to a fixed sequence makes generation fully deterministic:

  ```
  same-Math.random-stream run 1: j^FK]c5y
  same-Math.random-stream run 2: j^FK]c5y
  ```

  No other entropy source is consulted anywhere in index.js.
- `Math.random()` is not a cryptographic generator. In V8 it is a 52-bit draw from
  an xorshift128+ state, and the state is recoverable from a modest number of
  outputs (published tooling exists, e.g. `v8-randomness-predictor`). Because each
  output character is `floor(r * mask.length)` for a mask the attacker knows
  (default alphabets, or `chars` in most uses), a run of generated strings leaks
  those 52-bit values. Once the state is recovered, every later string from the
  same process — including tokens issued to *other* users — is computable.

**Impact:** A secret that an attacker can predict is not a secret. In a service
that issues per-user tokens or temporary passwords with this module, an attacker
who receives a token of their own can recover the generator state and predict
tokens issued to other users — crossing a trust boundary with permanent
compromise (an issued credential cannot be un-issued). Matches CVE-2017-16028,
which is why upstream replaced the generator in 3.0.0 with a cryptographic one
(`math-random`, exposed as `module.exports.isCrypto`). High, not critical: the
severity depends on the consumer using the output as a security token, and the
module itself is a general-purpose string generator.

**Fix:** Draw from a CSPRNG and reject out-of-range samples instead of scaling a
float — e.g. `crypto.randomInt(0, mask.length)` per character (Node >= 12.19), or
`crypto.randomBytes` with rejection sampling for older runtimes, keeping the
public pattern API unchanged.

findings.title: Fractional or negative length hangs the process until out-of-memory
findings.body:
A non-integer or negative `length` is never validated, so `while (length--)`
(index.js:80) never reaches a falsy value and the loop appends to `res` until the
process runs out of memory.

**Preconditions:** caller passes a fractional, negative, or `Infinity` length —
e.g. a length computed from a size in bytes, a percentage, or user input.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "require('./')('A',5.5)"     # no output, killed by timeout after 4s (exit 124)
$ node -e "require('./')('A',-5)"      # same
$ node -e "require('./')('A',Infinity)"  # same; V8 aborts with out-of-memory
```

`0.5--` evaluates to `-0.5`, still truthy, so the loop never terminates; `res`
grows without bound. `NaN` and non-numeric strings are falsy immediately, so the
failure is specific to fractional/negative values. No test in test.js passes a
non-integer length.

**Impact:** A caller's process hangs and then aborts on out-of-memory, taking down
whatever request triggered the call. Containment: only the caller's own process is
affected, and restarting clears it; the trigger requires a caller that does not
round its length. Low.

**Fix:** Validate the length once, before the loop — accept only non-negative
integers (`Number.isInteger(length) && length >= 0`), otherwise throw a
`TypeError`, and keep the loop bound to that validated integer.

findings.title: Pattern '?' without the chars option draws from the literal string "undefined"
findings.body:
When the pattern contains `?` but the caller supplies no `chars`, the mask picks up
the literal string `"undefined"`, and generated strings are drawn from its letters.

```js
if (pattern.indexOf('?') !== -1) mask += opts.chars;   // index.js:72
```

`opts.chars` is `undefined`, and `'' + undefined` is the 9-character string
`"undefined"`.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "var r=require('./'); console.log(r('?',8))"        # e.g. 'eufneniu'
# union of the characters produced by 3000 calls to r('?',3):
definu
```

No error and no warning: the call looks successful and returns a string of
letters from `d,e,f,i,n,u`. `r('?A',5)` mixes lowercase `definu` into what should
be an uppercase-only string. Untested in test.js: both `?` cases pass `chars`.

**Impact:** Callers who forget the `chars` option get tokens from a 6-letter
alphabet instead of an error, so the produced secret has far less entropy than its
length suggests. Requires caller misuse of a required option; the output is still
a valid string of the requested length, so damage is bounded. Info.

**Fix:** Only add `opts.chars` when it is a non-empty string, and throw a clear
error (or treat `?` as unusable) when `pattern` contains `?` without it — e.g.
`if (pattern.indexOf('?') !== -1) { if (typeof opts.chars !== 'string' || !opts.chars) throw new TypeError('randomatic expects `chars` when the pattern contains "?"'); mask += opts.chars; }`.

summary:
Review complete. Recording done.

**Summary:** The PR adds `lib/dns-sync.js`, which resolves a hostname by spawning a helper Node script through `shelljs`'s `shell.exec`. Its only guard is a hostname regex, and the regex is written with `\.` inside a JavaScript string literal — JavaScript drops the unknown escape, so the separator becomes "any character" and strings like `a;id` or `a;touch m2` pass validation. I reproduced arbitrary command execution through `resolve()` (`lib/dns-sync.js:31-33`), which is CVE-2017-16100, and recorded it as a high-severity finding. The other new lines (script path, `process.execPath`, `net.isIP` handling of `response.output`, valid/failed resolution) behaved correctly in my tests, so the change has one substantive defect: don't build a shell command from the hostname, and fix the validator's escaping.

findings.title: resolve() runs unvalidated hostnames through a shell, enabling command injection
findings.body:
`resolve()` runs attacker-supplied text through a shell. The hostname check it relies on
passes almost any short string, because the separator in the regex is written `\.` inside
a JavaScript string literal (`lib/dns-sync.js:10`). JavaScript drops the unknown `\.`
escape, so the regex compiles to `...)*` with a bare `.`, i.e. "any character". The
hostname is then interpolated unquoted into a command string and executed with
`shell.exec` (`lib/dns-sync.js:31-33`), so shell metacharacters are interpreted.

**Preconditions:** a caller passes a hostname that an attacker can influence (the intended
use is server startup, but the API takes a plain string). The module's own validation is
what callers rely on to make that safe.

**Evidence:** the regex accepts non-hostname strings:

```
$ node -e 'var re=new RegExp("^(([a-zA-Z0-9]|[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9\-]*[a-zA-Z0-9])\.)*([A-Za-z0-9]|[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9\-]*[A-Za-z0-9])$"); ["a;id","a;touch m2","x`id`y"].forEach(s=>console.log(s,re.test(s)))'
a;id true
a;touch m2 true
x`id`y true
```

Calling `resolve("a;touch m2")` creates the file `m2` in the process working directory and
returns `null`; `resolve("a;id")` executes `id`. Replacing `"`-quoted `node`/script with
`"/usr/bin/true"` and echoing the built command shows the shell receives
`... dns-lookup-script a;touch m2`.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution as the Node process user whenever a caller forwards
an untrusted hostname. An attacker crosses a trust boundary (data in, code out) and the
effect is permanent (commands can modify or exfiltrate anything the process can reach).
This is CVE-2017-16100; severity `high`.

**Fix:** do not involve a shell. Restore the invariant "the hostname is one argument,
never a command". Use `child_process.execFileSync(nodeBinary, [scriptPath, hostname])`
(or `spawnSync`) instead of `shell.exec(cmd)`, and fix the validator so it rejects
non-hostnames: escape the separator (`\\.`) or use a regex literal
`/^(([a-zA-Z0-9]|[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9-]*[a-zA-Z0-9])\.)*([A-Za-z0-9]|[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9-]*[A-Za-z0-9])$/`.

summary:
The pull request adds `lib/deep-extend.js` — the complete recursive merge implementation (upstream deep-extend 0.5.0) that `index.js` and `package.json`'s `main` already point at. It is the only reviewable file, so the whole library's behavior is new surface, and I traced the merge path and its array/special-value clone helpers end to end.

The implementation is otherwise faithful to the documented API (correct merging, array cloning, Buffer/Date/RegExp copies), but the merge target handling is unsafe: a `__proto__` key in a source object writes through to `Object.prototype`, which is CVE-2018-3750 and should block the merge. A related, distinct weakness lets a merge write into an inherited object property and so mutate a shared prototype object. I reproduced both with node; the smaller edge cases I checked (cycled/deep input recursion, frozen targets, `new Buffer` deprecation) did not rise to reportable findings.

findings.title: Merging untrusted input pollutes Object.prototype via a __proto__ key
findings.body:
`deepExtend(target, untrusted)` treats a `__proto__` key in a source object like any
other key. `src = target[key]` (lib/deep-extend.js:105) resolves to
`Object.prototype`, the both-objects branch takes `deepExtend(src, val)`
(lib/deep-extend.js:137), and the attacker's properties are written straight onto
`Object.prototype`. Every object in the process then inherits them.

This is CVE-2018-3750. Version 0.5.1 fixed it by refusing to read or write
`__proto__`; this file has no such check (no `__proto__` or `hasOwnProperty` guard
anywhere).

**Preconditions:** a caller merges attacker-controlled data (parsed JSON body, query
parameters, untrusted config) into an object. That is the library's main use; the
documented clone form `deepExtend({}, userInput)` is affected too.

**Evidence:** with node v24, from the repo root:

```
node -e '
var e = require("./lib/deep-extend");
e({}, JSON.parse("{\"__proto__\":{\"isAdmin\":true}}"));
console.log(({}).isAdmin);'      # -> true
```

The nested forms leak as well, because array elements are merged through
`deepExtend({}, item)` at lib/deep-extend.js:64:

```
node -e '
var e = require("./lib/deep-extend");
e({}, JSON.parse("{\"a\":[{\"__proto__\":{\"isAdmin\":true}}]}"));
console.log(({}).polluted);'     # also pollutes Object.prototype
```

**Impact:** high under the service/library policy in the review contract: one
request's payload changes every object for everyone the process serves, and nothing
the program can call undoes it while it runs. What the attacker can do depends on
which properties the host reads off plain objects (`isAdmin`, role flags, options,
module resolution settings). Severity rests on the consumer passing untrusted input
to this function; where it only merges trusted literals, impact is lower.

**Fix:** restore the invariant "source keys `__proto__` never reach a target". Skip
the key when iterating the source (`if (key === '__proto__') return;`) and read the
existing value only when it is an own property of the target
(`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, key) ? target[key] : undefined`).
Upstream 0.5.1+ does exactly this.

findings.title: Merge writes into an inherited object property, mutating the shared prototype
findings.body:
When the target inherits an object-valued property, `src = target[key]`
(lib/deep-extend.js:105) picks up the inherited object, and the both-objects branch
(`target[key] = deepExtend(src, val)`, lib/deep-extend.js:137) merges the source
into it. The shared prototype object is mutated, so the change is visible through
every other instance of that class, not just the object that was extended.

**Preconditions:** the caller passes an object whose prototype holds the merge
target (a class instance or settings object) and a source that contains the same
key. This is different from the `__proto__` key issue: no `__proto__` key is
involved, so skipping `__proto__` does not fix it.

**Evidence:** node v24, from the repo root:

```
node -e '
var e = require("./lib/deep-extend");
function Settings(){}
Settings.prototype.limits = { maxUploads: 10 };
e(new Settings(), JSON.parse("{\"limits\":{\"maxUploads\":999999}}"));
console.log(new Settings().limits);'
# -> { maxUploads: 999999 }
```

Equivalently `deepExtend(s, {limits: {...}})` where `s` has no own `limits`.

**Impact:** low. It silently corrupts shared configuration for every instance of
the class and leaves no own property behind that would reveal the write, but it
needs a consumer that models its options as prototype properties and merges
attacker-influenced data into an instance. The damage lasts until the process
restarts and is limited to that one prototype object.

**Fix:** read the existing value only when the target owns the key:
`src = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, key) ? target[key] : undefined;`
so an inherited object is treated as absent and replaced by a fresh clone.

summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/dns-sync.js`, a small wrapper that resolves a hostname by shelling out to `scripts/dns-lookup-script.js` via `shelljs`, and exports it through `index.js`. That design is the problem: the hostname is concatenated into a shell command string with no quoting or validation, so any name the caller does not fully control becomes arbitrary command execution.

I reproduced it in the checkout — `; id > file`, `$(...)`, backticks and `&&` payloads all execute, and a payload that prints an IP also controls the address `resolve()` returns. The rest of the file is otherwise straightforward and correct (the extension-less script path still resolves through Node's CLI, and error handling returns `null` as documented); no other issues warranted a finding.

findings.title: resolve() passes the hostname to a shell, so any caller-supplied hostname runs arbitrary commands
findings.body:
`module.exports.resolve(hostname)` interpolates `hostname` into a command string and
runs it through `shell.exec` (`lib/dns-sync.js:12` builds the string, `lib/dns-sync.js:16`
executes it). Nothing quotes or validates the value, so any caller that resolves a
name it does not fully control hands that actor arbitrary shell command execution as
the Node process user.

**Evidence:** reproduced in the checkout after `npm install`:

```
$ node -e "require('./index').resolve('example.com; id > /tmp/pwned.txt; echo 1.2.3.4')"
$ cat /tmp/pwned.txt
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

`$(...)`, backticks and `&&` payloads were also verified to execute. The return value
comes from `response.output` (`lib/dns-sync.js:18`), so an injected command that prints
an IP address also controls the address `resolve()` hands back to its caller.

**Impact:** command execution in the calling process. Hostname arguments are the
library's whole input surface — proxy configuration, URL/redirect targets, allowlist
and SSRF checks are the usual callers — so the actor who supplies the name gains the
capability the process itself holds, and can silently substitute the resolved address.
Reach crosses a trust boundary; arbitrary commands can leave permanent effects. No
repository policy redefines severity, so this is filed at `high`.

**Fix:** stop building shell text. Run the lookup script with an argument vector, e.g.
`child_process.execFileSync(process.execPath, [scriptPath, hostname])`, and reject
inputs that are not a plain hostname (or IP) before use; `shelljs` is then unnecessary.

summary:
The PR adds `src/renderer.js`, the headless-Chrome rendering layer behind the existing `/render/:url` and `/screenshot/:url` endpoints, re-instating the file the baseline tree requires but does not contain. The file is upstream rendertron as of the vulnerable commit; functionally it works, but it introduces no validation on the caller-supplied URL and leaves its Chrome targets open on every error path.

I recorded four findings: the unvalidated navigation that lets any caller read local files and reach internal hosts (the issue upstream later fixed as CVE-2017-18354), the tab/connection leak on failed renders, the interpolation of the URL into an evaluated script, and the async `Promise` executor that turns pre-`try` errors into requests that never answer. I checked reachability against `main.js`'s default config and against the repo's own tests, and corroborated the two main defects with the corresponding upstream fixes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can make Chrome read local files and internal hosts through /render
findings.body:
`GET /render/:url` and `GET /screenshot/:url` accept any URL from an unauthenticated caller and hand it to headless Chrome (`src/renderer.js:74`), then return the serialized page back to the caller (`src/renderer.js:189-193`, `src/main.js:100`). Chrome will happily load `file://` paths and internal HTTP endpoints, so any remote client can read local files and reach services that are only exposed on the host or its private network.

**Preconditions:** default deployment — no `config.json`, so `renderOnly` is unset and `isRestricted()` returns `false` unconditionally (`src/main.js:65-74`). The endpoints have no authentication (`src/main.js:43-59`).

**Evidence:** the request parameter goes straight to `Page.navigate({url: url})` (`src/renderer.js:74`) with no scheme or host check anywhere in `src/`. The repo's own tests depend on `file://` loads working: `/render/file://<abs path>` is expected to return the status code declared in that local file's `<meta>` tag (`test/app-test.js:112-127`), which is only possible if Chrome loaded and serialized the file. A caller asking for `/render/file:///etc/passwd`, `/render/file:///app/config.json`, `http://localhost:<debug-port>/json` or `http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/…` gets the fetched document in the response body. Setting `renderOnly` does not close this: the check is a raw `startsWith` prefix compare (`src/main.js:69`), so `http://allowed.host@169.254.169.254/` and `http://allowed.host.evil.tld/` pass, and a redirect from an allowed host is followed without re-checking the final URL.

**Impact:** remote file read and SSRF across a trust boundary, with the stolen content handed back to the requester; on App Engine/GCE the metadata server hands out service credentials. Upstream later fixed exactly this by rejecting non-`http(s)` protocols in `isRestricted` and adding a test asserting `file://` URLs return 403, which confirms the pre-fix behaviour.

**Fix:** restore one invariant in the renderer: only `http:`/`https:` URLs may be navigated, and the resolved host must not be loopback/private/link-local, re-checked after redirects. Also fail closed when `renderOnly` is unset.

findings.title: Failed renders leak their Chrome tab and DevTools connection, exhausting the service
findings.body:
Each failed render leaks a Chrome tab and its DevTools WebSocket: `CDP.Close` runs only after a successful load (`src/renderer.js:190`, `:220`), and the `catch` blocks just reject (`src/renderer.js:194-196`, `:222-224`).
