request and recoverable by changing the caller's casing, so `info`.

**Fix:** Merge defaults case-insensitively — e.g. scan `Object.keys(opts.headers)` with
`toLowerCase()` before defaulting, or set defaults only when no key matches. `_write.js:40-41`
has the same issue.

findings.title: Query parameters land in the URL fragment and are dropped when the url has a #
findings.body:
`options.data` is appended to the end of the whole URL string, so if the URL carries a
`#fragment` the parameters land in the fragment and never reach the server. `_read.js:27-30`
does `options.url += (isSearch ? '&' : '?') + qs.stringify(options.data)` and then reparses,
but `url.parse` only treats text before `#` as the path/query. The request is sent without
the parameters, and the caller has no way to tell.

**Preconditions:** an `options.url` containing `#`, plus `options.data`.

**Evidence:** Reproduced with Node v24.22.2: `_read({url:'http://localhost:<port>/y?a=1#frag', data:{b:2}})`
reaches a server that logs `req.url` as `/y?a=1` — `b=2` is gone. The same run without a
fragment sends `b=2` as expected.

**Impact:** Requests silently go out with missing query parameters — wrong pages, missing
filters, or an unfiltered default result set. Contained to that call and the caller can
work around it, so `low`.

**Fix:** Attach the query to the parsed components instead of the string: build the query
from `opts.query`, `opts.pathname`, and `opts.hash` (or use the WHATWG `URL` object and
`url.searchParams`) so the fragment stays last. `_write.js:30-34` has the same pattern for
`DELETE`.

summary: The change re-adds `src/index.ts`, the TypeScript `devalue` serializer, on top of a baseline that only carried the tests and build files; the PR is the escaping work that the CVE (`mishandles object keys → XSS`) is about. The key/value escaping now blocks the original attack (no raw `<` can reach the output from strings or keys), the package compiles, and the existing suite passes (45 tests). The main defect is that the new key escaping runs before `JSON.stringify`, which double-escapes every key that needs escaping and silently corrupts it; the repo's own key test asserts that corrupted output, so the suite does not catch it. Beyond that, a repeated empty `Set`/`Map` emits invalid JavaScript, own `__proto__` keys turn into prototype assignments, and the `RegExp` path skips escaping altogether. All four are contained to specific inputs and need small, local corrections.

findings.title: Object keys with unsafe characters are double-escaped and change value on deserialization
findings.body:
Object keys that need escaping are escaped twice, so the key that comes back from the
generated code is not the key that went in.

`safeKey`/`safeProp` call `escapeUnsafeChars` *before* `JSON.stringify` (src/index.ts:233,
src/index.ts:237). `escapeUnsafeChars` turns `<` into the six characters `\u003C`; the
following `JSON.stringify` escapes that backslash again to `\\u003C`. The emitted source
therefore contains a literal backslash sequence, which evaluates to the characters
`\`, `u`, `0`, `0`, `3`, `C` instead of `<`.

**Evidence:**

```js
devalue({ '<svg onload=alert("xss")>': 'bar' })
// '{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss\\")\\u003E":"bar"}'
// eval of the above -> key '"\\\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss\\")\\\\u003E"', not the input key

devalue({ 'a\nb': 1 })          // '{"a\\nb":1}'  -> key becomes 'a\\nb' (backslash + n)
devalue({ 'a\0b': 1 })          // '{"a\\0b":1}'
const o = {}; o['a\nb'] = o;    // cyclic form: '(function(a){a["a\\nb"]=a;return a}({}))'
devalue(o)
```

Any key containing `<`, `>`, `\b`, `\f`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\0`, U+2028 or U+2029 is
affected (the `unsafeChars` class, src/index.ts:2). Keys that match the bare-identifier
fast path are unaffected, as are all string *values* (which go through
`stringifyString`, src/index.ts:240).

**Impact:** round trip through server-rendered state silently changes or loses keys, so
client code reading the state sees `undefined` for those properties. The XSS hardening
this change intends still works (no raw `<` reaches the output), but it corrupts data.
Contained to the affected keys and undone by shipping the corrected escaping, hence low.

The existing test does not catch this: `test/test.ts:94` expects the double-escaped
output (`\\\\u003C`), so it asserts the corrupted form.

**Fix:** escape after serializing, so the backslashes introduced by escaping are the ones
that survive into the emitted source:

```ts
return /^[_$a-zA-Z][_$a-zA-Z0-9]*$/.test(key) ? key : escapeUnsafeChars(JSON.stringify(key));
return /^[_$a-zA-Z][_$a-zA-Z0-9]*$/.test(key) ? `.${key}` : `[${escapeUnsafeChars(JSON.stringify(key))}]`;
```

findings.title: Own __proto__ key is emitted as a prototype setter, dropping the key and injecting the prototype
findings.body:
An object that has its own `__proto__` key serializes to code that sets the revived
object's prototype instead of restoring the key, so the property disappears and the
attacker-chosen object becomes the prototype.

`safeKey` treats `__proto__` as a plain identifier (src/index.ts:233) and the object
literal path emits it unquoted (src/index.ts:119, src/index.ts:127). In a JS object
literal `__proto__: value` is a prototype-setter, not an own property. The shared-reference
path has the same problem through `safeProp`: `${name}.__proto__=${...}`
(src/index.ts:183, src/index.ts:237) assigns the prototype.

**Preconditions:** the value carries an own enumerable `__proto__` property. `JSON.parse`
produces one from normal JSON (`JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')`), which is
the usual way untrusted request/user data becomes server state that is then serialized.

**Evidence:**

```js
const p = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true},"name":"eve"}');
devalue({ user: p })
// '{user:{__proto__:{isAdmin:true},name:"eve"}}'
// evaluated: Object.keys(state.user) === ['name']   (key lost)
//            state.user.isAdmin === true            (attacker object is the prototype)
//            Object.getOwnPropertyNames(state.user) === ['name']

devalue([p, p])
// '(function(a){a.__proto__={isAdmin:true};a.name="eve";return [a,a]}({}))'
// evaluated: same - no own '__proto__', prototype replaced
```

The null-prototype branch (src/index.ts:122-124) loses the key as well, because
`Object.assign(Object.create(null), {__proto__: ...})` also skips it.

**Impact:** data supplied by an untrusted client can reshape the object graph on the
client and can make prototype-based lookups (`state.user.isAdmin`, feature flags,
defaults read off the prototype) return attacker-chosen values. It is contained to the
affected object and recoverable by emitting the key as a real property, hence low.

**Fix:** emit an own property for `__proto__` (e.g. use `Object.defineProperty` in the
generated code, or a quoted computed key `["__proto__"]`, which is a normal property in
an object literal), and do not use bare `.`-assignment for it in `safeProp`.

findings.title: Repeated empty Set or Map emits a dangling dot and makes the whole payload a SyntaxError
findings.body:
When an empty `Set` or `Map` is referenced more than once, the generated code contains a
dangling `.`, so the whole payload is invalid JavaScript and evaluating it throws.

The repeated-reference path joins the member mutations on `.` (src/index.ts:172,
src/index.ts:177). For an empty collection the array of methods is empty, `join('.')`
returns `''`, and the statement becomes `` `${name}.` ``.

**Preconditions:** the same empty `Set` or `Map` appears at least twice in the value
(counting nesting), which is what makes it take the shared-reference path
(`names` at src/index.ts:79-84).

**Evidence:**

```js
const s = new Set();
devalue([s, s])
// '(function(a){a.;return [a,a]}(new Set))'
// vm.runInNewContext of that: SyntaxError: Unexpected token ';'

const m = new Map();
devalue([1, m, m])
// '(function(a){a.;return [1,a,a]}(new Map))'
```

The non-repeated path is fine (`devalue(new Set())` → `new Set([])`).

**Impact:** the entire serialized payload becomes unparseable, so anything the app
serializes alongside it fails to hydrate; a `SyntaxError` in the inline script of a
server-rendered page. It needs that specific data shape and is fixed by correcting the
statement generation, so contained/recoverable → low.

**Fix:** only append the member statement when the collection is non-empty, e.g. build it
conditionally:

```ts
const entries = Array.from(thing);
if (entries.length) statements.push(`${name}.${entries.map(v => `add(${stringify(v)})`).join('.')}`);
```

findings.title: RegExp values bypass HTML escaping and can emit </script> into the generated source
findings.body:
RegExp values are inserted into the generated source as `thing.toString()` with no
escaping (src/index.ts:104 and src/index.ts:156), so a `RegExp` bypasses the HTML
escaping that every string and key goes through and can place `</script>` in the output,
ending the inline script element that the serialized state is meant to sit inside.

**Preconditions:** a `RegExp` reaches the serialized state whose text is not produced
verbatim from a pattern string, i.e. it has an own `source`/`flags` property or a
`toString` override. `walk` returns early for RegExps (src/index.ts:43-44) and never
applies the prototype/own-property checks (src/index.ts:56-68), so neither is rejected.
Ordinary patterns cannot produce `</script` because the engine escapes `/` in
`RegExp.prototype.source`, but they do emit raw `<`, `<script` and `<!--`.

**Evidence:**

```js
const r = /a/;
Object.defineProperty(r, 'source', { value: '</script><script>alert(1)</script>' });
devalue(r);
// '/</script><script>alert(1)</script>/'
// inlined: <script>window.state=/</script><script>alert(1)</script>/;</script>

class R extends RegExp { toString() { return '</script><script>alert(1)</script>'; } }
devalue(new R('x'));
// '</script><script>alert(1)</script>'

devalue(/<script>x/);      // '/<script>x/'     - raw '<' in the script element
devalue(/<!--<script>/);   // '/<!--<script>/'  - raw '<!--' (HTML script-data escape)
```

**Impact:** the module's contract is that its output is safe inside `<script>`; that
contract does not hold for RegExp values, giving either a full XSS breakout or a broken
script element. It requires an object of that shape, which ordinary request/JSON data does
not produce, so reach is limited and the severity is low.

**Fix:** serialize the source instead of calling `toString()`:
`new RegExp(${stringifyString(thing.source)}, ${stringifyString(thing.flags)})`.

## Summary

The PR re-adds `index.js`, the full implementation of npm `ssir`/`ssri` 5.2.1 (parse, stringify, `fromData`, `checkData`, `checkStream`, `integrityStream`, `create`). The file is byte-identical to the published 5.2.1 tarball, i.e. the pre-fix code for CVE-2018-7651: `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` (index.js:12) has an unbounded base64 group whose failure paths backtrack superlinearly (measured 471 ms → 2.0 s → 11.5 s for 16k/32k/64k characters), so untrusted metadata under `opts.strict` stalls the event loop; upstream's fix (`d0ebcdc`) bounds the digest to `{44,88}` characters. A second, smaller issue: `_parse`'s `acc[algo].push(...)` throws an uncaught `TypeError` for algorithm names that collide with prototype members, including a synchronous throw out of the promise-returning `checkStream`. Otherwise the code matches upstream 5.2.1 behaviour, and the rest of the probe leads (falsy `integrity` fail-open, size-check ordering, weak-algorithm acceptance, caller-mutable options) are API-design or caller-misuse matters rather than reportable failures.

findings.title: Strict SRI regex backtracks catastrophically on long base64 hash strings (CVE-2018-7651 ReDoS)
findings.body:
Parsing integrity metadata with `strict: true` backtracks quadratically (measured: worse than quadratic) in `STRICT_SRI_REGEX`, so a single attacker-supplied SRI string stalls the Node.js event loop for seconds to minutes. This is CVE-2018-7651; the added file is byte-identical to the vulnerable npm `ssri` 5.2.1 (`git diff` against upstream 5.2.1 is empty; blob `ba1bb6d`, the exact blob the upstream security fix `d0ebcdc` rewrites).

**Preconditions:** the caller uses `opts.strict` (documented as "recommended if the integrity strings are intended for use in browsers", README.md:104-110) and the string comes from untrusted metadata. The regex only fails — and therefore only backtracks — when the token ends in a byte outside `\x21-\x7E` (any non-ASCII character in a JSON manifest, or an internal space/newline when `opts.single` is set, index.js:140-142).

**Evidence:** index.js:12 `STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?))([?\x21-\x7E]*)$/`. On failure the engine retries every split point between the greedy `[A-Za-z0-9+/]+` and the overlapping `[?\x21-\x7E]*`, and each retry rescans the rest of the string.

    node -e "const s=require('./');for(const n of [16000,32000,64000]){const t=Date.now();s.parse('sha512-'+'A'.repeat(n)+'\u00ff',{strict:true});console.log(n,Date.now()-t,'ms')}"

    16000 471 ms   32000 2029 ms   64000 11525 ms   (growth factor 4.3x then 5.7x)

The same input through the verification entry point: `ssri.checkData(data, 'sha512-'+'A'.repeat(32000)+'\u00e9', {strict: true})` takes ~1.7-2.5 s, and `integrityStream`/`checkStream` pass `opts` straight into `parse` (index.js:247), so they are hit too. Long *valid* base64 needs no backtracking (1 ms at 32 000 chars), and non-strict parsing is unaffected — the cost is specific to the failing strict regex.

**Impact:** Availability only. Reach is broad: `parse` runs on the main thread, so one 64 KB malicious integrity string (a plausible `dist.integrity` value or CLI argument) blocks the whole process for ~11 s, and a few hundred KB blocks it for minutes — every concurrent request in that process stalls. Persistence is recoverable (the process finishes or is restarted). Broad x recoverable is medium; NVD also rates CVE-2018-7651 5.9 medium (CWE-400, availability high). Reach is discounted to low only if you weight the non-default `strict` opt-in heavily; the library's own README recommends strict for browser-bound metadata, and the input is untrusted by design.

**Fix:** bound the digest so the failing-match search space cannot grow with input length, restoring the invariant that strict parsing runs in linear time. Upstream's patch (commit `d0ebcdc`, ssri 5.2.2) does exactly this: `STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*$/`. Note it also tightens the third group from `[?\x21-\x7E]*` (which accepted any printable junk as "options") to `(?:\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*`, and updates the tests in test/integrity.js and test/stringify.js that rely on the looser form.

findings.title: Integrity metadata with an algorithm named after a prototype member throws TypeError
findings.body:
Any integrity string whose algorithm name is a member of `Object.prototype` (or of `Integrity`'s own prototype) makes parsing throw an uncaught `TypeError`. Attacker-controlled metadata can therefore crash a caller that only expects a parse result or a rejected promise.

**Evidence:** index.js:145-148

    if (!acc[algo]) { acc[algo] = [] }
    acc[algo].push(hash)

`acc` is `new Integrity()`, so `acc['toString']`, `acc['constructor']`, `acc['hasOwnProperty']`, `acc['isIntegrity']`, `acc['match']`, `acc['hexDigest']`, … are all truthy inherited values. The array is never initialised and `.push` fails.

    node -e "const s=require('./');for(const a of ['toString','constructor','match'])try{s.parse(a+'-AAAA')}catch(e){console.log(a,e.message)}"
    toString acc[algo].push is not a function
    constructor acc[algo].push is not a function
    match acc[algo].push is not a function

Reachable through the verification APIs with no `strict` opt-in, and it poisons otherwise-valid metadata — a valid hash plus one junk token is enough:

    ssri.checkData(Buffer.from('x'), '<valid sha512 sri> toString-AAAA')  // throws
    ssri.checkStream(stream, '<valid sha512 sri> toString-AAAA')          // throws synchronously

`checkStream` throws before the promise is constructed (index.js:229-233, the `parse` happens inside `integrityStream` at index.js:247, before `new P(...)`), so a caller doing `.catch(...)` cannot handle it. There is no prototype pollution — the assignment at index.js:147 is never reached — only a crash.

**Impact:** Availability. Anyone who can influence an integrity string (a registry `dist.integrity` field, a lockfile, a CLI argument) can make `parse`/`checkData`/`checkStream` throw where callers expect `false` or a rejection. Contained (one call, one process) and transient (restart/retry), so low. The contract break in `checkStream` (sync throw out of a promise-returning API) is what makes it more than a nit.

**Fix:** only treat own array entries as existing, e.g. `if (!Array.isArray(acc[algo])) { acc[algo] = [] }` in `_parse` (and the same pattern in `fromData` index.js:186-190 and `createIntegrity` index.js:311-316), so inherited prototype members can never be pushed into.

summary:
Verified my suggested regex fix removes the blowup without changing strict-parse behaviour (`?foo?bar` still parses, `?\x01\x02` still rejected).

## Summary

This PR re-adds `index.js`, the whole of `ssri@5.2.2`, to a tree whose baseline is upstream ssri 5.2.1 with that file removed. The code does close the original CVE-2018-7651 hole — the previously quadratic long-base64 case drops from 30 s to under a millisecond — but it replaces the options segment with a nested quantifier (`(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*`, `index.js:12`) that backtracks exponentially on runs of `?`, so a sub-100-byte integrity string still pins a core for seconds to minutes in any strict-mode parse path. The change also alters strict-parse semantics (digests shorter than 44 chars are now dropped), which breaks two assertions in the repository's existing tests (`test/integrity.js:76`, `test/stringify.js:111`), so `npm test` cannot pass as submitted. Both issues are recorded as findings; everything else in the file matches upstream ssri 5.2.2 behaviour, which this change does not alter.

findings.title: Strict-mode SRI parsing hangs exponentially on '?' runs (ReDoS)
findings.body:
Strict-mode integrity parsing still hangs for minutes on a short attacker-supplied
integrity string. `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` (`index.js:12`) ends in `(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)*`: an
outer `*` over a group whose body ends in `*`, and `[\x21-\x7E]` itself contains `?`.
A run of `?` can be split between the two quantifiers in ~2^n ways, so any trailing
character outside `[\x21-\x7E]` forces `$` to fail and the engine to try every split.

**Preconditions:** the consumer parses untrusted integrity metadata with
`opts.strict` — `parse`, `parse(s, {single: true})`, `checkData`, `checkStream`,
`integrityStream({integrity})`, `fromData`/`create`, all of which forward `opts` to
`new Hash` at `index.js:22-26`. In strict mode the match runs before the algorithm
whitelist (`index.js:28`), so the algorithm prefix is free-form.

**Evidence:** `\x00`, `\x7f` or any non-ASCII character survives `hash.trim()`
(`index.js:19`) and `split(/\s+/)` (`index.js:143`) and is rejected by `[\x21-\x7E]`.
Measured with Node 24 in this checkout:

```
s = 'sha512-' + 'A'.repeat(44) + '?'.repeat(n) + '\u0000'
ssri.parse(s, {strict: true})
n=20 (72 B)   11 ms      n=24 (76 B)   290 ms
n=22 (74 B)   61 ms      n=26 (78 B)  4.4–15 s
```

Roughly 2x per added `?`. A n=28 input (~80 bytes) ran 15–25 s; through
`ssri.checkData(data, craftedSri, {strict: true})` a 100-byte input burned 5 s.

This shape is not one the digest bound fixed: the previous form
`/^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/]+(?:=?=?))([?\x21-\x7E]*)$/` has a single-star options group
and measured flat (0.02 ms) on the same `?`-run inputs, while it was quadratic on
long padded base64 (`'A'*20000 + '='*20000 + '\x00'` = 8 s, `40000` = 30 s — the
CVE-2018-7651 shape, now ~0.5 ms). So the change closes the original hole but
introduces a new exponential path in the same expression.

**Impact:** one integrity string under 100 bytes pins a CPU core in the calling
process (npm/pacote-style consumers, or any service that validates client-supplied
SRI). Reach is contained to that process/request and a restart clears it, so `low`;
cheap re-triggering makes it a reliable denial of service against strict-mode
consumers. Graded down one tier because `opts.strict` is opt-in.

**Fix:** remove the nesting, e.g.
`const STRICT_SRI_REGEX = /^([^-]+)-([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{44,88})(\?[\x21-\x7E]*)?$/`
(a single optional options group also matches `?a?b`, since the class contains `?`).
Add a regression test that parses a long `?`-run and asserts it returns quickly.

findings.title: Change breaks two existing strict-mode tests and silently drops short digests
findings.body:
The added `index.js` changes what strict parsing accepts, and two assertions in the
repository's existing tests now fail. `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` (`index.js:12`) requires a
44–88 character digest, so `sha512-foo` no longer parses in strict mode; both failing
assertions feed non-conforming digests through strict API and expect them back.

**Evidence:** with the added `index.js` and `node_modules` installed:

- `test/integrity.js:76` — `ssri.parse('sha512-foo sha256-bar!').concat('sha1-bar!', {strict: true}).toString()`
  returns `''`, test expects `'sha512-foo'`. `concat` reparses its own stringified
  self under `strict` (`index.js:87-92`), so all entries are dropped.
- `test/stringify.js:111` — `ssri.stringify('sha512-foo sha256-bar', {sep: ' \r|\n\t', strict: true})`
  returns `''`, test expects `'sha512-foo \r \n\tsha256-bar'`.
- `test/parse.js:171` still passes (real 88-char digest).

`npm test` runs `standard` then `tap -J --coverage test/*.js` (`package.json:10-13`),
so the PR cannot pass CI as submitted. The other two strict assertions
(`test/integrity.js:17`) still pass by accident: a `sha512-foo` Hash built in
non-strict mode serializes fine because strict `Hash#toString` only checks
`BASE64_REGEX` and never the digest length (`index.js:41-66`), so strict parse and
strict stringify disagree.

**Impact:** red CI and a silent behaviour change for strict-mode consumers: metadata
that used to round-trip is now dropped without an error, and `concat` can return an
empty integrity that makes `pickAlgorithm` throw (`index.js:112-116`). Contained and
recoverable, so `info`.

**Fix:** update these two assertions to use real digests (the behaviour change is
correct per the SRI spec), and keep strict parse and strict stringify consistent on
the digest-length rule.

Verified the exploitation path myself with a jsdom reproduction against the real vendored MooTools and the added file; the finding is recorded. Final assessment: **Summary:** The PR adds the single file `jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js` (615 lines), the MooTools element-extension library that the Haddock template bundle already lists (`config/wro/wro-haddock.xml:40`) and that baseline callers such as `Wiki.js`, `Wiki.Behaviors.js`, `Prefs.js`, `Tabs/Columns/Flip` and `HighlightQuery.js` rely on. The file is a faithful copy of the pre-fix upstream version and its API usage matches the vendored MooTools 1.6.0 (including `Element.match`, `document.getElements`, the `!>` selector and the `.slick()` helpers), so the integration is sound. The blocking problem is `mapTextNodes`, which assigns callback output to `innerHTML` whenever it contains `<`. With the `.caps` behaviour passing unescaped, lowercased text nodes, ordinary wiki page text such as `%%caps /%` is parsed back into live markup — a stored XSS reachable by any page editor, reproduced end to end (the `onerror` fires once the broken image load fails). The upstream later added an `s === n.nodeValue` guard for exactly this; the PR should carry that (or an equivalent) before merge. The `HighlightQuery` highlight path I initially suspected is not exploitable — it escapes `<` before inserting `` — so that vector is not reported.

findings.title: mapTextNodes re-parses text as HTML, so any page editor can run script in visitors' sessions
findings.body:
`Element.implement.mapTextNodes()` re-parses callback output as HTML. For the `.caps` behaviour (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki/Wiki.Behaviors.js:210-216`) the callback returns the raw text node, lowercased and unescaped, so wiki page text that the renderer escaped becomes live markup and can run script in the browser of every visitor. **Preconditions:** the attacker can save a wiki page (editing is open by default; no ACL is configured in the shipped `jspwiki.properties`) and uses the `%%caps ... /%` style block. Default `jspwiki.translatorReader.allowHTML = false` (`jspwiki-main/src/main/resources/ini/jspwiki.properties:252`) is what makes the payload survive as text. **Evidence:** with `allowHTML=false`, `JSPWikiMarkupParser.flushPlainText()` escapes `<` to `<` (`JSPWikiMarkupParser.java:524-529`, `escapeHTMLEntities` at :655-668), so a page containing %%caps /% renders as `
<img src=x onerror=...>
`, and the DOM text node holds the literal characters ``. `mapTextNodes` (`moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:505-561`) then computes `s = fn(n.nodeValue)` (:525), sees `<` through `hasHTML` (:513, :527), assigns `dummy.innerHTML = s` (:530) and moves the parsed children back into the document (:534-537). Reproduced with jsdom + the vendored MooTools 1.6.0 and this file, running exactly the `.caps` call: before html: <img src=x onerror="window.__xss=1"> and <b>bold</b> before text node: and bold after html:
and bold
imgs in DOM: 1 onerror attribute preserved after the img's error event fires: window.__xss = 1 The `onerror` handler is attached and executes; in a browser `src=x` fails to load, so it fires without any user interaction. **Impact:** stored XSS in the wiki origin from ordinary page text. A user who may only edit page content gains script execution in the session of everyone who opens the page, including administrators (cookie/session theft, actions performed as the victim). The page persists, so the payload repeats for every visit. The same sink also silently rewrites entity references in page text (`&` becomes `&`), which the code itself flags at :532. The `HighlightQuery` caller (`moo-extend/HighlightQuery.js:61-67`) is not exploitable this way: it replaces `<` with `<` before wrapping matches in ``, so the only tags it can produce are `` elements. **Fix:** keep the invariant that mapping text nodes only rewrites text. Add the guard upstream later used for this file (`if( s === n.nodeValue )` before the `hasHTML` branch, i.e. leave nodes whose callback output is unchanged alone), or have `mapTextNodes` write results as text nodes and expose markup insertion through an explicit, sanitising API. Fixing only `.caps` re-introduces the bug for the next caller that forgets to escape.

summary:
The change adds `src/get-static-value.js`, restoring the vulnerable pre-fix implementation (blob `1dab05d`, identical to upstream `08158db^`) rather than the version fixed for CVE-2019-15657. I confirmed the file is a byte-for-byte match, then reproduced the exploit with an eslint `Linter` rule: `Function("globalThis.PWNED = 'scope-path'")()` runs inside the linter process, and `"".constructor.constructor(...)()` does the same with no scope at all.

Beyond the CVE, I reproduced three smaller defects in the newly added code: quoted/numeric object-literal keys collapse to a single `undefined` property, unbounded re-evaluation of const initializers can OOM a lint run on a ~500-byte file, and const values resolve to a shadowing binding at the use site.

The library's intended contract — a rule evaluating nodes from untrusted source — makes the code-execution issue high severity; the other three are correctness/availability issues confined to a single evaluation. I also recorded one knowledge concept so a later review can identify which version of the file a PR re-adds.

findings.title: getStaticValue calls functions resolved from the analyzed source, so linting untrusted code executes it
findings.body:
`getStaticValue` calls any function it can resolve from the analyzed AST. A lint rule that follows the documented usage — `getStaticValue(node, context.getScope())` on a node from the file being linted (docs/api/ast-utils.md:312-320) — executes attacker-controlled code inside the linter process, with that process's filesystem and credentials.

**Preconditions:** the rule uses `getStaticValue` or `getStringIfConstant` on a node from source it did not author. ESLint, editor integrations and CI runs normally do exactly that.

**Evidence:** `CallExpression` invokes the resolved callee (`src/get-static-value.js:179`, `:185`), `NewExpression` invokes the resolved constructor (`:283`), `TaggedTemplateExpression` invokes the resolved tag (`:342`), and `MemberExpression` returns live host objects (`:272`), so `.constructor` reaches `Function`. Driving the function the way test/get-static-value.js does (an eslint `Linter` rule that calls `getStaticValue(node, context.getScope())`), this source expression:

```js
Function("globalThis.PWNED = 'scope-path'")()
```

sets `globalThis.PWNED` to `"scope-path"`. The same works with no scope at all:

```js
"".constructor.constructor("globalThis.PWNED = 'x'")()
```

Both operands are plain string literals, so `getElementValues` resolves them and the call really runs.

**Impact:** high. Code under analysis crosses into code execution in the linting process: the payload can read or delete files, read environment variables and credentials, and send them out. Nothing in the library undoes it. This is CVE-2019-15657, fixed upstream in eslint-utils 1.4.2 (commit 08158db, "fix getStaticValue security issue").

**Fix:** never call a value that came from the AST. Keep an allowlist of known-safe built-ins (`String`, `Number`, `Math.*` members, `JSON.stringify`, `Object.keys`, ...) and call only when the resolved function is in it; treat `Object.freeze`/`seal`/`preventExtensions` as pass-through; apply the same allowlist to `NewExpression`; allow only `String.raw` as a template tag; and return `null` for member reads whose property descriptor is a getter.

findings.title: Object literals with quoted or numeric keys evaluate to a single 'undefined' property
Const initializers are re-evaluated without memoization, so a 500-byte input can exhaust memory
Const values resolve to a shadowing binding at the use site
findings.body:
A `const` value is resolved against the scope where it is *used*, not the scope where it is declared, so an unrelated shadowing binding changes the result.

**Evidence:** `Identifier` re-evaluates the declaration's initializer with the caller's `initialScope` (`src/get-static-value.js:230`), and `findVariable` starts from that scope and only descends (`src/find-variable.js:15`, `src/get-innermost-scope.js:11-25`). Running the test harness on

```js
const a = "outer"; const b = a;
function f() { const a = "inner"; b; }
```

returns `"inner"` for `b`, whose runtime value is `"outer"`. A parameter shadow gives the opposite error: `const b = a; function f(a) { b; }` returns `null`. There is also no declaration-order check: `const y = a; const a = 1; y` returns `1`, although the program throws `ReferenceError` when it evaluates `y`.

**Impact:** low. A rule gets a wrong constant and reports, or stays silent, wrongly. Contained to one evaluation and recoverable; no crash.

**Fix:** evaluate `def.node.init` in the scope that owns the variable (`variable.scope`), and resolve identifiers only when the declaration's range starts before the reference.

summary:
## Summary

The PR replaces the removed `js/src/tooltip.js` with the fixed implementation: sanitize/html handling in `setElementContent` (`js/src/tooltip.js:432-455`), sanitization of the `template` option inside `_getConfig` (`:695-697`), and `sanitize`/`whiteList`/`sanitizeFn` defaults that tooltip and popover share, with the three keys stripped from `data-*` config (`:29`, `:658-672`). I traced every attacker-reachable string to its only HTML sinks — the template parse at `:421-424` and `$element.html` at `:451` — and an independent check found no markup-driven path that bypasses sanitization; popover inherits the defaults via `...Tooltip.Default` (`js/src/popover.js:24-35`), and existing unit tests that exercise `html:true`, custom templates and DOM-node content still hold under a whitelist sanitizer.

The change is the correct fix for CVE-2019-8331, but it depends on `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js`, which this tree does not contain; unless that module is added, the source build breaks and the fix never lands — recorded as a low-severity finding.

findings.title: Added tooltip.js imports a sanitizer module that does not exist, so the XSS fix cannot build
findings.body:
The new `js/src/tooltip.js` imports `{ DefaultWhitelist, sanitizeHtml }` from `./tools/sanitizer` (`js/src/tooltip.js:8-11`), but this tree has no `js/src/tools/` directory. Nothing else in the repository supplies that module, so the whole sanitization half of the change is unreachable and source builds fail.

**Evidence:**

- `ls js/src/tools` → no such directory; `grep -rn sanitize js` matches only `js/src/tooltip.js`.
- Every JS build entry point pulls the new file in: `build/rollup.config.js:44` bundles `js/src/index.js`, which imports `./tooltip` (`js/src/index.js:11`); `build/build-plugins.js:39` builds `js/src/tooltip.js` alone. Rollup fails on an unresolvable relative import, so `npm run js-compile`, `npm run js-compile-plugins` and the karma test runs (which load the plugin builds, `js/tests/karma.conf.js`) cannot complete.
- The two sanitization sites — `js/src/tooltip.js:446-451` (html content) and `js/src/tooltip.js:695-697` (template) — are exactly the code that closes CVE-2019-8331. Without the module they never execute.
- The checked-in build output is still the pre-fix code: `js/dist/tooltip.js` and `dist/js/bootstrap.js` contain no `sanitize` symbol and still write html content directly.

**Impact:** As submitted, the security fix does not take effect anywhere: source builds break, and the shipped `dist/` artifacts remain the vulnerable ones. Graded low rather than high because the failure is loud at build time and blocks merge — nothing reaches users in a broken or silently-unfixed state — and the correction is mechanical.

**Fix:** Add the missing `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js` from the same upstream change, exporting `DefaultWhitelist` and `sanitizeHtml(unsafeHtml, whiteList, sanitizeFn)`. A PR that touches `js/src/tooltip.js` without it cannot be built or tested.

summary:
Recorded both findings. Closing summary:

**What the change does:** adds `src/get-static-value.js` (506 lines), the static-AST-value evaluator that `src/index.js` and `get-string-if-constant.js` already import. I diffed it against upstream `mysticatea/eslint-utils`: it is byte-identical to commit `08158db`, which is exactly the *post-fix* commit recorded for CVE-2019-15657 in the OSSF benchmark metadata (`prePatch` = 587cca2f, i.e. this repo's baseline tree). So the well-known RCE is **not** present: I reproduced the classic payloads with espree 5 plus a real ESLint scope and `Function("return 1")()`, `({}.constructor.constructor("process.exit(1)")())`, `Object.create(null, {a:{get:…}}).a` and `RegExp.$1` all return `null`; the `callAllowed` identity check (`:250`, `:261`, `:368`, `:429`) and the `isGetter` guard (`:127`, `:355`) hold.

**Assessment:** the security hardening is correct and complete relative to upstream, but the change imports only the source half of that upstream commit, so the repo's existing `test/get-static-value.js` still asserts the pre-fix behaviour and the suite goes red; a second, lower-impact deviation is that a computed `["__proto__"]` literal key rewrites the evaluated object's prototype instead of creating an own property. Otherwise the file is faithful upstream code; no `high` issue found.

**Not reached / notes:** I could not run `npm test` as shipped — `npm install` here leaves transitive packages missing (`wrappy`, `esrecurse`) and the `esm` loader from 2019 does not load on Node 24, so I verified behaviour with an esbuild bundle of `src/index.js` plus a clean eslint@5 install. The remaining unprobed surfaces are the lint-config fit of the new file (`npm run lint` against `@mysticatea/*` plugins) and the broader DoS class (exponential growth through `const`-chained template concatenation and array spread, `:146-151`, `:440-444`, which reproduced as a >120 s hang upstream-side but is inherent to static evaluation rather than this patch).

findings.title: New evaluator breaks the shipped test: 'new Array(2)' is expected to be static but now returns null
findings.body:
The added evaluator returns `null` for `new Array(2)`, but `test/get-static-value.js:78` still expects `{ value: new Array(2) }`, so the repository's own test suite fails as soon as this file lands.

**Evidence:** `CallAllowed`/`NewExpression` gate at `src/get-static-value.js:362-374` requires `callAllowed.has(Func)`; the set at `src/get-static-value.js:55-98` contains `Array.isArray` but not `Array`. Reproduced with espree 5 + `eslint.Linter` and a real scope: `getStaticValue` on `new Array(2)` returns `null`. In the test harness that path hits `assert.strictEqual(actual, expected)` (`test/get-static-value.js:135-136`), because `actual == null`, and throws. `new Array(len)` (line 79) still passes, so this one case is the only red assertion. The upstream commit that introduced these guards (`mysticatea/eslint-utils` 08158db, which this file is byte-identical to) changed that expectation to `null` and added six security regression cases (`Function(...)()`, `({}.constructor.constructor(...))`, `Object.create(null, {a:{get:...}}).a`, `RegExp.$1`, ...). This change imports only the source half.

**Impact:** `npm test` fails, so the fix cannot be merged or released as-is, and the security behaviour it adds (blocking `Function`, getters, `String.raw` on arbitrary tags) is left untested. Contained to CI, recoverable by editing the test.

**Fix:** Update `test/get-static-value.js:78` to `expected: null` and port the security regression cases from upstream 08158db, so the suite asserts the new restriction instead of the old behaviour.

findings.title: Computed '__proto__' key in an object literal rewires the evaluated object's prototype
findings.body:
A computed `["__proto__"]` key in an object literal rewrites the prototype of the value `getStaticValue` returns, so the evaluator reports members that the real object does not have.

**Evidence:** `src/get-static-value.js:384-391` builds the object with `object[key.value] = value.value`. For a computed key that assignment is a `[[Set]]` on `"__proto__"`, i.e. the prototype setter, not a new own property. Reproduced with espree 5 + a real ESLint scope: `({['__proto__']: {b: 2}}).b` evaluates to `{ value: 2 }`, while real JavaScript yields `undefined` (the literal has a plain own `__proto__` property and its prototype is `Object.prototype`). `({['__proto__']: {b: 2}})` also evaluates to `{}` with no own keys. The mutation stays inside the freshly created `{}` at line 377, so `Object.prototype` and other intrinsics are not polluted, and the CallExpression allow-list (`:250`, `:261`, `:368`) still blocks every call, so no capability is gained.

**Impact:** A rule that asks `getStaticValue` about an attacker-written object literal can be told that a property exists when it does not (or, with `Object.keys`, that it does not when it does). That is a wrong static value in the lint result, not a security escape: no code execution, no getter invocation, no shared-object mutation.

**Fix:** Skip the member when `key.value === "__proto__"` and the property is computed (or define properties with `Object.defineProperty(object, key.value, {value, ...})`), so the evaluated object matches JS semantics.

summary:
Filed one high-severity finding. Summary of the review:

**What the change does:** adds `src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs`, a new operation that runs the input through all 44 charsets in `IO_FORMAT` in either Encode or Decode mode, returning JSON and presenting it as an HTML table.

**Assessment:** the `run()` logic is sound — `cptable.utils.encode()` returns an array-like, which `Utils.arrayBufferToStr` (`new Uint8Array(...)`) accepts, so Encode mode works; all 44 code pages exist in the vendored cptable; and op registration is generated, so no config edit is needed. The blocking problem is in `present()`: the decoded value is interpolated into the table without `Utils.escapeHtml`, and the web app writes `presentType = "html"` output to `innerHTML` and evaluates embedded `<script>` — so crafted input runs script in the CyberChef origin, reachable automatically via a shared recipe/input URL. Two cosmetic defects (the table is closed with `<table>` at line 86, and errors always read "Could not decode." even in Encode mode) are not worth filings.

findings.title: Crafted input escapes the encoding table and executes script (XSS) in the CyberChef origin
findings.body: `TextEncodingBruteForce.present()` copies decoded input into the output table without HTML escaping, so a crafted recipe URL or pasted input executes arbitrary JavaScript in the CyberChef origin. `present()` interpolates `Utils.printable(encodings[enc], true)` directly into `${value}`. `Utils.printable` (`src/core/Utils.mjs:176-187`) only replaces control characters with dots; `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes pass through unchanged. The op declares `this.presentType = "html"` (`src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:37`), and the web app assigns that string to `innerHTML` and `eval`s any `

summary:
I reviewed the full diff, the three call sites, the pinned dependency versions, and reproduced the extraction paths locally.

**What the PR does:** re-adds `lib/util/extract.js` (278 lines) at the state that fixes CVE-2019-5484. Relative to the previous release, exactly one line differs (`lib/util/extract.js:133`): `isSymlink(entry)` → `isSymlink(_, entry)` returning `entry.type === 'symlink'`. The old signature received the entry name as its first argument, so it never matched a tar header and tar symlinks were written out unfiltered.

**Verification (local, using the versions pinned in `yarn.lock`):**
- `tar-fs@1.15.3` calls `ignore(name, header)` (`/tmp/tf/package/index.js:236`), so the two-argument `isSymlink` is correct. Extracting a tar containing absolute and relative symlinks now yields only the regular file; restoring the old signature leaves `evil -> /tmp/outside.txt` in the destination, reproducing the vulnerable behavior.
- `decompress-zip@0.2.2` filters entries with `file.type === 'SymbolicLink'` (`dz/package/lib/decompress-zip.js:100`), so `filterSymlinks` at `lib/util/extract.js:137` matches; a zip with a symlink entry extracts without the link.
- Path-traversal attempts stay contained: decompress-zip's `restrict` check rejects `../escape.txt`, and tar-fs's `path.join(cwd, path.join('/', header.name))` collapses `../../escape2.txt` into the destination directory.

The call sites (`UrlResolver.js:247`, `FsResolver.js:115`, `GitHubResolver.js:120`) pass the temp dir as `dst`, consistent with the `tmp.dir` extraction the function performs. I found no regression, no dead code, and no issue worth filing; existing findings list is empty, so there was nothing to update.

Verified the change empirically. Summary of my check:

**What the change does:** adds `index.js` (tar-fs 1.16.1 + one-line change). The single delta versus the pre-fix upstream code is at `index.js:264`: the hardlink source path went from `path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)` (which let `../../x` or `/abs/x` resolve outside `cwd`) to `path.join(cwd, path.join('/', header.linkname))`, clamping the target under `cwd` (this is upstream commit "force hardlink targets to be in the tar", the CVE-2018-20835 fix).

**Verification:**
- PoC tarball: `link` entry with `linkname` = relative path outside `cwd`, then a `file` entry of the same name. Against the pre-fix code (`/tmp/1.16.1`) the outside file is truncated and overwritten (`PWNED-VIA-hardlink`); against this change the extract fails with `ENOENT: ... link '<cwd>/outside-hardlink.txt' -> '<cwd>/evil'` and the outside file is untouched. Absolute-linkname traversal is likewise blocked.
- Legitimate relative and absolute-inside targets still resolve correctly (`path.join('/', 'sub/file')` → `<cwd>/sub/file`), so no regression for normal hardlinks.
- Repo suite: `standard` clean, `node test/index.js` 48/48 pass, including the "no abs hardlink targets" regression test at `test/index.js:315`.

**Out of scope:** extraction still permits a symlink entry to point anywhere (`index.js:257`, unvalidated `header.linkname`), and a following file entry of the same name overwrites the symlink target outside `cwd` — I reproduced this (`PWNED-VIA-symlink`) and confirmed it behaves identically on the pre-change 1.16.1 code, so it is a pre-existing hole this change neither touches nor makes reachable (upstream closed it years later via a resolved-target containment check). The related intermediate-symlink hardlink bypass is the same root cause. Not filed, since it is not introduced or worsened by this diff.

No findings recorded: the change is a correct, minimal fix for the hardlink path traversal, with the regression test passing.

The PR adds `index.js`, the `set-value` 3.0.0 implementation (path splitting with escape handling, a memoised key cache, and a `merge` option). The logic reproduces the documented behaviour for ordinary paths, but the traversal follows inherited properties and never filters prototype keys, so a caller-supplied path such as `a.__proto__.isAdmin` or `constructor.prototype.x` writes an own property onto `Object.prototype` — the unfixed CVE-2019-10747, which I reproduced against this checkout. A second, independent defect sits in the memo cache, which is a plain object keyed by the raw path: names like `constructor`, `toString` or `__proto__` hit inherited entries and the write lands on a stray `undefined` key or disappears. Both are recorded; I found no other change-introduced failure worth filing.

findings.title: Caller-controlled path pollutes Object.prototype via __proto__ and constructor.prototype
findings.body:
`set(obj, path, value)` walks a caller-supplied path and writes wherever the walk
lands. Path segments are never checked, and inherited properties count as objects,
so `__proto__.x` and `constructor.prototype.x` reach `Object.prototype` and install an
own property on it. Every object in the process then inherits that property. This is
CVE-2019-10747.

**Preconditions:** the caller of `set-value` passes a path built from untrusted input.
Common case: a server maps a parsed request body or query string onto a config object.

**Evidence:** with a local `is-plain-object` stub so `require('./')` resolves:

```
$ node -e "const set=require('./'); set({}, 'a.__proto__.isAdmin', true); \
  console.log(({}).isAdmin, 'isAdmin' in {})"
true true
$ node -e "const set=require('./'); set({}, 'constructor.prototype.p', 1); \
  console.log(({}).p)"
1
```

Both spellings work, and so do array paths (`['__proto__','p']`) and
`{ merge: true }`. The chain:

- index.js:26 splits the path into plain strings with no filtering.
- index.js:40-42 only asks `isObject(target[prop])`, so `target['__proto__']`
  (`Object.prototype`) and `target['constructor']` (the `Object` function, accepted at
  index.js:105-106) both pass and no fresh object is created.
- index.js:49 follows the inherited link: `target = target[prop]`.
- index.js:45 and index.js:57-59 write `target[prop] = value` onto the object reached
  in the previous step.

Grep finds no `__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype` or `hasOwnProperty` handling in
index.js, and test.js (206 lines) has no pollution test.

**Impact:** any object created later in the process inherits the attacker's key and
value — `({}).isAdmin === true`, `'isAdmin' in other`. This crosses a trust boundary
(untrusted input changes process-wide object behaviour) and is permanent for the life
of the process; nothing in the library undoes it. Downstream code that trusts
inherited properties for authorisation, options or defaults is exposed, and inherited
keys are classic gadget material for RCE chains in other libraries. Not raised to
`critical` because the repository defines no such policy.

**Fix:** reject path segments that resolve an inherited or prototype-mutating link
before descending — at minimum skip/throw on `__proto__`, `constructor` and
`prototype`, and require `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, prop)` (or
`Object.create(null)` intermediates) so the loop never follows an inherited
reference. Keep honouring legitimate own keys such as `constructor` on plain data.

findings.title: Paths named after Object.prototype members write the key undefined or silently drop the value
findings.body:
`split()` caches results in `set.memo`, a plain `{}`, and looks them up with a truthy
test. Paths named after `Object.prototype` members hit inherited values, so `split()`
returns a function or a prototype object instead of an array of keys. The loop then
does the wrong thing: the value is dropped, or it is written under the literal key
`undefined`.

**Evidence:**

```
$ node -e "const set=require('./');
  console.log(JSON.stringify(set({}, 'constructor', 'v')));
  console.log(JSON.stringify(set({}, 'toString', 'v')));
  console.log(JSON.stringify(set({}, 'a.b', 1)));"
{"undefined":"v"}
{}
{"a":{"b":1}}
```

Cause: index.js:65 `if (set.memo[id]) return set.memo[id]` finds
`set.memo['constructor'] === Object` (index.js:113) and returns it as the key list.
`keys.length` is then `Object.length === 1`, so the loop runs with
`prop = keys[0] === undefined` and writes `target['undefined']`. For `toString`
`keys.length` is 0 and the call is a silent no-op. The same applies to `valueOf`,
`hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable` and `__proto__` (the last
returns `Object.prototype`, so `set(obj, '__proto__', v)` silently does nothing).

**Impact:** ordinary property names — `constructor` is common on plain data — are
silently mis-set: the caller's object gains a stray `undefined` key while the intended
property is untouched, or the write disappears. A single call corrupts one object and
the caller gets no error, so the failure surfaces later as wrong data. Contained reach
and recoverable by rewriting the object, hence `low`.

**Fix:** cache in a prototype-free map (`set.memo = Object.create(null)`, plus an
`hasOwnProperty` guard), so only entries this module stored can be returned.

summary: This PR adds the whole of `st.js`, the static file server, and its content is byte-identical to the upstream v1.2.2 release — the release that fixes CVE-2017-16224 (the `//nodesecurity.org/%2e%2e` scheme-relative 301 open redirect). I confirmed the fix: that target now returns 403 here, while the previous release's file still answers `301 Location: //nodesecurity.org/%2e%2e/`, and the repository's own tests (`basic`, `dot-*`, `parent-path`) pass. The path-traversal guards themselves hold up against literal, encoded (`%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c`), double-encoded, overlong-UTF-8 and raw-socket payloads, so the CVE-specific hole is closed. I did find three unrelated defects in the added code: a single malformed request path kills the process, autoindex never responds on an empty directory, and a dot-enabled mount with a custom `url` can serve one directory above its root.

findings.title: Percent-encoded NUL byte in a request path kills the server process
findings.body:
One unauthenticated request with a percent-encoded NUL byte kills the whole Node process. `GET /a%00b HTTP/1.1` reaches `decodeURIComponent` (st.js:192) after the traversal and dot gates have passed, so `req.sturl` becomes `/a\u0000b`. `getPath` passes it to `path.join` (st.js:209), and `serve` hands it to `this.cache.fd.get` (st.js:250). That call runs the fd loader synchronously; `fs.open` rejects a path containing a NUL byte by throwing `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` (through `node_modules/async-cache/ac.js:63` and `node_modules/fd/index.js:47`), and nothing in st catches it. The throw unwinds out of the `'request'` listener as an uncaught exception, so the process exits.

**Preconditions:** none beyond default options (`st({path})`); the attacker needs no credentials and no file on disk.

**Evidence:** with `st({path:'/tmp/v/root'})` behind `http.createServer`, sending `GET /a%00b HTTP/1.1` produced no response and the server printed:

```
TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE]: The argument 'path' must be a string, Uint8Array, or URL without null bytes. Received '/tmp/v/root/a\x00b'
    at Object.open (node:fs:593:10)
    at AsyncCache.get (.../async-cache/ac.js:63:8)
    at Mount.serve (st.js:250:17)
```

and exited with code 1 (a normal `GET /f.txt` on the same server returned 200 first). A second malformed target, `GET http:// HTTP/1.1`, dies earlier: `url.parse('http://').pathname` is `null`, so `p.replace` throws at st.js:172 — same uncaught-exception exit.

**Impact:** availability only, but an unauthenticated remote client stops the service for every user with a single short request, repeatable at will. Reach is broad (everyone the server serves) and recovery is a restart, so medium under the repo's severity table.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that `getUriPath` returns only a plain path string, or `false`. Smallest change: reject the request when `url.parse(u).pathname` is not a string (st.js:169-172) and when the decoded path contains a NUL or other control character before returning it (after st.js:192). As defence in depth, the fd cache load should not be allowed to throw synchronously out of `serve` (surround the `cache.fd.get` continuation, or validate `p` once at st.js:247).

findings.title: Autoindex hangs forever on an empty directory listing
findings.body:
Autoindex never answers when a directory listing comes back empty: the request socket is held open with no status line until the client or a proxy times out, and the `readdir` cache entry stays pending, so later requests for the same directory pile onto the same unresolved load.

`_loadReaddir` sets `len = files.length` (st.js:550) and only completes via `next()`, which decrements and calls back once `len` reaches 0 (st.js:563-565). With zero files, `next()` is never called and `cb` never runs, so `async-cache` never resolves `_loading[p]` (`node_modules/async-cache/ac.js:42-43,60-81`) and `_loadIndex` (st.js:496) never answers. Two ordinary ways to get zero files: an empty directory, and a directory whose only entries are dotfiles while `dot` is off — the filter at st.js:546-549 empties the list.

**Preconditions:** default `index: true`; the served tree contains an empty directory (or a dotfile-only directory with `dot: false`). Empty directories are common (upload, cache and placeholder dirs).

**Evidence:** `st({path:'/tmp/v/root'})` with `/tmp/v/root/empty/` and `/tmp/v/root/dotted/` (containing only `.hidden`): `GET /empty/` and `GET /dotted/` produced no response within 1.5 s (a control request for `/f.txt` returned 200). After five interleaved requests, `mount._this.cache.readdir._loading` still held `{'/tmp/v/root/empty/': [...], '/tmp/v/root/dotted/': [...]}` — queued callbacks that are never invoked.

**Impact:** contained per request, but every request for such a directory hangs forever and leaks a queued callback holding `req`/`res`; an unauthenticated client can repeat it to grow the pending list and hold sockets, so low.

**Fix:** make the empty listing complete immediately — after the `len = files.length` assignment, call `cb(null, data)` (or `next()`) when `len === 0`, instead of relying only on the per-file decrement.

findings.title: Mount url matched as a raw string prefix lets a dot-enabled mount serve one directory above its root
findings.body:
With `dot` enabled and a non-root `url`, a request whose target starts with the mount URL followed by `..` is served one directory above `opt.path`. `getUriPath` checks for traversal on the raw path (st.js:182), then matches the mount with a plain string prefix test (st.js:189) and strips it by length (`u.substr(this.url.length)`, st.js:201). Because the prefix test has no segment boundary, `/assets../MARKER.txt` on a mount of `/assets` strips to `../MARKER.txt`, is forced to `/../MARKER.txt` (st.js:202), and `path.join(this.path, u)` (st.js:209) resolves to the parent of the root. The `..` is manufactured by the strip, so the traversal gate never sees it.

**Preconditions:** `st({path, url: '/assets', dot: true})` — both the non-root `url` option (documented in README as the normal sub-directory mount) and `dot: true` (needed by deployments serving `/.well-known`) are required. With `dot: false` the post-strip dot check at st.js:233 rejects the value with 403, which is why the default configuration is not affected.

**Evidence:** root `/tmp/v2/www`, marker `/tmp/v2/MARKER.txt`, `st({path:'/tmp/v2/www', url:'/assets', dot:true})`; `GET /assets../MARKER.txt HTTP/1.1` returned `200` with body `MARKER-OUTSIDE-ROOT\n` (`/tmp/v2/MARKER.txt`). `%2e%2e` and `..%5c` variants behave the same. Deeper payloads (`/assets..%2f..%2fX`) are rejected with 403, so the reach is exactly the parent directory of the root, with any file name in it.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client reads files outside the served root (e.g. `/var/www/*` when serving `/var/www/html`), which is the disclosure the mount's path boundary is supposed to deny. It needs two non-default settings and is bounded to one directory level up, so low.

**Fix:** match and strip the mount URL at a path-segment boundary: accept only `req.url === this.url` or a path starting with `this.url + '/'` (and reject anything else before stripping), so `getUriPath` can never return a value beginning with `..`.

summary:
Review complete. One finding recorded.

**What the change does:** PR #2 re-adds `index.js` (345 lines) — the full tar-fs 1.16.1 source — to a tree whose baseline was the upstream repo with that file removed. It is byte-identical to the published 1.16.1 package, i.e. the vulnerable commit before the 1.16.2 fix for CVE-2018-20835.

**Assessment:** The extraction logic contains the CVE-2018-20835 defect: `onlink` resolves an attacker-supplied hardlink target with `path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)` (`index.js:264`), so `..`-escaping or absolute linknames create a hardlink to an arbitrary file that a following plain entry then overwrites. I reproduced it with both absolute and relative linknames (outside file content replaced, inodes matched), and the repository's own `no abs hardlink targets` test (`test/index.js:315`) fails — it hangs waiting for an error and leaves `test/fixtures/outside` overwritten. The correct one-line fix is the upstream 1.16.2 change, which I verified against the published package.

I also probed the rest of the added file: entry names are neutralized by `path.join('/', header.name)`, and `validate` walks all ancestors so symlink-in-path traversal for file entries is blocked; remaining behaviour I could trigger (writing through a same-name symlink entry, a `validate` recursion hang on a `/`-named entry, the `opts.xfs` typo in `mkdirfix`) is pre-existing upstream behaviour that persists past 1.16.2, so I left it out of findings.

findings.title: Hardlink entries can target files outside the extraction root and overwrite them
findings.body:
`tar.extract()` resolves a hardlink entry's `linkname` with `path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)`, so a linkname containing `..` or an absolute path points outside the destination. `xfs.link` happily creates that hardlink inside the extraction directory, and a later plain file entry with the same name writes through it, replacing the contents of the outside file.

**Evidence:** `index.js:264` — `var srcpath = path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname)`. Entry names go through `path.join(cwd, path.join('/', header.name))` (`index.js:238`), which neutralizes `..`, but the hardlink target never gets that treatment. Reproduced with two entries, using the file itself:

```js
var s = tarStream.pack()
s.entry({type: 'link', name: 'stolen', linkname: '/tmp/outside/secret.txt'})  // or '../../target'
s.entry({name: 'stolen'}, 'PWNED')
s.finalize()
s.pipe(tar.extract(dest))
```

`/tmp/outside/secret.txt` changed from `ORIGINAL` to `PWNED`, and the inode of `dest/stolen` matched it. The relative form `linkname: '../../target'` behaves the same. The repository's own test `no abs hardlink targets` (`test/index.js:315`) does not pass: it hangs waiting for an error that never comes, and leaves `test/fixtures/outside` containing `overwrite`.

**Impact:** Anyone who extracts an untrusted tarball — build jobs, package installers, upload pipelines, CI running as root in a container — lets the archive author overwrite any file writable by the extracting user, e.g. `/etc/passwd`, `authorized_keys`, or files in the output tree belonging to another tenant. The write is permanent and requires no privilege the extractor did not already have.

**Fix:** Constrain the hardlink target to the destination just like entry names: `var srcpath = path.join(cwd, path.join('/', header.linkname))`, so an absolute or `..`-escaping linkname can only resolve inside `cwd` and `xfs.link` fails with `ENOENT`. This is the upstream 1.16.2 change.

summary:
Review complete. Diff verified byte-for-byte against published `set-value@3.0.1`, and the shipped suite passes (26 tests).

**What the change does:** it adds `index.js`, the full `set-value` implementation, including the CVE-2019-10747 mitigation — path segments are split, then `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` are filtered out before any property assignment (`index.js:28`, `index.js:101-103`).

**Assessment:** the mitigation holds for the documented API. I reproduced the standard payloads — `'__proto__.polluted'`, `'constructor.prototype.polluted'`, the array-path equivalents, and JSON `{"__proto__":...}` merged with `{merge: true}` — and none of them add an own or readable property to `Object.prototype`; the merge branch writes into a fresh `{}` (`index.js:57`), so it cannot reach it. Two durable caveats came out of the probes: the guard compares segments by identity, so an array path containing a boxed `String` would still reach `Object.prototype`, which is only exploitable if a caller passes non-primitive path elements rather than JSON-derived strings; and the traversal follows inherited values, so a path like `'toString.polluted'` writes onto a shared builtin function object (property injection, no `Object.prototype` write). I filed the one defect that is reachable from ordinary string paths — the memo cache answering lookups with inherited members — and left the rest unreported as out-of-contract input.

findings.title: single-segment path named after an Object.prototype member throws TypeError
findings.body:
Calling `set(target, path, value)` with a string path whose only segment names an
`Object.prototype` member throws a `TypeError` instead of writing the property. The
memo cache is a plain object and is looked up without an own-property check, so the
inherited member is returned in place of a segment array.

**Preconditions:** none beyond the documented string-path API — no options object and a
single-segment path.

**Evidence:**

```
require('.../index.js')({}, 'constructor', 1)
TypeError: (intermediate value)(intermediate value)(intermediate value).filter is not a function
    at set (.../index.js:28:53)
```

`split()` computes `id = createKey(path, options)` (index.js:64), which for a string path
with no options is just the path (index.js:89-91), then returns `set.memo[id]` whenever
that value is truthy (index.js:65). `set.memo = {}` (index.js:109) inherits from
`Object.prototype`, so `set.memo['constructor']` is `Object`, `set.memo['toString']` is a
function, and so on. `set()` then calls `.filter(isValidKey)` on that function
(index.js:28). Observed throws for `constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, `valueOf`,
`hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `toLocaleString`;
`'prototype'` and any multi-segment path (`'a.toString'`) are unaffected. The same call
with an options argument or an array path works, because `createKey` then produces a
compound id that is not an inherited member.

**Impact:** low. Any caller that sets a property from an untrusted or user-supplied key
name can be made to throw on the exact keys this filter was added to tolerate
(`__proto__`, `constructor`) and on ordinary keys like `toString`, and so can abort a
request or crash an unguarded handler; the actor can repeat the call at will, and a
restart or retry clears it. Contained to one call, so low under the reach/persistence
table in the review policy.

The same cache design also produces wrong-property writes on key collisions: after
`set(a, 'q;merge=true', 1)`, `set(b, 'q', {j: 2}, {merge: true})` writes to
`b['q;merge=true']` instead of merging into `b.q`, because `createKey` concatenates
`path + ';key=value'` without escaping (index.js:92-100).

**Fix:** do not let prototype members answer cache lookups — store the memo in a
`Map` (or `Object.create(null)` plus a `hasOwnProperty` check) and build the id
unambiguously (e.g. `JSON.stringify([path, options])` over the option fields actually
read), so an inherited member or a colliding string can never be returned as a keys
array.

summary:
## Summary

PR #2 adds `lib/util/extract.js` (278 lines), which is bower's archive extractor: it picks an extractor by extension/MIME, unpacks into a `dst-XXXXXX` temp directory, then moves the contents into the destination. That file is the CVE-2019-5484 fix area, and the copy under review has the symlink filter broken.

I reproduced both issues against the real dependency versions pinned in `yarn.lock` (`tar-fs@1.15.3`, `tar-stream@1.5.4`, `decompress-zip@0.2.2`). The tar symlink filter at `lib/util/extract.js:133` reads the entry from the wrong argument, so symlinks are never rejected and an archive can overwrite files outside the destination while extraction still reports success — that is the security regression this change introduces. A hardlink entry bypasses the same filter in both this version and the corrected one. The zip path, tar path traversal (`../`, absolute names), and other extractor behaviors I tested were contained; the remaining rough edges from probing (temp-dir leaks, non-atomic moves, dead `.gz` path) are long-standing upstream behavior and I left them unreported.

findings.title: Tar archives with a symlink entry overwrite arbitrary files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
`extract()` writes files outside the requested destination when a tar archive contains a symlink entry, so a malicious package archive can overwrite any file the installing user can write. The symlink filter is never applied: `isSymlink` (lib/util/extract.js:133) reads `entry.type` from its first argument, but `tar-fs` calls `ignore(name, header)` (`node_modules/tar-fs/index.js:236` in tar-fs 1.15.3, the version pinned in yarn.lock), so the first argument is the entry's path string and `entry.type` is always `undefined`. tar-fs then creates the symlink (`index.js:261-266`) and later entries whose path runs through it are written through the link.

**Preconditions:** The user installs a package whose archive is fetched and extracted by bower: `UrlResolver._extract` (lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:247) or `GitHubResolver` (lib/core/resolvers/GitHubResolver.js:120). The archive is a `.tar`/`.tar.gz`/`.tgz`.

**Evidence:** Built a tar with `tar-stream` containing `{name:'pwn', type:'symlink', linkname:'/tmp/repro/victim.sh'}` followed by `{name:'pwn'}` with attacker content, then ran the repo's `extract()` (with dependencies at the versions in yarn.lock) on it. Before: `victim.sh` contained `echo original`. After extraction the promise resolved successfully and `victim.sh` contained the attacker's bytes. Replacing `isSymlink(entry)` with `isSymlink(_, entry) { return entry.type === 'symlink'; }` makes the same archive harmless. The zip path is unaffected: decompress-zip's `filter` does receive the entry object and uses the `'SymbolicLink'` string (node_modules/decompress-zip/lib/decompress-zip.js:100).

**Impact:** Arbitrary file write/overwrite as the user running bower, from an untrusted archive (a malicious registry entry, URL endpoint or GitHub tarball). The extraction reports success, so nothing signals the escape. Embedded scripts placed in `~/.bashrc`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` or a global npm/bower config turn this into code execution. Reach crosses a trust boundary (archive author acts on the victim's filesystem); the effect is permanent. Remaining requirement is that the user installs the package, which is the normal use of the tool.

**Fix:** Filter symlinks by the tar header, not the path: `function isSymlink(_, entry) { return entry.type === 'symlink'; }`, and pass it to `tar.extract`'s `ignore` for both `extractTar` and `extractTarGz`.

findings.title: Tar archives with a hardlink entry overwrite files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
Hardlink (`type: 'link'`) entries are not filtered, so a tar archive can hard-link any file the user owns on the same filesystem into the extraction directory and then overwrite it with attacker content. The filter in `extractTar`/`extractTarGz` (lib/util/extract.js:66, :96) only recognizes symlinks, and `isSymlink` (lib/util/extract.js:133) matches `'symlink'`/`'SymbolicLink'` only. tar-fs 1.15.3 (yarn.lock) implements `case 'link'` as `xfs.link(path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname), name)` (node_modules/tar-fs/index.js:257-266), and an absolute `linkname` resolves to itself, so the link target is outside `dst`. A later entry with the same name is opened with `createWriteStream(name)` without unlinking (index.js:274), which truncates the shared inode.

**Preconditions:** The archive is a tar/tar.gz installed through `UrlResolver` or `GitHubResolver`; the target file is owned by the installing user and on the same filesystem as the extraction directory (the usual case for files in `$HOME`). Linux `fs.protected_hardlinks` does not block this for the user's own files.

**Evidence:** Built a tar with `{name:'pwn', type:'link', linkname:'/tmp/repro/victim.sh'}` followed by `{name:'pwn'}` containing `ATTACKER CONTENT`, then extracted it with the repo's `extract()` **with the symlink fix applied** (`isSymlink(_, entry)`). `victim.sh` went from `echo original` to `ATTACKER CONTENT`, its link count went from 1 to 2, and the promise resolved successfully.

**Impact:** Same arbitrary-file-overwrite outcome as the symlink escape, and it survives the symlink fix, so the intended protection is incomplete. Reach crosses a trust boundary (archive author writes the victim's files); the write is permanent. Discounted from high because the attack needs a same-filesystem file the victim owns, which bounds what can be targeted; installed packages are still arbitrary code, so the outcome is comparable.

**Fix:** Reject both link types in the same predicate, e.g. `function isLink(_, entry) { return entry.type === 'symlink' || entry.type === 'link'; }`, or pin a tar-fs release that resolves and confines `linkname` to the extraction root.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** it adds `st.js` (599 lines), which is byte-for-byte the `st@1.2.1` static file server — the release vulnerable to CVE-2017-16224.

**Assessment:** the file reintroduces a real, exploitable defect class. All request-path sanitisation in `serve` (`st.js:225-240`) runs on the raw `req.sturl`, while `getPath` decodes `%2e` and cuts the mount prefix by string length (`st.js:171-205`); one unauthorised request is enough to read dotfiles, escape a sub-path mount root, or get a 301 to an attacker-chosen domain. I reproduced each of these and confirmed `st@1.2.2` blocks all three, so they are reported as one high finding with three facets (two narrower findings folded into it as duplicates). Beyond the CVE, I also reproduced two independent defects that persist in upstream `st` 1.2.2: an encoded NUL in the path kills the whole process, and autoindex of an empty directory hangs the request and that cache key forever. Several other hypotheses (fd leak on client abort, gzip cache-fill accounting, autoindex escaping) were tested and did not hold.

findings.title: Checks run on the raw request path, so encoded dots disclose dotfiles, escape sub-path mounts, and redirect off-origin
findings.body:
`req.sturl` keeps the raw request pathname (st.js:225-226), while the checks that
gate what may be served run on that raw string and `getPath` decodes it
separately. Three exploitable consequences, all fixed together by the st 1.2.2
patch for CVE-2017-16224:

1. **Dotfiles and dot-directories are served under the default `dot: false`.**
   `GET /.secret` returns 403 but `GET /%2esecret` (or `/%2Esecret`) returns the
   file; `GET /%2ehidden-dir/` returns a full listing of a dot-directory.
2. **Sub-path mounts can be escaped.** With `st({path: P, url: '/static'})`,
   `GET /static%2e%2e/outside.txt` and `GET /static../outside.txt` serve files from
   the parent directory of `P`.
3. **Directory redirects point off-origin (the CVE as published).**
   `GET //evil.example/%2e%2e` answers `301` with
   `location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/`, a protocol-relative redirect to an
   attacker-chosen host.

**Evidence:** `getPath` decodes `%2e` to `.` (st.js:171-172), so the filesystem
path it builds at st.js:205 contains the dotfile/`..` segments; but the dot test at
st.js:240 inspects the still-encoded `req.sturl`, which has no `/.` segment, so it
passes. For sub-path mounts the `..` is glued to the mount name (`static..`), which
the traversal regex at st.js:183 does not match (it needs a separator on both
sides); the prefix test `u.indexOf(this.url) !== 0` (st.js:190) passes because the
string starts with `/static`, and `u.substr(this.url.length)` (st.js:202-203) then
cuts at a character rather than a segment boundary, leaving a leading `../...` that
`path.join` (st.js:205) resolves above the root. For the redirect, the same glued
`..` normalises away (st.js:189) so the mount root is served, and `autoindex`
copies the raw `req.sturl` into `location` (st.js:349-352).

Reproduced against this tree (default options, `st({path: '/tmp/v/root'})` and
`st({path: '/tmp/v/root/sub', url: '/static'})`):

```
/.secret                    403   |  /%2esecret                200 "SECRET"
/.hd/                       403   |  /%2ehd/                   200 listing
/.hd/x.txt                  403   |  /%2ehd/x.txt              200 "LEAK"
/static/a.txt               200 "INSIDE"
/static../outside.txt       200 "ESCAPED-TO-PARENT"
/static%2e%2e/outside.txt   200 "ESCAPED-TO-PARENT"
//evil.example/%2e%2e       301 location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/
```

st 1.2.2 answers 403 to every one of these: it splits `getUriPath` out, assigns the
normalised and decoded path to `req.sturl` before the dot check, and adds `|$` to
the traversal regex. Verified by running the same requests against
`st@1.2.2`.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client reads files the operator deliberately
excluded (typical mounts contain `.git` or `.env`), reads outside the mount root
for sub-path mounts (one level up, then arbitrary depth below that parent), and
gets a trusted-origin 301 to any domain it names. Severity from reach (a plain
request obtains data the `dot: false` policy and the mount root deny) and
persistence (data leaves; nothing undoes it): high, using the dotfile facet, which
needs no non-default option.

**Fix:** port the 1.2.2 change: compute one normalised, decoded url path, assign it
to `req.sturl`, run the dot test on that value, and apply the `..` test to the
decoded path (including a trailing `..`); additionally compare the mount prefix on
a segment boundary so `/static..` is not treated as being under `/static`.

findings.title: Sub-path mounts can be escaped with a glued dot-dot to serve the mount root parent directory
findings.body:
When a mount is configured with a sub-path `url` (e.g. `st({path: '/srv/public',
url: '/static'})`), a request whose `url` prefix is glued to `..` — with literal
dots or `%2e` — escapes the mount root and serves files from the root's parent
directory, including listings. `GET /static../outside.txt` and
`GET /static%2e%2e/outside.txt` both return the parent-level file with status 200.

**Evidence:** the traversal guard at st.js:183 only rejects `..` that has a
separator on both sides, so `static..` passes. `path.normalize` (st.js:189) keeps
the `static..` component intact, the mount-prefix test
`u.indexOf(this.url) !== 0` (st.js:190) passes because the string starts with
`/static`, and then `u.substr(this.url.length)` (st.js:202) cuts the prefix at a
character boundary rather than a path-segment boundary, leaving
`../outside.txt`; st.js:203 prepends `/` and `path.join(this.path, u)`
(st.js:205) resolves it to the parent. The dot check at st.js:240 sees the raw
`req.sturl` (`/static%2e%2e/...`), which has no `/.` segment, so it does not
interfere.

Reproduced against this tree with `st({path: '/tmp/v/root/sub', url: '/static'})`
and `/tmp/v/root/outside.txt` outside the mount root:

```
/static/a.txt                        -> 200 "INSIDE"
/static../outside.txt                -> 200 "ESCAPED-TO-PARENT"
/static%2e%2e/outside.txt            -> 200 "ESCAPED-TO-PARENT"
/static/%2e%2e/outside.txt           -> 403
```

Root mounts (`url: '/'`) are not escapable this way, because `substr(1)` of a
normalized absolute path never yields a leading `..`.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client reads and lists anything in the parent
directory of the mount root and below it — typically application config, `.env`,
data directories — crossing the boundary the mount is meant to draw. Base severity
would be high (boundary crossed, data leaves permanently); it is graded medium
because the escape is one directory level up, not arbitrary filesystem access, and
requires the sub-path `url` form (README:21-25, a documented configuration).

**Fix:** compare mount prefixes on path-segment boundaries and reject any
normalized path that does not contain `this.url` as a whole segment prefix (and
re-check for `..` segments after stripping the prefix), e.g. require
`u === this.url || u.indexOf(this.url + '/') === 0` before cutting, and re-run the
`..` test on the remainder.

findings.title: A request path containing an encoded NUL byte crashes the server process
findings.body:
Any request path that decodes to contain a NUL byte (for example
`GET /a.txt%00.txt`) raises an uncaught `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE]` inside
the request handler and exits the whole Node process. One unauthenticated request
takes the server down.

**Evidence:** `getPath` decodes percent-escapes with `decodeURIComponent` at
st.js:193 and nothing validates the result; the decoded string becomes the cache
key/file path at st.js:205-206 and is passed to `this.cache.fd.get(p, ...)` at
st.js:247. `async-cache` invokes the loader synchronously, so
`fd/index.js:47 fs.open` throws on the NUL inside `Mount.serve`, with no try/catch
in `serve` or in the caller. Reproduced with a plain `st({path: '/tmp/v/root'})`
mount:

```
TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE]: The argument 'path' must be a string,
Uint8Array, or URL without null bytes. Received '/tmp/v/root/a.txt\x00.txt'
    at Object.open (/workspace/.../node_modules/fd/index.js:47:10)
    at AsyncCache.get (.../async-cache/ac.js:63:8)
