    at Mount.serve (/workspace/.../st.js:247:17)
Node.js v24.22.2      <-- process exited, exit code 1
```

The current upstream fixed release (st 1.2.2) has the same behaviour, so this is
not part of the CVE-2017-16224 patch, but the whole file is added by this change.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated client can kill the service repeatedly; every
in-flight connection and all other users lose service. Severity is medium because
a restart restores it (recoverable) and no data is exposed, while the reach is
broad — the whole served application, not one request.

**Fix:** reject paths that are not valid after decoding — treat any NUL in the
decoded path as an invalid URL and return `false` from `getPath` (or validate the
final `p` before it reaches `fs`), so `serve` falls through to `next()`/404.

findings.title: Directory redirect reflects a protocol-relative path, allowing open redirect
findings.body:
The 301 that redirects a directory request to its trailing-slash form copies the
raw request path into `location`, so a path beginning with `//host` produces a
protocol-relative redirect to any attacker-chosen host.
`GET //evil.example/%2e%2e` answers `301` with `location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/`,
which browsers follow off-origin.

**Evidence:** `req.sturl` is the raw, un-normalised pathname (st.js:225-226).
`getPath` maps `//evil.example/%2e%2e` to the mount root: after `%2e` becomes `.`
(st.js:172) the guard at st.js:183 does not match (a trailing `..` has no separator
after it), `path.normalize` collapses the path to `/` (st.js:189), the prefix test
and `path.join` (st.js:190-205) resolve to the mount directory, and the dot check
at st.js:240 sees no `/.` segment. `autoindex` then redirects using `req.sturl`
st.js:349-352.

Reproduced with default options (`st({path: '/tmp/v/root'})`):

```
GET //evil.example/%2e%2e   -> 301  location: //evil.example/%2e%2e/
GET //evil.example/%2e.     -> 301  location: //evil.example/%2e./
```

**Impact:** an attacker-supplied link on the victim's own domain bounces the
visitor to an external site, which enables phishing and, where the site feeds this
endpoint a `redirect_uri`-style parameter, redirect-based token theft. Contained
(one victim per link) and recoverable, so low.

**Fix:** build the redirect target from the normalised, same-origin path instead of
the raw `req.sturl` (st 1.2.2 does this by assigning the sanitised path to
`req.sturl`), and reject paths where the leading `//` would make `location`
protocol-relative.

findings.title: Autoindex of an empty directory hangs the request forever and leaks its socket
findings.body:
Autoindex of an empty directory never responds: the client connection hangs until
timeout, and the directory's listing stays permanently broken for the life of the
process.

**Evidence:** `_loadReaddir` (st.js:538-563) sets `len = files.length` and relies on
the per-entry callback to call `next()`, which fires `cb` when `--len === 0`. For an
empty directory the loop body never runs, so `cb` is never called; `async-cache`
keeps the entry in `_loading` and every later `get()` for that key only appends a
callback. Reproduced with `st({path: '/tmp/v/root'})` and an empty
`/tmp/v/root/empty/`, six concurrent `GET /empty/`:

```
requests hung: 6  server connections: 6  (after 2.5 s, no bytes sent)
index._loading keys: [ '/tmp/v/root/empty/' ]
```

**Impact:** each request for an empty directory leaks an open socket, its `req`/
`res`, and a queued cache callback, and the listing never recovers without a
restart. Contained per request and recoverable by restart, so low.

**Fix:** call back immediately when there is nothing to stat, e.g.
`if (files.length === 0) return cb(null, data)` before the `forEach`, or make
`next()` handle the zero-length case.

summary:
Review complete. Two findings recorded.

The change adds `src/download.js`, which fetches the Visual C++ Build Tools installer and the Python MSI via `nugget` before `src/index.js` hands them to the installer. The download path skips transport and artifact integrity altogether — `strictSSL: false` (`src/download.js:33`) plus a plain-`http://` build tools URL (`src/constants.js:5`) with no checksum — and the fetched binaries are then executed with administrator rights, which I confirmed with a self-signed-certificate repro against nugget 2.0.0. The remaining issue is that download failures are logged and swallowed (`src/download.js:17`), so the postinstall step exits 0 with nothing installed. Everything else in the new file is ordinary error-message and proxy plumbing; no other defects found.

findings.title: Installer downloads skip certificate validation, so an on-path attacker can substitute code run as administrator
findings.body:
Downloaded installers are fetched with certificate verification turned off, and the
build tools installer is fetched over plain HTTP. An attacker on the network path can
substitute their own executable, which is then run with administrative rights.

**Preconditions:** an on-path attacker (hostile Wi-Fi, compromised router, or the
`PROXY` env var at `src/download.js:32`, which points nugget at an attacker-chosen
proxy) plus the documented install flow: the README tells users to run
`npm install --global windows-build-tools` from an elevated prompt, and
`ps1/launch-installer.ps1:43-48` refuses to continue without admin rights.

**Evidence:**
- `src/download.js:33` passes `strictSSL: false` to nugget, which forwards it to
  `request.defaults` (`nugget/index.js:28-34`), disabling certificate validation for
  every download, including the Python MSI over `https://`.
- `src/constants.js:5` fetches `BuildTools_Full.exe` over `http://`. That host answers
  with `302 Location: https://...`; the first response is unauthenticated, so an
  attacker can answer with a `200` body or their own redirect.
- Nothing verifies a checksum or signature afterwards: `src/download.js:46` resolves as
  soon as nugget reports success, and `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28` then runs
  `./BuildTools_Full.exe` and `:38` runs `msiexec.exe /i python-2.7.11.msi`.
- Reproduced with nugget 2.0.0 against a self-signed HTTPS server: with
  `strictSSL: false` nugget reported a successful 300 KB download from a host whose
  certificate Node rejects; with `strictSSL: true` the same request failed with
  `Error: self-signed certificate`.

**Impact:** High. Code of the attacker's choosing executes as the installing user, and
per the README and `launch-installer.ps1:43` that user is an administrator, on a machine
that is being configured for compiling native modules. Nothing in the system detects or
undoes the compromise, so the effect is permanent and crosses a trust boundary.

**Fix:** Validate the transport and the artifact. Drop `strictSSL: false` (or make it
opt-in via a documented env var), change the build tools URL in `src/constants.js:5` to
`https://`, and compare the downloaded file against a pinned SHA-256 before it is handed
to `install`; fail closed on mismatch.

findings.title: Failed download still exits 0, so postinstall reports success with nothing installed
findings.body:
When either download fails, `download` only logs the error and never calls its
callback, so the postinstall process exits with code 0 even though nothing was
downloaded or installed.

**Evidence:** `src/download.js:17` ends the chain with
`.catch((error) => console.log(error))`, which swallows the rejection; `cb()` is called
only on the success path at `:16`. The caller, `src/index.js:11`, therefore never runs
`install`, and the `postinstall` script (`package.json`, `node ./lib/index.js`) finishes
with no pending work and status 0.

**Impact:** `npm install --global windows-build-tools` and any CI job running it report
success while the toolchain is absent; the failure surfaces later as unrelated
`node-gyp` errors. Contained to one machine and cleared by re-running the install, so
low severity.

**Fix:** Propagate the failure instead of logging it — reject out of `download` and let
the top-level entry point print and `process.exit(1)` so a failed install is visible to
npm.

summary: PR #1 adds `src/download.js`, the missing piece that fetches the Visual C++ Build Tools and Python installers via `nugget` and then hands control to the install step. The download itself is the problem: it uses plain HTTP for the Microsoft installer, passes `strictSSL: false` (nugget 2.0.0 forwards it to `request`, disabling certificate verification — verified against a self-signed server), and applies no checksum or signature check before `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28` executes the binary in an elevated session. I also confirmed the error path swallows failures so `npm install` exits successfully with nothing installed. Both issues are recorded; the rest of the file (404 string sniffing, `resume` on stale files, missing timeout) is weak but I could not tie it to a failure worth a separate finding.

findings.title: Failed download silently skips installation and npm install still reports success
findings.body:
If either download fails, `download` logs the error and returns without ever calling its callback, so the install step never runs and the process still exits with status 0. `npm install` reports success for a package whose only job is to install the build tools.

**Evidence:** `src/download.js:13-18` — the chain ends with `.catch((error) => console.log(error))`, and `cb()` is only invoked on the success path (line 16). `src/index.js:11-15` uses that callback to start `install`, so nothing else observes the failure. Any transient network error, DNS failure, or dead URL takes this path.

**Impact:** The user gets a successful install with no compiler and no error message beyond a logged object, then hits confusing `node-gyp` failures later. Contained to that user's run and fixed by re-running, so low.

**Fix:** Make the failure observable — rethrow / call the callback with the error so `postinstall` exits non-zero, e.g. `.catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1) })` or pass the error through to `cb(error)`.

findings.title: Installers are downloaded over an unauthenticated channel and then executed as Administrator
findings.body:
The installers this package downloads are fetched without authenticating the server, and the bytes are then executed. An attacker on the network path can return their own `BuildTools_Full.exe` and it runs with Administrator rights.

**Evidence:**
- `src/download.js:31-38` builds the nugget request with `strictSSL: false`. nugget@2.0.0 forwards that option to `request.defaults` (`nugget/index.js:28-34`), and request 2.x turns it into `rejectUnauthorized = false`, so certificate verification is off for the HTTPS Python download. Confirmed against a self-signed server: with `strictSSL: false` the download succeeds, without it the request fails with `self-signed certificate`.
- The build tools installer is fetched over plain HTTP: `src/constants.js:5` (`http://download.microsoft.com/.../visualcppbuildtools_full.exe`). The Python mirror (`src/constants.js:1,11`) can also be pointed at `http://` via `PYTHON_MIRROR`.
- Nothing checks the result. No hash, signature, or Authenticode verification of the downloaded file exists anywhere in `src/`, `ps1/`, or `lib/`.
- The file is executed: `src/download.js:38` writes it into `%USERPROFILE%\.windows-build-tools` (`src/utils.js:32-63`), then `src/install/index.js:26` → `src/install/launch.js:27` spawns PowerShell, and `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:28` runs `./BuildTools_Full.exe` (line 38 does the same for the MSI). The script refuses to continue unless the session is elevated (`ps1/launch-installer.ps1:43-48`, surfaced as "run as Administrator" at `src/install/launch.js:35-41`), so the substituted binary executes with Administrator rights.

**Impact:** A network attacker (hostile Wi-Fi, DNS/ARP spoofing, transparent proxy) gets code execution as Administrator on every developer machine that installs this package. That crosses a trust boundary and the effect is permanent, so high.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant that the downloaded bytes come from Microsoft/Python and have not been altered. Use `https://` for the build tools URL, drop `strictSSL: false` (or make it opt-in via an explicit env var), and verify the downloaded file against a pinned checksum/signature before `install` runs — fail closed if verification fails.

summary:
Bash in this sandbox became unresponsive mid-review, but I had already completed the analysis with the read/grep tools. Findings: none — here is what I verified.

**What the change does.** PR #1 re-adds `xmpp/util.js` (158 lines) to this dojox fixture. The added blob is byte-identical to upstream dojo/dojox commit `6eb278356ca7b0ac7e9cba6067fcf077d2e3ad9a`, the recorded fix commit for CVE-2019-10785 (verified by diffing against both the pre-patch tree `d6b93d9e` and the post-patch commit fetched from GitHub; the benchmark metadata in `CVEs/CVE-2019-10785.json` names exactly those two commits and `xmpp/util.js:7` as the weakness site).

**Why I found nothing to report.**
- The defect the PR fixes is `xmlEncode` calling `.replace("&", ...).replace(">", ...)` etc., which escapes only the *first* occurrence of each character, so a roster name like `x" onmouseover="alert(1)"` produced a `name="…" onmouseover="alert(1)""` attribute in `RosterService.js:33`. The new version (`xmpp/util.js:5-21`) does a single global-regex pass over `& > < ' "` with a complete entity map, escapes every occurrence, and does not double-escape the replacements it just made. I hand-traced that payload and confirmed both quotes are escaped now; the map lookup `xmlEntityMap[match] || ''` can never take the fallback since every alternation branch is a key.
- Escaping is the only defence for attribute values, and I confirmed `xmlEncode` has exactly two callers repo-wide (`RosterService.js:33` and `:78`), both for attribute values, and there is no second, still-broken escaping helper in `xmpp/`.
- The rest of the file is unchanged upstream code and behaves the same before and after: `decodeJid`'s regex/switch mismatch (unmatched matches yield `"ARG"`) has no callers in the repo, `stripHtml`'s empty `for` loop is dead code, and `Base64.encode`'s per-char `charCodeAt` mishandles non-ASCII — all pre-existing upstream, none reachable as a security failure through this change.

**Residual risk (not filed).** `createElement` (`xmpp/util.js:92-109`) still concatenates attribute values without escaping, so callers must escape themselves; `RosterService.removeRosterItem` (`RosterService.js:241`) passes an unescaped `jid`, unlike `addRosterItem`. I could not trace attacker-controlled data into that value — roster JIDs come from the XMPP server, which already controls the channel — so it fails the evidence bar, and the code is untouched by this PR.

Overall: this is the correct, complete backport of the CVE-2019-10785 fix, and the patch approves cleanly.

Recorded three findings. Summary:

This PR adds `server/apps/routes/auth.js`, the admin authentication router (signup, login, first-run install, password reset, verify, logout), mounted at `/admin` with no middleware in front of it. The `.toString()` coercions on the query values close the NoSQL-injection hole those calls replaced, but the surrounding flow has real problems: the new `/admin/signup` route bypasses the `allowPublicRegistration` gate and places self-registered users in the all-permissions admin group, and `/admin/forgotpassword` overwrites the stored password hash with `null` while issuing a reset token. The missing-input paths in three handlers also leave unauthenticated requests hanging on an unhandled promise rejection. I would not merge without at least gating or removing `/admin/signup` and dropping `password: undefined` from the reset update.

findings.title: Password reset writes password: null to the user document, locking accounts out
findings.body:
`POST /admin/forgotpassword` writes `password: null` over the user's password hash as a side effect of issuing a reset token. The handler builds `{ token, password: undefined }` and passes it to `findByIdAndUpdate` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:88-90`). Mongoose keeps the `undefined` key in the `$set`, and the driver's BSON serializer writes it as `null` (`ignoreUndefined` defaults to false), so the stored document becomes `{ password: null, token: <new> }`. The user's previous password stops working immediately, and `server/utils/passport.js:43` (`if (user.token) return done(null, false)`) refuses login while a token is set, so the account is locked until the emailed reset link is used.

**Evidence:**
- `server/apps/routes/auth.js:88-90` — `const data = { token, password: undefined }` followed by `User.findByIdAndUpdate(user._id, data, { new: true })`.
- mongoose 4.11.13 `lib/services/query/castUpdate.js:24-49` copies every non-`$` key into `$set` including `undefined`; `lib/schema/string.js` returns `undefined` unchanged from `cast`.
- mongodb-core 2.1.15 `lib/wireprotocol/commands.js:59-63,185` and `lib/wireprotocol/2_6_support.js:239-240` default `ignoreUndefined` to `false`; bson 1.0.4 `lib/bson/parser/serializer.js:686-687` then serializes `undefined` as BSON null. (Reproduced with the pinned bson: serializing `{$set:{token:'abc',password:undefined}}` with `ignoreUndefined:false` yields a null field.)
- `server/models/UserSchema.js:33` — `token` is a plain string with no expiry, and `server/apps/routes/auth.js:99` does not await `sendEmail`, whose transport errors are only logged (`server/utils/emails/sendEmail.js:26-28`), yet the endpoint still answers `200 {success:true}`.

Trigger: plain `POST /admin/forgotpassword` with `{"email":"victim@example.com"}` by anyone, no session. The same request also confirms whether the address is registered (`auth.js:82-84` returns `400 There is no user with that email.` versus `200 {success:true}`), giving an existence oracle for any address.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller can invalidate the password of any account whose email they know and keep it unusable until the victim completes a reset; if mail is misconfigured or the link is lost, the lockout is permanent. Reach is broad (any user, one request each) and recovery is a supported action, hence medium.

**Fix:** write only the token — `User.findByIdAndUpdate(user._id, { token }, { new: true })` — and validate `email` before querying; the same `password: undefined` pattern exists at `server/graphql/mutations/users/resetPassword.js:23-26`.

findings.title: Unauthenticated POST /admin/signup creates a full administrator account
findings.body:
The new `/admin/signup` route is reachable by anonymous callers and the account it creates lands in the `admin` user group, so anyone who can reach the site can make themselves a full administrator. The route is registered unconditionally on the admin router (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:14`, mounted by `server/apps/admin.js:12` under `/admin` at `server/index.js:53`), while the only place `Site.allowPublicRegistration` (default `false`, `server/models/SiteSchema.js:20-23`) is enforced is the separate, opt-in route in `server/utils/public-registration.js:14,25`. The frontend never calls `/admin/signup` (`app/views/Auth/Install/index.js:39` and `app/views/Auth/Login/index.js:30` are the only auth calls), so the endpoint has no legitimate consumer.

**Evidence:**
- `server/apps/routes/auth.js:14` — `router.post('/signup', passport.authenticate('local-signup', strategyOptions))`, no middleware in front of it.
- `server/utils/passport.js:30-36` — the strategy does `new User(req.body)` and saves it.
- `server/models/UserSchema.js:39-47` — `pre('validate')` assigns the `slug: 'admin'` group when `usergroup` is unset, and it overwrites a client-supplied `usergroup` too (no `return` after `next()` on line 40), so the account can never land below admin.
- `server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:11-17` — the admin group gets every permission set to `true`; permissions are only checked as bits in resolvers such as `server/graphql/mutations/site/updateSite.js:16` (`canManageSite`) and `server/graphql/mutations/users/addUser.js:23`.

Reproduction on a stock install: `POST /admin/signup` with `{"username":"x","email":"x@y.tld","password":"p"}`, then `POST /admin/login` with the same credentials (the user has no `token`, so `server/utils/passport.js:43` does not block it), then `POST /graphql` with `mutation { updateSite(data:{siteUrl:"http://attacker"}) { siteName } }`.

**Impact:** unauthenticated network caller gains administrator capability over site settings, content, and users, and the new account persists — high under the reach (crosses a trust boundary, no credentials needed) × persistence (permanent) grading. Note that in `NODE_ENV=test` every request is auto-authenticated (`server/index.js:43-49`) and no test hits `/admin/signup`, so the suite cannot notice this.

**Fix:** drop the `/signup` handler from this router and keep registration on the gated route in `server/utils/public-registration.js`; if it must stay, put `publicMiddleware` (site setting check) in front of it and never default self-registered users into the admin group.

findings.title: Missing token, email or query parameter hangs the request and raises an unhandled rejection
findings.body:
Several handlers in this router dereference request input before validating it, inside `async` functions. Express 4.15.5 catches only synchronous throws from handlers (`lib/router/layer.js:94-98`), and the repo installs no `unhandledRejection` handler, no Express error middleware and no `server.timeout`, so the rejected promise is dropped: the client gets no response and the socket stays open.

**Evidence:**
- `server/apps/routes/auth.js:80` — `email.toString()` runs before any check that `email` exists. `POST /admin/forgotpassword` with no body throws `TypeError: Cannot read property 'toString' of undefined`.
- `server/apps/routes/auth.js:58` — `token.toString()` runs after only `password` is validated (`:53-56`). `POST /admin/setpassword {"password":"x"}` throws the same way.
- `server/apps/routes/auth.js:104` — `req.query.t.toString()` throws on `GET /admin/verify` with no query string (the URL in reset emails `server/utils/emails/templates/reset-password.html` is `/admin/verify?t=...`, easy to truncate).
- Same class at `server/apps/routes/auth.js:31` (`adminUserGroup._id` when no admin group exists) and `:34` (explicit `throw` inside the async handler).
- The `admin.get('*')` catch-all (`server/apps/admin.js:39`) never runs, because the matched route never calls `next()`.

**Impact:** each request from an unauthenticated caller produces an unhandled rejection and a request that never completes, held until Node's default 120 s socket timeout, so a small number of concurrent requests exhausts the server's sockets; on Node 15+ the default policy turns the same request into a process exit. One packet per request, no credentials. Reach is broad, the effect clears on retry/restart, hence low; not filed higher because the declared runtime is Node 8 (`package.json` engines), where it does not kill the process.

**Fix:** validate the fields before using them, e.g. return a 400 when `typeof email !== 'string' || !email` (and the same for `token` and `req.query.t`) — or wrap the async handlers so rejections reach `next(err)`.

summary:
I've completed the review. Verified the key exploit primitives locally against the locked Mongoose version and recorded four findings.

**What the change does:** adds a new 121-line auth router (`server/apps/routes/auth.js`) mounted at `/admin` — signup, login, first-user bootstrap, first-install probe, set-password, forgot-password, verify, logout.

**Assessment:** this is the pre-1.1.10 version of the file, so the change re-introduces CVE-2018-3783. The reset flows pass unvalidated request fields straight into Mongo filters, and `User.findOne({ token })` with a missing token becomes `{token: null}`, which matches the first token-less user — a one-request, unauthenticated account takeover that I confirmed at the query-construction level with Mongoose 4.11.13. The two related operator-injection paths (`/verify` token oracle, `/forgotpassword` email filter) and the ungated `/admin/signup` route, which lands new accounts in the all-permissions admin group, round out the findings. Everything else in the file (logout, first-install probe, missing async error handling, no rate limiting) is low value; no other concrete failure path justified a finding.

findings.title: /admin/setpassword matches users by an unvalidated token filter, letting an anonymous caller reset and log in as another account
findings.body:
`POST /admin/setpassword` selects the account to reset with `User.findOne({ token })` (server/apps/routes/auth.js:58), where `token` is whatever the request body carried. No authentication middleware guards this router (server/apps/admin.js:12; server/index.js:53), and the only check before the lookup is that `password` is non-empty (auth.js:53-56). Two unvalidated shapes let an anonymous caller match an account they do not own:

- **No `token` field at all.** `token` is `undefined`, and Mongoose 4.11.13 (`package.json:113`) rewrites undefined condition values to `null` in `lib/cast.js` before the query reaches the driver. Verified locally against the locked version:

  ```
  missing token  -> {"token":null}
  $gt injection  -> {"token":{"$gt":""}}
  ```

  MongoDB's `{token: null}` matches documents where the field is `null` **or missing**, so the query returns the first user in the collection — normally the admin created by `/firstuser` (auth.js:20-39), which never has a `token` value set.
- **An operator object instead of a string.** `{"token":{"$gt":""}}` (or `token[$ne]=x` urlencoded) survives casting on the `String` path, selecting any user who currently holds a reset token.

The handler then overwrites that user's password hash (auth.js:64), clears the token (auth.js:65, verified to emit `$unset`) and calls `req.login(user)` (auth.js:73), so the caller's session is authenticated as the victim. One request, no prior state.

**Preconditions:** none beyond network reachability of `/admin/setpassword`. The missing-token variant works on a fresh install; the operator variant needs any account to hold a pending reset token, which `/admin/forgotpassword` hands out at will (see the companion finding).

**Evidence:**
- `curl -X POST http://host/admin/setpassword -d 'password=pwned'` → `{token: null}` filter → first user's password replaced, `Set-Cookie` session for that user, `200 {"success":true}`.
- Query construction reproduced with the repository's Mongoose version and schema: `/tmp/repro13` script above printed the exact `_conditions` written above.
- `req.body` reaches the handler as a JS object for both JSON and urlencoded bodies (`bodyParser.json()` / `bodyParser.urlencoded({extended: true})`, server/index.js:30-31).
- Upstream fixed exactly this line in flintcms 1.1.10 (`User.findOne({ token: token.toString() })`), which is the release that closes CVE-2018-3783.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller obtains an authenticated session as another user — the first user is the site admin — and can then use `/graphql`, whose only guard is `loggedIn` (server/apps/graphql.js:14, server/utils/helpers.js:8-13). Reach crosses a trust boundary, and the attacker chooses the new credential, so the state is not undone by the service; this is `high` under the review policy (the policy defines no `critical`).

**Fix:** treat the reset token as a string credential. Reject requests whose `token` is missing or not a string with a 400 before querying; coercing (`String(token)`) inside the filter is the upstream minimal change but still lets `undefined` through as `"undefined"`.

findings.title: /admin/verify answers differently on filter matches, leaking the password-reset token of any account
findings.body:
`/admin/verify` uses the query parameter as the Mongo filter directly: `const token = req.query.t` then `User.findOne({ token })` (server/apps/routes/auth.js:104-105). Express's default extended query parser turns `?t[$regex]=^a` / `?t[$ne]=x` into objects, Mongoose 4.11.13 passes those operators through on the `String` path, and the handler answers differently on a hit and a miss: `302 Location: /admin/sp/[object Object]` when a user matches (auth.js:112) vs `302 Location: /admin` when none does (auth.js:108). The response is a boolean oracle over the token value.

**Preconditions:** some account holds a pending reset token. `/admin/forgotpassword` lets an anonymous caller create one on any chosen account (auth.js:87-90), and users who legitimately requested a reset have one while they wait.

**Evidence:**
- Cast check with the locked Mongoose version: `t $regex -> {"token":{"$regex":"^A"}}` (script in `/tmp/repro13`).
- With a pending token, `GET /admin/verify?t[$regex]=^A` redirects to `/admin/sp/[object Object]`; `?t[$regex]=^B` redirects to `/admin`. Repeating per character recovers the 16-character token returned by `randtoken.generate(16)` (auth.js:87). `?t[$ne]=x` answers whether any token exists at all.
- Tokens have no expiry (`server/models/UserSchema.js:33`), so a recovered token stays usable until it is redeemed.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller can extract another user's live password-reset token and then redeem it at `/admin/setpassword` with the correct string, taking over that account without ever seeing the email. Reach crosses a trust boundary; I did not run the full character-by-character extraction, which bounds this at `medium`.

**Fix:** accept only a string token. Reject non-string `req.query.t` (or build the filter with `String(req.query.t)`) so the value is matched literally, never as an operator.

findings.title: /admin/forgotpassword accepts a Mongo operator as the email filter, locking arbitrary accounts out of login
findings.body:
`/admin/forgotpassword` passes the request body field straight into the user lookup: `const { email } = req.body` then `User.findOne({ email })` (server/apps/routes/auth.js:79-80). A JSON body `{"email": {"$gt": ""}}` (or `email[$ne]=x`) is parsed to an object and cast to the operator by Mongoose 4.11.13, so `$gt: ""` matches the first user with a non-empty email. The handler then mints a token and writes it onto that account (auth.js:87-90).

Two consequences, both for an account the caller does not own:

- **Login lockout.** `local-login` refuses any user whose `token` is set: `if (user.token) return done(null, false)` (server/utils/passport.js:43). The owner cannot log in until they use the emailed reset link — and the attacker can re-plant a token at will.
- **Email enumeration.** A non-matching email returns the plaintext `400 "There is no user with that email."` (auth.js:82-85) while a match returns `200 {"success":true}`, and an operator such as `{"email":{"$regex":"^adm"}}` makes the endpoint a per-character oracle over every account's email address.

It is also the first step of the takeover chain: it puts a known-pending token on a chosen account that `/admin/verify` can then leak.

**Preconditions:** none for the enumeration and lockout; the victim must have an email matching the injected filter.

**Evidence:**
- Cast check with the locked Mongoose version and the repository's schema: `email $gt -> {"email":{"$gt":""}}`; body parsing confirmed for JSON and urlencoded (`server/index.js:30-31`).
- `curl -X POST /admin/forgotpassword -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":{"$gt":""}}'` → `200 {"success":true}`, token written on the first user; that user's subsequent `/admin/login` fails.

**Impact:** an unauthenticated caller can deny login to any account, including the admin, and can enumerate account emails; the victim can recover through the emailed reset link, so persistence is `recoverable` → `medium`.

**Fix:** validate `email` is a string (e.g. `typeof email === 'string'` → 400 otherwise) before the query; upstream 1.1.10 used `User.findOne({ email: email.toString() })`.

findings.title: Anonymous POST to /admin/signup creates an admin-group account even when public registration is disabled
findings.body:
`router.post('/signup', passport.authenticate('local-signup', strategyOptions))` (server/apps/routes/auth.js:14) is mounted unconditionally at `/admin/signup` (server/apps/admin.js:12) and creates a working account for any anonymous POST. The intended gate is elsewhere: public registration is opt-in and `Site.allowPublicRegistration` defaults to `false` (server/models/SiteSchema.js:22-25), enforced by `publicMiddleware` in server/utils/public-registration.js:12-19, which only mounts at the configured `global.FLINT.signupRoute`. That router is mounted after `/admin` (server/index.js:53 vs :55), so `/admin/signup` bypasses the setting entirely.

The account it creates is an admin. `local-signup` builds the user from the body with no usergroup (server/utils/passport.js:27-36), and the pre-validate hook then assigns the `admin` group (`server/models/UserSchema.js:39-47`), which holds every permission (`server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:11`). Passport logs the new user in during the same request (no `successRedirect`, so it proceeds), issuing a session cookie; the response itself is a 404 from the admin static handler, which does not matter.

**Preconditions:** none; the site setting that disables registration is ignored.

**Evidence:**
- Hook test with the locked Mongoose version: a `User` built without `usergroup` validates with `usergroup == admin group id`.
- `POST /admin/signup` with `{email, username, password}` returns a `Set-Cookie` for the new user; `GET/POST /graphql` then passes `loggedIn` (server/apps/graphql.js:14) and every mutation's `perms.*` check because the admin group has all permissions.
- The admin SPA has no signup view (`app/views/Auth/` contains only `Install`, `ForgotPassword`, `SetPassword`), so the endpoint serves no first-party UI flow.

**Impact:** on any deployment where public registration is disabled, an anonymous attacker obtains a full-admin session. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the account persists until an admin deletes it, so this is `high`. Note that the group assignment comes from the pre-existing `UserSchema` hook; the new route is what exposes it to anonymous callers.

**Fix:** remove the duplicate route, or gate it with the same `allowPublicRegistration` check used by server/utils/public-registration.js:12-19.

summary:
## Review summary

The PR adds `index.js` (the `https-proxy-agent` agent implementation) back to the tree. Its content is byte-for-byte the upstream post-fix blob `4e007128` from TooTallNate/node-https-proxy-agent commit `1c24219` ("Use `Buffer.from()`"), so relative to the baseline source at `c58d365d` the single substantive change is line 207: `new Buffer(proxy.auth)` → `Buffer.from(proxy.auth)`. That is precisely the fix for CVE-2018-3736 / CVE-2018-3739 (uninitialized-memory exposure and DoS when a numeric `auth` reached the `Buffer` constructor); I verified empirically that `Buffer.from` rejects every non-byte input and zero-fills array-likes, so no uninitialized-read path survives, and that the residual `TypeError` is contained by agent-base and surfaces as a request `'error'` rather than an uncaught throw.

I found no issues introduced by this change and recorded no findings. The surrounding code has long-standing quirks (missing `onend` → `fn`, buffering of unterminated proxy headers, header concatenation, the ignored `secureProxy` option), but they are unchanged upstream behaviour that this patch neither touches nor makes newly reachable. Note: the repo's own mocha suite cannot run on this sandbox's Node 24 because the bundled 1024-bit `ssl-cert-snakeoil` key is rejected by OpenSSL (`ee key too small`) — an environment limitation, not a defect in the change; I validated the agent end-to-end against a fake proxy instead.

No findings to record. Verification I ran:

- `lib/linux.js:4` passes the path as a single argv element to `execFile("cat", …)`, so no shell is spawned. I confirmed empirically: `macaddress.one("eth0; touch /tmp/pwned")` produced `cat: '/sys/class/net/eth0; touch /tmp/pwned/address': No such file or directory` and `/tmp/pwned` was never created.
- This matches the upstream CVE-2018-13797 fix (commit `358fd594`), which replaced `exec("cat /sys/class/net/" + iface + "/address")` with exactly this `execFile` form; the removed baseline `lib/linux.js:4` was the vulnerable `exec` version.
- Error path is handled (`lib/linux.js:6-9`), the signature matches the other platform modules and `index.js:70`, and `node test.js` passes on Linux (`execFile` defaults to utf8, so `out.trim()` is valid).
- `iface` still reaches the path unvalidated (e.g. `../../..`), but reading requires a file literally named `address`, the caller already controls the argument in-process, and the added code no longer reaches a shell — not reportable.

The `macosx.js`/`unix.js`/`windows.js` `exec` calls in the same tree remain shell-based and unfixed relative to upstream's full patch, but those files are untouched here and were equally reachable before this change, so they belong outside this review.

The PR re-adds the Linux backend for the `macaddress` library, which the baseline had removed so that `require('./index.js')` threw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on Linux, and it adds it in the post-fix, `execFile`-based form. That restores Linux support and closes the command-injection sink for that platform; the code is small, correct, and I found no issue worth reporting.

Covered the single changed file and its only caller (`index.js:78-112`); the rest of the repo is untouched by this PR.

**Summary:** The PR adds `lib/linux.js` to the `macaddress` library, which reads an interface's MAC address by running `cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/address` through `child_process.exec`. The interface name is concatenated directly into the shell string, so a caller-supplied `iface` with shell metacharacters executes arbitrary commands in the host process; I reproduced root command execution through the public `one(iface, callback)` API. The file is otherwise simple and correctly handles errors, but the shell use makes it unsafe as written — it should use `execFile`/`fs.readFile` (and reject non-interface-name input) before this can be merged.

findings.title: Interface name is interpolated into a shell command, allowing arbitrary command execution
findings.body:
`lib/linux.js` builds a shell command by string-concatenating the caller-supplied
interface name into `exec`. An `iface` value containing shell metacharacters runs
arbitrary commands in the host Node process.

**Preconditions:** the application passes a non-OS-controlled string to
`macaddress.one(iface, callback)` (or `.all()` under an interface name it can
influence). The library never validates `iface`.

**Evidence:** `lib/linux.js:5` — `exec("cat /sys/class/net/" + iface + "/address", ...)`.
`index.js:109` forwards `iface` unchanged to `_getMacAddress`. Reproduction:

```
node -e 'require("./index").one("eth0; id > /tmp/pwned; echo ", function(){})'
cat /tmp/pwned   # uid=0(root) gid=0(root) ...
```

The callback even reports success (`mac: "/address"`), so the failure is silent.

**Impact:** anyone who can set the interface name gets command execution with the
host process's privileges — a trust-boundary crossing on the standard use of a
public API (`README` documents `one([iface], callback)` with no restriction on the
value). This is CVE-2018-13797.

**Fix:** stop involving a shell. Use `child_process.execFile('cat', ['/sys/class/net/' + iface + '/address'], cb)`
or `fs.readFile('/sys/class/net/' + iface + '/address', 'utf8', cb)`, and reject
`iface` values that are not a plain interface name (`/^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]+$/`).

summary:
Verified both against the code and end-to-end repros. Summary:

The PR adds `lib/formats/ssh.js`, which parses OpenSSH one-line public keys (`ssh-rsa AAAA... comment`). The added file is byte-identical to sshpk 1.13.1, i.e. the version before the upstream fix for CVE-2018-3737 (sshpk 1.13.2, commit 46065d38).

Two issues are confirmed: `SSHKEY_RE2` backtracks quadratically on a long key string whose trailing newline survives the trim/replace at line 27 (a `\` after the newline does it), which I reproduced through the public `parseKey()` path — 40 KB of input costs ~2 s of blocked event loop; and comment-less keys get the literal string `"undefined"` as their comment (line 75), which also leaks into `toString('ssh')` output. The existing test suite passes; the one failure under `test/*.js` is an openssl sandbox issue unrelated to this change. The rest of the parser (partial-read comment recovery, `write`, error handling) behaves as upstream and shows nothing further worth reporting.

findings.title: Long ssh-format key strings make the parser backtrack quadratically and stall the event loop
findings.body:
`sshpk.parseKey()` on a long attacker-supplied string that reaches the
ssh-format parser blocks the Node event loop for seconds to minutes. The
regex `SSHKEY_RE2` (lib/formats/ssh.js:19) backtracks quadratically when the
trimmed input ends in a newline: `[a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n]+` first swallows the
whole body, then `(.*)$` cannot cross the trailing `\n`, and the engine
retries every starting position for the greedy group.

**Preconditions:** The trailing newline has to survive trimming at
lib/formats/ssh.js:27. A backslash after it makes that happen: `trim()` stops
at the `\` and `replace(/[\\\r]/g, '')` then deletes it, leaving the newline
in place. So `"ssh-rsa <long body>\n\\"` is parsed as `"ssh-rsa <long body>\n"`.

**Evidence:**

    $ node -e '
      var sshpk = require("./lib");
      [10000,20000,40000].forEach(function (n) {
        var s = "ssh-rsa " + "A".repeat(n) + "!\n\\\\";
        var t0 = Date.now();
        try { sshpk.parseKey(s, "ssh"); } catch (e) {}
        console.log(n, (Date.now()-t0) + "ms");
      });'
    10000 121ms
    20000 583ms
    40000 1981ms

Each doubling of the input multiplies the time by ~4, so a 1 MB key string
costs roughly an hour of CPU. Matching against `SSHKEY_RE2` alone shows the
same growth (8 ms / 37 ms / 121 ms / 584 ms / 1975 ms for 2.5k/5k/10k/20k/40k
body chars). `parseKey(data)` with no format argument defaults to `auto`
(lib/key.js:219), which sends any string starting with `ssh-`/`ecdsa-` to this
parser (lib/formats/auto.js:27-30), so a caller validating a user-supplied
public key reaches it without any extra step.

**Impact:** One request with a ~1 MB crafted key pins a CPU core and stalls
every other request in the process. The stall ends when the match finishes and
an attacker can repeat it at will, so this is a service-wide availability
issue (broad reach, recoverable). It does not leak data or corrupt keys.

**Fix:** Bound the match. The upstream fix (sshpk 1.13.2, commit 46065d38)
replaces the two regexes with forms that have no overlapping quantifiers:

    var SSHKEY_RE = /^([a-z0-9-]+)[ \t]+([a-zA-Z0-9+\/]+[=]*)([ \t]+([^ \t][^\n]*[\n]*)?)?$/;
    var SSHKEY_RE2 = /^([a-z0-9-]+)[ \t\n]+([a-zA-Z0-9+\/][a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n=]*)([^a-zA-Z0-9+\/ \t\n=].*)?$/;

Applied here, those regexes answer the same 20000-char input in 0.3 ms. A
hard cap on accepted key length (e.g. reject input over 16 KB before matching)
is a cheap second line of defense.

findings.title: Comment-less ssh-format keys get the literal comment "undefined"
findings.body:
Parsing any ssh-format public key that has no comment sets the key's
`comment` to the literal string `"undefined"` instead of leaving it unset, so
callers that rely on `key.comment` see a bogus value and re-serialising the
key writes `... undefined` as the comment.

**Evidence:**

    $ node -e '
      var sshpk = require("./lib");
      var k = sshpk.parseKey("ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTItbmlzdHAyNTYAAAA" +
        "IbmlzdHAyNTYAAABBBK9+hFGVZ9RT61pg8t7EGgkvduhPr/CBYfx+5rQFEROj8EjkoGIH2xy" +
        "pHOHBz0WikK5hYcwTM5YMvnNxuU0h4+c=", "ssh");
      console.log(JSON.stringify(k.comment));'
    "undefined"

When `SSHKEY_RE` matches without a comment, group 3 and group 4 are both
undefined, so the comment-recovery branch at lib/formats/ssh.js:75 runs with
`var data = m[2] + m[3]` and builds `data` from the base64 body concatenated
with the string `"undefined"`. The trailer computed from that string starts
with the base64 body, so it passes the `/^[a-zA-Z0-9]/` test at
lib/formats/ssh.js:89 and is stored as the comment. For longer bodies the
junk after the consumed bytes is the base64 body itself plus `undefined`.

**Impact:** Wrong metadata on a correctly parsed key: `key.comment` no longer
reports the "(unnamed)" default that `Key.parse` sets (lib/key.js:237-238),
and `toString('ssh')` appends the garbage comment to the output, so a
round-trip through sshpk alters the key line. Nothing is authenticated on the
comment, so the damage is a corrupted display/serialisation value, not a
security decision.

**Fix:** Do not concatenate an absent group:

    var data = m[2] + (m[3] ? m[3] : '');

which is the change upstream made in sshpk 1.13.2 (commit 46065d38) together
with a test that asserts `comment === '(unnamed)'` for a comment-less key.

summary:
Recorded three findings. Summary:

The PR adds the full `index.js` of https-proxy-agent 2.1.1 to the baseline tree. It is functional but reproduces CVE-2018-3739 (filed as CVE-2018-3736): `proxy.auth` goes unvalidated into `new Buffer()` at `index.js:207`, leaking uninitialized heap into the `Proxy-Authorization` header on Node 4–7 and throwing/leaking sockets for non-string values. Two further evidence-backed defects exist in the added file: proxy connection options bleed into the destination TLS handshake, so `rejectUnauthorized: false` for a self-signed proxy also disables endpoint verification, and IPv6 targets generate a malformed `CONNECT` line and `Host` header.

The connection, buffering, and non-200 replay logic was also probed; its weaker edges (silent hang on an incomplete proxy response, tail bytes after the 200 header discarded, unbounded buffering) need a misbehaving proxy and did not justify separate findings. Overall the change should not merge without the `auth` fix.

findings.title: Unvalidated proxy auth leaks heap memory into the Proxy-Authorization header and crashes on non-string values
findings.body:
`proxy.auth` is copied from the caller's options without any type check and passed
straight to `new Buffer()`. On Node 4–7 (the versions `.travis.yml` targets) that call
returns uninitialized memory when `auth` is a number, so stale process heap is
base64-encoded into the `Proxy-Authorization` header of the CONNECT request sent to the
proxy. Non-string, non-numeric values throw instead of reporting a configuration error:
the exception escapes the connection callback, the request fails as an uncaught
`TypeError` (or, on older Node, a swallowed rejection that hangs forever), and the
socket to the proxy is never destroyed.

**Preconditions:** the attacker must control the structured options object handed to
`new HttpsProxyAgent(...)` (e.g. JSON-decoded config) — a proxy URL string is safe,
because `url.parse()` yields a string `auth` (`index.js:27`).

**Evidence:** `index.js:35` copies `auth` verbatim; `index.js:204-208` only checks
truthiness before `new Buffer(proxy.auth).toString('base64')`.

Reproduction with a local proxy that records the bytes it receives:

* Node 6.11.5, `auth: 1024` → the proxy reads `Proxy-Authorization: Basic AQAA…`
  (1024 decoded bytes, 368 of them nonzero stale heap); Node 8 and later zero-fill, so
  no disclosure there.
* Node 24, `auth: {}` → uncaught `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]` at `index.js:207`,
  process exit code 1 when the request has no `error` listener; with a listener the
  request errors and the proxy TCP socket stays open (5 requests → 5 open, 0 closed),
  because agent-base only emits `error` (`node_modules/agent-base/index.js:117-124`).
* Node 6/8, `auth: {}` → `UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning` and the request hangs
  silently.

**Impact:** heap contents are disclosed to the proxy/network on Node 4–7, and any
non-string `auth` crashes or hangs the client. This is CVE-2018-3739 (duplicated as
CVE-2018-3736); upstream fixed it in 2.2.0 by switching to `Buffer.from`.

**Fix:** reject non-string `auth` (at construction, or skip the header) and build the
header with `Buffer.from(proxy.auth, 'utf8')`.

findings.title: Proxy-only rejectUnauthorized setting also disables verification of the destination server
findings.body:
Options given to `HttpsProxyAgent` are meant for the proxy connection, but they are also
merged into the TLS handshake with the destination. A client that sets
`rejectUnauthorized: false` (the documented workaround for a self-signed proxy, and
what this repo's own tests do) therefore also stops verifying the certificate of the
HTTPS server it ultimately talks to, silently.

**Evidence:** `index.js:33` calls `Agent.call(this, opts)`, so agent-base keeps the
proxy options as `this.options` and merges them into every request's options
(`node_modules/agent-base/index.js` `addRequest`, `Object.assign({}, this.options,
ownOpts)`). `index.js:148-153` then passes that merged object to `tls.connect` for the
endpoint. Repro: a CONNECT proxy plus a self-signed HTTPS server; a request with no
request-level TLS options fails with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`, while the same
request through `new HttpsProxyAgent({host, port, rejectUnauthorized: false})` succeeds
and returns the body. The README describes those options as passed to the proxy's
`net.connect()`/`tls.connect()`, not to endpoint validation.

**Impact:** an application that trusts a self-signed corporate proxy also accepts any
certificate for the real endpoint, so a network attacker can MITM the destination
traffic. The severity is reduced because it needs the non-default
`rejectUnauthorized: false` (or a proxy-specific `ca`) setting.

**Fix:** keep proxy-only connection options out of the object agent-base merges into
request options (store them separately and pass only socket/servername plus the
request's own TLS options to `tls.connect`).

findings.title: IPv6 destination hosts produce a malformed CONNECT request and Host header
findings.body:
Requests whose destination is an IPv6 literal produce a malformed CONNECT request and
`Host` header because `opts.host` is interpolated without brackets. `url.parse()`
returns `::1` (no brackets) for `https://[::1]:443`, so the proxy receives
`CONNECT ::1:443 HTTP/1.1` and `Host: ::1`, which RFC 7231 authority-form / RFC 3986
IP-literal syntax does not allow. Strict proxies reject the request, and permissive
ones may treat `443` as part of the address.

**Evidence:** `index.js:201-202` builds `opts.host + ':' + opts.port` and
`index.js:212-216` builds the `Host` header the same way, with no `net.isIPv6` check.
Reproduction against a local server that records the CONNECT bytes:

    CONNECT ::1:443 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: ::1\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n

Upstream later added `net.isIPv6(opts.host) ? '[' + opts.host + ']' : opts.host`.

**Impact:** HTTPS/WSS requests to IPv6 endpoints cannot be tunnelled through a proxy.
Contained and recoverable — the process keeps working and only that request fails.

**Fix:** bracket IPv6 literal hosts when composing both the request line and the `Host`
header.

summary: All five findings are recorded. ## Summary This PR adds `selectize-plugin-a11y.js`, a 140-line Selectize.js plugin that turns the widget into an accessible combobox (role/aria wiring, an assertive live region that announces the highlighted option, and an Enter handler on the control). The change re-introduces a known DOM XSS: `speak()` concatenates the active option's text into an HTML string and injects it with `.html()` into a hidden region in `document.body`. I reproduced it end-to-end with real selectize 0.12.4 and jQuery 3.3.1 in jsdom — a label of `` executes even though Selectize escapes the label at render time, because `.text()` hands the raw payload back to the plugin. That is the only high-severity issue; the remaining findings are accessibility/behaviour defects in the plugin's core job (`haspopup` misspelling, no accessible name in the README-documented setup, Enter reopening a single-select list after selection) and an observer leak on `destroy()`. Each low finding was reproduced or verified in jsdom rather than argued from reading alone.

findings.title: Option labels are parsed as HTML in the live region, executing attacker script in the host app's origin
findings.body:
Option labels are inserted into the live region as HTML, so any app that shows untrusted labels in a Selectize dropdown runs attacker script in its own origin. `speak()` builds a string by concatenation and injects it with `.html()` (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:28-29`). Its only caller passes the active option's text (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:52`), and the region is a hidden `
` appended to `document.body` (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:97`). **Evidence** Round-trip in jsdom with real selectize 0.12.4 (as in `examples/api.html`), jQuery 3.3.1 and the plugin file verbatim. Select source label ``, then open the dropdown and highlight that option (`setActiveOption`, what arrow keys and hover do — the observer reacts to the `active` class at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:46-53`): ``` option rendered by selectize default render.option: "
<img src=x onerror=\"window.__xss=1\">
" -> $target.text() passed to speak(): "" live region innerHTML: "
" img in live region: true | attached to document: true window.__xss after error event: 1 ``` Selectize's default renderer escapes the label (which is why the escaped text is what `.text()` returns), so the plugin's own sink — not the host app's `render.option` — is enough to execute. `
").text(msg);` then `this.$region.html($msg);` (equivalently `this.$region.text(msg)`). `aria-live` with `aria-relevant="additions"` still announces the added child.

findings.title: Combobox is created without aria-haspopup because the attribute is spelled haspopup
findings.body:
The combobox is created with a literal `haspopup` attribute instead of `aria-haspopup`, so
no `aria-haspopup` is ever present and assistive technology cannot report that the control
opens a popup.

`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:118` passes the key `haspopup: "listbox"` to `self.$control_input.attr({...})`.
jQuery applies attribute names verbatim; nothing else in the file sets the ARIA name.

**Evidence**

Rendered markup from the plugin with selectize 0.12.4 in jsdom:

```
<input type="text" ... role="combobox" aria-expanded="false" haspopup="listbox" aria-owns="zgyrzplujx" aria-label="Country">
has aria-haspopup? undefined | has haspopup? listbox
```

`haspopup` appears only at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:118`, so nothing else relies on it.

**Impact**

Every widget using the plugin ships an invalid attribute and a missing combobox state:
screen readers do not announce the popup type, and validation/axe tooling flags the unknown
attribute. The plugin's only purpose is a correct accessible combobox, so its headline
behaviour is silently absent. No data exposure; low.

**Fix**

Rename the key to `"aria-haspopup": "listbox"` at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:118`.

findings.title: Enter on a single-select dropdown reopens it immediately after selecting
findings.body:
After a single-select value is chosen with Enter, the dropdown reopens immediately and focus
is pulled back into the hidden text input.

`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:109-113` binds `keydown` on `self.$control`, which also receives
the bubbled event from `self.$control_input`, and calls `$(this).click()` on Enter without
checking whether Selectize already handled the key.

**Evidence**

Selectize's own handler processes Enter (selectize.js 0.12.4, `onKeyDown` KEY_RETURN case)
and selects the active option: `addItem` → `isFull()` → `close()`, and in single-select mode
`hideInput()` plus `$control_input.blur()`, which clears `isFocused`. The plugin's handler
then runs `$(this).click()`; Selectize's `onClick` sees `!isFocused`, so it focuses and
`openOnFocus` reopens the list.

Reproduced in jsdom with the plugin file and selectize 0.12.4, Enter dispatched on the
control input with an active option:

```
immediately after Enter:        isOpen= false  items=["2"]
after microtasks:               isOpen= true   aria-expanded: "true"
control classes: selectize-input items has-options full has-items focus input-active dropdown-active
selected label in item div: "France"
```

**Impact**

Every keyboard user of a single-select widget sees the list reopen and focus leave the
selected item right after choosing; the re-announcement also interrupts speech. Visual and
focus regression only — the value is still selected correctly. Low.

**Fix**

Do not synthesize a click when the event was already handled: bail out when
`e.isDefaultPrevented()`, or bind on `$control_input` and skip while the dropdown is open
with an active option (`self.isOpen && self.getActiveOption()`).

findings.title: destroy() leaves MutationObservers attached, retaining each destroyed widget and its callbacks
findings.body:
`destroy()` removes the live region but never disconnects the three MutationObservers, so
each destroyed widget stays reachable and its callbacks keep firing against detached nodes.

`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:58-73` creates the observer inside `domListener()` and never
stores or disconnects it; `destroy()` (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:133-139`) only calls
`self.accessibility.liveRegion.$region.remove()`.

**Evidence**

Instrumented the `MutationObserver` constructor in jsdom, created a widget with the plugin,
destroyed it, then mutated the detached `$dropdown` / `$control` nodes:

```
observer callbacks fired AFTER destroy from detached nodes: 1
region still in body: 0
dropdown detached from document: true
```

The file contains no `disconnect()` call.

**Impact**

Apps that create and destroy widgets — SPA components, modals, framework wrappers — leak
one observer plus the full Selectize instance, wrapper markup and jQuery data per instance
for the page's lifetime, and the callback still walks `self.$dropdown` / `self.$control_input`
after teardown. No user-visible misbehaviour unless widgets are recreated often, so low.

**Fix**

Keep the observer on `self.accessibility.liveRegion`, add a teardown helper that calls
`observer.disconnect()`, and call it from the `destroy` wrapper before removing the region.

findings.title: Combobox has no accessible name in the setup the README documents
findings.body:
Following the README, the combobox ends up with no accessible name: `aria-label` is only set when an ancestor carries an undocumented `data-accessibility-selectize-label`, and placing that attribute on the `` (`$input.attr('tabindex', -1).hide().after(self.$wrapper)`), so a `closest()` walk from `$wrapper` skips any attribute on the ` -> closest() found: false rendered: (no aria-label)
``` Neither `README.md` nor `examples/api.html` mentions `data-accessibility-selectize-label`, so an app that copies the documented setup gets the first result. **Impact** Screen-reader users are told only "combobox" with no name for the field, on every widget set up as documented; the selected value is also not reflected, so the control reads as empty. Accessibility correctness only, no data exposure; low. **Fix** Set the name through a supported ARIA path rather than a custom data attribute — e.g. accept a `label` option, or fall back to an existing `

summary: Reviewed the change: it re-adds `src/run.js`, the process helper every command in the package goes through. The exec-based `run()` is a shell sink, and the callers in `src/index.js` and `src/check-out-tag.js` interpolate remote URLs, tags, and file names into it unquoted; I reproduced command execution through a crafted remote URL. I also confirmed a smaller robustness defect in the new `runWithSpawn` error handling. Both are recorded; the shell injection is the one that matters.

findings.title: Crafted remote URL, tag, or file name runs arbitrary shell commands
findings.body:
`run()` executes its command string through a shell, and callers build that string by
interpolating values that can come from outside the program. A remote URL, tag, or
ignored file name containing shell metacharacters runs extra commands as the user who
started git-diff-apply.

**Evidence:**
- `src/run.js:10` calls `promisify(exec)(command)`, which passes the string to `/bin/sh`.
- `src/index.js:225` builds `git clone ${remoteUrl} ${_tmpDir}` with no quoting.
- Tag and file names get the same treatment: `src/index.js:127` (`git diff ${startTag} ${endTag}`),
  `src/check-out-tag.js:6` (`git rev-parse ${tag}`), `src/index.js:116,118` (`git ls-files ${ignoredFile}`,
  `git checkout -- ${ignoredFile}`).
- Reproduction against this checkout: calling `run("git clone " + url + " /tmp/dest")`
  with `url = "/tmp/dummy; echo INJECTED > /tmp/pwned.txt; echo"` created `/tmp/pwned.txt`
  and still resolved. The shell ran the injected `echo`.

**Impact:** Anyone who can influence one of those values — a remote URL taken from a
project config, CI variable, or issue text, or a tag name from the repository being
applied — can run arbitrary commands with the developer's or CI job's privileges and
read or alter its files and credentials. `git clone` of an attacker-named repository
is a normal first step of this tool, so the value is naturally externally supplied.
NVD rates CVE-2019-10776 9.8; this repository's policy caps findings at `high`.

**Fix:** Stop routing data through a shell. Use the argument-array path that already
exists (`runWithSpawn`, `src/run.js:15`) for `clone`, `rev-parse`, `checkout`, `diff`,
`ls-files`, and `apply`, so no value is parsed by the shell. Keep `exec` only for
`startCommand`/`endCommand`, which are documented as shell commands.

findings.title: runWithSpawn leaves an unhandled error event when the command cannot spawn
findings.body:
`runWithSpawn` never settles its promise when the command cannot be started. The child
`error` event has no listener, so Node throws it as an uncaught exception and the
process dies; the awaiting caller gets no rejection to catch.

**Evidence:** `src/run.js:16-39` only handles `'close'` and the two stdio streams.
Running it with a command that does not exist
(`runWithSpawn('definitely-not-a-binary-xyz', ['--version'], { cwd: '/tmp' })`) raised
`uncaughtException: ENOENT spawn ... ENOENT` and the promise never settled.

**Impact:** `isGitClean` (`src/git-status.js:6`) is called inside the try/catch at
`src/index.js:199-203` that is meant to report "Not a git repository". When git is
missing or `cwd` does not exist, the process instead exits with an uncaught `ENOENT`
stack trace. Contained and cosmetic — an error message rather than wrong behaviour.

**Fix:** Add `child.on('error', reject)` (guarding against settling twice) so spawn
failures reject like non-zero exits do.

summary:
The change is a single new file that rewrites limdu's liblinear wrapper to drop shell command strings. The command-injection goal is met — every spawn now goes through `execFileSync` with an argument vector. Recording is done.

**Findings recorded (3):**
- medium — `SvmLinear.isInstalled()` is now unconditionally false, so the constructor always throws
- medium — string `learn_args` breaks `trainBatch` (all documented callers pass a string)
- low — `darum` typo in the multi-label guard

**Summary:** The PR replaces the shell-composed `execSync` calls in `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js` with `execFileSync` and an argument array, which removes the command-injection vector that motivated the change. It is not shippable as-is: the same sweep converted the install probe to a form that can never succeed (execFile does not split `'liblinear_train .'`), so the classifier cannot be constructed even with liblinear installed, and it changed `learn_args` from a string to an array without migrating the README, demos or tests, so training would still throw after the probe is fixed. The repo's tests hide both because they skip silently when `isInstalled()` is false.

findings.title: SvmLinear.isInstalled() always returns false, so every SvmLinear construction throws
findings.body:
`SvmLinear.isInstalled()` can never return true, so the constructor's guard throws and the classifier cannot be used at all, even on a machine with liblinear installed.

**Evidence:** `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:46` now calls `child_process.execFileSync('liblinear_train .')`. `execFile` does not run a shell or split the string, so the whole 17-character string is used as the executable path and the spawn fails every time:

```
$ printf '#!/bin/sh\nexit 0\n' > /tmp/bin/liblinear_train && chmod +x /tmp/bin/liblinear_train
$ PATH=/tmp/bin:$PATH node -e "require('child_process').execFileSync('liblinear_train .')"
Error: spawnSync liblinear_train . ENOENT   (code=ENOENT, path="liblinear_train .")
$ PATH=/tmp/bin:$PATH node -e "require('child_process').execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])"   # works
```

The catch at `:47-49` turns that ENOENT into `false`, and the constructor at `:37-41` then throws `Cannot find the executable 'liblinear_train'`. The previous code (`execSync('liblinear_train .')`, shell-split, same file upstream at 92c045d3) did return true: a reference liblinear build exits 0 for a directory argument (`train .` writes `..model`, exit 0), which is what upstream relied on.

The repo's own tests hide the break: `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90-93`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:12` and `test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:95-98` only `console.warn` when `isInstalled()` is false, so SvmLinear coverage silently drops to zero while the suite stays green.

**Impact:** SvmLinear is exported from `classifiers/index.js:11` as a public classifier; every user and both demos (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:16`, `SvmLinearMulticlassDemo.js:25`) now throw at construction. Reach is broad (all consumers of the wrapper) and the failure repeats on every call, but nothing is destroyed, so medium.

**Fix:** Pass the argument list separately: `child_process.execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])`.

findings.title: Documented string learn_args makes SvmLinear.trainBatch throw TypeError
findings.body:
`learn_args` changed from a shell-argument string to an array, but every documented and in-repo caller still passes a string, so `trainBatch` throws before liblinear is ever invoked.

**Evidence:** `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:28` stores `opts.learn_args || []` and `:94` builds `this.learn_args.concat([learnFile, modelFile])`. With a string, `String.prototype.concat` flattens the array into a single string, and `:95` then calls `.join` on it:

```
$ node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify("-c 20.0".concat(["x.learn","x.model"])))'
"-c 20.0x.learn,x.model"
$ node -e 'var cp=require("child_process"); try{cp.execFileSync("echo","a b")}catch(e){console.log(e.name,e.message.split("\n")[0])}'
TypeError The "args" argument must be of type object. Received type string
```

Reproduced end to end against the file with `isInstalled` forced true: `trainBatch({...})` throws `TypeError: args.join is not a function` (`SvmLinear.js:95`) for `{learn_args: "-c 20.0"}`; with `learn_args: ["-c","20.0"]` it succeeds.

String usages that are now broken, none of which this change updated: `README.md:442`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:91`, `test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:18`, `test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:96`, `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:18`, `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearMulticlassDemo.js:27`. The sibling wrapper `SvmPerf.js:31` is still string-based, so the two APIs now disagree. Before this change the string was interpolated into a shell command (`execSync(this.train_command+" "+this.learn_args+" "+learnFile+" "+modelFile)`) and worked.

**Impact:** training throws for every caller that uses the documented option, i.e. the whole documented surface of the wrapper. The damage is currently masked by the `isInstalled()` break (which stops the constructor first), so it will surface as soon as that is fixed — fixing only `isInstalled` leaves SvmLinear still unable to train. Broad reach, recoverable, medium.

**Fix:** Normalise one way in the constructor and keep the documented type working, e.g. `this.learn_args = Array.isArray(opts.learn_args) ? opts.learn_args : String(opts.learn_args || "").split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean)`, and build `args` as an array unconditionally so `:95` and `:97` always see an array.

findings.title: Multi-label guard in SvmLinear.trainBatch throws ReferenceError on 'darum'
findings.body:
The multi-label guard in `trainBatch` references an undeclared variable, so a dataset whose samples carry more than one output label crashes with a `ReferenceError` instead of the intended diagnostic.

**Evidence:** `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:68-74`:

```js
if (_.isArray(datum.output))
  if (datum.output.length > 1) {
    console.log("Multi-label is not allowed")
    console.log(JSON.stringify(darum.output, null, 4))   // :72 — "darum" is not defined
    process.exit(0)
  }
```

Reproduced by calling `trainBatch` with the array-output shape that limdu's own multi-label tests use (`test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:67-70`, `output: ['A','B']`):

```
Multi-label is not allowed
ReferenceError: darum is not defined
    at SvmLinear.<anonymous> (classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:72:34)
```

The whole file is new in this change (the baseline tree has no `SvmLinear.js`), so the defect ships with it; it is inherited from the upstream version of the file and is untouched by the execSync→execFileSync part of this change.

**Impact:** a caller that feeds array labels to `SvmLinear` directly gets an unhandled `ReferenceError` instead of an actionable message. The neighbouring `process.exit(0)` is also a hazard: once the log line is fixed, the guard would terminate the host process with a success exit code on bad input. Contained to the offending dataset and nothing is persisted, so low.

**Fix:** use `datum.output` at `:72`, and replace `process.exit(0)` with `throw new Error("Multi-label is not allowed")` so a library call cannot kill the process.

summary:
The pull request adds `lib/conversion.js`, the package's public entry point: a factory that stores global options, plus `convert()`, which clones the per-call options, writes `html`/`header`/`footer` to temp files, derives the input URL and output PDF path, and dispatches to the `phantom-server` or `dedicated-process` strategy. The file matches upstream 0.6.0/0.6.1 byte for byte; the tree it lands in is the pre-fix code for CVE-2020-7763.

The change works for its documented happy path, but it hands the caller's `url` and `html` to PhantomJS with no scheme restriction of its own while the only local-file guard, in unchanged `conversionScriptPart.js`, blocks just the literal `file:///` prefix — so arbitrary server files are readable with `allowLocalFilesAccess` false, both through `url: 'file:///...'` and through protocol-less paths in the HTML. Two smaller defects sit in the new file: unsanitized `tmpId` escapes `tmpDir`, and non-string `header`/`footer` throw from inside a callback and crash the process.

findings.title: Untrusted HTML or a caller-supplied url reads arbitrary local files even with allowLocalFilesAccess false
findings.body:
Converting untrusted HTML, or opening a caller-supplied `url`, lets the page read any file the
server process can read, even with `allowLocalFilesAccess` left at its documented default
(`false`).

**Preconditions:** the service passes document HTML that comes from an untrusted source (report
templates, user uploads) or forwards a user-controlled `url`.

**Evidence:**

- `lib/conversion.js:63` keeps the caller's `url` verbatim (`opt.url = opt.url || ...`);
  `lib/conversion.js:12-14` writes `html` to a temp file that PhantomJS opens with JavaScript
  enabled (`lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:8`).
- The only restriction is `lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:20-28`: it returns early when
  `request.url` starts with `body.url`, and aborts only requests whose URL starts with the
  literal `file:///`.
- `conversion({ url: "file:///etc/passwd" })` therefore opens that file directly — the document
  request matches the early return at :20-22 — and renders its contents into the PDF with
  `allowLocalFilesAccess` false and no `html` at all.
- HTML that navigates to a path without a protocol, e.g.
  `document.write(window.location='/etc/passwd')` or the advisory's `c:/windows/win.ini`,
  produces a request URL without the `file:///` prefix and slips past the check at :25.
- Both paths are CVE-2020-7763 / GHSA-6h7f-qwqm-35pp ("Arbitrary File Read"). Upstream commit
  b5d2da2 fixes the HTML vector by aborting every non-http(s) request and adds a regression test
  for protocol-less paths; the `body.url` early return is still there, so the `url` vector
  survives that fix.

**Impact:** An untrusted document author reads any file the Node/PhantomJS process can read —
credentials, config, other tenants' temp files — and gets the content back as a PDF. Untrusted
actor, secret data crossing a trust boundary, default configuration, permanent disclosure:
graded `high`. The file under review (`lib/conversion.js`) is the exported entry point that
forwards both `url` and `html` with no scheme check of its own; the remaining defect lives in
`conversionScriptPart.js`.

**Fix:** enforce one rule — local files are readable only when `allowLocalFilesAccess` is true.
In `lib/conversion.js`, reject a `url` whose scheme is not `http`/`https`/`data`. In
`lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js`, abort every request that is not `http(s):`/`data:` instead
of allowlisting the `file:///` prefix, and stop letting the `body.url` prefix short-circuit the
check for local schemes.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tmpId traverses out of tmpDir and writes PDF and HTML to an arbitrary directory
findings.body:
`tmpId` reaches `path.join` unvalidated, so a caller-supplied value places the temp HTML and the
PDF outside `tmpDir`.

**Evidence:**

- `lib/conversion.js:56` `var id = opt.tmpId || uuid();`
- `lib/conversion.js:12` `path.resolve(path.join(options.tmpDir, id + type + ".html"))`
- `lib/conversion.js:64` `opt.output = path.resolve(path.join(options.tmpDir, id + ".pdf"))`

Node resolves `path.join("/tmp/t", "../../evil" + "html.html")` to `/evilhtml.html`; `id` of
`a/../../../etc/x` resolves to `/etc/xhtml.html` (verified with `path.join`/`path.resolve` on
node 24). The same id is reused for `header.html`, `footer.html`, and the `.pdf` output, so the
path escape covers every file the conversion writes.

**Impact:** A service that forwards a request-scoped id into `tmpId` lets that id choose the
directory the write lands in and overwrite another request's `<id>html.html`/`<id>.pdf`; the
content is attacker HTML. Severity `low`: the caller normally sets `tmpId` itself, the appended
suffix (`html.html`, `.pdf`) limits which existing file names can be hit, and the visible damage
is contained to the files the conversion writes.

**Fix:** derive `id` from `uuid()` and accept a caller id only when it matches
`/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/`, rejecting anything containing a path separator or `..` before it reaches
`path.join`.

findings.title: A non-string header or footer throws from inside a callback and crashes the process
findings.body:
A non-string `header` or `footer` throws inside `writeHtml`'s async callback, so the error becomes
an uncaught exception and kills the process instead of reaching `cb`.

**Evidence:**

- `lib/conversion.js:9-14` calls `fs.writeFile(htmlPath, opt[type], cb)` after only a truthiness
  check on `opt[type]`. Node throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` synchronously for a number, object or
  array (verified: `fs.writeFile("/tmp/x", {a:1}, cb)` throws immediately).
- `html` is written first (`lib/conversion.js:20-21`); `header`/`footer` are written inside its
  callback (`:24-32`), so a bad type there throws from inside a callback with no try/catch —
  uncaught, `process.exit`.
- A bad `html` type throws synchronously out of `convert()` (`:36`) rather than calling back with
  an error, which breaks the callback contract for the same input class.

**Impact:** A caller that forwards an unvalidated request field such as `header: {...}` from a
JSON body takes down the whole node process; repeatable by any requester that can reach that
field. Severity `low`: it needs the calling service to pass a non-string, and the library's
documented input is a string.

**Fix:** validate/coerce `html`, `header` and `footer` in `convert` (accept only strings and
Buffers, report anything else through `cb(err)`), and wrap the writes so no type error escapes a
callback.

summary:
Working tree is clean (`git status` empty) and both findings are recorded.

**Summary.** The PR adds one file, `src/run.js`, giving the package back its `exec`-based `run()` helper plus a `spawn`-based `runWithSpawn()`. Since every other module in the tree builds shell command strings by concatenation (`git clone ${remoteUrl} ...` at src/index.js:225, `git rev-parse ${tag}` at src/check-out-tag.js:6, `git ls-files ${ignoredFile}` at src/index.js:116, and others), restoring the exec helper restores shell injection on values like remote URLs and refnames — the exact defect of CVE-2019-10776, which upstream fixed by routing those calls through spawn. I reproduced injection through `remoteUrl` and through a git tag name that git accepts verbatim, including a second-order case where raw `exec` stdout is re-interpolated into the next command. The spawn helper also lacks an `error` listener, so a failed spawn crashes the process and leaves its promise unsettled; that one is minor. The change needs the exec path removed or fully replaced by argv-style spawn calls before it is safe to merge.

findings.title: Commands run through exec, so a remote URL or tag name can inject shell commands
findings.body:
`src/run.js` runs every command through `child_process.exec`, which starts a
shell (`/bin/sh -c`). Callers build those command strings by concatenating
values that are data, not shell code: `git clone ${remoteUrl} ${_tmpDir}`
(src/index.js:225), `git diff ${startTag} ${endTag} --binary > ${patchFile}`
(src/index.js:127), `git ls-files ${ignoredFile}` / `git checkout -- ${ignoredFile}`
(src/index.js:116,118), `git rev-parse ${tag}` (src/check-out-tag.js:6) and
`git tag ${tag}` (src/commit-and-tag.js:8). Nothing quotes or escapes them, so a
`;`, `$(...)`, backtick or `|` in a URL or refname runs an arbitrary command as
the invoking user.

**Preconditions:** a caller supplies a `remoteUrl` / `startTag` / `endTag` /
`ignoredFiles` value that a third party influenced — e.g. a URL from config or
CI, or a tag name enumerated from a remote repo. Git does not sanitise this
input class: `;`, `$`, backtick, `|`, `&`, `(`, `)` and `${IFS}` are all legal in
refnames (only space, `~^:?*[\`, `..` and `@{` are rejected), so "git validated
the tag" is not a defence.

**Evidence:** reproduced with dependencies installed. `remoteUrl` of
`/tmp/ozrepro/remote$(touch${IFS}/tmp/oz_url_injected)` (a syntactically valid
URL path) produced `git clone /tmp/ozrepro/remote$(touch ...) /tmp/tmp-XXXX`;
`/tmp/oz_url_injected` appeared and the apply reported success, so the victim gets
no signal. The same held for a real URL with a query string
(`https://example.invalid/org/repo.git?ref=main&x=$(touch${IFS}/tmp/...)`), and
for `endTag = "v2$(touch${IFS}/tmp/oz_tag_injected)"` through
`git rev-parse v2$(...)` at src/check-out-tag.js:6.

There is also second-order injection: src/check-out-tag.js:7 and
