src/index.js:177,183 re-interpolate raw `exec` stdout into the next shell
command, so stdout that happens to contain a newline or `;` becomes a new
command.

**Impact:** remote, unauthenticated code execution as the user running
git-diff-apply, with nothing written to the user's output to reveal it. The
package's own version is 0.22.1 (package.json), the range affected by
CVE-2019-10776 / GHSA-84cm-v6jp-gjmr; upstream fixed it by routing `git clone`
through the spawn helper (upstream commit 106d61d). Reach crosses a trust
boundary and the effect is permanent, so high.

**Fix:** `run()` must not pass a shell a string built from values. Either delete
the exec path and express every git invocation as `runWithSpawn(cmd, argv)` —
the helper for that already exists in this same file (src/run.js:15) and is used
by src/git-status.js:6 and src/git-remove-all.js:11 — or keep `run` only for
fixed command literals and add shell quoting for the argument values. The
`>` redirect in createPatchFile (src/index.js:127) becomes a
`fs.createWriteStream` pipe, as upstream did.

findings.title: runWithSpawn has no 'error' listener, so a failed spawn crashes the process and never settles
findings.body:
`runWithSpawn` (src/run.js:15-40) attaches listeners for `stdout`, `stderr` and
`close` but never for `error`. A `spawn` that cannot start the process — git not
on `PATH`, a deleted or unreadable `cwd`, `EACCES`, `E2BIG` from a large
`git add -f ...files` argv (src/git-remove-all.js:61) — emits `error`
asynchronously. With no listener Node raises an uncaught exception, and because
`close` never fires, the returned promise never settles either.

**Evidence:** reproduced on Node 24. Spawning a missing binary printed
`UNCAUGHT ENOENT spawn ... ENOENT` and no `close` followed; a nonexistent `cwd`
also resolved `spawn` and then threw `UNCAUGHT ENOENT -2`. The caller that
expects a rejection breaks: `isGitClean` is wrapped in try/catch at
src/index.js:199-203 exactly to turn a failure into `'Not a git repository'`,
and bin/git-diff-apply.js:42-47 only handles a rejected promise. The exec path
in the same file does reject on `ENOENT`, so the two helpers disagree.

**Impact:** an environment problem becomes a process crash (or a hung promise if
the host installs an `uncaughtException` handler) instead of the intended error.
Contained to one run and cleared by fixing the environment, so info.

**Fix:** add `child.on('error', reject)` in the promise body before resolving on
`close`.

summary:
Review complete.

**What the change does:** it re-adds the package entry point `angular-http-server.js` (124 lines), which serves a static SPA directory, falls back to `index.html` for unknown routes, and delegates request-to-file resolution to `./lib/get-file-path-from-url` — the helper introduced to block directory traversal. The path-handling code itself looks sound: the URL is resolved against an absolute `basePath`, and the `returnDistFile`/CORS/port options are unchanged in behaviour.

**Assessment:** the change as checked out cannot run. The helper it requires is not in the tree, so the CLI and the package's `main` entry both throw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before serving anything; I reproduced this after `npm install`. Minor secondary rough edges I did not file: `getPort()` throws `new Exception(...)` (`angular-http-server.js:95`), an undefined identifier, so a non-numeric `-p` value yields a `ReferenceError`; and `--open` builds its URL from `argv.ssl` only (`:43`), so `--https --open` opens an `http://` URL against a TLS listener.

findings.title: Added entry point requires a missing module, so the server crashes on every start
findings.body:
The added entry point requires a module that is absent from the tree, so the package
crashes on every start. `angular-http-server.js:12` does
`require('./lib/get-file-path-from-url')`, but `git ls-tree -r HEAD` contains no `lib/`
directory. `package.json` exposes this file as both `main` and `bin`, so every
invocation — CLI or `require('angular-http-server')` — exits with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`
before parsing arguments or serving a request.

**Evidence:** after `npm install`, `node angular-http-server.js --path example -p 9311`
prints:

```
Error: Cannot find module './lib/get-file-path-from-url'
Require stack:
- /workspace/.../angular-http-server.js
    at Object.<anonymous> (.../angular-http-server.js:12:28)
```

`test/mocha.opts` also lists `lib/**/*.spec.js`, so the expected companion module and
its tests are missing from the change.

**Impact:** the server cannot run at all, so the request-path resolution this commit
introduces (and the directory-traversal handling it is meant to restore) is not
present in the tree; the change is unusable rather than merely degraded. Reach is
broad (every user of the package) and the breakage persists until a follow-up commit,
but it is a local dev tool, fails loudly at startup, and exposes no data, so it stops
at medium.

**Fix:** ship `lib/get-file-path-from-url.js` (the file that returns `'dummy'` for
rejected paths) together with this entry point, or point the require at a module that
exists in the tree.

summary:
Findings recorded. Summary:

The PR re-adds `index.js` at the state where the parser no longer forces `remarkable`'s `html: true` (the upstream CVE-2018-3770 fix): `index.js:28` now defaults to `{breaks: true}`, so raw HTML in markdown is escaped before it reaches PhantomJS. I verified the default path is safe end-to-end with the repo's own dependencies — injected `<script>` and `onerror` handlers render as literal text in the PDF — and confirmed the fix works on both remarkable 1.7.1 and 1.7.4.

The fix is incomplete in one documented configuration: it never sets `html` explicitly, so remarkable's `commonmark` preset (`html: true`) re-opens the injection path and attacker markdown executes in the renderer; I reproduced the script actually rewriting the PDF. The stale README default is a smaller follow-on. Verdict: request changes for the preset gap, otherwise sound.

findings.title: commonmark preset still lets markdown HTML run as JavaScript in the PDF renderer
findings.body: `index.js:28` stops forcing `html: true` but never turns raw HTML off, so remarkable's preset decides. The documented `commonmark` preset sets `html: true`, and markdown HTML then reaches PhantomJS unescaped and runs as JavaScript — the CVE-2018-3770 path is still open for any caller that picks that preset. **Preconditions:** the library caller passes `remarkable: { preset: 'commonmark' }`. README.md:137-143 lists `commonmark` as a supported preset and describes presets as a formatting convenience, not as an opt-in to executing HTML. **Evidence:** var p = markdownpdf({remarkable: {preset: 'commonmark'}}) // markdown: // rendered HTML: // PDF text: "EXECMARKplain" (script ran; the document was rewritten) // same input, default preset: PDF text keeps the script as literal text - `index.js:28` — `extend({breaks: true}, opts.remarkable)`; no `html` key. - `index.js:29`, `index.js:43` — `preset` is defaulted to `'default'` and forwarded to `new Remarkable(...)`, whose constructor applies preset options before per-key options, so `html` comes from the preset. - remarkable 1.7.1/1.7.4 `lib/configs/commonmark.js:8` — `html: true` (`default.js:8` and `full.js:8` are `false`). - `index.js:117` writes that HTML to the tmp file; `phantom/render.js:22` `page.setContent(...)` runs it with PhantomJS's default `javascriptEnabled = true` (no `page.settings` anywhere in the repo); `phantom/render.js:44-52` renders after the load event, i.e. after execution. **Impact:** untrusted markdown (a README, issue body or docs page the caller did not write) executes attacker JavaScript inside the local renderer, which can read local files and make network requests — the script-execution primitive of CVE-2018-3770. Reach crosses a trust boundary, but it needs a non-default preset, so one tier down: medium. The default and `full` presets are safe. **Fix:** make the safe value explicit rather than inherited, so a preset cannot reopen it: after `index.js:29` add `if (opts.remarkable.html == null) opts.remarkable.html = false`. Optionally set `page.settings.javascriptEnabled = false` in `phantom/render.js` as defense in depth.

findings.title: README documents raw HTML as enabled by default after the change turns it off
findings.body:
The change makes inline HTML in markdown escape by default, but README.md still documents the old behaviour, so an upgrade silently changes output and users have no stated way to get raw HTML back. **Evidence:** README.md:133 says `Default value: { html: true, breaks: true }` while `index.js:28` now defaults to `{breaks: true}` and remarkable's `default` preset has `html: false`. README.md:255-266 shows an example passing `html: true`, which still works, but nothing says it is now required. Converting markdown such as `
…
` or `
` now emits `<div …>` into the PDF. **Impact:** documented behaviour and the code disagree; users relying on the documented default get visibly different PDFs after upgrading, and the security rationale for the change is nowhere stated. Information/low: no failure beyond wrong documentation, recoverable by passing `html: true`. **Fix:** update README.md:133 to `{ breaks: true }` and note in the `options.remarkable` section that raw HTML is passed through only when `html: true` is set explicitly.

summary: The PR adds a single file, `lib/conversion.js`, the factory and request pipeline for phantom-html-to-pdf: it clones request options, writes `html`/`header`/`footer` into temp files, derives the `file://` URL and PDF output path from `tmpId`, and hands the request to one of the two phantom strategies. The code is upstream 0.6.0 unchanged, and it carries the library's known weakness: request options are forwarded to filesystem sinks without validation, which is exactly the CWE-22 class of CVE-2020-7763. I reproduced two of the issues directly (path traversal via `tmpId`, and cross-instance option bleed); the third is traced statically because phantomjs is not installed. The rest of the file is small, and its remaining rough edges (temp files never deleted, a synchronous throw for a bad option combination) are documented behaviour or low-impact API choices rather than defects worth filing.

findings.title: Caller-supplied headerFile/footerFile/htmlFile are read into the PDF, bypassing allowLocalFilesAccess
findings.body:
`writeHtmlFile` only overwrites `opt[type + "File"]` when the matching `html`/`header`/`footer` string is truthy (lib/conversion.js:9-13), so any `headerFile`, `footerFile` or `htmlFile` supplied by the caller survives into the phantom request. Phantom reads those paths with `fs.open` and renders them into the PDF header/footer (lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:112, :124), and `htmlFile` becomes the document URL (lib/conversion.js:63). That read path is independent of `allowLocalFilesAccess`, which only aborts `file:///` page resource requests in the page's request handler (lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:25), so local files can be pulled into the returned PDF with the guard at its default.

**Preconditions:** the application forwards request-derived options; `header`/`footer` are absent, which is the normal case for a request that only sets `headerFile`.

**Evidence:** with `{html:'x', headerFile:'/etc/passwd'}`, lib/conversion.js:9 returns early, so `opt.headerFile` stays as given; lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:104 treats `body.headerFile` as present and :112 reads it, and the contents are returned as header markup in the PDF. The same holds for `footerFile` (:120-127) and for `htmlFile` when `html` is omitted (:63).

**Impact:** whoever can set request options reads arbitrary server files back through the generated PDF — confidential data disclosure that persists because temp files are never deleted. Medium: crosses a trust boundary with permanent disclosure, discounted because the non-default `*File` keys must be forwarded by the caller.

**Fix:** delete `opt.htmlFile`, `opt.headerFile` and `opt.footerFile` before `writeHtml`, so these options only ever point at files this module just created.

findings.title: Caller-controlled tmpId escapes the temp directory and writes attacker HTML to arbitrary paths
findings.body:
`convert()` builds every temp filename from the caller-supplied `tmpId` without sanitising it, so a `tmpId` containing `../` resolves outside `options.tmpDir`. The `html`, `header` and `footer` strings are then written to those paths, and the PDF output path is derived the same way. **Preconditions:** the application forwards request-derived options to the converter, or lets callers pick `tmpId` (the option exists to name the temp files). **Evidence:** `var id = opt.tmpId || uuid()` (lib/conversion.js:56) flows into `path.join(options.tmpDir, id + type + ".html")` (lib/conversion.js:12) and `id + ".pdf"` (lib/conversion.js:64); `path.join` normalises `..`. Reproduced: a converter with `tmpDir: '/tmp/oztest'` called with `{html:'attacker html', header:'

hdr

', tmpId:'../pwn'}` wrote `/tmp/pwnhtml.html` containing `attacker html` plus `/tmp/pwnheader.html`, while `/tmp/oztest` stayed empty. `path.resolve(path.join('/srv/app/tmp','../../../../etc/cron.d/xhtml.html'))` resolves to `/etc/cron.d/xhtml.html`. The same `id` is reused for `id + "settings.html"` (lib/dedicatedProcessStrategy.js:12). **Impact:** arbitrary file creation and overwrite with attacker-controlled content wherever the process can write — pages served by the same host (stored XSS under the app origin), another tenant's report files, the PDF itself. Medium: writing outside the intended directory crosses a trust boundary and a clobbered file is not restorable, discounted because it needs the non-default `tmpId` option fed from untrusted input. **Fix:** reduce `id` to one path component and verify containment — `path.basename(id)` plus a rejection of ids containing `/`, `\` or `..`; or keep `uuid()` as the file stem and use a sanitised `tmpId` only as a prefix.

findings.title: A second converter instance silently reconfigures every existing one
findings.body:
`options` is a module-level variable (lib/conversion.js:7) that every factory call overwrites (lib/conversion.js:82) and that each conversion reads at request time (lib/conversion.js:12, :64, :68, :70). Creating a second converter therefore changes `tmpDir`, `strategy`, `numberOfWorkers`, `timeout` and the rest for converters created earlier.

**Preconditions:** the application creates more than one converter instance (the library's own test does, test/test.js:7 and :31).

**Evidence:** reproduced — `factory({tmpDir:'/tmp/ozA', strategy:'none'})`, then `factory({tmpDir:'/tmp/ozB', strategy:'none'})`, then the first converter called with `{html:'tenant A doc'}` wrote `23857a22-28c8-4421-aea3-0e7b262bb767html.html` into `/tmp/ozB`; `/tmp/ozA` stayed empty.

**Impact:** one instance's documents and header/footer content are written into another instance's directory, so per-instance tmpDir, retention and cleanup settings no longer apply, and an in-flight request can be dispatched to a different strategy than the one its instance was built with (lib/conversion.js:68-71). Low: contained to a single application's converter instances and needs the application to create several.

**Fix:** move `options` into the factory closure — `module.exports = function (opt) { var options = opt || {}; ... }` — and keep `convert.options` pointing at that per-instance object.

summary: Review complete. One finding recorded. **What the change does:** PR #1 adds `js/tooltip.js` back to the tree at the exact upstream commit that fixes CVE-2018-14042 (`2a5ba23ce8`, "Fix/xss issues on data attributes"). The file is byte-identical to upstream: the only substantive lines are `js/tooltip.js:54` and `:207`, which route the `viewport` and `container` options through `$(document).find(...)` instead of `$(...)` / `$tip.appendTo(...)`. **Assessment:** the fix is correct and complete. I reproduced the payloads on jQuery 1.9.1 through 3.7.1: `$(document).find('')` throws `Syntax error, unrecognized expression` from Sizzle and creates no element, while the pre-fix form `$(payload)` still creates the `` (and `data-container` values reach it via `getOptions` at line 87). Nothing in the rest of the 520-line file is new relative to the pre-fix copy at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:1323,1476`, so the review reduces to those two lines; the one regression I could reproduce is the shadow-root/cross-document container case, recorded as `info`. Two out-of-scope observations worth knowing, neither filed because the identical code already ships in the untouched `dist/` bundle: `dist/js/bootstrap.js` and `dist/js/bootstrap.min.js` still contain the vulnerable tooltip and are what `package.json` `main` and the npm package point at, so the built artifact needs regenerating at release; and `js/tooltip.js:432` (`$(this.options.template)`, reachable from `data-template`) remains a DOM-creation sink — the CVE-2019-8331 class of issue, not addressed by this change.

findings.title: Element containers outside the main document are silently dropped by the tooltip container/viewport fix
findings.body:
Element-typed `container` and `viewport` values now pass through jQuery's
`find()`, which filters by containment in the main `document`. A container or
viewport that lives elsewhere — inside a shadow root, or in another document
such as an iframe — matches nothing, so the tooltip is never inserted into the
DOM. When the lost value is `viewport`, `show()` throws.

**Preconditions:** an application passes an element or jQuery object as the
`container` or `viewport` option, and that element is inside a shadow root or a
different document. The documented `container: 'body'`-style string form and any
element inside the main document are unaffected.

**Evidence:**

- `js/tooltip.js:207` — `$tip.appendTo($(document).find(this.options.container))`.
  For non-string arguments jQuery's `find()` returns
  `jQuery(selector).filter(... jQuery.contains(document, this) ...)`, so an
  element outside `document` yields an empty set and `appendTo` is a no-op.
  The tooltip stays detached (`isConnected: false`, `offsetWidth` 0) while
  `inserted.bs.tooltip` and `shown.bs.tooltip` still fire at
  `js/tooltip.js:208` and `:235`, so the page sees no error.
- `js/tooltip.js:54` — same wrapping for `viewport`. The resulting empty jQuery
  object is truthy, so the `if (!this.$viewport) return delta` guard at
  `js/tooltip.js:387` does not fire and `getPosition` dereferences
  `$element[0].tagName` at `js/tooltip.js:360` — `TypeError: Cannot read
  properties of undefined (reading 'tagName')` escapes `show()`.
- Reproduction with jsdom + the repo's vendored jQuery 1.12.4, same shadow-root
  container and viewport, pre-fix form (`$(el)` / `$tip.appendTo(el)`) restored
  for comparison:

  ```
  old: {"containerParent":"DIV","tipIsConnected":true,"viewportLen":1,"vpShow":"no throw"}
  new: {"containerParent":null,"tipIsConnected":false,"viewportLen":0,
        "vpShow":"THREW TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'tagName')"}
  ```

  An iframe-document container behaves the same way (`parent:"iframec"` →
  `null`). Selector strings, `document.body`, `document.documentElement` and
  in-document jQuery objects (e.g. `container: $tooltip` in
  `js/tests/unit/tooltip.js:1138`) return the element under both forms.
- Pre-fix behavior for these cases is at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:1476` and
  `:1323`.

**Impact:** contained and low incidence — an uncommon option value plus a
shadow-root or cross-document host. The failure is silent for `container` and a
hard `TypeError` for `viewport`. Graded `info` because it needs a non-default
setting and a hosting arrangement (web component or iframe) that classic
Bootstrap 3 pages rarely use. The XSS fix itself holds: HTML-shaped strings
throw `Syntax error, unrecognized expression` from Sizzle and create no
elements, on jQuery 1.9.1 through 3.7.1.

**Fix:** scope the document lookup to strings and pass anything else through
unchanged:
`this.options.container ? $tip.appendTo(typeof this.options.container === 'string' ? $(document).find(this.options.container) : $(this.options.container)) : $tip.insertAfter(this.$element)`,
and the same test at line 54 for `viewport`.

summary:
The PR adds `index.js`, the markdown-to-PDF pipeline: remarkable renders markdown to HTML, the HTML is written to a temp file, and PhantomJS `execFile`s `phantom/render.js` to produce the PDF, exposed as a duplex/`stream-from-to` API.

I reviewed all 144 lines plus the code they feed into (`phantom/render.js`, `bin/markdown-pdf`, tests, README). The headline problem is the `{html: true, breaks: true}` default at index.js:28: I reproduced end-to-end, with this repo's own code and PhantomJS 2.1.1, that markdown containing `<script>` or `<iframe src="file://…">` reads local files into the PDF and beacons them to a remote host — CVE-2018-3770, and the upstream fix was exactly to drop `html: true` from the defaults. I also confirmed two lower-impact defects: failed conversions throw an unhandled stream error (process crash, callback never runs), and `md += chunk` corrupts multi-byte characters split across chunk boundaries. Overall the pipeline is otherwise straightforward and well-scoped; the security default is the change-blocking issue.

findings.title: Untrusted markdown can run script and read local files into the PDF
findings.body: Rendering attacker-supplied markdown lets that markdown inject raw HTML and JavaScript into the PhantomJS page, which then reads local files into the PDF and can send them to a remote host. `index.js:28` defaults `opts.remarkable` to `{html: true, breaks: true}`. Remarkable then passes raw HTML through to the generated document (`index.js:77`), which is written verbatim to the temp `.html` file (`index.js:98`) and spliced into the page body by `phantom/render.js:20`. `phantom/render.js:22` loads it with `page.setContent(html, 'file:///markdown-pdf.html')`, so inline ` produced a PDF whose text contained the secret file's contents; an `

findings.title: Conversion errors crash the process instead of reaching the caller's callback
findings.body:
When a conversion fails, `index.js` reports it with `outputStream.emit('error', err)`
(`index.js:90`, `:95`, `:120`) and nothing ever listens on that stream. Under the documented
`.from(...).to(path, cb)` API the error is unhandled: the process throws and exits, and the
caller's callback is never called. The output stream is also never `end()`ed, so a consumer that
does attach a listener waits forever.

**Preconditions:** any failed conversion — PhantomJS missing or exiting non-zero (bad
`paperFormat`, failed `phantomjs-prebuilt` install), or a tmp-file creation error.

**Evidence:** reproduced with the same dependency set (`duplexer@0.1.1`, `stream-from-to@1.4.2`,
`through2`). A stream whose output emits `error` and is used through
`.from.string(...).to(path, cb)` throws `Unhandled 'error' event` (re-emitted by
`duplexer/index.js:85`) and the process exits with code 1; `cb` never ran. `stream-from-to`'s
`to()` only listens for `finish` on its write stream, and `index.js` registers no listener.

**Impact:** a failed render takes down the host process instead of returning an error to the
caller, and leaves temp files and the pipeline behind. Contained to the calling process and
recoverable on retry, hence low.

**Fix:** surface failures through the streams contract — attach an `error` handler to
`outputStream` (or `destroy(err)` the returned duplex) and end the stream, so `.to()`/pipe
consumers see a normal stream error rather than an uncaught exception.

findings.title: Multi-byte characters at chunk boundaries are corrupted in the generated PDF
findings.body:
The markdown accumulator coerces each stream chunk to a string on its own
(`md += chunk` at `index.js:37`). A multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is
decoded as two broken halves and becomes U+FFFD replacement characters in the PDF.

**Preconditions:** input larger than one stream chunk (64 KiB for `fs.createReadStream`, which
`stream-from-to` uses for `.from(path)`) with a non-ASCII character at a boundary.

**Evidence:** the same coercion in isolation:

    const b = Buffer.from('中文测试中文测试'); let md = ''
    md += b.slice(0, 5); md += b.slice(5)
    // "中\uFFFD\uFFFD测试中文测试" — not equal to b.toString()

**Impact:** silent corruption of non-ASCII text (CJK, accents, emoji) in the output with no
error, for users converting large documents. Low: contained to the affected document and visible
in the output.

**Fix:** collect chunks as Buffers and decode once at flush, e.g. push into an array and
`Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8')` in the `flush` handler, or set the stream to
`{encoding: 'utf8'}` via `through2({encoding: 'utf8'}, ...)` so the split is handled by the
stream's string decoder.

summary:
Coverage is complete: the change adds a single file, so I reviewed all 290 lines, reproduced the failures, and cross-checked against the upstream 1.10.0 release, which fixes the injection with `spawn`.

**Summary.** The PR adds `lib/growl.js`, a desktop-notification library that builds a shell command string from the message and options and runs it with `child_process.exec`. Escaping is done with `JSON.stringify`, which quotes for JSON, not for the shell, so `$(...)` and backticks in a message or title are executed by `/bin/sh` — the CVE-2017-16042 command injection; I reproduced it. Two smaller defects also reproduced: the priority block pushes the descriptor object (`[object Object]`), drops numeric priorities, and throws when the platform config has no priority flag; and `options.exec` overwrites the module-level notifier config, so every later call in the process runs the custom command. Overall assessment: do not merge; replace the shell invocation with an argument-array call (`execFile`/`spawn`), which removes the injection without changing the API.

findings.title: Priority option renders "[object Object]", drops numeric values, and throws for Linux-Growl
findings.body:
The priority block is broken on every platform, in three ways:

1. It pushes the whole priority descriptor object instead of its flag:
   `args.push(cmd.priority, options.priority)` at lib/growl.js:216, where
   `cmd.priority` is `{cmd: '-u', range: [...]}`. The notifier receives
   `[object Object]` as an argument.
2. The range check compares a string with the numeric entries of the range, so numeric
   priorities are compared against `undefined`. On Darwin and Windows the documented
   numeric priorities (`growl('m', {priority: 2})`) are silently dropped.
3. `cmd.priority` does not exist for the `Linux-Growl` and `Custom` types, so
   `cmd.priority.range` at lib/growl.js:214 throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties
   of undefined`.

**Evidence:** reproduced by stubbing `os`/`child_process`/`fs` (non-Darwin, no
`growl` binary):

```
growl('m', { priority: 'normal' })
# CMD: "notify-send [object Object] normal \"m\""
growl('m', { priority: 2 })          // Linux named range: dropped silently
growl('hi', { exec: 'echo X %s', priority: 2 })
# TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'range')
```

With a `growl` binary present (`Linux-Growl`, lib/growl.js:74-78) any `priority`
option throws.

**Impact:** a documented option either renders garbage into `notify-send` (which then
shows `[object Object]` as the notification summary instead of the message),
is ignored, or crashes the calling process. Contained to the caller, so severity is
low.

**Fix:** push `cmd.priority.cmd`, guard the block with `if (options.priority &&
cmd.priority)`, and normalise both sides before the range check (compare
`String(entry) === String(priority)`).

findings.title: Untrusted notification text is executed by the shell, allowing command injection
findings.body:
`growl()` builds a shell command by joining arguments and running it with
`child_process.exec`, and escapes user text with `JSON.stringify`. JSON quoting is not
shell quoting: inside the double quotes that `JSON.stringify` produces, `$(...)` and
backticks are still evaluated by `/bin/sh`. Any message, title, subtitle, url, image,
sound or name value that reaches `growl()` runs as a shell command in the caller's
process and with its privileges.

**Preconditions:** the application passes text it does not fully control (a filename,
a chat/CI/build message, a user-supplied title) to `growl()`. That is the normal use of
a notification library.

**Evidence:** reproduced on Linux with a fake `notify-send` on `PATH`:

```
growl('$(touch /tmp/pwn-stamp)', { title: 'hello' })
# executes: notify-send "hello"  "$(touch /tmp/pwn-stamp)"
# -> /tmp/pwn-stamp created
```

A title is equally injectable: `growl('body', { title: '`touch /tmp/pwn-title`' })`
creates the file. The escaping happens at lib/growl.js:12 (`quote = JSON.stringify`),
:192-203, :233-274 and the command runs at lib/growl.js:289 (`exec(args.join(' '))`).
The `Custom` branch inherits the same flaw at lib/growl.js:281-283.

**Impact:** untrusted notification text becomes arbitrary command execution as the
host process (build agent, editor plugin, daemon). This crosses a trust boundary and
gives the attacker a capability they were not granted; nothing supported undoes
executed code, so severity is high.

**Fix:** never involve a shell. Pass the program and its arguments as an array to
`execFile`/`spawn` and drop `quote()` entirely, e.g.
`execFile(cmd.pkg, args, fn)`. For the `Custom` type, split the caller's command on
whitespace and pass the message as a separate argument instead of interpolating it into
a shell string.

findings.title: options.exec overwrites the shared cmd config, changing every later notification in the process
findings.body:
`cmd` is a module-level variable holding the platform's notifier configuration
(lib/growl.js:13, assigned at :25-118). When a caller passes `options.exec`,
lib/growl.js:170-176 overwrites that module-level variable instead of using a local
one, so the custom command sticks for the rest of the process: every later `growl()`
call, with or without `options.exec`, runs the caller's custom command and loses its
title, image, sticky and priority options.

**Evidence:** reproduced with a real `exec`:

```
g('first',  { exec: 'echo CUSTOM %s' })   // CUSTOM first
g('second', {})                           // CUSTOM second   <- expected: notify-send
g('third',  {})                           // CUSTOM third
```

**Impact:** one call with `exec` silently redirects all subsequent notifications in the
library's process to the wrong program, with the message text still routed there. Only
a process restart restores the platform default, so severity is low (contained to the
calling process, recoverable by restart).

**Fix:** build the command config in a function-local variable and leave the shared
`cmd` untouched, e.g. `var cfg = options.exec ? {type:'Custom', pkg: options.exec,
range: []} : cmd;` and use `cfg` throughout `growl()`.

summary:
I reviewed the full diff, verified the upstream lineage of the added file, built the project, and ran the fixture suite.

**What the change does:** it adds `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js` (81 lines). The baseline tree imports this module from `lib/rules_inline/links.js:4` and `lib/rules_core/references.js:3` but ships without the file, so the tree could not build. The added file is byte-identical to upstream remarkable v2.0.0, i.e. the CVE-2019-12043 fix: the bare-destination branch breaks on ASCII control characters (`code < 0x20 || code === 0x7F`, lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js:52) instead of only 0x09–0x0D.

**Verification:**
- `rollup -c` builds `dist/cjs` and `dist/umd` cleanly, so the previously missing module resolves.
- All 118 fixtures under `test/fixtures/remarkable` pass against the built tree (expected HTML == rendered HTML, same comparator as `test/utils.js`).
- Payloads now render as text rather than links: `[x](\u0000javascript:alert(1))`, tab and VT variants, and the reference-definition forms `[r]:\u0000javascript:alert(1)`. Encoded-scheme attempts stay blocked in both branches (`javascript:`, `a`, `:`, `%3A`), and control characters reaching the angle-bracket branch are percent-encoded by `normalizeLink` before validation and rendering, so they cannot form a `javascript:` scheme.

**Assessment:** a small, correct security fix that restores a broken module and closes the control-character XSS path; no regressions found, and I recorded no findings. One non-blocking gap: the PR does not carry upstream's regression fixture for the control-character case in `test/fixtures/remarkable/xss.txt`, so the fix is untested in this tree—a test-only gap, not a defect in the change.

Review complete. Summary:

**What the change does.** PR #1 adds `lib/formats/ssh.js`, the reader/writer for the `ssh-rsa AAAA… comment` public-key text format that `lib/key.js:31` and `lib/formats/auto.js:24-27` already require — without it the package cannot load. The added file is byte-identical (md5 `96b257d…`) to upstream `joyent/node-sshpk` commit `46065d3`, the patch named in GHSA-2m39-62fm-q8r3 / CVE-2018-3737.

**Assessment: approve.** I reproduced the published HackerOne PoC (`'ssh-rsa a' + ' '.repeat(199999) + 'x\nx'`) through `parseKey` and it completes in ~5 ms at 200 KB; the pre-fix regexes (still present in the baseline tree at `4d01aede`) go quadratic on the same input (>6 s at 40 KB, ~4× per doubling), so the change removes the ReDoS rather than adding it. An exhaustive adversarial sweep (thousands of whitespace/`=`/newline/base64-comment shapes, 10 KB→1.6 MB) showed linear time for both `SSHKEY_RE` and `SSHKEY_RE2`, and the fix's own regression cases (key with no comment; comment containing `=` plus trailing newline) parse and round-trip correctly.

`npm test` passes 536/537; the single failure (`test/fingerprint.js:117`, `parseFingerprint('59:a4:…:878')` not throwing) is in `lib/fingerprint.js`, untouched by this change and unrelated to the ssh format. Beyond the CVE I found no defect that this change introduces: the lenient fallback read (`ssh.js:46-58`) and the comment-recovery heuristic (`ssh.js:62-93`) are documented upstream design, behave identically in the pre-fix version, and the only output-side concern (an unsanitized `key.comment` in `write`, `ssh.js:110-111`) needs a caller to supply an untrusted, newline-bearing comment and persist it itself — outside this system, so not filed. No findings recorded.

The PR re-adds `lib/growl.js` as the upstream fix for CVE-2017-16042: it replaces the shell-based `exec(args.join(' '))` with `spawn(cmd, argv)` and drops the `JSON.stringify` quoting. The injection itself is genuinely closed — caller-controlled values (`msg`, `title`, `image`, `url`, …) reach the child as discrete argv elements, never through a shell; I confirmed that per platform branch with stub binaries.

The conversion was done without accounting for what the shell used to do. Under `exec` the joined string lost empty and `undefined` tokens and errors went to the callback; under `spawn` they become real arguments and unhandled events. That produces two medium findings (a missing notifier now aborts the host process, and titled Linux notifications lose their body) and three low ones (callbacks never fire, a literal `"undefined"` argument on `sticky`, and a hang when a notifier writes past the pipe buffer). All were reproduced against the added code with node 24 and stub notifiers.

findings.title: Missing notifier binary aborts the host process instead of reporting an error
findings.body:
`growl()` starts the notifier child process and never listens for `'error'` on it (`spawn(cmd_to_exec, args)` at `lib/growl.js:288`). If the binary is missing — `notify-send` on Linux, `growlnotify` on Windows/macOS, or the `options.exec` path — Node emits `'error'` on a `ChildProcess` with no listener and throws, aborting the caller's process. Before this change the failure went to the callback, so a machine without the optional notifier only lost a notification.

**Preconditions:** the selected notifier binary is not on `PATH` — the default on Linux without `libnotify-bin`, and the norm in containers and CI.

**Evidence:** on Linux with no `notify-send` on `PATH`:

```
$ node -e "require('./lib/growl')('hi')"
Error: spawn notify-send ENOENT
Emitted 'error' event on ChildProcess instance ...
    at ChildProcess._handle.onexit (node:internal/child_process:316:19)
```

The same throw happens for `growl('x', {exec: 'echo hi'})` (`spawn echo hi ENOENT`). Running the repo's `test.js` dies at the first custom-notifier case.

**Impact:** any application that calls `growl()` on a host without the notifier installed is killed by an uncaught exception rather than losing a cosmetic notification. That is a denial of service for every consumer of the library in that environment (`broad` reach, recoverable by installing the binary or upgrading the library), so `medium`.

**Fix:** keep the child handle and attach a handler, e.g. `var child = spawn(cmd_to_exec, args); child.on('error', function (err) { fn(err); });`, so a spawn failure is reported through the existing callback instead of escaping.

findings.title: Notification callbacks are never called
findings.body:
The `fn` argument of `growl(msg, options, fn)` is accepted (`lib/growl.js:167`) but never invoked on the normal path: the result of `spawn()` at `lib/growl.js:288` is discarded, so no `close`, `exit` or `error` event is wired to `fn`. `fn` only runs in the unsupported-platform early return (`lib/growl.js:178`). Every caller that waits for the callback to know a notification was delivered waits forever.

**Evidence:** with a `notify-send` stub on `PATH` so the spawn succeeds:

```
$ PATH=/tmp/fb:$PATH node -e "
    require('./lib/growl')('hi', {}, function (err, out) { console.log('CALLBACK', err, out); });
    setTimeout(function(){ console.log('timeout, still no callback'); }, 500);"
timeout, still no callback
```

`Readme.md` documents the callback and `test.js` passes one, so the documented contract is broken.

**Impact:** callers cannot observe completion or failure; failures become silent (and, per the separate missing-error-handler issue, sometimes fatal). Library-wide, no data loss: `low`.

**Fix:** handle the child to completion and call `fn` once: attach `child.on('error', ...)` and `child.on('close', function (code) { fn(code === 0 ? null : code, out, err); })`, collecting `stdout`/`stderr` if the callback signature is to be honoured.

findings.title: Titled Linux notifications lose their message body
findings.body:
On Linux the `Linux` branch pushes `cmd.msg` between the title and the message (`lib/growl.js:262-265`), and for `notify-send` `cmd.msg` is the empty string (`lib/growl.js:82`). Under the old `exec` the joined command string collapsed the empty token, so `notify-send T  hello` reached the shell as two arguments. `spawn` passes each array element as a separate argument, so the empty string survives and `notify-send` reads it as the body: the summary is the title, the body is empty, and the real message becomes a third positional argument that `notify-send` does not define.

**Preconditions:** Linux host with `libnotify-bin` (the default `Linux` branch) and a `title` option.

**Evidence:** with a `notify-send` on `PATH` that logs its argv:

```
$ node -e "require('./lib/growl')('hello',{title:'T'})"
ARG[T]
ARG[]
ARG[hello]
```

The old behaviour produced `ARG[T]` `ARG[hello]`. `Readme.md` ("Message with title") and `test.js:18` exercise exactly this call.

**Impact:** every titled Linux notification loses its body — the only visible text is the title. It affects all Linux users of the option (broad, recoverable only by a code change): `medium`.

**Fix:** do not push an empty placeholder — only push `options.title` when `cmd.title`/`cmd.msg` is falsy, so the title and message are the two positional arguments `notify-send` expects.

findings.title: "undefined" reaches the notifier's argv when sticky is set
findings.body:
`lib/growl.js:208` pushes `cmd.sticky` whenever `options.sticky` is set, but the `Darwin-NotificationCenter` and `Linux-Growl` command tables have no `sticky` key (`lib/growl.js:27-40`, `67-77`). `spawn` converts `undefined` in the argv array to the literal string `"undefined"` instead of dropping it, so the notifier receives a stray positional argument.

**Preconditions:** `sticky: true` on macOS with `terminal-notifier` installed, or on a Linux host with a `growl` binary on `PATH`. `Readme.md` and `test.js:6` use `growl('5 new messages', { sticky: true })`.

**Evidence:** with faked `os.type()` and a logging `terminal-notifier` stub:

```
$ node -e "var os=require('os'); os.type=function(){return 'Darwin';};
            require('./lib/growl')('5 new messages',{sticky:true})"
ARG[undefined]
ARG[-message]
ARG[5 new messages]
```

`ARG[undefined]` is absent under the old `exec`, where `Array.join` rendered the missing value as nothing and the shell dropped it.

**Impact:** a malformed command line to `terminal-notifier`/`growl`, which the notifier must reject or read as a positional argument; `sticky` has no effect on these two platforms in any case. Sticky output and a specific binary are needed to hit it, so `low`.

**Fix:** guard the push — `if (options.sticky && cmd.sticky) args.push(cmd.sticky);` — so no `undefined` element enters argv.

findings.title: Unread child stdio pipes hang the caller when a notifier writes more than a pipe buffer
findings.body:
The child spawned at `lib/growl.js:288` gets piped stdio by default, and the code never reads `child.stdout` or `child.stderr`. The old `exec` drained both. A notifier that writes more than the pipe buffer (~64 KB) blocks on write forever while the parent waits for the child to exit, so the caller's process hangs.

**Preconditions:** an `exec` command (or notifier) that writes more than roughly 64 KB to stdout or stderr.

**Evidence:** with a stub `exec` command emitting 200 KB:

```
$ node -e "require('./lib/growl')('x',{exec:'/tmp/fb2/bigout'})"
exit=124            # killed by `timeout 10`, process never exits
```

**Impact:** a hang (denial of service) in the caller's process instead of a delivered notification. It needs a user-supplied command that is more verbose than a normal notification, so `low`.

**Fix:** drain the pipes (`child.stdout.resume(); child.stderr.resume();`) or pass `stdio: 'ignore'`, since the output is not used by the module.

summary:
The PR re-adds `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js`, the helper that `lib/rules_inline/links.js` and `lib/rules_core/references.js` import but which the baseline tree lacks, so it restores the Markdown link parser.

The added code is the pre-fix version of the file: line 52 rejects only U+0009–U+000D, so other ASCII control characters reach the `href` of a link, image or reference definition. Because `validateLink` only trims whitespace and the plain destination branch skips `normalizeLink`, a prefixed control character such as U+000E makes `javascript:alert(1)` pass validation and reach the browser, where URL parsing strips leading C0 controls — CVE-2019-12043. I reproduced it against this PR's source and recorded one high finding. The upstream fix is a single-line change to that check plus a regression fixture.

findings.title: Control characters in link destinations bypass validateLink and produce javascript: hrefs
findings.body:
Link destinations containing an ASCII control character are accepted, and the control character is copied into the rendered `href`. Browsers strip leading C0 controls before parsing a URL, so `[x](\x0Ejavascript:alert(1))` renders `x`, which runs `javascript:alert(1)` on click. Any application that renders untrusted Markdown (comment, README, issue body, chat message) gets stored XSS in the viewer's browser. This is the defect described by CVE-2019-12043; the file re-added by this PR is the pre-fix version. **Preconditions:** none beyond the default configuration — the app renders attacker-controlled Markdown with default options. **Evidence:** - `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js:52` breaks only on `code > 0x08 && code < 0x0e`, i.e. U+0009–U+000D. U+0000–U+0008, U+000E–U+001F and U+007F fall through to `pos++` (line 69) and stay inside the destination slice (line 74). - The plain destination branch never calls `normalizeLink`/`encodeURI`; only the `<...>` branch does (line 26). So the control character reaches `href` raw. - `lib/parser_inline.js:157` `validateLink` does `url.trim().toLowerCase()` and compares the text before `:` with `BAD_PROTOCOLS`. `String.prototype.trim` removes only whitespace, not U+000E, so `split(':')[0]` is `"\x0Ejavascript"` and validation passes. - `escapeHtml` (`lib/common/utils.js:111`) escapes only `[&<>"]`, so the control character survives into the attribute. - Reproduced against this PR's source (`npx esbuild lib/index.js --bundle`, then `new Remarkable().render(...)`): ``` [x](javascript:alert(1)) ->

[x](javascript:alert(1))

(rejected) [x](\u000Ejavascript:alert(1)) -> x (bypass) [x](\u0001javascript:alert(1)) -> x (bypass) [x](\u007Fjavascript:alert(1)) -> raw U+007F in href [x](<...>) -> href="%0Ejavascript:..." (encoded, harmless) ``` A scan over U+0000–U+007F shows the exploitable set is U+0001–U+0008 and U+000E–U+001F (U+0000 becomes U+FFFD and U+007F is not stripped by the URL parser). The same path is reachable through reference definitions (`lib/rules_core/references.js:31` calls the same helper) and through images. - Upstream fix (remarkable 2.0.1) replaces line 52 with `if (code < 0x20 || code === 0x7F) { break; }`; `validateLink` is unchanged between the two versions, so this loop is the only mitigation. **Impact:** untrusted Markdown yields HTML that executes attacker script in the reader's origin on click. The attacker crosses a trust boundary and gains script execution in another user's session, permanently for stored content. Severity: high. **Fix:** reject all ASCII control characters in the destination loop, matching the upstream fix: replace line 52 with `if (code < 0x20 || code === 0x7F) { break; }`. Add the regression fixtures from upstream `test/fixtures/remarkable/xss.txt` (`[x](\x0Ejavascript:alert(1))` must render as literal text).

summary:
I verified the change against upstream and empirically tested the pollution vectors.

**What the change is:** PR #1 re-adds `request/util.js` (214 lines) to the dojo tree, byte-identical to dojo's `1.16.2` / `master` version, i.e. the release carrying the CVE-2020-5258 prototype-pollution fix. The load-bearing line is `request/util.js:47` (`name !== '__proto__'` in `deepCopy`).

**Evidence gathered**

- `diff` against upstream `1.16.2` and `master` `request/util.js`: identical; against `1.16.1`/`1.15.2` the only delta is that guard (`tval !== sval` → `name !== '__proto__' && tval !== sval`), which is exactly the security fix.
- Harness run of the shipped `deepCopy`/`deepCreate` (all `has()` flags registered by `request/xhr.js:18-44`, module id `./util` matches `request/xhr.js:5`, so the file loads and is reachable through `xhr`/`node`/`iframe`/`script`): payloads `{"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"}}`, nested `{"a":{"__proto__":…}}`, `{"constructor":{"prototype":…}}`, `{"list":[{"__proto__":…}]}`, and the `deepCreate` path all leave `Object.prototype` clean.
- Same harness with the guard stripped pollutes `Object.prototype` for the `__proto__` payloads, confirming the guard is the mechanism and is present here. (`constructor`/`prototype` was never a global-pollution vector for this code — it lands as an own property on the copy target.)
- No test regression: `tests/unit/request/util.js` exercises `deepCopy` for plain values, `Date`, `FormData`, `Blob`, and `Element`; the `native-*` feature flags it gates on are all registered in `request/xhr.js`.

**Assessment:** the change is the complete, unmodified upstream fix for the CVE. I found no incomplete-fix vector (own-vs-inherited `__proto__`, nested objects, arrays, or the `deepCreate` wrapper) and no other defect in the added lines worth reporting, so I record no findings and recommend approval.

Review complete. Recorded two findings.

**Summary:** The PR adds `bl.js`, the full `bl` BufferList implementation; the content is byte-identical to upstream commit `84e1852`, i.e. the released CVE-2020-8244 fix (`consume()` normalisation at `bl.js:239-242`, plus the "no uninitialized memory" guard at `bl.js:201-202`), while `package.json` and the test suite still sit at the pre-fix 3.0.0 state. I reproduced the CVE-2020-8244 attack (`append('a'); consume(-1024); slice(1)`) against this file and it no longer inflates `length` or exposes allocUnsafe bytes, and the bundled suite passes 753/753. The defects that remain are in the new copy/truncation arithmetic: the guard returns memory `copy()` never filled, and fractional offsets slip past it. Substance is sound, so this is approvable with those two corrections.

findings.title: slice() with fractional offsets returns an uninitialized byte from the allocUnsafe pool
copy() with a destination buffer returns bytes it never wrote

summary:
The PR adds `lib/parser.js`, the regex-based `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header parser that the baseline tree had removed, restoring the package to its 0.1.3 behaviour. The whole file is new code, and the parser is reachable from both documented entry points (`generateResponse` on the server with the client's header, `activate` on the client with the server's header).

The file is the pre-fix variant of CVE-2020-7662: `QUOTED` at lib/parser.js:5 lets a bare backslash match both alternatives, so an unterminated quoted parameter causes exponential backtracking in `EXT_LIST.test` — 45 backslashes block the event loop for 33 seconds, reproduced through `Extensions.generateResponse`. I recorded that as the one finding; the rest of the file (offers bookkeeping, `serializeParams`, numeric coercion) behaves as the upstream 0.1.4 release does, and the existing 79-test suite passes. Aside from the ReDoS I found no change-specific defect worth filing.

findings.title: Unterminated quoted extension parameter causes exponential regex backtracking and blocks the event loop
findings.body:
`Parser.parseHeader` runs a backtracking regex that grows exponentially. A
remote peer that sends a `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` value containing a quoted
parameter with many backslashes and no closing quote blocks the Node event loop
for minutes, stalling every connection the process serves.

**Preconditions:** the normal documented server path — `exts.generateResponse(clientOffer)`
with the client's header (README.md:120-132), or the client path
`exts.activate(serverHeader)` (README.md:89-105). No authentication and no
non-default setting are needed; only one header, ~60 bytes.

**Evidence:** `QUOTED` (lib/parser.js:5) has two overlapping ways to consume a
backslash: `\\[\x00-\x7f]` and the trailing class `[^\x00-\x08\x0a-\x1f\x7f"]*`,
which still matches a bare `\`. With no closing quote, every split of *n*
backslashes between the two alternatives is tried, so `EXT_LIST.test(header)`
(lib/parser.js:18) is exponential in *n*:

    backslashes=20    0.4 ms
    backslashes=30   19.0 ms
    backslashes=35  243.6 ms
    backslashes=40  2676.6 ms
    via Parser.parseHeader: 45 -> 33480 ms

Reproducer (from the repo root):

    node -e 'var E=require("./lib/websocket_extensions");
             var h="permessage-deflate; client_max_window_bits=\"" + "\\".repeat(40);
             var t=Date.now(); try{ new E().generateResponse(h) }catch(e){}
             console.log(Date.now()-t)'

The backslash is a legal `quoted-string` character in RFC 7230, so the value is
well-formed input up to the missing quote, and it is attacker-supplied.

**Impact:** any unauthenticated client that can open a WebSocket handshake can
hold the process's single thread for an unbounded time (each extra backslash
multiplies the cost by ~10). Reach is broad — the whole server stalls for
everyone it serves — and the stall is re-triggerable at will, so a running
service is effectively down until restarted. This is the denial-of-service issue
fixed in websocket-extensions 0.1.4.

**Fix:** remove the ambiguity: exclude backslash from the second alternative so
only the escaped-pair branch can consume it —
`QUOTED = /"((?:\\[\x00-\x7f]|[^\x00-\x08\x0a-\x1f\x7f"\\])*)"/` (lib/parser.js:5),
matching the 0.1.4 release.

summary: **Summary.** The PR restores `bl.js` (382 lines, `bl` v3.0.0) to a repo whose baseline omitted it. The file is byte-identical to upstream `bl.js` immediately before rvagg/bl's "Fix uninitialized memory access" commit, so it re-adds CVE-2020-8244: `consume()` does unchecked arithmetic on `this.length`, and the resulting desync makes `slice()`/`copy()`/`_read()` return `allocUnsafe`/`Buffer.concat` padding that was never written — I reproduced disclosure of freed heap contents and the `NaN`/fractional/`Infinity` state corruption that follows. The shipped test suites (`test/test.js`, `test/indexOf.js`) still pass, because the regression test for this bug only exists in the fixed upstream tree. One medium finding recorded; the other edge-case quirks I probed (leading zero-length buffer breaking `indexOf`, `end()` callback handling, `shallowSlice(start > end)`) are long-standing upstream behaviours rather than part of this change's intent, so I did not file them.

findings.title: Negative consume() inflates length and leaks uninitialized heap memory through slice()
findings.body:
`consume()` accepts any number without validation. A negative value makes it *add*
to `this.length` instead of subtracting (`bl.js:242`), so the list claims more bytes
than it holds. The next `slice()`/`copy()`/`toString()` then hands back a buffer
padded with uninitialized heap memory (`bl.js:181`, `bl.js:157-161`, loop
`bl.js:183-198` runs out of buffers before filling `dst`), and a leftover tail of
`dst` is never written or truncated (`bl.js:200`). This is CVE-2020-8244; the file
re-added here is byte-identical to upstream `bl.js` immediately before upstream's
"Fix uninitialized memory access" commit.

**Preconditions:** the embedding application passes a value derived from untrusted
input into `consume()` and that value can come out negative, zero-length-cheaply
(e.g. `bl.consume(offset - bl.length)`), or `NaN`/fractional. The library's own
stream path only passes positive integers, so plain `pipe()`/`write()` use is not
enough on its own.

**Evidence:**

```
const BufferList = require('./bl.js')
const bl = new BufferList()
bl.append(Buffer.from('a'))
bl.consume(-1024)          // bl.js:234-247
bl.length                  // 1025, real content 0 bytes
bl.slice(1).length         // 1024 uninitialized bytes
```

Leaking live memory (Node 24, marker written into freed 64 KiB buffers first):

```
$ node --expose-gc /tmp/poc2.js
iter 0 len 65535 nonzero 445 secretAt 64
LEAK: SECRETMARKER1
```

State corruption follows the same root cause: `consume(NaN)` sets `this.length` to
`NaN` and `consume(1.5)` to `4.5`, after which every read throws
`RangeError: The value of "size"/"length" is out of range`; `consume(-Infinity)`
sets `length` to `Infinity`. `bl.js:99-106` `_read()` also pushes `slice(0, size)`
of the inflated length, so the stream emits the garbage bytes downstream and then
leaves `length > 0` with `_bufs` empty.

**Impact:** process heap contents (tokens, request bodies, other tenants' data in a
shared process) are returned to whoever receives the slice/`toString()`/stream
output — a trust-boundary crossing whose damage cannot be undone. Severity is
`medium` rather than `high` because it needs the caller to feed a non-positive or
non-integer value into `consume()`; the library itself never does.

**Fix:** restore the invariant `this.length === sum(_bufs[i].length)`. Normalize the
argument at the top of `consume()` — `bytes = Math.trunc(bytes)` and
`if (Number.isNaN(bytes) || bytes <= 0) return this` — and, as a second safeguard,
`copy()` should return `dst.slice(0, bufoff)` when `dst.length > bufoff` instead of
the full unwritten buffer (also move `bufoff += l` before the `break`). This is
exactly upstream's fix for CVE-2020-8244.

summary:
The PR adds `request/util.js` (214 lines, identical to upstream dojo at the baseline commit), restoring the helper module used by every request transport (`deepCopy`, `deepCreate`, `deferred`, `parseArgs`, `checkStatus`, and the `is*` helpers). Compared with dojo 1.16.2 the file differs in exactly one line: the copy loop lacks the `name !== '__proto__'` guard.

That missing guard is CVE-2020-5258. I reproduced it against the module in this tree: `deepCopy({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}'))` and the nested and `deepCreate` variants all write attacker keys onto `Object.prototype`, and all four transports (`xhr.js:203`, `node.js:23`, `iframe.js:349`, `script.js:124`) feed request options into that path unchecked. One medium finding is recorded with the one-line fix and the upstream regression test.

The rest of the file matches shipped upstream code; I probed the other helpers (`deepCopyArray`, `isElement`, `parseArgs`, `deferred`, `checkStatus`) and found no defect that is both new to this change and materially wrong in normal use, so nothing else is reported. Overall the change is a faithful re-add of the module except for the security bug, which should be fixed before merge.

findings.title: deepCopy in request/util.js pollutes Object.prototype via a __proto__ key (CVE-2020-5258)
findings.body:
`request/util.js` `deepCopy` (added by this PR) writes attacker-chosen keys onto
`Object.prototype` when the source object carries a `"__proto__"` key. Any code that
passes an object built from parsed JSON as `options` to `dojo/request`, `dojo/request/xhr`,
`dojo/request/node`, `dojo/request/script` or `dojo/request/iframe` is a sink; the
polluted key is then visible to every object in the page or Node process. This is
CVE-2020-5258.

**Evidence**

`request/util.js:43-66`:

```js
exports.deepCopy = function(target, source) {
    for (var name in source) {          // :44  "__proto__" from JSON.parse is an own enumerable key
        var tval = target[name],        // :45  target.__proto__ === Object.prototype for a plain target
            sval = source[name];
        if (tval !== sval) {            // :47  upstream fix adds: name !== '__proto__' &&
            ...
            if (tval && typeof tval === 'object') {
                exports.deepCopy(tval, sval);   // :55  recurses with target === Object.prototype
```

`exports.deepCreate` (`:82`) ends in `exports.deepCopy(target, properties)` (`:94`), so
the same sink is reached through the option-copy path used by every transport:
`request/xhr.js:203`, `request/node.js:23`, `request/iframe.js:349`, and directly by
`request/script.js:124` (`util.deepCopy({}, options)`).

Reproduced against the module in this tree (same-realm AMD shim loading the repo files):

```
$ node repro.js
top: 1        # util.deepCopy({}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"top":1}}')) -> ({}).top
hdrA: 1       # util.deepCopy({}, JSON.parse('{"headers":{"X":{"__proto__":{"hdrA":1}}}}'))
hdrD: 1       # util.deepCreate({headers:null}, ...same nested payload) -> xhr/node path
```

The upstream fix is exactly one line, dojo 1.16.2 `request/util.js:47`:
`if (name !== '__proto__' && tval !== sval) {`. Diffing this file against dojo 1.16.2
shows no other difference. Upstream also added the regression test
`.deepCopy should ignore the __proto__ property` in `tests/unit/request/util.js`;
this tree's test file has no `__proto__` case.

**Preconditions:** application code passes an object derived from untrusted input (e.g.
`JSON.parse` of a request body, query or config value) as the `options` argument of a
dojo request. Nothing inside the library sanitises that object.

**Impact:** the attacker controls keys added to `Object.prototype` for the lifetime of
the page or Node process, which is broad reach with a recoverable outcome (a reload or
restart clears it, the attacker can retrigger it at will), and the trigger needs the
application to forward untrusted data as request options, so `medium`. In a Node
service this is shared state across all requests the process serves.

**Fix:** skip the `__proto__` key in the copy loop, as upstream does:
`if (name !== '__proto__' && tval !== sval) {` at `request/util.js:47`, plus the
upstream regression test in `tests/unit/request/util.js`.

summary:
Review complete. No findings recorded.

**What the change does:** it re-adds `lib/pdfinfo.js`, the child-process wrapper behind `index.js`. The wrapper now spawns `pdfinfo` with `execFile`/`execFileSync` and an argv array (`lib/pdfinfo.js:26`, `lib/pdfinfo.js:36`) instead of building a shell string, and the filename is stored raw (`lib/pdfinfo.js:6`) rather than quote-wrapped.

**Verification:** I ran the wrapper against a spy `pdfinfo` on `PATH` with a filename containing `; touch …; echo $(id)` and backticks. The whole payload arrived as one argv element, no shell ran, and the marker file was never created. A repo-wide grep finds no `exec`, `execSync`, `spawn`, or `shell: true` anywhere else, so no shell-injection path remains, and the file matches the upstream fix commit (`5cc59cd`) byte for byte.

**Assessment:** the change is the correct minimal fix for CVE-2018-3746 and I'd approve it. Residual nits in the new file stay below threshold and I did not file them: `getInfoSync` throws with `err.msg` (nonexistent, so the message is `undefined`) and `getInfo` passes `self.options.addtional` (typo, so the third callback argument is `undefined` only on errors), plus a per-error `console.info` claiming poppler-utils is missing. Those cost diagnostics, not data or capability — a caller discarding an error's detail can retry and see it again, so they grade below `info`. Loop bounds in the untouched `lib/utils.js:19` drop pdfinfo's last output line (`PDF version`); that is pre-existing code the diff does not modify.

PR #2 adds the whole `lib/pdfinfo.js` module (66 lines) that `index.js` already required: a `pdfinfo` wrapper with `add_options`, `getInfo`, and `getInfoSync`. The design pastes the filename and options into a single string run by `/bin/sh`, which I reproduced as arbitrary command execution via `$( )`, backticks, or a stray quote — even with the binary absent. Several smaller defects sit in the same error-handling code: a misspelled `additional` drops the documented third callback argument on failure, `err.msg` erases the real cause in the sync path, and the `error()`/`success()` setters register handlers nothing calls. The change should not merge as written; switching to `execFile`/`spawn` with an argv array fixes the security issue and is a small, contained edit.

findings.title: Filename interpolation into a shell command allows arbitrary command execution
findings.body:
Filenames passed to the constructor are pasted into a shell command line, so any
character the shell interprets runs on the host.

The constructor stores `'"' + filename + '"'` (lib/pdfinfo.js:6) and both query
paths join it into a single string handed to `child_process`: `execSync('pdfinfo ' +
...)` at lib/pdfinfo.js:26 and `exec('pdfinfo ' + ...)` at lib/pdfinfo.js:36. Both
run the string through `/bin/sh`. Double quotes do not stop command substitution or
backticks, so no quote-breaking is even needed.

**Evidence:** against this checkout, with the pdfinfo binary absent:

```
const pdfinfo = require('./lib/pdfinfo.js');
new pdfinfo('/tmp/$(touch /tmp/pwned_sub).pdf').getInfoSync();   // /tmp/pwned_sub created
new pdfinfo('/tmp/`touch /tmp/pwned_bt`.pdf').getInfoSync();     // /tmp/pwned_bt created
new pdfinfo('/tmp/x.pdf"; touch /tmp/pwned_async; echo "')
  .getInfo(function () {});                                      // /tmp/pwned_async created
```

`add_options` routes into the same join (lib/pdfinfo.js:14,16), so an option string
may also contribute shell tokens.

**Impact:** high. Any party who controls a path handed to this library — the normal
case for a metadata extractor reading user-supplied or uploaded files — gets
arbitrary command execution as the Node process. That crosses a trust boundary and
the effect is permanent (files moved or destroyed, secrets read). Separately, a
filename containing whitespace-separated flags is reinterpreted as pdfinfo options.

**Fix:** stop using a shell. Call `execFile`/`spawn`/`execFileSync('pdfinfo',
[...args, filename])` with the filename as one argv element, and pass options as
separate argv entries. Quoting or escaping the filename is not sufficient.

findings.title: Error callback receives undefined params because of the addtional typo
findings.body:
The error branch of `getInfo` passes `undefined` as the third callback argument
instead of the command arguments the README documents.

lib/pdfinfo.js:46 reads `self.options.addtional` (misspelled). The property set in
the constructor is `additional` (lib/pdfinfo.js:6), so the expression is always
`undefined`. The success branch at lib/pdfinfo.js:40 uses the correct name, so the
argument is present on success and missing on failure.

**Evidence:** with `pdfinfo` absent, `new pdfinfo('/tmp/missing.pdf').getInfo(cb)`
invokes `cb` with arguments `(Error, null, undefined)`; setting
`options.additional` before the call does not change that.

**Impact:** low. Consumers that inspect the third argument on the error path — to
log the command that failed, per README "commandline params passed to pdfinfo cmd" —
get `undefined` and throw on `.length`/`.join`, masking the original error. Reach is
contained to callers of this library and a supported retry reproduces it.

**Fix:** spell it `self.options.additional`.

findings.title: getInfoSync failures surface as 'pdfinfo error: undefined'
findings.body:
`getInfoSync` reports every failure as `pdfinfo error: undefined`, discarding the
actual cause.

lib/pdfinfo.js:29 rethrows `new Error("pdfinfo error: " + err.msg)`, but Node error
objects have no `msg` property; the message is `err.message`, and for `execSync`
failures the useful data sits on `err.stderr`, `err.stdout` and `err.status`.

**Evidence:** `new pdfinfo('/tmp/missing.pdf').getInfoSync()` throws
`Error: pdfinfo error: undefined`, even though the child's stderr is
`/bin/sh: 1: pdfinfo: not found`.

**Impact:** info. No data is corrupted, but callers cannot tell a missing binary
(exit 127) from an unreadable or corrupt PDF (exit 1), and the async path at
lib/pdfinfo.js:46 at least forwards `stderr`. Reach is contained to the caller of
the sync API.

**Fix:** include `err.message` and `err.stderr` (or rethrow `err` unchanged) so the
failure cause survives.

findings.title: error() and success() register callbacks that are never invoked
findings.body:
`error()` and `success()` store callbacks that no code path ever invokes, so
chaining them silently has no effect.

lib/pdfinfo.js:52-60 assign `this.options.error` and `this.options.success` and
return `this`, but `getInfo` (lib/pdfinfo.js:34-50) and `getInfoSync`
(lib/pdfinfo.js:23-31) never read either property. Failures in `getInfo` are only
written to stdout via `console.info` (lib/pdfinfo.js:44).

**Evidence:** `new pdfinfo('/tmp/missing.pdf').error(function () {
console.log('handled'); }).getInfo()` never logs; only the install hint is printed.
The chain does not throw, so the caller believes a handler is registered.

**Impact:** info. A caller that registers an error handler and omits the `getInfo`
callback cannot detect failure at all, but the supported `cb(err, ...)` form works
and the new module is not yet in a release.

**Fix:** invoke `this.options.success` / `this.options.error` from the corresponding
branches of `getInfo`, or delete the two methods so the API does not promise
behavior it lacks.

summary:
The change adds `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts`, TinyMCE's SAX HTML parser, at the 4.9.9 state — the version released before the security fix in 4.9.10. I compiled and ran the added file against the real `Schema`/`DomParser`/`Serializer` modules and against an HTML parser to check behavior end to end, and compared it with the upstream 4.9.10 file and the 5.x rewrite to see which hardening is missing here.

The parser is otherwise faithful and consistent with its call sites, but the CDATA sanitization step is the pre-fix implementation, so I filed one high-severity finding for it (details recorded). I did not file the other leads the sweep raised (`data-mce-type` bypassing attribute validation, `constructor` key lookups, duplicate attributes) — they are long-standing upstream design in every later version and not regressions this change introduces.

findings.title: Crafted CDATA content escapes the comment wrapper and runs script
findings.body: Crafted CDATA content keeps an intact `-->` after sanitization, so it closes the comment that the editor wraps it in and the remaining markup becomes live HTML. Any HTML that reaches the editor's parser (initial content, `setContent`, HTML paste) can therefore run script in the editor page's origin. `trimComments` (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:59-61`) strips `` with a single `replace`.
