summary:
Review complete.

The PR adds one file, `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts` (538 lines) — the pure-JS HTML SAX parser that `DomParser`, `Serializer`, the media plugin and `TrimHtml` depend on. The added content is byte-identical to upstream TinyMCE 4.9.10, i.e. release code that contains the CDATA `trimComments` loop from the CVE-2019-1010091 fix; the rest of the tree here is 4.9.9.

I verified the parser's behaviour by bundling `DomParser`/`Serializer`/`Schema` with esbuild and running payloads through them, and checked the comment/CDATA/attribute paths in `Writer`, `InitContentBody` and `DomSerializerFilters`. Three issues are recorded: a CDATA sanitizer bypass that survives `getContent()`, an attribute-whitelist bypass via `data-mce-type`, and a parser crash on an element named `constructor`.

Scope note, not filed: the media-plugin half of the same upstream security release (`src/plugins/media/main/ts/core/Sanitize.ts`, `HtmlToData.ts`, `UpdateHtml.ts`) is untouched in this tree, so this change alone does not bring the repository up to the 4.9.10 security baseline.

findings.title: CDATA body is re-emitted unescaped, so a leading > escapes the comment and renders live attacker HTML
findings.body: A ``, so anything the body places after a `>` becomes live markup. Because the CDATA body never becomes a node, it is never subject to schema or attribute filtering (`on*` stripping, URL checks), which makes it a sanitizer bypass: content that is inert inside the editor executes script in the page that renders `getContent()` output. **Preconditions:** attacker-controlled HTML reaches the editor (paste, or `setContent` via an API/CMS path with untrusted content) and the stored editor output is later rendered as HTML — the same threat model as CVE-2019-1010091. **Evidence:** - `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:503-504` sends the CDATA body to `cdata()`; `trimComments` (`:59-65`) strips only `` and `--!>`, so a bare `>` survives. - `src/core/main/ts/api/html/DomParser.ts:433-435` stores it as a `#cdata` node; `src/core/main/ts/init/InitContentBody.ts:97-106` parks it in the editor DOM as the inert comment ``; `src/core/main/ts/dom/DomSerializerFilters.ts:139-148` converts that comment back to `#cdata` on output; `src/core/main/ts/api/html/Serializer.ts:63-65` → `src/core/main/ts/api/html/Writer.ts:128-129` writes `` with no escaping. - Round trip through this tree (`DomParser({validate: true})` → `Serializer({validate: true})`): `]]>` comes back byte-identical. The comment-token payloads are handled correctly — `]]>` comes back inert, so the `trimComments` fix works for its case. - Browser parsing (jsdom, same tokenizer rules): `body.innerHTML = ']]>'` yields one live `img` element with `onerror="alert(1)"`. The trimming step can also turn inert input into live input: `

findings.title: An element named constructor throws a TypeError and aborts parsing
findings.body:
Element named `constructor` makes the parser throw. `specialElements` / `shortEndedElements` are plain objects created by `Tools.makeMap`, so the lookup at `SaxParser.ts:458` resolves `constructor` to `Object.prototype.constructor`. That value is truthy, so the code treats it as the special-element end-tag regexp and calls `.exec` on a function, aborting `parse()` with `TypeError: endRegExp.exec is not a function`.

**Evidence:** with this tree, `SaxParser({ validate: true }).parse('<constructor>x</constructor>')` throws that TypeError; the throw escapes `DomParser.parse`, so `setContent`/paste of such markup fails and the content is lost. Same class of lookup exists at `:327` (`value in shortEndedElements`) and `:330`.

**Impact:** a sandboxed-correctness failure on attacker-supplied or accidental markup (content loss / editor error), not script execution. Contained to the single parse and recoverable by retrying with different content.

**Fix:** consult the schema maps with own-property semantics (`Obj.has` / `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`) instead of property access on plain objects.

findings.title: data-mce-type on attacker content skips attribute validation, so srcdoc survives into the editor page
findings.body:
Any element carrying a `data-mce-type` attribute is treated as editor-internal (`SaxParser.ts:358`), and for such elements the whole schema attribute whitelist is skipped (`:210`, `if (validate && !isInternalElement && …)`). Only `on*` names and the URL attributes listed in `filteredUrlAttrs` (`:172`) are still filtered (`:262`). An attacker who controls the inserted HTML can therefore pick any other attribute — `srcdoc` is the dangerous one — and it reaches the output untouched, even with `validate: true`.

**Evidence:** with this tree, `DomParser({validate: true})` → `Serializer({validate: true})`:
- `<iframe srcdoc="<script>alert(1)</script>"></iframe>` → `<iframe></iframe>` (stripped, as intended)
- `<iframe data-mce-type="x" srcdoc="<script>alert(1)</script>"></iframe>` → unchanged, `srcdoc` preserved.
`data-mce-type` itself always passes (`:55-57`, `data-` prefix) and `DomParser.ts:425-434` never forwards `remove_internals`, so the element is not removed either. `InitContentBody.ts:45` builds the editor parser from `editor.settings`, which leaves `isInternalElement` active for content coming from paste or `setContent`.

**Impact:** an iframe `srcdoc` document runs in the embedding page's origin, so content inserted into the editor can execute script in the editor/CMS page (and persists in saved output) — the sanitizer that is supposed to strip such markup never sees it. Scored medium rather than high because the bypass is demonstrated at the parser/serializer level and the final execution step rests on standard `srcdoc` semantics, which I could not exercise in a real browser here.

**Fix:** don't let untrusted `data-mce-type` widen the allow-list. Either filter `data-mce-*` attributes out of parsed input (they are editor-generated markers, not author content), or keep applying the schema/attribute denylist while skipping only the editor's own bookkeeping attributes.

summary:
The change adds `lib/parser.js`, byte-identical to `websocket-extensions@0.1.4` — it is the CVE-2020-7662 fix, differing from 0.1.3 only by dropping `\` from `QUOTED`'s ordinary-character class (`lib/parser.js:5`). I reproduced the vulnerability on 0.1.3 (`'a; b="' + '\\'.repeat(40)` took 2.5 s and grew ~4× per four bytes) and confirmed the new regex is linear (0.9 ms at 100 000 backslashes); a fuzz sweep across all four regexes and 42 adversarial input families found no remaining super-linear matching, and the shipped suite passes 79/79.

The three findings are in the new file's serializer and duplicate-parameter handling, not in the fix itself. The stateful `NOTOKEN` regex makes header output depend on earlier calls in the same process and can emit unquoted values that split into extra offers; backslashes and empty strings do not survive a serialize/parse round trip; and duplicate parameter names make `parseHeader` quadratic. Only the last is on attacker-supplied input, and header size limits keep it at info. Overall the fix is correct and complete for the CVE.

findings.title: Global NOTOKEN regex leaks lastIndex, so serializeParams emits unquoted values and can inject offers
findings.body:
`Parser.serializeParams` can emit an unquoted parameter value that contains `,` or `;`, so the header it produces is invalid or splits into extra extension offers. The cause is the module-level `NOTOKEN` regex, declared with the `g` flag (lib/parser.js:4) but used with `.test()` (lib/parser.js:63). `test()` on a global regex keeps `lastIndex` between calls, so the quote decision depends on the previous value that was serialized.

**Evidence:**
- Two serializations in one process alternate: `Parser.serializeParams('a', {k: 'p q'})` returns `a; k="p q"` on the first call and `a; k=p q` on the second.
- `Extensions.generateOffer()` (lib/websocket_extensions.js:50) shows it end to end: three successive calls for an extension whose session returns `{note: 'hello world'}` give `deflate; note="hello world"`, then `deflate; note=hello world`, then back to the quoted form. The unquoted form is rejected by `parseHeader`, and `Extensions.activate()` throws `SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header`.
- Injection: after one call that leaves `NOTOKEN.lastIndex === 2`, `Parser.serializeParams('deflate', {b: 'a,b'})` returns `deflate; b=a,b`, which reparses as two offers: `[{deflate,{b:'a'}},{b,{}}]`.

**Impact:** low. The library sends a malformed or differently-shaped `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header depending on unrelated earlier calls in the same process; a strict peer fails the handshake. A parameter value can also become an extra offer on the wire. It stays low because the values come from extension code rather than free-form peer input, and the failure is per-handshake and recoverable.

**Fix:** make the regex stateless where it is tested. Drop the `g` flag from `NOTOKEN` (it is only used with `.test`), or use `/[^…]/.test(value)` created inside `serializeParams`.

findings.title: Backslash and empty-string param values do not round-trip through serializeParams and parseHeader
findings.body:
Quoted parameter values do not survive a serialize/parse round trip: `serializeParams` escapes `"` but not `\` (lib/parser.js:64), while `parseHeader` deletes every backslash instead of unescaping pairs (lib/parser.js:34). Empty-string values get a related failure: `NOTOKEN.test('')` is false, so the value is written unquoted as `key=`.

**Evidence:**
- Value ending in a backslash: `Parser.serializeParams('a', {b: 'a\\'})` returns `a; b="a\"`. Feeding that back to `Parser.parseHeader` throws `SyntaxError: Invalid Sec-WebSocket-Extensions header: a; b="a\"`, because the trailing backslash escapes the closing quote.
- Value with an interior backslash: `Parser.serializeParams('a', {b: 'a\\\\b'})` gives `a; b="a\\b"`, which reparses as `{b: 'ab'}` — both backslashes are dropped by lib/parser.js:34. Escape sequences that arrive from the peer are destroyed the same way: `parseHeader('a; b="c:\\\\dir"')` yields `c:dir`.
- Empty string: `Parser.serializeParams('a', {b: ''})` returns `a; b=`, which `parseHeader` rejects as a syntax error (lib/parser.js:6, 18).

**Impact:** low. Any extension parameter whose value contains a backslash produces either a header the peer (or this library's own parser) rejects, breaking the handshake, or a silently altered value after a round trip. `serializeParams` output is used directly as the wire header in `generateOffer` (lib/websocket_extensions.js:50) and `generateResponse` (lib/websocket_extensions.js:105).

**Fix:** make the two directions inverse. Escape `\` before `"` on output (`value.replace(/\\/g, '\\\\').replace(/"/g, '\\"')`), unescape with `/\\\\(.)/g` on input rather than deleting backslashes, and treat the empty string like any other non-token value so it is emitted as `""`.

findings.title: parseHeader copies the parameter array per duplicate name, making parsing quadratic in header size
findings.body:
`parseHeader` is quadratic in the number of parameters that share a name, so a large `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header costs far more CPU than its size suggests. Each duplicate assigns `offer[key] = [].concat(offer[key])` and then pushes (lib/parser.js:40-43), copying the whole accumulated array once per duplicate. The regexes are not involved; the cost is the array copy.

**Evidence:** `Parser.parseHeader('a' + ';x="q"'.repeat(n))`
- n=4000 (24 KB): 24.6 ms, n=8000 (48 KB): 81.7 ms, n=16000 (96 KB): 809 ms, n=32000 (192 KB): 6584 ms.
- Control with unique parameter names at the same sizes: 4.7 / 11.3 / 21.1 / 37.4 ms, i.e. linear.

The input reaches this code from the peer: `Extensions.generateResponse(header)` parses the client's header (lib/websocket_extensions.js:94) and `activate` parses the server's (lib/websocket_extensions.js:61).

**Impact:** info. The header is attacker-supplied and unauthenticated, but an HTTP header size limit bounds the payload: at Node's default 16 KB cap (n≈2700) the parse costs about 10 ms, which is a few times the linear baseline rather than a denial of service. Reaching the hundred-millisecond-to-second range needs a raised `maxHeaderSize` or a transport that does not cap header length. The path is also unchanged from upstream 0.1.3, so this PR neither introduces nor fixes it.

**Fix:** append to the existing array instead of copying it — `if (hasOwnProperty.call(offer, key)) offer[key].push(data); else offer[key] = [data]` — keeping the "single value or array" shape while making the cost linear.

summary:
I've completed the review of the change (one 141-line file, fully read; the injected-vs-escaped behavior verified against real jQuery 3.3.1 + jsdom, and the plugin's DOM hooks — `$control` `.items`/`.dropdown-active`, `$dropdown_content` — verified against the selectize 0.12.4 build its example page loads). **Summary:** The PR re-adds `selectize-plugin-a11y.js`, a Selectize.js accessibility plugin that injects combobox/listbox ARIA attributes and announces the active option through a hidden live region. The live-region sink here is the *patched* form — `$container.text(msg)` then `$region.html($container)` (lines 28–30) — so CVE-2019-15482's XSS (upstream 1.0.4's `$('
' + msg + '
')`) is not present; I confirmed markup in the option text renders as escaped text, not as an element. The change is otherwise faithful to upstream 1.1.0 and its required hooks exist in the Selectize version the example uses. I recorded one `info` correctness note (the `haspopup` attribute name), which has no security impact; I found no exploitable or otherwise material defect in the added code.

findings.title: Combobox popup attribute set as haspopup, not aria-haspopup
findings.body:
`setup()` writes the popup attribute as `haspopup` instead of `aria-haspopup`, so the
combobox never advertises that it owns a popup. Assistive technology sees a
combobox with `aria-expanded` but no popup type, which is the one semantic the
plugin exists to provide.

**Evidence:** `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:116`-`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:124` sets the
attribute map on `self.$control_input`; line 119 is `haspopup: "listbox"`. jQuery
passes the key through verbatim, so the DOM ends up with `haspopup="listbox"` and no
`aria-haspopup` attribute. Nothing else in the file sets `aria-haspopup`.

**Impact:** Only an accessibility correctness defect: screen readers do not announce
"has popup, listbox". No security consequence and no effect on mouse or
keyboard use.

**Fix:** Rename the key to `"aria-haspopup": "listbox"` in the `attr` object at
line 119.

summary:
Tests pass (57/57) and lint is clean, so the change restores the missing module without breaking documented behavior.

**What the change does:** adds `lib/reduce_object.js`, the reducer that `adapters/object.js:1` and `extra/functions_clone.js:2` / `extra/functions_extend.js:2` already require — at the parent commit the package could not load at all because this file was absent.

**Assessment:** the implementation is a straightforward `Object.keys().reduce()` copier, but it introduces no guard for unsafe keys. I reproduced prototype pollution through both the `mutable` and default `immutable` entry points, including via nested keys, and recorded it as one high finding; that is the only issue in the diff.

findings.title: Merging JSON with a __proto__ key pollutes Object.prototype for the whole process
findings.body:
`lib/reduce_object.js` assigns every own key of `source` onto the accumulated
target without filtering `__proto__`, so merging attacker-controlled JSON
writes into `Object.prototype` and every object in the process inherits the
injected properties.

**Preconditions:** the host app passes data an attacker controls (request body,
config file, deserialized message) to `deeply`/`deeply.mutable` — the library's
documented use. Default flags, no special configuration.

**Evidence:** `Object.keys(source)` returns `__proto__` for `JSON.parse`'d
input, and `acc[key] = merge(acc[key], source[key])` at
`lib/reduce_object.js:19` then reads `acc.__proto__` (the target's prototype),
merges into it, and writes back:

```
$ node -e "var d=require('./index.js');
  d.mutable({}, JSON.parse('{\"__proto__\":{\"polluted\":\"yes\"}}'));
  console.log(({}).polluted)"
yes
```

The default (`immutable`) export is affected too, as are nested keys
(`{"a":{"__proto__":{...}}}`). After the call `Object.keys(Object.prototype)`
contains the injected key, and later merges and every fresh object carry it.
Note the repository at the parent commit could not load at all
(`adapters/object.js:1` requires the missing file), so this commit is what
makes the merge path reachable.

**Impact:** Prototype pollution of the whole process from merged input. In a
server that merges per-request JSON, one request sets properties on every
object created afterwards — the usual escalation is bypassing authorization
checks or reaching RCE through a gadget in another dependency. Reach: the
pollution crosses from attacker-supplied data into global state shared by all
requests. Persistence: until the process restarts, and the attacker can
re-trigger it at will. Hence high.

**Fix:** restore the invariant that only own, non-prototype keys are copied:
skip `__proto__` (and, defensively, `constructor`/`prototype`) inside the
reducer before assigning, e.g.
`if (key === '__proto__') { return acc; }` at the top of the callback, or
assign through `Object.defineProperty` instead of `acc[key] = ...`. Upstream
3.1.0 does exactly this in `isUnsafeKey()`.

summary:
The PR re-adds `xmpp/util.js` (147 lines) to the dojox tree — the XMPP helper module with `xmlEncode`, `encodeJid`/`decodeJid`, `createElement`, `stripHtml`/`decodeHtmlEntities`/`htmlToPlain` and Base64 wrappers. I checked the file against upstream history: it is the pre-fix revision, and the one confirmed defect is that `xmlEncode` escapes only the first occurrence of each XML metacharacter, which reproduces deterministically and feeds unescaped values into stanza attributes built by `createElement`.

Other candidates in the file (no attribute escaping in `createElement`, `stripHtml`'s regex gaps, `decodeJid`'s incomplete escape table, the unused `htmlToPlain`) lack a reachable production path in this tree or need a cooperating server, so I left them unreported.

findings.title: xmlEncode escapes only the first occurrence of each XML metacharacter
findings.body:
`dojox.xmpp.util.xmlEncode` replaces only the first occurrence of each of `& > < ' "`, so its output is not XML-safe. Any value with two or more special characters keeps the extra ones raw. Both callers use the result as an attribute value in an outbound XMPP stanza, so attacker-influenced text can break out of the attribute or the element.

**Evidence:**

- `xmpp/util.js:6-8` chains `String.prototype.replace` with string patterns, which each replace one leftmost match:
  `.replace("&", "&").replace(">", ">").replace("<", "<").replace("'", "'").replace('"', """)`.
- Reproduction (function extracted and run under Node):
  - `"a&b&c"` → `"a&b&c"`
  - `""><script>alert(1)</script>"` → `""><script>alert(1)</script>"` (raw `<` and `>` survive)
  - `"Tom & Jerry <3 <3"` → `"Tom & Jerry <3 <3"`
- The only callers feed the result straight into an unescaped attribute value (`xmpp/util.js:85-88` appends `attr + '="' + attributes[attr] + '" '`, no encoding): `xmpp/RosterService.js:33` and `xmpp/RosterService.js:78` both put it in `{name: xmlEncode(...)}`.
- The value is attacker-influenced: `xmpp/xmppSession.js:405` copies the `name` attribute of an inbound roster-push `<item>` into `this.session.roster[x].name`, and `xmpp/RosterService.js:74-80` re-encodes and re-sends that stored name with `xmlEncode`.

**Impact:** A remote XMPP peer that controls a roster item name (or any application data reaching these calls) can keep a second `"` or `<` raw. The `"` closes the `name="…"` attribute early and the `<` breaks element well-formedness, letting the attacker inject attributes or elements into the stanza the victim's client sends under its own credentials. Values that later reach an HTML renderer — the shipped widget renders roster-derived names and message bodies with `innerHTML` at `xmpp/widget/ChatSession.js:24` — become script. This is the defect CVE-2019-10785 was filed for; upstream fixed exactly this line in dojo/dojox commit `6eb27835` ("fixes potential xss by properly encoding xml") by replacing it with a global regex, and then with `dojo.string.escape`. Severity is `medium`: the escaping failure itself is deterministic and reachable, but turning it into script execution needs a consumer that renders the value as HTML, which is outside this library.

**Fix:** Restore the invariant "every occurrence of every XML metacharacter is escaped". Replace the five single-shot replaces with one global pass, e.g. `return dojo.string.escape(str);` (as upstream did), or `str.replace(/[&<>'"]/g, function(c){ return xmlEntityMap[c]; })`, keeping the existing null/empty handling.

summary: The PR adds `index.ts`, restoring the upstream 1.0.8 implementation of `@actions/http-client`, including the cross-host redirect check that removes the `Authorization` header before following a 302 to another hostname. The file is byte-identical to the upstream fixed release (`cde0b32`), and the security tests at `__tests__/basics.test.ts:182-226` are satisfied by it. I found no regression in the changed file, but I recorded one medium finding: the redirect protection only covers per-request headers, so credentials from the library's own auth handlers or from `requestOptions.headers` are still forwarded across hostnames (reproduced locally).

findings.title: Authorization from auth handlers and default client headers still leaks on cross-host redirects
findings.body:
The cross-host redirect fix only removes `Authorization` from the per-call `headers` argument. Credentials supplied through the library's own auth handlers, or through the client's default `requestOptions.headers`, are re-added on every redirect and are still sent to the new hostname.

**Preconditions:** The client authenticates with `BearerCredentialHandler`, `BasicCredentialHandler`, or `PersonalAccessTokenCredentialHandler`, or with an `Authorization` entry in the `requestOptions.headers` passed to the `HttpClient` constructor. A server the client contacts returns a redirect (301/302/303/307/308) whose `Location` names a different hostname.

**Evidence:** The added strip loop at `index.ts:390-397` deletes only from `headers`. `_prepareRequest` then rebuilds the outgoing headers from `this.requestOptions.headers` via `_mergeHeaders` (`index.ts:553`, `index.ts:570-583`) and lets every handler call `prepareRequest`, which writes `options.headers['Authorization']` (`index.ts:561-565`, `auth.ts:17-19`, `auth.ts:43-45`, `auth.ts:71-73`). Reproduced with the compiled package and two local servers: a request from `http://127.0.0.1:18081` redirecting to `http://localhost:18080` delivered `Bearer SECRET-TOKEN` (handler) and `SECRET-DEFAULT` (`requestOptions.headers`) to the second host, while a per-call `{Authorization: 'SECRET-ADDL'}` was correctly dropped.

**Impact:** This is the CVE-2020-11021 credential disclosure surviving the fix for the library's advertised authentication mechanism: an Authorization token is disclosed to an unrelated host. Reach crosses a trust boundary and the disclosure is permanent (the token can be reused), but it requires a redirect to an attacker-controlled hostname, so medium.

**Fix:** Strip `Authorization` from the final merged request headers for the redirected request, not just from the `headers` argument. E.g. after `this._prepareRequest(verb, parsedRedirectUrl, headers)` returns `info`, when `parsedRedirectUrl.hostname !== parsedUrl.hostname`, delete any case-insensitive `authorization` key from `info.options.headers` before `requestRaw`.

summary:
Review complete. All five findings are recorded (repo working tree left clean; only ignored `node_modules` from the reproduction).

The PR re-adds `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js` (300 lines), the liblinear wrapper, at the pre-fix revision of upstream limdu. Training and batch classification build shell command strings from constructor options and run them with `child_process.execSync`; upstream's own remedy (CVE-2020-4066) is `execFileSync` with an argument array, and I reproduced the injection with both learner options and a tainted model path. Beyond the injection, the class silently reuses a stale model after `trainBatch`, loses its model through `toJSON`/`fromJSON`, leaks training data into the current directory under default options, and has a `ReferenceError` typo in its multi-label guard. I checked the `isInstalled()` probe with a real liblinear build and it behaves correctly, so I did not report it.

Overall: request changes — the shell sinks must go before this file ships, and the retraining and serialization defects are worth fixing in the same pass.

findings.title: Shell metacharacters in learner options execute arbitrary commands during SvmLinear training
findings.body:
`SvmLinear.trainBatch` and `SvmLinear.classifyBatch` build a shell string from constructor options and run it with `child_process.execSync`. Any shell metacharacter in `learn_args`, `model_file_prefix`, `train_command` or `test_command` becomes a second command, so library input can execute arbitrary commands as the Node process user.

**Preconditions:** The embedding application must place attacker-influenced text into one of those options — for example a `model_file_prefix` derived from a user or tenant name, or `learn_args` assembled from configuration or request data. The library does not quote or validate them.

**Evidence:**
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:100` concatenates `this.train_command + " " + this.learn_args + " " + learnFile + " " + modelFile`; `:103` runs it with `child_process.execSync`.
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:146`/`:148` do the same for `this.test_command`, `this.test_file`, the stored model path and the output path.
- The model path is stored at `:110` (`this.modelFileString = modelFile`) and reused at `:146`, so one tainted `model_file_prefix` reaches both sinks.
- Reproduced with a stub `liblinear_train` on `PATH` and a model written in liblinear format:
  - `new SvmLinear({learn_args: '-c 20; touch /tmp/pwned_args #', model_file_prefix: '/tmp/argsmod'})` followed by `trainBatch(...)` created `/tmp/pwned_args`. The child process received only `["-c","20","/tmp/argsmod_..."]` — the shell had split the string at `;`.
  - `model_file_prefix: '/tmp/x;touch${IFS}pwned_rel;#'` also fired (no spaces needed, so no directory precondition).
  - Setting `classifier.modelFileString = '/tmp/m;touch /tmp/pwned_test #'` before `classifyBatch` created `/tmp/pwned_test`; without `#` the call still returned normally, so the injection is silent.
- `model_file_prefix` is written to disk first (`classifiers/svm/svmcommon.js:15-17`), so a prefix containing `/` fails with `ENOENT` before the shell runs; prefixes without a path separator inject without any precondition.

**Impact:** Arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the hosting process, and permanent (commands can exfiltrate or destroy anything the process can reach). Reach depends on the caller forwarding data into these options, which is the usage the published advisory for this library describes; where that happens this crosses a trust boundary.

**Fix:** Pass arguments without a shell. Keep `this.learn_args` as an array and call `child_process.execFileSync(this.train_command, this.learn_args.concat([learnFile, modelFile]))`, and `child_process.execFileSync(this.test_command, [testFile, this.modelFileString, "/tmp/out_"+this.timestamp])`. This is what upstream limdu 0.9.4→0.9.5 changed (`learn_args` became an array). The `execSync('liblinear_train .')` probe at `:48` should become `execFileSync` for the same reason.

findings.title: Retraining a SvmLinear classifier keeps predicting with the previous model
findings.body:
A trained `SvmLinear` keeps using its first model after `trainBatch` runs again. `trainBatch` writes a new model file and updates `this.modelFileString`, but the parsed weight map is only rebuilt inside `setModel`, which `classify` calls only when `this.mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` is missing. After the first training and classification the old map stays, so later trainings are ignored and predictions stay those of the first model, with no error.

**Evidence:**
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:65-113` — `trainBatch` sets only `this.modelFileString` (`:110`); it never touches `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight`.
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:158-159` — `classify` calls `setModel` only when the map is absent; same guard in `getModelWeights` at `:124-125`.
- Reproduced with the real liblinear binaries: train on `{0,0→0, 1,1→0, 0,1→1, 1,2→1}`, call `classify([0,2])` (returns 1, correct), then retrain on the same inputs with the labels flipped and call it again. The retrained classifier still returns 1, while a fresh classifier trained only on the second dataset returns 0. `getModelWeights()` after the second training returns the first model's weights; the two model files on disk differ (their `label` lines are `0 1` and `1 0`).
- The shipped demo does exactly this: `classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:37` retrains the same instance inside a cross-validation loop.

**Impact:** Silent wrong predictions for every caller that retrains an instance — cross-validation, incremental data refresh, or any meta-classifier that reuses an instance. Nothing errors, so the stale model can go unnoticed. Reach is broad (every retraining user) and the damage is recoverable by constructing a fresh classifier, which is why this is medium rather than high.

**Fix:** Invalidate the cached model at the end of `trainBatch` — e.g. `this.setModel(modelFile)` after a successful run, or `delete this.mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` so the next `classify` reloads.

findings.title: Saved SvmLinear models serialize no weights and reload throws on first classify
findings.body:
`SvmLinear.toJSON` returns `this.mapFeatureToWeight`, a field this class never assigns, and `fromJSON` writes that same unused field. A serialized SvmLinear therefore carries no model, and the first `classify` after `fromJSON` throws a `TypeError` from `fs.readFileSync(undefined)` instead of classifying.

**Preconditions:** Use the documented save/load path, e.g. `EnhancedClassifier.toJSON()` / `fromJSON()` or `JSON.stringify` on the classifier, then classify after reload.

**Evidence:**
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:227-233` — `toJSON` returns `mapFeatureToWeight`; `fromJSON` sets it. Every other reference in the file is to `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` (`:118`, `:126`, `:176`) or `allLabels` (`:85-86`, `:119`). A repo-wide grep finds `mapFeatureToWeight` only at these two lines.
- Delegation into it: `classifiers/EnhancedClassifier.js:493` (`this.classifier.toJSON(callback)`) and `:505` (`fromJSON`); `classifiers/multilabel/BinaryRelevance.js:225` and `:233`.
- Executed: training an `EnhancedClassifier({classifierType: SvmLinear})`, calling `toJSON()` and `JSON.stringify` produced `{"pastTrainingSamples":[]}` — the classifier state was dropped silently. Reloading in a fresh instance and calling `classify` throws `TypeError: The "path" argument must be of type string. Received undefined` at `:159` (`setModel(this.modelFileString)`).
- `classifiers/svm/SvmPerf.js:125-131` has the same pair, but that class really does use `mapFeatureToWeight`, so the bug is unique to the new file.

**Impact:** Saved models are lost with no warning and reload fails at the first classification. Recoverable by retraining, contained to the caller that saved, hence low.

**Fix:** Serialize the state the class actually uses — `{mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight: ..., allLabels: ...}` — and restore both in `fromJSON`; restoring only the weight map is not enough, because `classify` dereferences `this.allLabels` at `:161`.

findings.title: Multi-label guard throws ReferenceError instead of rejecting the dataset
findings.body:
The multi-label guard in `trainBatch` references an undefined variable, so a dataset whose `output` is an array of length > 1 crashes with `ReferenceError: darum is not defined` instead of the intended "Multi-label is not allowed" message.

**Evidence:**
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:74` — `console.log(JSON.stringify(darum.output, null, 4))`, while the callback parameter at `:69` is `datum`.
- Reproduced: `trainBatch([{input:[0,0],output:[0]},{input:[1,1],output:[0,1]}])` prints "Multi-label is not allowed" and then throws `ReferenceError: darum is not defined`.
- The line behind the typo, `:75` `process.exit(0)`, would terminate the host process if reached; a library should throw instead.

**Impact:** A caller passing multi-label data gets an opaque `ReferenceError` from inside the library rather than a clear rejection. Once the typo is fixed, the same path silently kills the host process — worth replacing with a thrown `Error` while correcting the name. Low: it needs invalid input and leaves no persistent damage.

**Fix:** `console.log(JSON.stringify(datum.output, null, 4))` and `throw new Error("Multi-label is not allowed")` instead of `process.exit(0)`.

findings.title: Default SvmLinear settings write training data into the current directory
findings.body:
With the default options, `SvmLinear` writes its training data and model into the current working directory as `null_<timestamp>.learn` and `.model`, not into the system temp folder as the class documents. Training data is thus left on disk in the process CWD, and training fails outright when the CWD is read-only.

**Evidence:**
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:31` — `this.model_file_prefix = opts.model_file_prefix || null`.
- `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:96-97` — the prefix is passed as `this.model_file_prefix+"_"+this.timestamp`, which stringifies to `"null_<ms>_<pid>"`; this is always truthy, so `svmcommon.writeDatasetToFile` takes its `if (model_file_prefix)` branch (`classifiers/svm/svmcommon.js:15-17`) and never reaches the `temp.openSync` fallback at `:19-21`.
- Reproduced: `new SvmLinear({learn_args:'-c 20'})` then `trainBatch(...)` in an empty directory left `null_1793555646948_1558.learn` (the full training set) and `null_1793555646948_1558.model` there.
- Nothing in the class deletes these files afterwards.
- The same defaults reach the tests: `test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:91` and `test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:16` bind no `model_file_prefix`.

**Impact:** Training data is persisted in a location nobody cleans up (information exposure on shared or web-served directories), and default construction fails with an `EACCES`/`EROFS` from `fs.openSync` on read-only filesystems such as container images or serverless runtimes — contrary to the documented behavior at `:14`. Contained and recoverable, hence low.

**Fix:** Pass `this.model_file_prefix` to `writeDatasetToFile` unchanged (so a null prefix selects the `temp.openSync` path) and append the timestamp only when a prefix is given.
